intro.x: **A note on time, for all six.** A puzzle set is one arrangement followed by about five questions. Nobody solves the arrangement in 45 seconds. The honest target is 3 to 6 minutes for the arrangement and 15 to 20 seconds for each question after it.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Exact Mechanics & Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **Central law.** Everybody grows older by the same number of years. So the gap between two people never changes, while their ratio does change. The total of a group grows by (number of people) x (years).
A **unit** is one part of a ratio. If ages are 4 : 7, the ages are 4 units and 7 units. Every Ages question is solved by finding the value of 1 unit.
Base operations

items.x: **Find 1 unit.** Match a real number to its parts, then divide.
Sum given: 1 unit = sum / (sum of parts). Ages 4 : 7, sum 66: 1 unit = 66 / 11 = 6.
Gap given: 1 unit = gap / (difference of parts). Ages 4 : 7, gap 18: 1 unit = 18 / 3 = 6.
One age given: 1 unit = that age / its part.
**Move a total in time.** New total = old total + people x years (minus for “ago”). Three people, average 33 now: total 99; five years ago the total was 99 - 15 = 84.
**Average to total.** Total = average x people. Always convert first; never work with the average itself.
**Gap stays fixed.** If A is 6 years older than B today, A was 6 years older ten years ago and will be 6 years older forever.
**Join two ratios.** A : B = 4 : 5 and B : C = 3 : 4. Make B the same in both: multiply the first by 3 and the second by 5. A : B : C = 12 : 15 : 20.

blocks.x: Percent and fraction words into ratios
Read “A is p% more than B” as A : B. Read “A is p% of B” differently: it is plain p : 100.

rows: Words about A compared with B

blocks.x: Calculation facts to keep ready

items.x: Tables of 7, 9, 11, 13, 17 and 23 up to x10. The sum of parts is often one of these.
Squares up to 30 and cubes up to 10, for product questions.

lead.x: Worked examples below are real questions from the papers. “Hence” means after; “ago” means before.

items.title: Present ratio plus one real number
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 4 : 7” followed by a sum, a difference, one age, or a third person placed between them (“12 years older than A and 6 years younger than B”).
**Shortcut engine: unit method.**

items.x: Decide what the real number measures: sum, gap or one age.
1 unit = real number / matching parts. Then read the asked age.

blocks.x: **Worked example (SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 Sep 2025, Shift 1).** Sarah : Farah = 4 : 7. Marah is 12 years older than Sarah and 6 years younger than Farah. Farah’s age four years ago? Farah minus Sarah = 12 + 6 = 18 years = 7 - 4 = 3 units, so 1 unit = 6. Farah = 42, four years ago = 38.

**Wording clues.** Two ratios or multiples for the same pair at two dates, and both people are shifted by the same years each time. “Seven years hence 2 : 1, three years hence 5 : 2.” Percent words count too: “150% more” is 5 : 2.
**Shortcut engine: equal-gap method.**

items.x: Write both ratios in the same person order. Find each ratio’s gap (bigger part minus smaller part).
Multiply the ratios so both gaps become equal (use the LCM of the gaps).
Now one person’s parts change by some units between the two dates. Those units = the years between the dates. That gives 1 unit.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 24 Aug 2024, Shift 1).** Seven years hence A : B = 2 : 1; three years hence 5 : 2. Find B now. Gaps are 1 and 3, so write 2 : 1 as 6 : 3. A moves from 5 parts (3 years hence) to 6 parts (7 years hence): 1 unit = 4 years. B three years hence = 2 units = 8, so B now = 5.

**Unknown time variant (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023).** “x years hence 7 : 5, x + 4 years hence 4 : 3, A is 26 now.” Gaps 2 and 1, so 4 : 3 becomes 8 : 6. A moves 7 to 8 = 1 unit = 4 years. A at the first date = 28, so x = 2. B at the first date = 20, so B now = 18.

items.title: Different time shift for each person
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “The ratio of A’s age five years hence to B’s age five years ago is 16 : 5”, or “A’s age 8 years hence is twice B’s age 2 years hence”. The two people are moved by different years, so the gap is not fixed and the equal-gap method fails.
**Shortcut engine: cross rule.** Let the base ratio be m : n, the target ratio r : s, and the shifts p for the first person and q for the second (hence is plus, ago is minus).

items.x: Top = r x q - s x p.
Bottom = s x m - r x n.
1 unit = Top / Bottom. Ages on the base date are m units and n units.

blocks.x: This is the one-line balance s x (m units + p) = r x (n units + q) already solved for you. The cross rule is used because no pure ratio shortcut exists when the shifts differ.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 1).** A : B = 9 : 5 now. A five years hence to B five years ago = 16 : 5. Sum of ages after 10 years? m = 9, n = 5, r = 16, s = 5, p = +5, q = -5. Top = 16 x (-5) - 5 x 5 = -105. Bottom = 5 x 9 - 16 x 5 = -35. 1 unit = 3. Ages 27 and 15; after 10 years the sum is 42 + 20 = 62.

**No present ratio variant (SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 Sep 2025, Shift 2).** X ten years ago to Y six years ago = 2 : 3; X four years hence to Y six years hence = 5 : 6. Treat the first ratio as the base and count shifts from its dates: X moves from -10 to +4, so p = 14; Y moves from -6 to +6, so q = 12. Top = 5 x 12 - 6 x 14 = -24. Bottom = 6 x 2 - 5 x 3 = -3. 1 unit = 8. X = 16 + 10 = 26, Y = 24 + 6 = 30, difference 4. The paper carried no answer key for this question; 4 is my computed answer.

items.title: Shifted ratio plus a sum, average or gap
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** One ratio or multiple at shifted dates, plus a real sum, average or “older by” for the present. No second ratio.
**Shortcut engine: shift the total, or shift the gap.**

items.x: Apply each person’s own shift to the sum (or to the gap) so the number sits on the same dates as the ratio.
Shifted sum / sum of parts = 1 unit. Or shifted gap / difference of parts = 1 unit.
Undo the shift to get the present age.

blocks.x: **Worked example, sum (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2024, Guidely paper).** A four years ago to B six years hence = 2 : 3. Average of present ages 19. Find A. Present sum = 38. Shifted sum = 38 - 4 + 6 = 40 = 5 units, so 1 unit = 8. A four years ago = 16, A now = 20.

**Worked example, gap (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** A three years ago to B five years ago = 4 : 5. A is 4 years younger than B. Find B. B five years ago minus A three years ago = 4 - 5 + 3 = 2 years = 1 unit. B five years ago = 10, B now = 15.

items.title: Three or more people linked, with a total
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** A third name appears with “older than”, “younger than” or “average of all three”. Often one ratio plus one “older by” plus an average.
**Shortcut engine: units plus extras = total.**

items.x: Convert the average to a total, and move the total to the date of the ratio.
Write each person as units plus an extra number of years. Add: (total units) + (total extras) = total.
Solve for 1 unit, then read the asked age and move it to the asked date.

blocks.x: If there is no ratio at all, pick the youngest person as the base: total = people x base + extras.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 12 Dec 2021, Set 1).** Five years ago Palani : Baba = 7 : 5. Ramar is 17 years older than Baba. Average of the three is 39. Baba’s age 2 years hence? Total now = 117; five years ago = 117 - 15 = 102. Then: 7 units + 5 units + (5 units + 17) = 102, so 17 units = 85 and 1 unit = 5. Baba then = 25, now = 30, two years hence = 32.
**Wording clues.** “Average age of a family of 5”, “a teacher joins”, “a child was born”, “one member leaves”.
**Shortcut engine: total bookkeeping and the deviation method.**

items.x: Work in totals: total = average x people. Each living person adds 1 year per year. A person not yet born adds nothing.
One person joins: new person = new average + (old count x rise in average).

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS PO Prelims, 23 Aug 2025, Shift 2, inside a quantity comparison).** 21 people average 64; one joins and the average becomes 64.5. New person = 64.5 + 21 x 0.5 = 75. Second part: 14 members average 30 and a baby is born now. Average after 4 years = (420 + 14 x 4 + 4) / 15 = 480 / 15 = 32.
**Wording clues.** One option says “Cannot be determined”. Three people but the facts feel thin.
**Shortcut engine: count fresh facts.** You need as many fresh facts as people. A sentence that can be built from earlier sentences is not fresh.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2022, Adda247 paper).** Six years ago Amit + Den = 20, so now Amit + Den = 32. Mohit is 6 younger than Amit. Average of Mohit and Den is 13, so Mohit + Den = 26. But Mohit + Den = (Amit - 6) + Den = 32 - 6 = 26 already. The third sentence is not fresh: three people, two fresh facts. Answer: cannot be determined.

**Shortcut engine.** Parts x parts = parts squared. Ages 2 : 3 with product 864: 2 units x 3 units = 6 square units = 864, so unit squared = 144 and 1 unit = 12. Three ages multiplied give unit cubed. For “sum and product”, move the sum to the product’s date and find the factor pair with that sum.

**Shortcut engine.** Translate the sentence into a ratio or gap using the phrase table in Section 4, then use the unit method. Example: “I am twice as old as you were when I was as old as you are now” always gives 4 : 3. With a sum of 63, 7 units = 63, so the speaker is 36.

items.title: One person across time, or “after how many years”
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** The years between two dates equal the difference in parts. “His age after 15 years will be 5 times his age 5 years ago”: the two dates are 20 years apart = 5 - 1 = 4 units, so 1 unit = 5. He was 5 then and is 10 now. For two known ages (25 and 17) and a wanted ratio 5 : 3: the gap 8 = 2 units, so the ages were 20 and 12, which was 5 years ago.

items.title: An x or a blank inside the data
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** Ignore the x at first. Solve the people with the engines above, then read x at the end. Example (Sreedhar model test 53): Karan is x + 7 and Riya is x - 1; after 5 years the ratio is 19 : 15. The gap is 8 years = 4 units, so 1 unit = 2. Karan after 5 years = 38, so x + 12 = 38 and x = 26.

lead.x: Nine original questions, one per Core archetype plus the product and phrasing traps. Every answer and every elimination hack was checked by script. Try each before reading the method.

body.x: The ratio of the present ages of Meena and Tara is 5 : 8. Kiran is 9 years older than Meena and 6 years younger than Tara. Find the age of Tara five years ago (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Let the ages be 5x and 8x. Then 5x + 9 = 8x - 6, so x = 5. Tara = 40, five years ago 35.
**30-second exam method.** Kiran sits between them, so Tara - Meena = 9 + 6 = 15 years. That gap is 8 - 5 = 3 units, so 1 unit = 5. Tara = 8 x 5 = 40. Five years ago = 35. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** Tara’s present age must be a multiple of 8, so (option + 5) must divide by 8. Only 35 + 5 = 40 works. Back-check: Meena 25, Kiran 34 = 25 + 9 = 40 - 6. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (C) 40 is Tara’s present age. Read the last line again: “five years ago”.

body.x: Four years ago, the ratio of the ages of P and Q was 5 : 3. Eight years hence, the ratio of their ages will be 4 : 3. Find the present age of Q (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Two equations: 3(P - 4) = 5(Q - 4) and 3(P + 8) = 4(Q + 8). Solve together.

**30-second exam method.** Gaps are 2 and 1. Double the second ratio: 4 : 3 becomes 8 : 6. Now P goes from 5 parts to 8 parts = 3 units in 4 + 8 = 12 years, so 1 unit = 4. Q four years ago = 3 units = 12. Q now = 16. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** (Q - 4) and (Q + 8) must both divide by 3. Only 16 passes (12 and 24). Back-check: P = 24; eight years hence 32 : 24 = 4 : 3. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** The years between the dates are 4 + 8 = 12, not 8. “Ago” and “hence” add up. Option (A) 12 is Q’s age four years ago.

body.x: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 3 : 4 and the product of their present ages is 432. Find the sum of their ages five years hence (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** 3x times 4x = 432, so 12x squared = 432, x squared = 36, x = 6.

**30-second exam method.** Parts x parts = parts squared. 3 x 4 = 12 square units = 432, so unit squared = 36 and 1 unit = 6. Ages 18 and 24, sum 42. Two people, five years each: 42 + 10 = 52. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** The present sum is 7 units, so (option - 10) must divide by 7. Only 52 - 10 = 42 works. Back-check: 18 x 24 = 432. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** 432 / 12 = 36 is the unit squared, not the unit. Take the square root. Option (A) 42 is the present sum; option (B) 47 adds five years for only one person.

items.title: Drill 4. Phrasing trap (A2 with percent words)

body.x: Six years ago, Ravi’s age was 200% more than Sonu’s age. Ten years hence, Ravi’s age will be 66 2/3% more than Sonu’s age. Find the present age of Sonu (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** R - 6 = 3(S - 6) and R + 10 = (5/3)(S + 10). Solve together.

**30-second exam method.** 200% more = 3 : 1. 66 2/3% more = 5 : 3. Gaps are 2 and 2, already equal. Ravi goes from 3 parts to 5 parts = 2 units in 6 + 10 = 16 years, so 1 unit = 8. Sonu six years ago = 1 unit = 8. Sonu now = 14. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** (Sonu + 10) must divide by 3. Only 14 + 10 = 24 works. Back-check: Ravi = 30; ten years hence 40 : 24 = 5 : 3. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** “200% more than” is 3 times, not 2 times. “200% of” would be 2 times. The same trap appears as “two times more than”.

body.x: The ratio of the present ages of Anil and Bina is 7 : 4. The ratio of Anil’s age two years ago to Bina’s age six years hence is 4 : 3. Find the present age of Bina (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Let the ages be 7x and 4x. Then 3(7x - 2) = 4(4x + 6), so 5x = 30 and x = 6.
**30-second exam method.** Cross rule with m : n = 7 : 4, r : s = 4 : 3, p = -2, q = +6. Top = 4 x 6 - 3 x (-2) = 30. Bottom = 3 x 7 - 4 x 4 = 5. 1 unit = 6. Bina = 4 x 6 = 24. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** (Bina + 6) must divide by 3. Only 24 + 6 = 30 works. Back-check: Anil = 42; 40 : 30 = 4 : 3. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** The equal-gap method does not work here because the two people are moved by different years. Also watch the sign: “ago” is minus.

body.x: The ratio of Kavya’s age three years ago to Lata’s age seven years hence is 3 : 5. The average of their present ages is 26 years. Find the present age of Kavya (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** 5(K - 3) = 3(L + 7) and K + L = 52. Solve together.
**30-second exam method.** Present sum = 26 x 2 = 52. Shifted sum = 52 - 3 + 7 = 56 = 3 + 5 = 8 units, so 1 unit = 7. Kavya three years ago = 21. Kavya now = 24. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** (Kavya - 3) must divide by 3. Only 24 - 3 = 21 works. Back-check: Lata = 28; 21 : 35 = 3 : 5. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** 26 is the average, not the sum. Option (E) 28 is Lata’s age.

items.title: Drill 7. Three people with a total (A5)

body.x: Five years ago, the ratio of the ages of Uma and Vani was 4 : 3. Wasim is 14 years older than Vani. If the average of the present ages of all three is 33 years, find the age of Wasim two years hence (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Let the ages five years ago be 4x and 3x. Then (4x + 5) + (3x + 5) + (3x + 19) = 99, so x = 7.

**30-second exam method.** Total now = 99. Five years ago = 99 - 3 x 5 = 84. Then Uma 4 units, Vani 3 units, Wasim 3 units + 14. So 10 units + 14 = 84 and 1 unit = 7. Wasim then = 35, now = 40, two years hence = 42. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** Vani’s age five years ago = option - 2 - 5 - 14 = option - 21, and it must divide by 3. Only 42 - 21 = 21 works. Back-check: 33 + 26 + 40 = 99. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Three people each lose 5 years, so subtract 15, not 5. Option (B) 40 is Wasim’s present age.

body.x: Four years ago, the average age of a husband, his wife and their son was 26 years. Six years ago, the average age of the wife and the son was 18 years. Find the present age of the husband (in years).

items.x: **Conventional method.** H + W + S - 12 = 78 and W + S - 12 = 36. Subtract.
**30-second exam method.** Total of three now = 26 x 3 + 4 x 3 = 90. Wife and son now = 18 x 2 + 6 x 2 = 48. Husband = 90 - 48 = 42. **Answer (D).**
**Option elimination hack.** No safe divisibility hack here. Two multiplications and one subtraction are faster than testing options.
**IBPS trap warning.** Add the years once per person: 4 x 3 = 12 and 6 x 2 = 12. Adding 4 and 6 only once gives a wrong total.

body.x: Six years ago, the sum of the ages of Asha and Dev was 34 years. Mohan is 4 years younger than Asha. If the average of the present ages of Mohan and Dev is 21 years, find the present age of Dev.

items.x: **Conventional method.** A + D = 46, M = A - 4, M + D = 42. Three unknowns, try to solve.

**30-second exam method.** Asha + Dev now = 34 + 12 = 46. Mohan + Dev = 42. But Mohan + Dev = (Asha - 4) + Dev = 46 - 4 = 42 already. The last sentence is not fresh, so only two facts exist for three people. **Answer (D).**

**Option elimination hack.** Test two options. Dev 20 gives Asha 26, Mohan 22, and 22 + 20 = 42 fits. Dev 22 gives Asha 24, Mohan 20, and 20 + 22 = 42 also fits. Two options fit, so the answer cannot be fixed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Do not pick “Cannot be determined” just because the question looks long. Pick it only after you show that one sentence repeats another.

blocks.x: Which engine to use

rows: Present ratio + sum, gap or one age
Same pair at two dates, same shift for both
Make gaps equal; change in parts = years between dates
Each person shifted by different years, two ratios
Unit = (r x q - s x p) / (s x m - r x n)
One shifted ratio + present sum, average or gap
Apply each person’s shift to the number first
Three or more people with an average
Average x people, move the total, then add up
Family, class, member joins or is born
New person = new average + old count x rise
Need one fresh fact per person
Divide, then take the square root

blocks.x: Universal fallback

When a question fits no engine, use the **one-date balance**. Put every person on one single date as units plus extra years. Use the one real number in the question to write a single balance line, and solve for 1 unit. If even that is unclear, plug in the middle option: build every age from it and test the sentence you have not used yet. Move up or down from there.
Phrase to maths

rows: “A is twice as old as B”
“A is two times more than B”, “200% more”
“Father was 28 when the son was born”
“I was as old as you are now when you were born”
“A is as much younger than B as he is older than C”
A = average of B and C; the gap itself stays unknown
“I am twice as old as you were when I was as old as you are now”
“Present age is 6/5 of the age at marriage 8 years ago”
“Sum of ages of A and B after 5 years”
“Average of A, B and C is 33”
“Ratio of B and A” after an earlier “A and B”

blocks.x: Red flags

items.x: **Wrong date.** The question often asks an age “4 years hence” or “5 years ago”. The present age is usually sitting among the options.
**Wrong person.** Finding A when B was asked. Similar names are used on purpose (one bank question uses Yuvan and Yuvansh as two people).
**Average used as sum.** Multiply by the number of people first.
**Years added once for a group.** Three people over 5 years add 15.
**Parts squared.** A product gives unit squared; take the root.

**Fractional ages are allowed.** One IBPS Clerk 2025 paper had the answer 42.5 years. Use divisibility hacks only when every option is a whole number, never when “None of these” is an option, and always back-check.
**Equal-gap misuse.** It works only when both people move by the same years.

What was tested

items.x: **Answers.** All 266 bank questions were rewritten as relations and solved by script. 258 match the answer key. 7 could not be machine-solved (cannot-be-determined items, a fill-in-the-blanks item and a “possible total” item) and were checked by hand; all 7 agree with the key. 1 does not match (see below).

**Methods.** The three mechanical engines were run by script on every question that uses them and compared with the solved ages: equal-gap on 45, shift the total or gap on 35, cross rule on 20. All 100 pass. The unit method, units + extras and total bookkeeping are direct arithmetic, so their only check is the answer check.
**Sister-exam questions.** All 11 were solved by script. Ten match the key printed in the paper. The SBI Clerk 20 Sep 2025 Shift 2 paper printed no key; the answer 4 is computed.
**Drills and ladder.** All 9 drill answers were solved by script, and each divisibility hack was tested to leave exactly one option. All 36 ladder answers were re-checked against the solver.

blocks.x: What failed and was fixed

items.x: The equal-gap method fails when the two people are shifted by different years. Those questions were split into archetype A3 with the cross rule.

The cross rule was first written only for “present ratio given”. The SBI Clerk question with two shifted ratios broke it. It was rewritten to count shifts from the first ratio’s dates and re-tested on 7 such questions.
“Cannot be determined” and “x inside the data” started as one archetype and were split, because only the first has PYQ support.
Drills 2 and 4 first had two options passing the divisibility test. One option in each was changed.

sample.x: **Sample.** Papers opened on the web: 14 (3 IBPS Clerk Prelims spot-checks, 4 SBI Clerk Prelims, 3 IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims, 4 IBPS PO Prelims). PYQs found: 21 IBPS Clerk Prelims questions from 21 paper labels (2016-2025, taken from your bank) plus 11 sister-exam questions from 9 papers. Bank questions used: 245 (30 constructed, 150 Guidely, 65 Sreedhar; 13 are repeats). The floor of 8 target-exam shifts plus 6-10 sister questions is met. All papers are memory-based reconstructions, so wording and numbers may differ from the real exam.

intro.x: Age questions look different every time, but they all rest on one fact: **everybody grows older at the same speed**. So the gap between two people never changes.

This path has nine short lessons. Each one adds a single new idea to the one before it, shows it on one question, lets you try one, and then gives you a few real questions of exactly that kind. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. From here, the **Quick revision** tab has everything on one page for the days before the exam, and the Course in each bank has many more Ages questions of every kind.

One last thing to carry with you: some questions offer the option "Cannot be determined". Choose it only when you can show that one sentence of the question says nothing new. A question that merely looks long almost always has an answer.

lessons.title: A ratio and one real number
lessons.plain: The simplest kind: you are told the ratio of two ages today, and one real number.

teach.x: We start with the question every other Ages question is built on.
You are given a ratio such as 4 : 7 for two people's ages today. Read it as **parts**: the first person has 4 equal parts, the second has 7. Nobody has told you how big a part is.
Then the question gives you one real number. It is always one of three things, and each one matches a number of parts:

items.x: their **sum**, which matches the parts added together;
their **difference**, which matches the parts subtracted;
**one person's age**, which matches that person's parts.

teach.x: Divide the real number by the matching parts and you have the size of one part. After that, every age in the question is a multiplication.

tags: The plain form: the real number is the sum.
The same question, as a real paper asked it.
The real number is one person's age, and at a future date.
The ratio arrives in two pieces that must be joined first.
The sum is hidden inside an average, and the answer is not among the numbers.

example.q: The ages of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 7 and the sum of their ages is 66 years. Find B's age.
steps: Read the ratio as parts: A has 4 parts, B has 7.
The real number is a sum, so match it to the parts added: 4 + 7 = 11 parts.
One part = 66 / 11 = 6 years.
B has 7 parts: 7 x 6 = 42.

checks.q: The ages of P and Q are in the ratio 5 : 6 and the sum of their ages is 44 years. How old is Q?
checks.why: 5 + 6 = 11 parts = 44, so one part is 4. Q has 6 parts: 6 x 4 = 24. (20 is P's age.)

checks.tag: The real number is a difference
checks.q: The ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 8. B is 12 years older than A. How old is A?
checks.why: A difference matches the parts subtracted: 8 - 5 = 3 parts = 12, so one part is 4. A = 5 x 4 = 20. (32 is B.)

checks.tag: A third person stands between them
checks.q: The ages of M and T are in the ratio 3 : 5. K is 4 years older than M and 6 years younger than T. How old is T?
checks.why: K sits between them, so T is 4 + 6 = 10 years older than M. That gap is 5 - 3 = 2 parts, so one part is 5. T = 5 x 5 = 25.

lessons.title: Older, younger and totals
lessons.plain: New: no ratio at all. People are described as "4 years older than" someone, with a sum or an average.

teach.x: Some questions never mention a ratio. They describe people by **how much older or younger** they are, and then give a sum or an average.
Two habits solve all of these.
**Habit 1: turn an average into a total at once.** Average 35 for three people means a total of 35 x 3 = 105. Work with the 105.

**Habit 2: pick one person as the base and write everyone else from them.** If Neha is 5 years older than Sukruti, write Sukruti as the base and Neha as "base + 5". Usually the youngest person makes the easiest base.
Now add everybody up. You get "so many bases, plus some extra years = the total". Take the extra years off the total, divide by the number of people, and you have the base.

tags: Two people: a gap and a sum.
A chain: each person is described from the one before.
"Twice as old" mixed with "older than".
Three people around one base, with an average.
The total belongs to the past, and one age to the future.

example.q: A is 6 years older than B, and C is 3 years younger than B. The average of their ages is 31 years. Find A's age.
steps: Average to total: 31 x 3 = 93.
Take B as the base. Then A = B + 6 and C = B - 3.
Add all three: B + (B + 6) + (B - 3) = 3 B + 3.
So 3 B + 3 = 93, which gives 3 B = 90 and B = 30.

checks.q: X is 5 years older than Y and the sum of their ages is 41 years. How old is Y?
checks.why: Y is the base and X is base + 5, so 2 bases + 5 = 41. Two bases = 36, and Y = 18. (23 is X.)

checks.q: A is as much younger than B as he is older than C. The sum of the ages of B and C is 50 years. How old is A?
checks.why: A is the same distance from B and from C, so A sits exactly in the middle. The middle of two numbers is their average: 50 / 2 = 25.

text.x: When three people are equally spaced, for example "A is 5 years older than B, and B is 5 years older than C", the **middle person's age is the average** of all three.
So if their average is 30, B is 30 straight away, A is 35 and C is 25. No equation needed. Look for this whenever the two gaps are the same.

lessons.title: The same two people at two dates
lessons.plain: New: two ratios for the same pair, at two different times. No sum, no age given.

teach.x: Now a question gives you two ratios and nothing else: "Four years ago the ratio was 3 : 5. Eight years hence it will be 3 : 4." It looks as if there is no real number to start from. There is one, hidden in the dates.
Here is the idea. The **gap** between two people never changes. If B is 8 years older than A today, B was 8 years older four years ago and will be 8 years older for ever.

In a ratio, the gap is the difference of the two numbers. In 3 : 5 the gap is 2 parts. In 3 : 4 the gap is 1 part. But it is the same gap in years, so those parts are different sizes, and that is why the two ratios cannot be compared yet.
**Step 1.** Make the gaps equal. Multiply 3 : 4 by 2 and it becomes 6 : 8, with a gap of 2 parts. Now both ratios are written in parts of the same size.
**Step 2.** Watch one person. A was 3 parts at the first date and is 6 parts at the second. A has grown by 3 parts.
**Step 3.** A also grew by the years between the two dates. So those 3 parts **are** those years, and that gives you one part.
Remember from the Basics: "ago" and "hence" sit on opposite sides of today, so the years between them add up.

tags: Today and a later date; the gaps are already equal.
Past and future, and the question asks for a sum.
"Twice" and "three times" instead of ratios.
Neither date is today.
Both dates are in the future, and given in reverse order.

example.q: Four years ago the ratio of the ages of A and B was 3 : 5. Eight years hence it will be 3 : 4. Find B's present age.
steps: Gaps: 3 : 5 has a gap of 2 parts, 3 : 4 has a gap of 1 part.
Make them equal: write 3 : 4 as 6 : 8. Both gaps are now 2 parts.
Watch A: 3 parts at the first date, 6 parts at the second. A grew by 3 parts.
Years between the dates: 4 + 8 = 12. So 3 parts = 12 years and one part = 4.
Four years ago B was 5 parts = 20, so B is 24 now.
Check: A is 16 now. Eight years hence they are 24 and 32, which is 3 : 4.

checks.q: The ratio of the present ages of two sisters is 2 : 3. After 10 years it will be 4 : 5. How old is the younger sister now?
checks.why: Both gaps are already 1 part. The younger sister goes from 2 parts to 4 parts, so 2 parts = 10 years and one part = 5. She is 2 x 5 = 10 now.

checks.tag: The question asks about a third date
checks.q: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 3 : 5. After 6 years it will be 2 : 3. What was the ratio of their ages 6 years ago?
checks.why: Gaps are 2 and 1, so write 2 : 3 as 4 : 6. A goes from 3 parts to 4 parts: one part = 6 years. Today they are 18 and 30. Six years ago they were 12 and 24, which is 1 : 2. Find today's ages first, then move to the date asked.

lessons.title: Two dates, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: the same question as the last lesson, but the ratios are hidden inside percent words or a changed order.

teach.x: Real papers rarely hand you the two ratios neatly. They dress them up. The method from the last lesson does not change at all; you only have to **uncover the ratios first**.
There are three common disguises.
**Percent words.** "A's age was 200% more than B's age" is a ratio. Call B 100; then A is 300, so A : B = 3 : 1. If this step feels shaky, the Basics lesson on percent words takes five minutes.

**A changed order.** "The ratio of A to B is 3 : 2. After four years the ratio of **B to A** will be 7 : 10." The second ratio is written the other way round. Turn it so both ratios read A : B before you do anything else: 10 : 7.

**An unknown number of years.** "x years hence the ratio will be 7 : 5, and x + 4 years hence it will be 4 : 3." You do not need x to begin. The two dates are 4 years apart whatever x is, and that is all the method asks for.
So the routine is: uncover both ratios, put them in the same order, and then do exactly what you did in the last lesson.

tags: The second ratio is written the other way round.
Both ratios are hidden in percent words.
The number of years is a letter.
Percent words, plus a third person brought in by an average.

example.q: Five years ago A's age was 100% more than B's age. Five years hence A's age will be 50% more than B's age. Find B's present age.
steps: Uncover the first ratio: 100% more means B is 100 and A is 200, so A : B = 2 : 1.
Uncover the second: 50% more means 150 against 100, so A : B = 3 : 2.
Gaps: 2 : 1 has a gap of 1 part, and 3 : 2 has a gap of 1 part. Already equal.
Watch A: 2 parts, then 3 parts. A grew by 1 part.
Years between the dates: 5 + 5 = 10. So one part = 10 years.
Five years ago B was 1 part = 10, so B is 15 now.
Check: A is 25 now. Five years hence they are 30 and 20, and 30 is 50% more than 20.

checks.q: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 5 : 3. After 6 years the ratio of the ages of B and A will be 2 : 3. How old is A now?
checks.why: Turn the second ratio round: A : B = 3 : 2. Gaps are 2 and 1, so write 3 : 2 as 6 : 4. A goes from 5 parts to 6 parts: one part = 6 years. A is 5 x 6 = 30 now. (18 is B.)

checks.q: Four years ago B's age was 2/3 of A's age. Four years hence B's age will be 3/4 of A's age. How old is A now?
checks.why: "B is 2/3 of A" means A : B = 3 : 2. "B is 3/4 of A" means A : B = 4 : 3. Both gaps are 1 part. A goes from 3 parts to 4 parts in 8 years, so one part = 8. A was 24 four years ago and is 28 now.

lessons.title: One ratio at another date, plus a sum or a gap
lessons.plain: New: only one ratio, and it belongs to the past or the future. The real number belongs to today.

teach.x: This kind gives you one ratio, but not for today. For example: "A's age 3 years ago and B's age 7 years hence are in the ratio 3 : 5." Then it gives a real number for **today**: a sum, an average, or "A is so many years younger".
The ratio and the real number are talking about different dates, so they cannot be matched yet. The fix is to **move the real number to the dates of the ratio**.

**If the real number is a sum.** Change it the same way the ratio changed each person. In the example A is taken back 3 years and B is taken forward 7 years, so the sum changes by - 3 + 7. That moved sum now matches the parts added together.

**If the real number is a gap.** When both people are moved by the same number of years the gap does not change, and it matches the parts subtracted. This is the most common form: "A father is 30 years older than his son. In 5 years he will be three times as old."
After that it is lesson 1 again: real number / matching parts = one part. Then bring the person back to today.

tags: A gap today, and one ratio in the future.
An average today, and "twice" in the future.
Each person at a different past date, with a gap.
Each person at a different date, with an average.
The same, and the last line asks for something further.

example.q: The ratio of K's age 3 years ago to L's age 7 years hence is 3 : 5. The average of their present ages is 26 years. Find K's present age.
steps: Average to total: 26 x 2 = 52 today.
Move the total to the dates of the ratio: K goes back 3, L goes forward 7. So 52 - 3 + 7 = 56.
That 56 matches the parts added: 3 + 5 = 8 parts. One part = 7.
K's age 3 years ago was 3 parts = 21.
Bring K back to today: 21 + 3 = 24.
Check: L is 52 - 24 = 28. Seven years hence L is 35, and 21 : 35 is 3 : 5.

checks.q: A father is 24 years older than his son. In 4 years the father will be three times as old as his son. How old is the son now?
checks.why: In 4 years the ratio is 3 : 1, a gap of 2 parts. The gap in years is still 24, so one part = 12. The son will be 12 then, so he is 8 now. (12 is his age in 4 years.)

checks.tag: A sum today and "times" in the past
checks.q: The sum of the present ages of a mother and her daughter is 50 years. Five years ago the mother was 4 times as old as her daughter. How old is the daughter now?
checks.why: Move the sum back five years: two people, so 50 - 10 = 40. Then the ratio was 4 : 1, which is 5 parts = 40, so one part is 8. The daughter was 8 then and is 13 now. (8 is her age five years ago.)

lessons.title: Three people: a ratio, an "older than", and a total
lessons.plain: New: lessons 1 and 2 together. Two people are tied by a ratio, a third by "older than", and there is one total for all.

teach.x: This is the form the Clerk paper sets most often, and you already own both halves of it.

Two of the people are given as a ratio, so they are **parts**. The third is described as "17 years older than" one of them, so the third is **parts plus some extra years**. Then there is an average or a sum for all three.
The routine:

items.x: Turn the average into a total.
If the ratio belongs to another date, move the total to that date. Remember that three people each change, so the total changes by 3 x the years.
Write each person as parts, or parts plus extra years, and add them all up.
You get "so many parts + extra years = total". Take the extra years away and divide.

teach.x: The only place people slip is step 2: three people going back 5 years lose 15 years between them, not 5.

tags: Everything at today's date.
No "older than": three parts, at a past date.
The ratio is hidden in a fraction.
The full exam form: past ratio, "older than", average, and a future answer.
The total covers only two of them; the third arrives through another average.

example.q: Five years ago the ratio of the ages of U and V was 4 : 3. W is 14 years older than V. The average of the present ages of all three is 33 years. Find W's present age.
steps: Average to total: 33 x 3 = 99 today.
The ratio is for five years ago, so move the total there: 99 - 3 x 5 = 84.
Five years ago: U was 4 parts, V was 3 parts, and W was 3 parts + 14 (W is always 14 older than V).
Add them: 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 parts, plus 14 years, equals 84.
So 10 parts = 70 and one part = 7.
W five years ago = 3 x 7 + 14 = 35. Today W is 40.
Check: today U is 33, V is 26, W is 40. Total 99.

checks.q: The ages of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3. C is 4 years older than B. The sum of all three ages is 68 years. How old is B?
checks.why: A is 2 parts, B is 3 parts, C is 3 parts + 4. That is 8 parts + 4 = 68, so 8 parts = 64 and one part = 8. B = 3 x 8 = 24. (28 is C.)

lessons.title: When each person is moved by a different number of years
lessons.plain: New: you know today's ratio, and a second ratio where one person is moved forward and the other back.

teach.x: Look closely at this sentence: "The ratio of A's age 2 years **ago** to B's age 6 years **hence** is 4 : 3." The two people are standing at different dates. In lesson 3 the gap stayed fixed because both people moved together. Here it does not, so making the gaps equal will give a wrong answer. This is the one place where a short equation is the honest method.
It is a small one. You are also told today's ratio, say 7 : 4. So:

items.x: Write today's ages in parts: A is 7 parts, B is 4 parts.
Move each person as the sentence says: A becomes "7 parts - 2", B becomes "4 parts + 6".
Those two are in the ratio 4 : 3. To remove a ratio, **cross-multiply**: multiply each side by the other side's number. That gives 3 x (7 parts - 2) = 4 x (4 parts + 6).
Open the brackets and collect the parts on one side.

teach.x: Why cross-multiplying works: "X : Y = 4 : 3" means X is 4 pieces when Y is 3 of the same pieces. So 3 lots of X and 4 lots of Y are both 12 pieces, which makes them equal.
How to tell this kind from lesson 3: check whether both people are moved by the **same** years. Same years, use the gap. Different years, use this.

tags: The two shifted ages are equal.
A proper ratio after the shifts.
"Twice" instead of a ratio, both moved forward.
Opposite directions, and the answer is a sum at a later date.

example.q: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 7 : 4. The ratio of A's age 2 years ago to B's age 6 years hence is 4 : 3. Find B's present age.
steps: Today: A is 7 parts, B is 4 parts.
Move them as the sentence says: A is 7 parts - 2, and B is 4 parts + 6.
They are in the ratio 4 : 3, so cross-multiply: 3 x (7 parts - 2) = 4 x (4 parts + 6).
Open the brackets: 21 parts - 6 = 16 parts + 24.
Collect: 5 parts = 30, so one part = 6.
Check: A is 42. Two years ago A was 40; six years hence B is 30. 40 : 30 is 4 : 3.

checks.q: The ratio of the present ages of P and Q is 3 : 1. P's age 5 years ago is twice Q's age 5 years hence. How old is Q now?
checks.why: P is 3 parts, Q is 1 part. 3 parts - 5 = 2 x (1 part + 5), so 3 parts - 5 = 2 parts + 10 and one part = 15. Q is 15. (45 is P.)

text.x: Once the equation feels natural, you can skip writing it. Say today's ratio is **m : n**, the second ratio is **r : s**, and the shifts are **p** for the first person and **q** for the second (hence is plus, ago is minus).
**One part = (r x q - s x p) / (s x m - r x n)**
With the worked example above: m : n = 7 : 4, r : s = 4 : 3, p = -2, q = +6. Top: 4 x 6 - 3 x (-2) = 30. Bottom: 3 x 7 - 4 x 4 = 5. One part = 6, the same answer.
It is only the equation solved in advance. If you ever doubt the signs, write the equation out instead; it takes a few seconds more and cannot go wrong.

lessons.title: One person at two dates, and "after how many years"
lessons.plain: New: the question compares a person with their own younger self, or asks when a ratio will come true.

teach.x: Two small relatives of what you already know. Neither has appeared in the Clerk papers we checked, but both are common in practice sets and each takes a minute to learn.

**One person, two dates.** "His age after 15 years will be 5 times his age 5 years ago." Treat his two ages as a ratio, 5 : 1. He grew from 1 part to 5 parts, which is 4 parts, and he grew by the years between the two dates. So those 4 parts are those years. It is lesson 3 with one person instead of two.

**After how many years.** "A mother is 36 and her daughter is 12. After how many years will the mother be twice as old?" Use the gap. The gap is 24 years today and will be 24 years on that day too. On that day the ratio is 2 : 1, a gap of 1 part. So one part is 24, the daughter will be 24, and that is 12 years from now.
**"When he was born."** A sentence like "the father was 28 when his son was born" is simply giving you the gap: the father is always 28 years older.

tags: After how many years: use the gap.
One person, a past date and a future date.
"When his son was born" gives the gap.
Percent words for one person's two ages.
A fraction for one person, then a second person.

example.q: A man's age after 12 years will be 3 times his age 4 years ago. Find his present age.
steps: His two ages are in the ratio 3 : 1.
From 1 part to 3 parts he grew by 2 parts.
Years between the two dates: 4 + 12 = 16. So 2 parts = 16 and one part = 8.
Four years ago he was 1 part = 8.
Today he is 8 + 4 = 12.
Check: after 12 years he is 24, and 24 is 3 times 8.

checks.q: A mother is 40 years old and her son is 10. After how many years will she be three times as old as her son?
checks.why: The gap is 30 years and stays 30. At 3 : 1 the gap is 2 parts, so one part = 15. The son will be 15, which is 5 years from now. (15 is his age then, not the wait.)

lessons.title: Family and group averages
lessons.plain: New: no ratios. A group's average changes because time passes, someone joins, or a child is born.

teach.x: The last kind is about groups: a family, a class, an office. There is usually no ratio. Everything is done with totals.
Keep three rules in front of you.
**1. Always work in totals.** Total = average x number of people. Do this for every average in the question before you think about anything else.
**2. A total grows by people x years.** A family of 4 with a total of 100 today had a total of 100 - 4 x 5 = 80 five years ago. A child who was not born yet adds nothing for those years.
**3. To find one person, subtract totals.** The total of everyone, minus the total of the others, is the person you want.
When someone joins a group, the same rule finds them: new total minus old total is the newcomer's age.

tags: Take one person out of a total.
Three small groups joined into one.
A past average and a future sum.
Someone joins and the average moves.
A child is born in between.

example.q: Four years ago the average age of a husband, his wife and their son was 26 years. Six years ago the average age of the wife and the son was 18 years. Find the husband's present age.
steps: All three, four years ago: 26 x 3 = 78.
Bring that to today: three people, four years each, so add 12. Total today = 90.
Wife and son, six years ago: 18 x 2 = 36.
Bring that to today: two people, six years each, so add 12. Their total today = 48.
The husband is the difference: 90 - 48 = 42.

checks.q: The average age of 5 people is 20 years. A sixth person joins and the average becomes 21 years. How old is the sixth person?
checks.why: Old total = 20 x 5 = 100. New total = 21 x 6 = 126. The newcomer is 126 - 100 = 26.

checks.q: The average age of 6 friends is 30 years. One of them, aged 40, leaves the group. What is the average age of those who remain?
checks.why: Total = 30 x 6 = 180. Take out the 40: 140 is left for 5 people. 140 / 5 = 28.

text.x: If one person joins and the average rises, you can find the newcomer in one line:
**newcomer = new average + (old number of people x rise in the average)**
Five people average 20; a sixth joins and the average becomes 21. Newcomer = 21 + 5 x 1 = 26.
Why it works: the newcomer brings the new average for themselves, and also has to lift each of the old members by the rise. If the average falls instead, subtract.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Exact Mechanics & Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **Central law.** Call the sum invested 100%. In simple interest (SI) every year adds the same slice, so total interest % = rate x years. In compound interest (CI) each year’s interest is charged on the grown amount, so the yearly increases multiply instead of adding. Almost every question is solved by finding what 1% of the sum is worth.
Base operations

items.x: **SI total percent.** Interest % = rate x years. 12% for 5 years = 60% of the sum. Amount = 100% + that.
**Sum from interest.** 1% of the sum = interest / (rate x years). Interest 2,880 at 20% for 6 years: 120% = 2,880, so 1% = 24 and the sum is 2,400.
**Rate or time from interest.** Interest as a % of the sum, divided by the one you know. Interest 1,800 on 4,000 in 3 years: 45% / 3 = 15% a year.
**CI for 2 years.** Effective % = 2 x rate + (rate x rate) / 100. At 20%: 40 + 4 = 44%. Multiply the sum by this once.
**CI for 2 years at two different rates a and b.** Effective % = a + b + (a x b) / 100. At 10% then 15%: 25 + 1.5 = 26.5%.
**CI for 3 years.** Use the table below, or apply the 2-year % and then one more year.
**Months and days.** Time = months / 12 or days / 365. 146 days = 2/5 year, 73 days = 1/5 year, 219 days = 3/5 year.
**Half-yearly and quarterly.** Half-yearly: halve the rate, double the number of periods. Quarterly: quarter the rate, four periods a year.

blocks.x: CI effective percent (learn by heart)
Rate as a fraction (sum : amount after one year)
Use the fraction table backwards: an amount of 12,167 after 3 years at 15% is 23 x 23 x 23 parts, so the sum is 20 x 20 x 20 = 8,000.
Calculation facts to keep ready

items.x: Half-yearly at 20% for one year is the same 21% as 10% for two years. Quarterly at 20% for one year is 21.55%; for nine months 15.7625%.
Non-linear warning: CI does not scale with the rate. Doubling the rate from 10% to 20% takes 2-year CI from 21% to 44%, more than double.

lead.x: Sixteen archetypes cover the bank and the sister-exam questions. In this sample the papers ask SI far more than CI, and CI almost always arrives as a 2-year calculation after an SI step. The classic “difference between CI and SI” formula question did not appear in any of the 30 papers; it is Insurance only. “Papers” counts paper labels.

rows: SI first, then CI on the same sum or rate
Two SI deposits: total, difference or ratio of interest
Becomes n times, or interest is a fraction of the sum
SI against CI, or two CI deposits, on linked sums
Same sum, rate or time changed
Plain SI: find the missing value
Plain CI: find interest, amount, sum or rate
Rate changes from year to year
Interest or amount reinvested in a second scheme
Difference between CI and SI, same sum and rate
CI amounts or interests of consecutive years
SI and CI both given for 2 years

lead.x: Worked examples below are real questions from the papers.

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “A man invested Rs X at simple interest … and received Rs … as interest. If he invests the same amount (or X + something, or at R + 5%) at compound interest for two years, find …”
**Shortcut engine: 1% value, then the 2-year table.**

items.x: SI part: total % = rate x years. Divide to get the sum (or the rate).
Adjust the sum or rate as the question says.
CI part: multiply by the 2-year effective % for interest, or by 100% + that for amount.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 3).** A sum at 10% SI for 3 years earns 1,800. Amount at 20% CI for 2 years? 30% = 1,800, so the sum is 6,000. At 20% for 2 years the amount is 144% = 8,640.

**Rate version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023, Adda247 paper).** 4,000 earns 1,800 in 3 years at R% SI. Interest on 5,000 at (R - 5)% CI for 2 years? 1,800 / 4,000 = 45% in 3 years, so R = 15. New rate 10%: 21% of 5,000 = 1,050.
**Wording clues.** Two schemes, two people or one sum split in two parts, all at simple interest. The question gives the total, the difference or the ratio of the two interests.
**Shortcut engine: one percent per deposit.**

items.x: For each deposit write its total % (rate x years).
Turn the sentence into one balance: total, difference or ratio of the two interests.
If one sum is “X + 1,400”, take the % of the extra 1,400 out as a plain number first.

blocks.x: **Worked example (SBI Clerk Prelims, 21 Sep 2025, Shift 1).** Scheme X: 3,000 at 6% for 9 years. Scheme Y: P at 12% for 6 years. Y’s interest is 1,260 more. X earns 54% of 3,000 = 1,620. Y earns 1,620 + 1,260 = 2,880 = 72% of P, so 1% = 40 and P = 4,000.

**Extra-sum version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017).** X at 8% and (X + 1,400) at 12%, both for 2 years; interests differ by 880. Second earns 24% of X plus 24% of 1,400 = 336. First earns 16% of X. So 8% of X + 336 = 880, 8% of X = 544, X = 6,800.

items.title: Becomes n times, or interest is a fraction of the sum
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “Doubles in 5 years”, “becomes 1.6 times”, “interest is three-fifths of the amount invested”, “interest is 16/25 of the principal and years equal the rate”.
**Shortcut engine.** Becoming n times means interest = (n - 1) x 100% of the sum. At SI, time is proportional to (n - 1).

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 4).** A sum doubles in 5 years at SI. When is it 12 times? Doubling needs 1 sum of interest in 5 years. Twelve times needs 11 sums: 11 x 5 = 55 years.
**Fraction version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 5 Oct 2025, Shift 1).** 3,400 at 12% for (x + 1) years earns three-fifths of the sum. Three-fifths = 60%; 60 / 12 = 5 years; x = 4.

items.title: SI against CI, or two CI deposits
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** The same sum, or two sums in a given ratio, placed in two schemes of which at least one is CI. The question gives the total or the difference of the two interests.
**Shortcut engine: effective percent on each side.**

items.x: Replace each scheme by one %: SI = rate x years; CI = table value.
Same sum: the difference (or total) of the two % equals the given rupees. Sums in a ratio: multiply each part by its % and add.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 24 Aug 2024, Shift 1).** X at 20% CI for 2 years and X at 30% SI for 2 years; interests differ by 896. CI = 44%, SI = 60%. 16% = 896, so 1% = 56 and X = 5,600.

**Ratio version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 5 Dec 2020).** Sums 2 : 3 at 20% and 10% CI for 2 years; total interest 1,208. Interest = 2 x 44% + 3 x 21% = 0.88 + 0.63 = 1.51 parts = 1,208. 1 part = 800. Total = 5 parts = 4,000.

items.title: Same sum, rate or time changed
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “Had the rate been 5% higher”, “at (X + 5)% for 3 years”, “is Rs 1,500 more than the interest at 12%”.
**Shortcut engine.** Only the change in total % matters: extra interest = sum x (new rate x new years - old rate x old years)%.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** SI at 15% for 5 years is 1,500 more than at 12% for 5 years. Extra = 3% x 5 = 15% = 1,500. Sum = 10,000.
**Shortcut engine.** Total % = rate x years, then 1% value.
**Worked example (IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims, 13 Dec 2025, Shift 1).** P at 20% for 6 years earns 2,880. Find P - 200. 120% = 2,880, 1% = 24, P = 2,400, answer 2,200.
**Shortcut engine.** 2-year or 3-year effective % from the table. To go backwards from an amount, use the fraction table.

**Worked example (IBPS PO Prelims, 22 Aug 2026, Shift 2).** P at 25% CI for 2 years. Amount minus interest = 2,000. Find the CI on (P + 800). Amount minus interest is simply the sum, so P = 2,000. 56.25% of 2,800 = 1,575.
**Shortcut engine.** The gap between the two amounts is pure interest for the years in between. Find one year’s interest, then subtract back to year zero.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023, Guidely paper).** Amount 6,960 after 2 years and 8,400 after 5 years. Three years’ interest = 1,440, so 480 a year. Sum = 6,960 - 2 x 480 = 6,000.

items.title: Rate changes from year to year
items.label: Seen once

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** SI: add the yearly rates into one total %. CI: use a + b + ab/100 for two years, or multiply the yearly factors.
**Worked example (IBPS PO Prelims, 23 Aug 2025, Shift 2).** SI on 6,000: 10% for 2 years, then 15% for 3 years. Total = 20 + 45 = 65% = 3,900.
**Shortcut engine.** Work scheme by scheme. Read carefully whether the interest or the whole amount moves on. Going backwards, undo the last scheme first.

**Worked example (IBPS PO Prelims, 24 Aug 2025, Shift 1).** 12,500 at r% SI for 2 years; the interest goes into 10% CI for 2 years and becomes 3,630. Undo the CI: 121% = 3,630, so the interest was 3,000. 3,000 / 12,500 = 24% in 2 years, so r = 12.
**Shortcut engine.** Two years: difference = rate% of rate% of the sum. Three years: difference = sum x (rate/100) squared x (3 + rate/100).
Example: difference 240 for 2 years at 20%. 4% of the sum = 240, so the sum is 6,000. To find the rate instead: (rate/100) squared = difference / sum, then take the square root.

items.title: SI and CI both given for 2 years
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** CI minus SI is one year’s interest on the first year’s SI. Rate = (CI - SI) / (half of SI). Example: SI 800, CI 832. First-year SI = 400; extra 32 is 8% of 400, so the rate is 8% and the sum is 400 / 8% = 5,000.

**Shortcut engine.** Convert, then use the normal table. 20% half-yearly for 1 year = 10% for 2 periods = 21%. 20% quarterly for 9 months = 5% for 3 periods = 15.7625%. 40% quarterly for 1 year = 10% for 4 periods = 46.41%.

**Shortcut engine.** At CI, times multiply while years add. Doubles in 4 years, so 8 times = 2 x 2 x 2 takes 12 years. Non-linear warning: at SI, 3 times in 15 years means 5 times in 30 years; at CI it would be 9 times in 30 years.

items.title: CI amounts or interests of consecutive years
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** The jump from one year’s amount to the next is exactly the rate. 4,840 after 2 years and 5,324 after 3: the rise 484 is 10% of 4,840. Sum = 4,840 x 100 / 121 = 4,000. Yearly interests grow the same way: 660 then 726 means 10%.

**Shortcut engine.** Equal yearly instalments: write the fraction ratio and add the present values. At 10% for two instalments, an instalment of 121 parts pays off 110 + 100 = 210 parts of loan, so instalment = loan x 121 / 210 (6,300 gives 3,630). For three instalments at 10%: loan x 1,331 / 3,310. Unequal part-payments: roll forward one year at a time (add interest, subtract the payment).

lead.x: Eleven original questions: one per Core archetype plus the non-linear trap. Every answer was checked by script. Try each before reading the method.

body.x: A man invested Rs P at 15% p.a. simple interest for 4 years and earned Rs 2,700 as interest. Find the value of P + 500.

items.x: **Conventional method.** P x 15 x 4 / 100 = 2,700, so P = 4,500.
**Option elimination hack.** No divisibility shortcut is needed; one division finishes it.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 4,500 is P itself. The question asks P + 500.

body.x: A man invested Rs X at 12% p.a. simple interest for 5 years and received Rs 3,000 as interest. If he invests Rs (X + 1,000) at 20% p.a. compound interest for 2 years, find the interest received (in Rs).

items.x: **30-second exam method.** 60% = 3,000, so X = 5,000. New sum 6,000. 20% for 2 years = 44%. 44% of 6,000 = 2,640. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** The answer is 44% of a whole number of hundreds, so it must divide by 44. Only 2,640 does. Back-check: 2,640 / 44 x 100 = 6,000 = X + 1,000. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 2,400 is simple interest at 20% for 2 years. CI adds the 4% “interest on interest”.

body.x: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a certain sum for 2 years at 15% p.a. is Rs 180. Find the sum (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** P x (1.15 x 1.15 - 1) - P x 0.30 = 180, so 0.0225 P = 180.
**30-second exam method.** Two-year difference = 15% of 15% = 2.25% of the sum. 2.25% = 180, so 1% = 80 and the sum is 8,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** Test 15% of 15% on the middle option: 15% of 8,000 = 1,200; 15% of 1,200 = 180. It fits at once.
**IBPS trap warning.** The difference depends on the rate squared. If the rate doubles to 30%, the difference becomes four times (9%), not double.

body.x: A sum of money becomes 2.5 times itself in 6 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 6 times itself at the same rate?

items.x: **Conventional method.** 1.5 P = P x r x 6 / 100, so r = 25%. Then 5 P = P x 25 x t / 100, so t = 20.
**30-second exam method.** “2.5 times” means interest of 1.5 sums in 6 years. “6 times” means interest of 5 sums. Time = 6 x 5 / 1.5 = 20 years. **Answer (D).**
**Option elimination hack.** None. The proportion is one line.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 14.4 comes from 6 x 6 / 2.5, which forgets to remove the original sum. Always subtract 1 from “times” first.

items.title: Drill 5. Rate and time both changed (I3)

body.x: The simple interest on a certain sum at 9% p.a. for 4 years is Rs 1,440 less than the simple interest on the same sum at 12% p.a. for 5 years. Find the sum (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** P x 60 / 100 - P x 36 / 100 = 1,440.
**30-second exam method.** First case 9 x 4 = 36%. Second case 12 x 5 = 60%. Gap 24% = 1,440, so 1% = 60 and the sum is 6,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Do not subtract the rates first. 3% x 4 years gives 12,000 and 3% x 5 years gives 9,600; both are wrong because the years also changed.

items.title: Drill 6. Two SI deposits with a ratio (I4)

body.x: Scheme A offers simple interest at 8% p.a. for 5 years and the amount invested in it is Rs 4,500. Scheme B offers simple interest at 12% p.a. for 4 years and the amount invested in it is Rs P. If the ratio of the interest received from scheme A to that from scheme B is 5 : 8, find P.

items.x: **Conventional method.** (4,500 x 40) / (P x 48) = 5 / 8. Cross-multiply.
**30-second exam method.** A earns 40% of 4,500 = 1,800. That is 5 parts, so 1 part = 360 and B earns 8 parts = 2,880. B’s total is 48%, so 1% = 60 and P = 6,000. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Check the order of the ratio. “A to B is 5 : 8” puts A on 5. Reversing it gives 2,343.75, which is not an option, so a strange number is a signal to re-read.

body.x: A sum of money amounts to Rs 5,520 in 3 years and to Rs 6,240 in 6 years at simple interest. Find the rate of interest per annum.

items.x: **Conventional method.** P + 3I = 5,520 and P + 6I = 6,240. Solve for I and P.
**30-second exam method.** Three extra years add 720, so one year’s interest is 240. Sum = 5,520 - 3 x 240 = 4,800. Rate = 240 / 4,800 = 5%. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Divide the yearly interest by the original sum, not by 5,520. The amount already contains interest.

items.title: Drill 8. SI against CI on the same sum (L2)

body.x: A man invested Rs X in scheme A at 10% p.a. compound interest (compounded annually) for 2 years and the same amount in scheme B at 12% p.a. simple interest for 2 years. If the difference between the interests is Rs 180, find X.

items.x: **Conventional method.** X x 0.24 - X x 0.21 = 180.
**30-second exam method.** CI at 10% for 2 years = 21%. SI = 12 x 2 = 24%. Gap 3% = 180, so 1% = 60 and X = 6,000. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** CI is not always the bigger one. Here the SI scheme has the higher rate and earns more, so subtract in the right direction.

items.title: Drill 9. Rate changes with the years (K8)

body.x: A man borrowed a sum at simple interest. The rate is 6% p.a. for the first 2 years, 9% p.a. for the next 3 years and 12% p.a. for the period beyond 5 years. If he pays Rs 9,000 as total interest at the end of 8 years, find the sum borrowed (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** P x (6 x 2 + 9 x 3 + 12 x 3) / 100 = 9,000.
**30-second exam method.** Total = 12 + 27 + 36 = 75%. 75% = 9,000, so 1% = 120 and the sum is 12,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** “Beyond 5 years” up to 8 years is 3 years, not 8. Count each slab’s own years.

body.x: A man invested Rs 10,000 in scheme A at r% p.a. simple interest for 3 years. He invested the interest received from scheme A in scheme B at 20% p.a. compound interest for 2 years. If the amount received from scheme B is Rs 4,320, find r.

items.x: **Conventional method.** I x 1.44 = 4,320 gives I = 3,000. Then 10,000 x r x 3 / 100 = 3,000.
**30-second exam method.** Undo scheme B first: 144% = 4,320, so the interest invested was 3,000. That is 30% of 10,000 over 3 years, so r = 10. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Only the interest moved to scheme B, not the whole 13,000. And 4,320 is an amount, so divide by 144%, not 44%.

items.title: Drill 11. Plain CI with a twist (K1)

body.x: A man invested Rs P at 30% p.a. compound interest for 2 years. The difference between the amount received and the compound interest earned is Rs 3,000. If he had invested Rs (P - 500) at the same rate for the same period, find the compound interest received (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Amount - CI = P, so P = 3,000. CI on 2,500 = 2,500 x (1.3 x 1.3 - 1).
**30-second exam method.** Amount minus interest is the sum itself: P = 3,000. New sum 2,500. 30% for 2 years = 69%. 69% of 2,500 = 1,725. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 1,500 is simple interest (60%). Option (E) 2,070 is the CI on the full 3,000.

blocks.x: Which engine to use

rows: SI data, then “at compound interest for 2 years”
Find sum or rate, then use 21%, 44%, 32.25% …
Two SI schemes, total, difference or ratio of interest
Write each total %, then one balance
Same sum, rate or years changed
(new rate x years - old rate x years)% = extra interest
Amounts after two different years at SI
Gap / years between, then subtract back

blocks.x: Universal fallback

When a question fits no engine, use the **100% line**. Call the unknown sum 100%. Walk through the question one step at a time, writing each interest or amount as a % of that sum, until you reach the rupee figure given. That rupee figure equals some % of the sum, so 1% is known and everything follows. If the unknown is a rate or a time instead, plug in the middle option and compare the result with the given figure.

blocks.x: Red flags

items.x: **Amount or interest.** Check which one the last line asks for. Both usually sit among the options.
**CI is not linear.** You cannot halve or double CI when the rate or the years change. Recompute from the table.
**CI is not always larger.** When the SI scheme has the higher rate, SI can earn more.
**Answer is not the sum.** “Find P - 200” or “find 3.12X” appear in real papers; finish the last step.
**Extra sum.** For “X + 1,400” take the interest on 1,400 out as a plain number before balancing.
**Decimals are allowed.** Answers such as 1,814.4 or 7.5% are common here. Use divisibility hacks only when every option is whole and none is “None of these”, and always back-check.
