intro.x: Interest is the extra money you get back for lending. This topic has two kinds, and one habit handles both: **call the sum 100% and find what 1% is worth.**
There are nine short lessons. The first four are about simple interest, the fifth introduces compound interest, and the rest put the two together the way the exam does. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the tables and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more interest questions.

One kind is left for later on purpose: loans repaid in instalments. It has not appeared in the Clerk papers we checked, and it is easier once everything above feels natural. You will find it in Quick revision.

lessons.title: What simple interest is
lessons.plain: The starting point: interest is a slice of your money, and simple interest adds the same slice every year.

teach.x: When you lend money, you get back a little more than you gave. Four words describe that, and every question in this topic uses them:

items.x: **Sum** or **principal**: the money you put in.
**Rate**: the slice of the sum you earn each year, written as a percent. "8% per annum" means 8% of the sum every year. ("Per annum", often shortened to p.a., simply means "each year".)
**Interest**: the extra money earned.
**Amount**: the sum and the interest together. Amount = sum + interest.

teach.x: In **simple interest** the slice is always cut from the original sum, so every year adds exactly the same. That makes it easy: add the yearly slices up.
**Interest percent = rate x years.**
At 7% for 4 years you earn 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 28% of the sum. On Rs 3,000 that is 28% of 3,000 = Rs 840.

Now the habit that makes this whole topic light: **think of the sum as 100%, and ask what 1% is worth.** If the question gives you the interest instead of the sum, you work backwards through 1%. The example shows how.

tags: Forwards: find the interest.
Find the rate.
Find the time, from an amount.
Find the sum, with a half year.
Extra information that is not needed.

example.q: A sum earns Rs 1,440 as simple interest in 4 years at 9% per annum. Find the sum.
steps: Interest percent = rate x years = 9 x 4 = 36%.
So 36% of the sum is Rs 1,440.
1% of the sum = 1,440 / 36 = Rs 40.
Check: 9% of 4,000 is 360 a year, and 360 x 4 = 1,440.

checks.q: What is the simple interest on Rs 6,000 at 5% per annum for 4 years?
checks.why: 5 x 4 = 20% of the sum. 20% of 6,000 = 1,200. (300 is one year only; 7,200 is the amount, not the interest.)

checks.q: What is the simple interest on Rs 4,000 at 9% per annum for 8 months?
checks.why: 8 months is 8/12 = 2/3 of a year. Interest percent = 9 x 2/3 = 6%. 6% of 4,000 = 240. (360 is a full year.)

lessons.title: "It doubles", "1.6 times", "three-fifths of the sum"
lessons.plain: New: no rupees at all. The question only says how the money grew compared with itself.

teach.x: Some questions never mention an actual amount of money. They say "a sum doubles in 8 years" or "the interest is three-fifths of the sum".
You do not need rupees. Because you already think of the sum as 100%, these phrases are simply telling you the **interest percent**.
The one thing to be careful about: "becomes 3 times" describes the **amount**. The interest is what was added on top of the original 100%, so it is 200%, not 300%.
Once you have the interest percent, last lesson's rule does the rest: interest percent = rate x years. Know two of the three and you can find the third.

tags: Doubles: find the rate.
A decimal multiple.
Interest as a fraction of the sum; the rupees are a distraction.
A fraction, and the time hides inside (x + 1).
Two stages: it doubles, then when is it 12 times?

example.q: A sum becomes 1.8 times itself in 4 years at simple interest. Find the rate. In how many years will it become 3 times itself?
steps: 1.8 times means the amount is 180%, so the interest is 80%.
80% came in 4 years, so the rate is 80 / 4 = 20% a year.
To become 3 times, the amount is 300%, so the interest needed is 200%.
At 20% a year, 200% takes 200 / 20 = 10 years.

checks.q: A sum of money triples in 10 years at simple interest. What is the rate per annum?
checks.why: Triples means the amount is 300%, so the interest is 200%. 200% in 10 years is 20% a year. (30% would be the answer if the interest were 300%.)

checks.tag: Rate and years are the same number
checks.q: The simple interest on a sum is 9/25 of the sum, and the number of years is equal to the rate percent. What is the rate?
checks.why: 9/25 is 36%. Interest percent = rate x years, and here both are the same number, so that number times itself is 36. The rate is 6% (for 6 years).

text.x: If a sum becomes **n times** in some years at simple interest, the time to become **m times** is:
**those years x (m - 1) / (n - 1)**
Doubles in 5 years, when 12 times? 5 x (12 - 1) / (2 - 1) = 55 years.
The "minus 1" is there because the interest is what was added on top of the original sum. It is the same reasoning as the lesson, packed into one line.

lessons.title: One sum, two situations
lessons.plain: New: the same money is looked at twice, with a different rate or a different number of years, and you are told the difference.

teach.x: A very common kind compares two situations for the **same sum**. "If the rate had been 2% higher, the interest for 3 years would have been Rs 360 more."
You could work out both interests and subtract. There is a much shorter way: **look only at what changed.**
Here the only change is 2% more each year, for 3 years. That is 2 x 3 = 6% of the sum, and that 6% is the Rs 360. So 1% is Rs 60 and the sum is Rs 6,000. The original rate was never needed.
The same thinking solves another favourite: **amounts at two dates**. "A sum amounts to Rs 5,200 after 2 years and Rs 5,800 after 5 years."

items.x: Nothing changed between the two dates except 3 more years of interest. So 5,800 - 5,200 = Rs 600 is the interest for 3 years.
In simple interest every year adds the same, so one year is Rs 200.
Walk back from the first date: two years of interest is Rs 400, so the sum is 5,200 - 400 = Rs 4,800.

teach.x: Whenever you see two situations for one sum, ask yourself: **what is the only thing that is different?** That difference is pure interest.

tags: The rate goes up.
Two rates named outright.
Borrow at one rate, lend at another.
Amounts at two dates.
The same, written with letters.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum at 11% per annum for 4 years is Rs 960 more than the simple interest on the same sum at 8% per annum for 4 years. Find the sum.
steps: What changed? Only the rate: 11 - 8 = 3% more each year.
Over 4 years that is 3 x 4 = 12% of the sum.
So 12% of the sum is Rs 960, and 1% is Rs 80.
The sum is 100 x 80 = Rs 8,000.

checks.q: If the rate of simple interest is raised by 3% per annum, the interest on a sum for 2 years goes up by Rs 240. What is the sum?
checks.why: The change is 3% a year for 2 years, which is 6% of the sum. 6% = 240, so 1% = 40 and the sum is 4,000.

checks.tag: The time changes, not the rate
checks.q: The simple interest on a sum at 8% per annum for 5 years is Rs 600 more than the interest on the same sum at the same rate for 3 years. What is the sum?
checks.why: What changed? Two more years at 8%, which is 16% of the sum. 16% = 600, so 1% = 37.5 and the sum is 3,750.

lessons.title: Two deposits
lessons.plain: New: two different sums, or one sum split in two, each earning simple interest at its own rate.

teach.x: Now there are two pots of money. Each has its own rate, and sometimes its own number of years. The question gives the total interest, the difference, or asks for the ratio.
The first step is always the same: **write each pot's interest percent** (rate x years) next to it. After that there are three shapes.
**Both sums are known.** Just work out each interest and compare. Rs 450 at 20% for 2 years earns 40% of 450 = Rs 180.
**The sums are linked by a letter**, such as X and X + 1,400. Write each interest using X, then use the total or the difference the question gives you. It is one line of algebra.

**One sum is split into two parts.** Use this small trick: pretend the **whole** sum was lent at the lower rate. Compare with the real interest. The extra money can only have come from the part at the higher rate, earning the extra percent. The example below shows it.
If the question says the two parts earn **equal** interest, the parts are in the opposite ratio of their interest percents: the part with the smaller percent must be bigger.

tags: Both sums known; the catch is the order of the ratio.
One sum split in two; the total interest is given.
Two sums linked by a letter; the difference of interest is given.
Split so that the two interests are equal.
Linked by a multiple, different years, and a twist in the last line.

example.q: Rs 10,000 is lent in two parts for one year, one part at 6% and the other at 9% simple interest. The total interest is Rs 720. How much was lent at 9%?
steps: Pretend all Rs 10,000 was lent at the lower rate, 6%. The interest would be Rs 600.
The real interest is Rs 720, which is Rs 120 more.
That extra can only come from the 9% part, which earns 9 - 6 = 3% more than we pretended.
So 3% of that part is Rs 120, and the part is Rs 4,000.
Check: 9% of 4,000 = 360, and 6% of the other 6,000 = 360. Total 720.

checks.q: A invests Rs 2,000 at 10% simple interest for 3 years. B invests Rs 3,000 at 5% simple interest for 4 years. What is the ratio of A's interest to B's interest?
checks.why: A earns 10 x 3 = 30% of 2,000 = 600. B earns 5 x 4 = 20% of 3,000 = 600. The interests are equal, so 1 : 1.

lessons.title: What compound interest is
lessons.plain: New: interest that earns interest. Each year's slice is cut from the grown amount, not from the original sum.

teach.x: In simple interest the yearly slice never changes. **Compound interest** (CI) is different in one way only: at the end of each year the interest is **added to your money**, and next year's slice is cut from that bigger amount.
Take Rs 6,000 at 10% a year.

items.x: Year 1: 10% of 6,000 = 600. You now have 6,600.

teach.x: The total interest is 600 + 660 = Rs 1,260. Simple interest would have given 600 + 600 = 1,200. The extra Rs 60 is the interest earned on the first year's interest.
Going year by year always works, and you should do it that way until it feels natural. For **two years** there is also a quick route. The interest percent for two years is:
**rate + rate + (rate x rate) / 100**
At 10%: 10 + 10 + 1 = 21%. And 21% of 6,000 is 1,260, the same answer in one step. The first two pieces are the two yearly slices; the last piece is the interest on interest.
If the rate is different in each year, the same idea holds: first rate + second rate + (first x second) / 100.
These two-year percents come up so often that it helps to recognise them. There is no need to memorise the table today; it will stick with practice.
For three years, do two years first and then one more year on the amount.

tags: Plain two years: find the interest.
The question asks for the amount.
A different rate in each year.
Backwards: find the rate from how much it grew.
Two and a half years.

example.q: Find the compound interest on Rs 8,000 at 20% per annum for 2 years.
steps: Year 1: 20% of 8,000 = 1,600. The money is now 9,600.
Year 2: 20% of 9,600 = 1,920. The money is now 11,520.
Compound interest = 1,600 + 1,920 = Rs 3,520.
Quick route to confirm: 20 + 20 + (20 x 20) / 100 = 44%, and 44% of 8,000 = 3,520.

checks.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 5,000 at 20% per annum for 2 years?
checks.why: Year 1: 1,000, giving 6,000. Year 2: 20% of 6,000 = 1,200. Total 2,200. (2,000 is the simple interest; 7,200 is the amount.)

checks.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 1,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years?
checks.why: Year 1: 100, giving 1,100. Year 2: 110, giving 1,210. Year 3: 121, giving 1,331. Interest = 100 + 110 + 121 = 331. (1,331 is the amount.)

text.x: Some rates are simple fractions, and then compound interest becomes a ratio. 20% is 1/5: every year, each 5 rupees become 6.
So after one year, sum : amount = 5 : 6. After two years, 25 : 36. After three, 125 : 216.
This is most useful backwards. "A sum amounts to Rs 7,200 in 2 years at 20%": 36 parts = 7,200, so one part is 200 and the sum, 25 parts, is Rs 5,000.

lessons.title: Simple interest first, then compound interest
lessons.plain: New: lessons 1 and 5 in one question. The first half hides a number; the second half uses it.

teach.x: This is the form the Clerk paper sets most often in this topic. It has two halves, and you already know both.

**First half: a simple interest story with one thing missing.** Usually the sum is missing ("a sum at 10% for 3 years earns Rs 1,800"), and sometimes the rate is. Find it exactly as in lesson 1, through 1%.
**Second half: compound interest for two years**, using what you just found. Use the two-year percent from lesson 5.
So the routine is two short steps:

items.x: From the simple interest story, find the missing sum or rate.
Apply the two-year compound percent to the sum the second half asks about.

teach.x: Before you mark, read the last line once more. It asks either for the **interest** or for the **amount** (sum + interest). Both will be among the options.

tags: The smallest version: same sum, same rate.
Find the sum, then a new rate; it asks for the amount.
An awkward rate, 8%.
This time the rate is missing, and it changes.
The rate is missing, and the second half uses a different sum.

example.q: The simple interest on a sum at 12% per annum for 5 years is Rs 3,000. If the same sum is invested at 20% per annum compound interest for 2 years, find the amount received.
steps: First half: interest percent = 12 x 5 = 60%. So 60% of the sum is 3,000.
1% is 50, so the sum is Rs 5,000.
Second half: compound interest at 20% for 2 years is 44%.
The question asks for the amount: 5,000 + 2,200 = Rs 7,200.

checks.q: The simple interest on a sum at 5% per annum for 4 years is Rs 800. What is the compound interest on the same sum at 10% per annum for 2 years?
checks.why: 5 x 4 = 20% of the sum is 800, so the sum is 4,000. Compound interest at 10% for 2 years is 21%, and 21% of 4,000 = 840.

lessons.title: The same question, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the method. The numbers are wrapped in letters such as P, R and (R + 5).

teach.x: Recent papers dress the last lesson up with letters. "A man invested Rs **P** at 18% simple interest for three years and received Rs **(0.5P + 100)** as interest. If he invests Rs **(P + 3,500)** at ..."
It looks heavier than it is. Take it one piece at a time.

**A letter in the interest.** "18% for 3 years" is 54% of P, which you can write as 0.54 P. The question says that same interest is 0.5 P + 100. Two ways of writing one thing must be equal: 0.54 P = 0.5 P + 100. Take 0.5 P from both sides: 0.04 P = 100, so P = 2,500.
**A changed sum, such as (P + 3,500).** Once you know P, this is just a number. Work it out before you touch the second half.
**A changed rate, such as (R + 5)% or (R - 5)%.** Find R from the first half, adjust it, and only then use the two-year percent.
So the routine from the last lesson gains one middle step:

items.x: Find the letter from the simple interest story.
Work out the new sum and the new rate as plain numbers.
Apply the two-year compound percent.

tags: The new sum is (P + 4,400).
An amount is given instead of the interest; the rate becomes (R + 5).
A letter inside the interest itself.
The compound half has to be done first.

example.q: A man invested Rs P at 15% per annum simple interest for 4 years and received Rs (0.5P + 300) as interest. If he invests Rs (P + 1,000) at 10% per annum compound interest for 2 years, find the interest.
steps: Simple interest percent = 15 x 4 = 60%, so the interest is 0.6 P.
The question says the interest is 0.5 P + 300. So 0.6 P = 0.5 P + 300.
That leaves 0.1 P = 300, so P = 3,000.
Compound interest at 10% for 2 years is 21%. 21% of 4,000 = 840.

checks.q: Rs P is invested at 10% per annum simple interest for 2 years and the interest received is Rs (P - 4,000). What is P?
checks.why: 10 x 2 = 20%, so the interest is 0.2 P. Then 0.2 P = P - 4,000, which gives 0.8 P = 4,000 and P = 5,000. Check: 20% of 5,000 is 1,000, and 5,000 - 4,000 is 1,000.

lessons.title: Simple against compound
lessons.plain: New: both kinds of interest on linked sums, and you are told how far apart they are.

teach.x: Here the question puts simple and compound interest side by side and gives you the gap between them. Do what you did in lesson 3: turn each side into a **percent of the sum** and compare the percents.

**Same sum, different schemes.** Rs X at 20% compound interest for 2 years earns 44% of X. The same X at 30% simple interest for 2 years earns 60% of X. The gap is 16% of X. If the question says the gap is Rs 896, then 1% is 56 and X is 5,600.

**Same sum, same rate, 2 years.** This one has a pattern worth knowing. Compound interest beats simple interest by exactly the interest on the first year's interest. As a percent of the sum that is **(rate x rate) / 100**. At 5% the gap is 0.25% of the sum; at 10% it is 1%; at 20% it is 4%.

**Both interests given for 2 years.** "Simple interest is Rs 800 and compound interest is Rs 832." One year's simple interest is 400. The extra 32 is the rate applied to that 400, so the rate is 32 / 400 = 8%. And if 8% of the sum is 400, the sum is 5,000.
**Two sums in a ratio.** Call them 2 parts and 3 parts. Apply each scheme's percent to its own parts, add, and match the total to the rupees given.

tags: Same sum and rate, 2 years: find the sum.
Both interests given: find the rate and the sum.
A different rate for each scheme.
Two compound schemes on sums in a ratio.
Three years.

example.q: A man invests Rs X in scheme A at 10% per annum compound interest for 2 years, and the same Rs X in scheme B at 12% per annum simple interest for 2 years. Scheme B gives Rs 150 more interest. Find X.
steps: Scheme A: compound interest at 10% for 2 years is 21% of X.
Scheme B: simple interest is 12 x 2 = 24% of X.
The gap is 24 - 21 = 3% of X.
So 3% of X is Rs 150, and 1% is Rs 50.

checks.q: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is Rs 50. What is the sum?
checks.why: Same sum, same rate, 2 years: the gap is (10 x 10) / 100 = 1% of the sum. 1% = 50, so the sum is 5,000.

text.x: For the same sum and rate, the gap between compound and simple interest after **2 years** is (rate x rate) / 100 percent of the sum. You have used that already.
After **3 years** the gap, as a percent of the sum, is:
**3 x (rate x rate) / 100 + (rate x rate x rate) / 10,000**
So "the difference between compound and simple interest for 3 years at 10% is Rs 155" means 3.1% of the sum is 155, and the sum is Rs 5,000.

lessons.title: Three smaller ideas to finish
lessons.plain: New: interest added every half year, compound money that doubles, and amounts from one year to the next.

teach.x: These have not appeared in the Clerk papers we checked, but they are common in practice sets. Each is a small step from what you know.

**1. Compounded half-yearly.** Sometimes interest is added to your money every six months instead of every year. Then each half year is its own "year": **halve the rate and double the number of periods.** 8% a year, compounded half-yearly, for 1 year is 4% applied twice. Using the two-step rule: 4 + 4 + 0.16 = 8.16%. (Quarterly works the same way: a quarter of the rate, four periods a year.)

**2. "It doubles" in compound interest.** In simple interest, doubling again takes the same extra money. In compound interest, the whole amount is multiplied each time. If a sum doubles in 4 years, then in the next 4 years it doubles again (4 times), and in the next 4 again (8 times). So think in **multiplications**: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2, three doublings, 12 years.

**3. From one year to the next.** In compound interest, one more year multiplies your money by the same number every time. So if you know the amount after 2 years and after 3 years, dividing one by the other shows the rate. 5,324 / 4,840 = 1.1, which means the money grew by 10% in that year. The same works for the interest of two neighbouring years: 726 / 660 = 1.1, again 10%.
After you know the rate, walk back to the start by dividing instead of multiplying.

tags: Interest added every half year.
Doubling under compound interest.
The amounts of two neighbouring years.
The interests of two neighbouring years.

example.q: A sum amounts to Rs 6,050 in 2 years and to Rs 6,655 in 3 years at compound interest. Find the sum.
steps: One more year took 6,050 to 6,655. Divide: 6,655 / 6,050 = 1.1.
So the money grows by 10% each year.
Two years at 10% multiplies the sum by 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21.
Walk back: sum = 6,050 / 1.21 = Rs 5,000.
Check: 5,000 becomes 5,500, then 6,050, then 6,655.

checks.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 10,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly?
checks.why: Half-yearly means 10% applied twice. 10 + 10 + 1 = 21%, and 21% of 10,000 = 2,100. (2,000 would be the answer if interest were added only once a year.)

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Exact Mechanics & Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **Central law.** A percent is a fraction of some base, so always ask “percent of what?”. A change of p% multiplies the base by (100 + p)/100 or (100 - p)/100. Changes one after another multiply; they do not add. Most questions end by finding what 1% (or one fraction part) of the base is worth.
Base operations

items.x: **Percent of a number.** Build it from 10% and 1% blocks. 35% of 840: 10% = 84, so 30% = 252 and 5% = 42; total 294.
**Whole from a part.** “45% is 378”: 1% = 378 / 45 = 8.4, so the whole is 840.
**Change factor.** Up 20% is x 6/5. Down 20% is x 4/5. Up 12.5% is x 9/8. Use the fraction table.
**Two changes in a row.** Net % = a + b + (a x b)/100, with minus signs for decreases. Up 10% then down 20%: 10 - 20 - 2 = -12%.
**Going backwards.** Divide by the factor. A value of 81,000 after two falls of 10% was 81,000 / 0.81 = 1,00,000.
**Changing the base.** If A is 1/n more than B, then B is 1/(n + 1) less than A. 25% more (1/4) turns into 20% less (1/5).
**“Of the remaining” chain.** Multiply the fractions that are kept. Spend 25%, then 20% of the rest, then 20% of the rest: kept = 3/4 x 4/5 x 4/5 = 48%.
**Equal percents.** If x% of A = y% of B, then A : B = y : x (swap the numbers).
**Price times quantity.** With spending fixed, a price rise of 1/n needs a cut of 1/(n + 1) in quantity; a price fall of 1/n buys 1/(n - 1) more.

blocks.x: Fraction table (learn by heart)
Base-change pairs

rows: A is this much more than B
B is this much less than A

blocks.x: Calculation facts to keep ready

items.x: Three rises of 10% multiply to 1.331; two give 1.21. Three falls of 10% give 0.729; two give 0.81.
Rises of 20%: 1.44 after two, 1.728 after three. A rise of 25% then a fall of 20% cancels exactly.
Non-linear warning: a rise and a fall of the same p% do not cancel. The result is a fall of (p x p)/100 percent.

lead.x: Fourteen archetypes cover the usable bank and the sister-exam questions. The salary-spending chain (“of the remaining”) is the clear leader: 9 of the 27 papers carry it. Elections, pass marks, Venn sets and mensuration percentages have many bank questions but none in the papers; they are Insurance. “Papers” counts paper labels.

rows: Two groups, each with its own percent
Constant part (fresh and dry fruit, dilution)
Fraction with numerator and denominator changed
Percent change in area or volume

lead.x: Worked examples below are real questions from the papers.

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “Spends 25% of his income on food. From the remaining he spends 20% on rent … and saves the rest.” A ratio split of one slice (“in the ratio 3 : 1 : 1”) is common.
**Shortcut engine: multiply what is kept.**

items.x: For each “of the remaining” step, write the fraction kept (spend 20%, keep 4/5).
Multiply the kept fractions: that is the final share of the income.
Final share = given rupees gives 1% of income. If a step says “of his income” instead, subtract that % directly, do not multiply.

blocks.x: **Worked example (SBI Clerk Prelims, 22 Feb 2025, Shift 1).** Spends 25% on food, 20% of the remaining on rent, 20% of the remaining on education, and saves 19,200. Kept = 3/4 x 4/5 x 4/5 = 48%. 48% = 19,200, so 1% = 400 and the income is 40,000.

**Difference version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2022, Adda247 paper).** 60% on accommodation, 15% of the remaining on entertainment, rest saved. Accommodation minus savings = 3,510. Remaining 40%; savings = 85% of 40 = 34%. Gap = 60 - 34 = 26% = 3,510, so 1% = 135 and the salary is 13,500.
**Wording clues.** “Increased by 10% in the first year and decreased by 20% in the second”, “increases by 10% every year”, “two years ago”.
**Shortcut engine: multiply the factors.**

items.x: Two steps: net % = a + b + ab/100. Three or more: multiply the fraction factors.
Forward: multiply. Backward (“was … years ago”): divide.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 2).** 25,000 rises 10% then falls 20%. Net = 10 - 20 - 2 = -12%. Answer 22,000.
**Backward version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023, Guidely paper).** Up 10% every year; 2,66,200 in 2022. Average of 2019 and 2020? 2019 = 2,66,200 / 1.331 = 2,00,000. 2020 = 2,20,000. Average 2,10,000.
**Wording clues.** “45% of X is equal to 60% of Y”, “5% of X is 25% more than Y”, “A is 20% more than B”, followed by a sum, difference or average.
**Shortcut engine: turn the sentence into a ratio.**

items.x: x% of A = y% of B gives A : B = y : x. “A is p% more than B” gives A : B = (100 + p) : 100.
Match the given sum, difference or average to its parts and find 1 unit.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2021).** 45% of X = 60% of Y; the average of X and Y is 20 less than X. Find 60% of Y. X : Y = 60 : 45 = 4 : 3. Average = 3.5 units = 4 units - 20, so 1 unit = 40. Y = 120 and 60% of it is 72.
**“More than” version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** 5% of X is 25% more than Y; X - Y = 96. X/20 = 5Y/4, so X : Y = 25 : 1. Gap 24 units = 96, 1 unit = 4, X = 100.

items.title: Two groups, each with its own percent
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** Boys and girls, males and females, two schools or two teams. Each group has its own pass %, graduate % or growth %, and a combined figure is given or asked.
**Shortcut engine: one line per group.**

items.x: Write each group as a % or ratio of the total.
Apply that group’s own % to it.
Add or compare the two lines and match with the given number.

blocks.x: **Worked example (SBI Clerk Prelims, 22 Feb 2025, Shift 1).** 40% of a town are male. 40% of the females are graduates, and 540 females are not. Find the males. Females = 60% of the town; non-graduate females = 60% of 60 = 36% = 540. 1% = 15, so males = 40% = 600.

**Count version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 4).** 360 passed; 60% of boys and 40% of girls passed; 66 2/3% of the passed boys is 160. Passed boys = 160 x 3/2 = 240 = 60% of boys, so boys = 400. Passed girls = 120 = 40% of girls, so girls = 300. Total 700.
**Shortcut engine.** All shares are “of the total”, so they add to 100%. The unnamed share = 100% minus the rest; match it to its number.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 1).** 40% science fair, 25% sports, the rest (315) cultural. Rest = 35% = 315, so 1% = 9. Difference between science and sports = 15% = 135.
**Shortcut engine.** Draw three boxes: income = expenditure + savings. Put 100 on whichever box the percent is “of”, fill the other two, then scale.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 3).** Income is 25% more than expenditure; expenditure is 24,000. Expenditure 100, income 125, savings 25. Savings = 25% of 24,000 = 6,000.
**Shortcut engine.** Price x quantity = spending. For “a price cut lets him buy k kg more for Rs S”: the money saved (cut % of S) is exactly what buys the extra k kg at the new price.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 3 Sep 2022, Slot 2).** A 16.66% cut buys 3 kg more for Rs 180. Saved = 1/6 of 180 = 30. So 3 kg cost 30 at the new price: new price 10. Original = 10 x 6/5 = 12.
**Shortcut engine.** One ingredient does not change (fruit pulp, pure alcohol). Find its weight first; then it is a known % of the new total.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017, Guidely model paper).** Fresh fruit is 68% water; dry fruit is 20% water. From 100 kg fresh: pulp = 32 kg. In dry fruit pulp is 80%, so dry fruit = 32 / 0.8 = 40 kg.

items.title: Fraction with numerator and denominator changed
items.label: Seen once

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** New fraction = old fraction x (numerator factor / denominator factor). To get the old one, multiply the new one by the upside-down of that.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** Numerator down 25% (x 3/4), denominator up 250% (x 7/2), result 6/5. Combined factor = 3/4 / 7/2 = 3/14. Original = 6/5 x 14/3 = 28/5.
**Shortcut engine.** Write every piece as a % of the same number and combine.
**Worked example (IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims, 13 Dec 2025, Shift 1).** A number raised 40% and the same number cut 80% differ by 360. 140% - 20% = 120% = 360, so the number is 300.

**Shortcut engine.** Two students around the pass mark: maximum marks = (marks short + marks extra) / (difference of their %). Scores 30% and fails by 30; scores 45% and passes by 15: 45 marks = 15%, so the maximum is 300.

**Shortcut engine.** Write the chain: voters on the list, votes polled, valid votes, winner and loser. Each % applies to the level just above it. Winning margin = (winner % - loser %) of valid votes. Example: 20% of polled votes invalid, winner gets 58% of valid and wins by 1,920. Margin = 16% of 80% = 12.8% of polled = 1,920, so 15,000 were polled.

items.title: Percent change in area or volume
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** Area uses two changes: a + b + ab/100. Each side up 20% gives 44%. Volume needs three factors: each edge up 30% gives 1.3 x 1.3 x 1.3 = 2.197, a rise of 119.7%. Non-linear warning: the area change is never just double the side change.
**Shortcut engine.** At least one = A + B - both. Neither = 100% - at least one. Example: 35% fail English, 25% fail Maths, 10% fail both. Failed at least one = 50%, so passed both = 50%.

lead.x: Ten original questions, one per Core archetype. Every answer and every trap value was computed by script. Try each before reading the method.

body.x: In a housing society, 45% of the residents own a car, 30% own only a bike and the rest own neither. If 175 residents own neither, find the difference between the number of car owners and bike-only owners.

items.x: **Conventional method.** 0.25 T = 175 gives T = 700. Then 0.45 T - 0.30 T = 105.
**30-second exam method.** The rest = 100 - 45 - 30 = 25% = 175, so 1% = 7. The gap asked is 45 - 30 = 15% = 105. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** The answer is 15 x (1%) and 1% = 7, so it must divide by 7 and by 15. Only 105 does. Back-check: 700 residents, 315 and 210. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Do not find the total first unless asked. Go straight from 25% to 15%.

body.x: Meera spends 40% of her monthly salary on rent and 25% of the remaining on food, and saves the rest. If her savings are Rs 9,000 more than the amount spent on food, find her monthly salary (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Food = 0.25 x 0.6 S = 0.15 S. Savings = 0.45 S. 0.30 S = 9,000.
**30-second exam method.** Remaining after rent = 60%. Food = a quarter of 60 = 15%. Savings = 45%. Gap = 30% = 9,000, so 1% = 300 and the salary is 30,000. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** “25% of the remaining” is 15% of salary, not 25%. Taking 25% of salary gives a 10% gap and option (E) 90,000.

body.x: The price of an article was increased by 25%, then decreased by 20% and then increased by 10%. If the final price is Rs 1,650, find the original price (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** P x 1.25 x 0.8 x 1.1 = 1,650.
**30-second exam method.** Up 1/4 then down 1/5 cancel exactly (5/4 x 4/5 = 1). Only the 10% rise is left: 110% = 1,650, so the original is 1,500. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** Once the first two changes cancel, 110% of the right option must equal 1,650. Only 1,500 works. Back-check: 1,500, 1,875, 1,500, 1,650. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Adding the changes (25 - 20 + 10 = 15%) gives about 1,435, option (B). Changes multiply; they never add.

body.x: A’s salary is 25% more than B’s salary, and B’s salary is 40% less than C’s salary. By what percent is A’s salary less than C’s salary?

items.x: **Conventional method.** A = 1.25 B and B = 0.6 C, so A = 0.75 C.
**30-second exam method.** Put C = 100. B = 60. A = 60 + a quarter of 60 = 75. A is 25 below C’s 100: 25% less. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed; put 100 on the last person named as the base.
**IBPS trap warning.** 40 - 25 = 15 is option (A). Each percent has a different base, so they cannot be subtracted.

body.x: In a company, 60% of the employees are male. 30% of the males and 45% of the females are graduates. If the number of non-graduate employees is 1,280, find the total number of employees.

items.x: **Conventional method.** Graduates = 0.6 x 0.3 T + 0.4 x 0.45 T = 0.36 T. Then 0.64 T = 1,280.
**30-second exam method.** Take 100 employees: 60 males, 40 females. Graduates = 18 + 18 = 36. Non-graduates = 64% = 1,280, so 1% = 20 and the total is 2,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Do not average 30% and 45%. Each applies to a group of a different size.

body.x: Ravi’s monthly income is 20% more than Sunil’s. Ravi saves 25% of his income and Sunil saves 30% of his income. If Ravi’s monthly expenditure is Rs 4,000 more than Sunil’s, find Sunil’s monthly income (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** 0.75 x 1.2 S - 0.7 S = 4,000.
**30-second exam method.** Sunil’s income 100: he spends 70. Ravi’s income 120: he spends three-quarters = 90. Gap 20 units = 4,000, so 1 unit = 200 and Sunil earns 20,000. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (D) 24,000 is Ravi’s income. The question asks Sunil’s.

body.x: A reduction of 20% in the price of sugar enables a buyer to get 4 kg more for Rs 640. Find the original price of sugar per kg (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** 640 / (0.8 p) - 640 / p = 4.
**30-second exam method.** Money saved = 20% of 640 = 128. That 128 buys the extra 4 kg at the new price: new price = 32. Original = 32 x 5/4 = 40. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** The new price is 4/5 of the answer and 640 must split evenly at both prices. 640 / 40 = 16 kg and 640 / 32 = 20 kg: 4 kg more. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 32 is the reduced price. The question asks the original price.

body.x: Fresh dates contain 72% water and dry dates contain 16% water. How many kg of dry dates can be obtained from 150 kg of fresh dates?

items.x: **Conventional method.** Pulp = 0.28 x 150 = 42. Dry weight x 0.84 = 42.
**30-second exam method.** Pulp never changes: 28% of 150 = 42 kg. In dry dates pulp is 84%, so dry dates = 42 / 0.84 = 50 kg. **Answer (D).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (A) 42 is only the pulp. Dry dates still hold 16% water, so the answer is larger.

body.x: If the numerator of a fraction is increased by 40% and the denominator is decreased by 30%, the resultant fraction is 8/5. Find the original fraction.

items.x: **Conventional method.** 1.4 n / 0.7 d = 8/5, so n/d = 8/5 x 0.7/1.4.
**30-second exam method.** Numerator x 7/5, denominator x 7/10: the fraction is multiplied by 7/5 / 7/10 = 2. The original is half of 8/5 = 4/5. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (C) 16/5 comes from multiplying by 2 again. Going back to the original means dividing.

body.x: A number is increased by 30%, and the same number is decreased by 45%. If the difference between the two results is 450, find the number.

items.x: **Conventional method.** 1.3 x - 0.55 x = 450.
**30-second exam method.** The two results are 130% and 55% of the number. Gap = 75% = 450, so the number is 600. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (E) 3,000 comes from 45 - 30 = 15%. One change goes up and the other down, so the gap is 30 + 45 = 75%.

blocks.x: Which engine to use

rows: Several shares “of the total”, one left over
Product of kept fractions = final share
a + b + ab/100; divide to go back
“x% of A = y% of B”, “p% more than”
A : B = y : x; then units
Put 100 on the base, fill, scale
Saved money buys the extra quantity
Two students around the pass mark

blocks.x: Universal fallback

When a question fits no engine, use the **100 method**. Put 100 on the quantity every other percent ultimately hangs from (total salary, total votes, the third person). Rewrite every other quantity as a plain number out of that 100, one sentence at a time. The rupee or head-count figure given will equal some number of those units, which fixes 1 unit. If two different bases appear and cannot be linked, plug in the middle option instead and test it.
Phrase to maths

rows: A quarter of what is left, not of the total
“25% of his income” in the middle of a chain
A quarter of the total; subtract it directly
“B is what percent less than A”
“x% of A is equal to y% of B”
“20% of the votes polled were invalid”
Valid = 80% of polled, not of the list

blocks.x: Red flags

items.x: **Wrong base.** Most wrong options come from applying a percent to the total when it belongs to “the remaining”, or the other way round.
**Adding successive changes.** Up 25% then down 20% is no change, not +5%.
**Averaging two group percents.** Weight each by the size of its group.
**Direction words.** “More” and “less” versions of the same number often both appear as options.
**Stopping early.** Finding the total when the question asks a difference, or one person’s income when it asks the other’s.
**Decimals and fractions are allowed.** Answers such as 28/5, 37.5% and 12.5 appear. Use divisibility hacks only when every option is whole and none is “None of these”, and always back-check.

**Rung 2. 60 seconds each.**

intro.x: A percent is a fraction of a whole, written out of a hundred. Almost every mistake in this topic comes from one place: forgetting **which whole** a percent is measured against.
So these ten short lessons keep returning to one question: "percent of what?" The first three build the tools. The rest are the settings the exam uses, one at a time. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the fraction table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
The ideas here are also the foundation for Profit & Loss, Interest and Data Interpretation, so time spent making them comfortable is repaid several times over.

lessons.title: A percent of a number, forwards and backwards
lessons.plain: The starting point: what 1% is worth, and three small questions that everything else is built from.

teach.x: Percent means "out of a hundred". The whole of anything is 100%, and the surest way to work with it is to find what **1%** is worth.
Three small questions come up again and again. Learn to tell them apart and this topic becomes calm.
**1. Find a percent of a number.** "What is 24% of 450?" 1% of 450 is 4.5, so 24% is 24 x 4.5 = 108.

**2. Find the whole from a part.** "35% of a number is 168." Go backwards: 1% is 168 / 35 = 4.8, so the number is 480. If a question then asks for 60% of that number, you do not even need the 480: 60 x 4.8 = 288.
**3. Find what percent one number is of another.** "72 is what percent of 450?" Put the part over the whole and multiply by 100: 72 / 450 x 100 = 16%.

A **percent change** is the third question in disguise: the change, over the **starting** value. A price that goes from Rs 400 to Rs 500 has changed by 100, and 100 / 400 = 25%. Always divide by where it started, not where it ended.
The same thinking handles shares of one whole. If 40% of students chose science and 25% chose sports, the rest are 100 - 40 - 25 = 35%. Give that 35% its real number and you have 1%.

tags: What percent is one number of another?
A percent change.
A part is known: jump straight to another part.
The number after an increase is known.
Shares of one whole.

example.q: 18% of a number is 81. What is 40% of the same number?
steps: 18% of the number is 81, so 1% is 81 / 18 = 4.5.
There was no need to find the number itself. (It is 450, if you want to check: 40% of 450 = 180.)

checks.q: 45 is what percent of 180?
checks.why: Part over whole: 45 / 180 = 1/4, and one quarter is 25%.

checks.tag: Two percents of the same number
checks.q: The difference between 62% of a number and 38% of the same number is 96. What is the number?
checks.why: Both percents are of the same number, so subtract them first: 62 - 38 = 24%. 24% = 96, so 1% = 4 and the number is 400.

text.x: **x% of y is always the same as y% of x.** So when a percent looks awkward, try it the other way round.
16% of 25 looks fiddly. But 25% of 16 is a quarter of 16, which is 4. Same answer.
It works because both are just x times y, divided by 100.

lessons.title: "More than", "less than", and which one is the 100
lessons.plain: New: two things are compared by a percent. The whole skill is knowing which of them counts as 100.

teach.x: "A's income is 60% more than B's income." Sentences like this compare two things, and the percent is always measured against the one that comes **after "than"**. So B is the 100, and A is 160.
This small habit removes most of the confusion in the topic: **find the word "than" (or "of"), call that thing 100, and write the other one beside it.**
Now the classic trap. "A is 60% more than B. B is what percent less than A?" It is tempting to say 60%. But the second sentence has a different thing after "than": now **A** is the base.

items.x: A is 160 and B is 100. The gap is 60.
Measured against A, that is 60 / 160 = 37.5%.

teach.x: The gap in numbers is the same both ways. The percent is different because the base is different.

When three things are involved, give the 100 to the one the others are described against. "Two numbers are 20% and 50% more than a third number": the third is 100, so the two are 120 and 150. Now any question about them is ordinary arithmetic.
If the description is a chain, such as "A is 30% less than B, and B is 50% more than C", start from the end of the chain: C is 100, so B is 150, and A is 30% less than 150, which is 105.

tags: The classic turn-around.
Two things described against a third.
A chain of three.
A percentage error.

example.q: P is 20% more than Q, and R is 40% less than Q. P is what percent of R?
steps: Both are described against Q, so Q is the 100.
P is 20% more: 120.
R is 40% less: 60.
P as a percent of R: 120 / 60 x 100 = 200%.

checks.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's salary. B's salary is what percent less than A's salary?
checks.why: B is 100 and A is 125. The gap is 25, but now A is the base: 25 / 125 = 20%. (25% is the tempting wrong answer.)

checks.q: A is 20% less than B. B is what percent more than A?
checks.why: B is 100 and A is 80. The gap is 20, but now A is the base: 20 / 80 = 25%.

text.x: If A is **1/n more** than B, then B is **1/(n + 1) less** than A. The bottom number simply goes up by one.
25% more is 1/4 more, so the way back is 1/5 less: 20%. And 50% more (1/2) turns into 1/3 less: 33 1/3%.
It also runs in reverse. If A is 1/n less than B, then B is 1/(n - 1) more than A: 20% less (1/5) turns into 1/4 more, which is 25%.

lessons.title: "40% of A equals 60% of B"
lessons.plain: New: two different percents of two numbers are equal. That sentence is really a ratio.

teach.x: "40% of A is equal to 60% of B." A smaller share of A matches a bigger share of B, so A must be the bigger number. How much bigger? **Swap the two percents and you have the ratio.**
Why it works: try it. If A is 3 and B is 2, then 40% of 3 is 1.2 and 60% of 2 is 1.2. They match. Each number takes the other one's percent.
Once the sentence has become a ratio, you are back in familiar country. The question will give one real number, and you match it to parts exactly as in the Basics:

items.x: one of the numbers itself;
their sum or their difference;
their average, which is half the parts added together.

teach.x: Find one part, and every number in the question follows.

Some questions hide the sentence a little: "5% of X is 25% more than Y". Translate one phrase at a time. 5% of X is X / 20. "25% more than Y" is 1.25 Y. So X / 20 = 1.25 Y, which gives X = 25 Y, a ratio of 25 : 1.

tags: One of the numbers is given.
No numbers at all: one as a percent of the other.
The difference is given.
The average is given.
The sentence itself is in disguise.

example.q: 40% of X is equal to 50% of Y, and the sum of X and Y is 180. Find X.
steps: Swap the percents to get the ratio: X : Y = 50 : 40 = 5 : 4.
The real number is a sum, so add the parts: 5 + 4 = 9 parts = 180.
One part = 20.
Check: Y is 80. 40% of 100 is 40, and 50% of 80 is 40.

checks.q: 30% of A is equal to 20% of B. What is the ratio A : B?
checks.why: Swap the percents: A : B = 20 : 30 = 2 : 3. A needs the bigger percent to keep up, so A is the smaller number.

lessons.title: One change after another
lessons.plain: New: a value goes up or down by a percent, and then changes again. The second change is taken on the new value.

teach.x: A town's population rises 10% this year and falls 20% next year. It is tempting to add them and say "10% down overall". That is not right, and seeing why is the whole lesson.
The second change is 20% of the **new** population, not of the original one. The base has moved.
The safe method is to go **one step at a time**. Start with 25,000. Up 10%: add 2,500 to get 27,500. Down 20%: 20% of 27,500 is 5,500, leaving 22,000.

There is a tidy way to write each step. A rise of 10% turns 100 into 110, which is multiplying by 1.1. A fall of 20% turns 100 into 80, which is multiplying by 0.8. So the two years together are 25,000 x 1.1 x 0.8 = 22,000.
This also explains a famous surprise: up 20% and then down 20% does not bring you back. 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96, which is a 4% fall.

**Going backwards.** If you are given the value **after** the changes and asked for the value before, divide instead of multiplying. A machine worth Rs 81,000 after losing 10% a year for two years was worth 81,000 / 0.9 / 0.9 = Rs 1,00,000.

tags: Up and down by the same percent.
A population over two years.
The story begins "two years ago".
Backwards: find the earlier value.
Two rises, and then he spends a share.

example.q: The population of a town is 20,000. It increases by 10% in the first year and by 25% in the second year. Find the population after two years.
steps: Year 1: 10% of 20,000 is 2,000. The population is 22,000.
Year 2: 25% of 22,000 is 5,500. The population is 27,500.

checks.q: The price of a shirt is raised by 10% and then reduced by 10%. What is the net change?
checks.why: 1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99, so 100 becomes 99: a 1% decrease. The fall is taken on the higher price, so it removes a little more than the rise added.

text.x: For two changes of **a%** and **b%** one after the other, the overall change is:
Write a fall as a negative number. Up 10% then down 20%: 10 - 20 + (10 x -20) / 100 = -10 - 2 = -12%. So 25,000 falls by 12% to 22,000.
Up 20% then down 20%: 20 - 20 - 4 = -4%. The last piece, (a x b) / 100, is the part that simple adding forgets.

lessons.title: "Of the remaining"
lessons.plain: New: money is spent in stages, and each stage takes a percent of what is left, not of the whole.

teach.x: "A man spends 20% of his income on rent and 25% **of the remaining** on food." The two words "of the remaining" matter. The 25% is not a quarter of his income; it is a quarter of what is left after rent.
This is last lesson's idea wearing different clothes: each stage works on a new, smaller base. So the method is the same. **Keep track of what is left after each stage.**

items.x: Start with 100%.
Rent takes 20%, so 80% is left.
Food takes 25% of that 80%, which is 20%. So 60% is left.

teach.x: The 60% that is left is his saving. If the question says he saves Rs 19,800, then 60% is 19,800, so 1% is 330 and his income is Rs 33,000.
In multiplying form: what is left = 0.8 x 0.75 = 0.6 of the income.
Two things to watch for.

**Fixed amounts mixed in.** If a stage is a plain number of rupees ("he spends Rs 12,000 on his children"), subtract it as rupees at that point and carry on. This kind is easier to do in rupees from the start.

**Which pieces the question compares.** Sometimes it gives the difference between two of the pieces, not the saving. Write every piece as a percent of the income first, and then compare the pieces the question names.

tags: The saving is given.
What is left is given.
The difference between two of the pieces is given.
Rupees and a fraction mixed in.
Not money at all: people sorted in layers.

example.q: A woman spends 30% of her salary on rent and 20% of the remaining on travel. She saves the rest, which is Rs 28,000. Find her salary.
steps: Start with 100%. Rent takes 30%, so 70% is left.
Travel takes 20% of that 70%, which is 14%. So 70 - 14 = 56% is left.
That 56% is her saving: 56% = 28,000.
1% = 500, so her salary is Rs 50,000.
Check: rent 15,000 leaves 35,000; travel 7,000 leaves 28,000.

checks.q: A man spends 40% of his income on rent and 50% of the remaining on food. He saves the rest, which is Rs 6,000. What is his income?
checks.why: After rent, 60% is left. Food takes half of that, so 30% is left. 30% = 6,000, so 1% = 200 and the income is 20,000.

lessons.title: Income, expenditure and savings
lessons.plain: New: three amounts tied together by one fact: what you earn is what you spend plus what you save.

teach.x: Every question of this kind stands on a single line:
**income = expenditure + savings**
Know any two and you have the third. The percent words just tell you how two of them compare, and you already know how to read those from lesson 2.
"His income is 25% more than his expenditure." Expenditure comes after "than", so it is the 100. Income is 125. Savings are the gap: 25.
The harder form changes two of the three and asks about the third: "He saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 20% and his expenditure by 10%. By what percent do his savings change?"
Do not try to combine the percents in your head. **Call the income 100 and write all three numbers, before and after.**
Savings went from 25 to 37.5. The change is 12.5 on a starting value of 25, which is 50%. Savings always swing by more than income does, because they are the small number left over.

tags: Income described against expenditure.
Spending as a percent of salary.
Income and expenditure both change.

example.q: A man saves 25% of his income. His income increases by 20% and his expenditure increases by 10%. By what percent do his savings increase?
steps: Call the income 100. He saves 25, so he spends 75.
New income: 20% more than 100 is 120.
New expenditure: 10% more than 75 is 82.5.
New savings: 120 - 82.5 = 37.5.
Change in savings: 37.5 - 25 = 12.5, measured against the starting 25. 12.5 / 25 = 50%.

checks.q: A person's income is 20% more than his expenditure. If his monthly expenditure is Rs 15,000, what are his monthly savings?
checks.why: Expenditure is the 100, so income is 120 and savings are 20, which is one fifth of the expenditure. One fifth of 15,000 is 3,000. (18,000 is the income.)

checks.tag: A ratio instead of a percent
checks.q: A man's income and expenditure are in the ratio 5 : 3. If he saves Rs 8,000 a month, what is his income?
checks.why: Savings are the gap between income and expenditure: 5 - 3 = 2 parts. 2 parts = 8,000, so one part = 4,000 and the income is 5 x 4,000 = 20,000.

lessons.title: Price, quantity and spending
lessons.plain: New: the price changes, and the question asks how much you can now buy, or how much less you must use.

teach.x: Here too one line holds everything together:
**money spent = price x quantity**
There are two kinds of question.

**Kind 1: keep the spending under control.** "The price of sugar rises by 20%. By what percent must a family cut its use so that its spending rises by only 8%?" Use the multipliers from lesson 4. The price is multiplied by 1.2. The spending is to be multiplied by 1.08. So the quantity must be multiplied by 1.08 / 1.2 = 0.9, which is a cut of 10%.
If the spending is to stay exactly the same, the quantity must be multiplied by 1 / 1.2. A 25% rise in price, for example, needs 1 / 1.25 = 0.8: a 20% cut.
**Kind 2: "a fall in price lets him buy 5 kg more for Rs 800".** This one looks awkward but has a lovely shortcut. Think about the money, not the percent.

items.x: If the price falls by 20%, then buying the **old** quantity now costs 20% less. On Rs 800 that frees up Rs 160.
That freed money is what buys the extra 5 kg, at the **new** price.
So the new price is 160 / 5 = Rs 32 a kg.
The new price is 80% of the old one, so the old price was 32 / 0.8 = Rs 40.

teach.x: Read the last line carefully: some questions ask for the new price and some for the original.

tags: Keep the rise in spending small.
A price fall buys more.
The same, with a percent that is really a fraction.

example.q: A 25% fall in the price of sugar enables a person to buy 4 kg more for Rs 480. Find the original price per kg.
steps: A 25% fall frees up 25% of the money: 25% of 480 = Rs 120.
That Rs 120 buys the extra 4 kg at the new price. New price = 120 / 4 = Rs 30 a kg.
The new price is 75% of the original. Original price = 30 / 0.75 = Rs 40.
Check: at Rs 40 he bought 12 kg; at Rs 30 he buys 16 kg. That is 4 kg more.
example.answer: The original price was Rs 40 per kg.

checks.q: The price of tea rises by 25%. By what percent must a family reduce its consumption so that its spending on tea stays the same?
checks.why: The price is multiplied by 1.25, so the quantity must be multiplied by 1 / 1.25 = 0.8. That is a 20% cut. (Not 25%: the cut is measured against the new, higher spending.)

checks.q: A 25% rise in the price of oil means a person gets 2 litres less for Rs 400. What is the new price per litre?
checks.why: The same thinking, turned round. His old quantity would now cost 25% more: Rs 500. He has only Rs 400, so he is Rs 100 short, and that Rs 100 is the 2 litres he must give up. New price = 100 / 2 = Rs 50. (Old price was 40: 10 litres then, 8 litres now.)

text.x: To keep spending unchanged when the price rises by **1/n**, cut the quantity by **1/(n + 1)**. It is the same turn-around as in lesson 2.
Price up 25% (1/4): use 1/5 less, which is 20%. Price up 20% (1/5): use 1/6 less, 16 2/3%. Price up 50% (1/2): use 1/3 less.
And if the price falls by 1/n, you can use 1/(n - 1) more: a 20% fall (1/5) lets you buy 25% more.

lessons.title: Two groups, each with its own percent
lessons.plain: New: boys and girls, men and women. Each group has a different percent, and the question mixes them.

teach.x: "In a town of 8,000 people, 55% are males. 40% of the males and 30% of the females are graduates." There are two groups, and each has its own percent. The important rule is simple: **a percent belongs to its own group.** 40% of the males is 40% of the number of males, never 40% of the town.
So the first move is always to **split the total into the two groups**, and only then apply each group's percent.

items.x: Males: 55% of 8,000 = 4,400. Females: the other 3,600.

teach.x: A small table keeps this tidy, with one row for each group. Fill in whatever the question gives you and work towards the empty boxes.

The harder form hides the sizes of the groups. "A village has 5,000 people. The men increase by 10% and the women by 15%, and the population becomes 5,600." Use the same trick as the two-deposit questions in the interest topic: **pretend everyone grew at the lower percent.**

items.x: If all 5,000 grew by 10%, the rise would be 500.
The real rise is 600, which is 100 more.
That extra comes only from the women, who grew by 15 - 10 = 5% more than we pretended.
So 5% of the women is 100: there are 2,000 women and 3,000 men.

tags: Both group sizes can be found at once.
Group sizes hidden: each group grows differently.
One group stays fixed while the other grows.
Work backwards from those who passed.
No numbers at all: call the class 100.

example.q: A village has 6,000 people. If the number of men increases by 5% and the number of women by 10%, the population becomes 6,400. How many men are there?
steps: Pretend everyone grew by the lower percent, 5%. The rise would be 5% of 6,000 = 300.
The real rise is 6,400 - 6,000 = 400, which is 100 more.
That extra comes from the women, who grew 10 - 5 = 5% more than we pretended.
5% of the women is 100, so there are 2,000 women.
Check: men rise by 200, women by 200. Total rise 400.

checks.q: A school has 500 students, of whom 60% are boys. 50% of the boys and 40% of the girls play a sport. How many students play a sport?
checks.why: Split first: 300 boys and 200 girls. 50% of 300 = 150, and 40% of 200 = 80. Together 230.

lessons.title: The part that does not change
lessons.plain: New: water dries out of fruit, or water is poured into a solution. One ingredient stays exactly the same.

teach.x: "Fresh grapes contain 80% water. Dry grapes contain 20% water. How much dry grapes come from 40 kg of fresh grapes?"
Both percents in this question are about water, and that is what makes it confusing, because the water is the thing that changes. The way through is to **follow the part that does not change.**
When grapes dry, only water leaves. The solid part, the pulp, stays exactly the same weight. So:

items.x: Find the pulp in the fresh grapes. They are 80% water, so 20% pulp: 20% of 40 kg = 8 kg.
That same 8 kg of pulp is in the dry grapes. Dry grapes are 20% water, so 80% pulp.
So 8 kg is 80% of the dry grapes. 1% is 0.1 kg and the dry grapes weigh 10 kg.

teach.x: Notice that the percent of pulp changed from 20% to 80% while the pulp itself never changed. The percent moved only because the total around it shrank.

The same idea solves **adding water to a solution**. A 60-litre solution is 20% alcohol, so it holds 12 litres of alcohol. Pour in water and the alcohol is still 12 litres. If it must now be 15% of the mixture, then 15% is 12 litres, so the mixture is 80 litres, and 20 litres of water were added.
Whenever a question has a "before" and an "after" percent, ask: **which ingredient was not touched?** Work with that one.

tags: Drying: water leaves.
The same, from a real paper, with awkward percents.
Diluting: water is added.

example.q: A 50-litre solution contains 30% acid. How many litres of water must be added so that acid becomes 20% of the new solution?
steps: Which part does not change? The acid. Acid now = 30% of 50 = 15 litres.
After adding water, the acid is still 15 litres, and it must be 20% of the new solution.
20% = 15 litres, so 1% = 0.75 and the new solution is 75 litres.
Water added = 75 - 50 = 25 litres.

checks.q: Fresh fruit contains 90% water and dry fruit contains 10% water. How much dry fruit can be obtained from 45 kg of fresh fruit?
checks.why: The pulp does not change. Fresh fruit is 10% pulp: 4.5 kg. Dry fruit is 90% pulp, so 4.5 kg is 90% of it and the dry fruit weighs 5 kg. (4.5 kg is the pulp alone.)

checks.q: A 40-litre mixture of milk and water contains 10% water. How many litres of water must be added so that water becomes 25% of the mixture?
checks.why: Water is being added, so the milk is the part that does not change: 90% of 40 = 36 litres. Afterwards milk is 75% of the mixture, so the mixture is 36 / 0.75 = 48 litres. Water added = 8 litres.

lessons.title: Marks, votes, overlaps and fractions
lessons.plain: New: four familiar exam settings. Each one is an idea you already have, in a particular costume.

teach.x: These last four are less about new ideas than about recognising old ones. Three of them have not appeared in the Clerk papers we checked, but all are regulars in practice sets.

**1. Pass marks.** "A student with 30% fails by 30 marks. Another with 45% gets 15 marks more than the pass mark." Both are measured against the same pass mark. The first is 30 below it and the second 15 above, so they are 45 marks apart. They are also 45 - 30 = 15% apart. So 15% of the maximum is 45 marks, and the maximum is 300.

**2. Elections.** Votes come in layers, and each percent belongs to its own layer, just like lesson 5. Total votes, then valid votes, then each candidate's share **of the valid votes**. With two candidates, if the winner has 58% of the valid votes the loser has 42%, so the winning margin is 16% of the valid votes.

**3. Failed in one subject or both.** "35% failed in English, 25% failed in Maths, 10% failed in both." Adding 35 and 25 counts the "both" students twice, so take them off once: 35 + 25 - 10 = 50% failed in at least one subject. The rest, 50%, passed in both.

**4. A fraction whose top and bottom change.** "The numerator is decreased by 25% and the denominator increased by 250%." Use multipliers. Down 25% is x 0.75. Up 250% is x 3.5 (the original 1, plus 2.5 more). So new fraction = old fraction x 0.75 / 3.5. To get the old fraction back, undo that: multiply the new fraction by 3.5 / 0.75.

tags: Pass marks.
Votes, with invalid ones removed first.
Voters who stayed at home.
Failed in one subject or both.
A fraction changed top and bottom.

example.q: In an election between two candidates, 10% of the votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of the valid votes and won by 1,800 votes. How many votes were polled?
steps: Work in layers. Call the votes polled 100%. Valid votes are 90% of them.
Of the valid votes, the winner has 60% and the loser 40%. The margin is 20% of the valid votes.
20% of 90% is 18% of the votes polled.
Votes polled = 10,000.
Check: 9,000 valid; 5,400 against 3,600; margin 1,800.

checks.q: A student who scores 40% fails by 20 marks. Another who scores 55% gets 10 marks more than the pass mark. What are the maximum marks?
checks.why: One is 20 below the pass mark and the other 10 above, so they are 30 marks apart. They are also 55 - 40 = 15% apart. 15% = 30 marks, so the maximum is 200.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Exact Mechanics & Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **Central law.** A partner’s claim on the profit is his money multiplied by the time it stayed in the business. Call this his **weight** (capital x months). Profits are shared in the ratio of the weights. So there are three linked ratios: capital, time and profit, with profit = capital x time.
Base operations

items.x: **Weight.** Weight = capital x months. Cancel common factors first: 24,000 for 12 months and 30,000 for 4 months is 24 x 12 : 30 x 4 = 288 : 120 = 12 : 5.
**Share from total.** One part = total profit / sum of weights. Each share = his parts x one part.
**Total from one share.** One part = his share / his parts. Total = one part x sum of parts.
**Months for a late joiner or early leaver.** Joined after 4 months in a 12-month year: 8 months. Left after 4 months: 4 months. Left 4 months before the end: 8 months.
**Capital changed midway.** Split that partner’s time into blocks and add: 9,000 for 8 months then 12,000 for 4 months = 72 + 48 = 120 (in thousands).
**The triangle.** Profit ratio = capital ratio x time ratio. So time ratio = profit ratio / capital ratio, and capital ratio = profit ratio / time ratio, taken term by term.
**Joining three capitals.** A : B = 3 : 5 and B : C = 15 : 11. Make B the same: 9 : 15 : 11.
**Fractions as a ratio.** 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4 becomes 6 : 4 : 3 after multiplying by 12.

blocks.x: Conversion grid

rows: 4 months at 1 part + 8 months at 2 parts
8 months at full + 16 months at half

blocks.x: Calculation facts to keep ready

items.x: Always cancel zeros and common factors before multiplying. Weights are only ever needed as a ratio.

Non-linear warning: profit depends on the product of capital and time. Sharing in the capital ratio alone is wrong whenever the times differ, and going backwards means dividing the ratios, not multiplying them.

items.title: Profit known, find capital, time or a ratio
items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Wording clues.** “The profit shares are in the ratio 2 : 1. Find X.” “B’s share is Rs 21,000 out of a total profit of Rs 49,000.” “Find the ratio of their investment periods.” “After X months B left.”
**Shortcut engine: the triangle, term by term.**

items.x: Turn the profit data into a ratio. If one share and the total are given, subtract to get the other share first.
Write the known side (capitals or months) under it.
Divide profit by the known side, term by term, to get the missing side as a ratio. Then match with any real number given.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023, Adda247 paper).** A starts with 8,000; after six months B joins with X. B gets 21,000 of 49,000. Profits A : B = 28 : 21 = 4 : 3. Months 12 and 6. Capital ratio = 4/12 : 3/6 = 1/3 : 1/2 = 2 : 3. A’s 2 parts = 8,000, so X = 12,000.
**Ratio version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 12 Dec 2021, Set 2).** Investments 3 : 2 : 1, profits 5 : 4 : 2. Times = 5/3 : 4/2 : 2/1 = 5 : 6 : 6.

**Months version (SBI Clerk Prelims, 21 Sep 2025, Shift 1).** Ravi 9,000 and Sohan 6,000; Sohan leaves after Y months; Sohan gets 1,500 of 4,500. Profits 3,000 : 1,500 = 2 : 1. Ravi’s weight = 9 x 12 = 108, so Sohan’s is 54 = 6 x Y. Y = 9.

**“X and X + something” version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 12 Dec 2021, Set 1).** x for 24 months, x + 4,000 for 16 months; B gets 1,440 of 2,400. Profits 960 : 1,440 = 2 : 3. Capital ratio = 2/24 : 3/16 = 4 : 9. The 5-part gap is 4,000, so 1 part = 800 and x = 3,200.
**Wording clues.** “After 3 months A withdrew Rs 600”, “doubles his investment”, “increased his investment by 50%”, “withdraws half”.
**Shortcut engine: time blocks.**

items.x: For each partner list his blocks: capital x months for every stretch between changes.
Add the blocks to get one weight per partner. Then share as usual.

blocks.x: **Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 3 Sep 2022, Slot 2).** A starts with 1,800. After three months B joins with 1,200 and A withdraws 600. Total profit 500. A = 18 x 3 + 12 x 9 = 162. B = 12 x 9 = 108. Ratio 3 : 2. A gets 300.

**Step-down version (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 4).** Rohit invests twice Shikhar’s sum, halves it after 8 months and halves it again after 8 more; 2 years in all. Rohit = 2 x 8 + 1 x 8 + 0.5 x 8 = 28. Shikhar = 1 x 24 = 24. Ratio 7 : 6.
**Wording clues.** “After 4 months B left”, “C joined after 6 months”, “invested for 8 months and 10 months”. All capitals and times are given; a share, the total or a ratio is asked.
**Shortcut engine.** Weight = capital x months for each partner, simplify, then one part = known rupees / matching parts.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 Oct 2025, Shift 2).** A 24,000 and B 30,000; B leaves after 4 months; profit 3,400. Weights 24 x 12 : 30 x 4 = 12 : 5. One part = 3,400 / 17 = 200. B gets 1,000.

**Difference version (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2024, Guidely paper).** Frenz invests 1.2p for 8 months, Dolly p for 12 months; Frenz gets 600 less. Weights 9.6 : 12 = 4 : 5. One part = 600. Total = 9 parts = 5,400.
**Shortcut engine.** Time cancels, so profit ratio = capital ratio.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 5 Oct 2025, Shift 1).** A 4,000, B 6,000, C X, one year. B gets 2,400 of 7,200, which is one-third. So B’s capital is one-third of the total: total 18,000 and X = 8,000.

items.title: Capital changed midway and an unknown to find
items.label: Seen once

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** Build each weight with time blocks, keeping the unknown as it is. Set weight ratio = profit ratio and cross-multiply once. No pure ratio shortcut exists here because the unknown sits inside a sum of blocks, so one line with X is used.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2022, Adda247 paper).** P invests X and Q invests X + 100. After three months P withdraws 40%. P gets 210 of 530. P’s weight = 3X + 9 x 0.6X = 8.4X. Q’s weight = 12(X + 100). Profits 210 : 320 = 21 : 32. One line: 32 x 8.4X = 21 x 12(X + 100), so 268.8X = 252X + 25,200 and X = 1,500.

**Shortcut engine.** Take the deductions off the top as a percent of the profit. Share only what is left in the weight ratio. Add back any salary to the working partner. Example: capitals 3 : 2, working partner A gets 10% of 15,000 = 1,500; the other 13,500 is split 3 : 2, so A gets 8,100 more: 9,600 in all.

items.title: Profit as a percent of investment, shared rent
items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** If profit is p% of the total investment and times are equal, each partner’s profit is p% of his own investment. For a shared pasture, weight = animals x months and the rent is split like a profit.

lead.x: Seven original questions: one per Core archetype, the phrasing and product traps, and one Insurance type. Every answer was computed by script. Try each before reading the method.

body.x: A, B and C started a business by investing Rs 4,500, Rs 6,000 and Rs 7,500 respectively for one year. If the total profit at the end of the year is Rs 9,600, find the difference between the profit shares of C and A (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Shares = 9,600 x 4,500 / 18,000 and 9,600 x 7,500 / 18,000; subtract.
**30-second exam method.** Capitals 45 : 60 : 75 = 3 : 4 : 5, twelve parts. One part = 9,600 / 12 = 800. C minus A = 2 parts = 1,600. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** The answer is 2 parts and one part is 9,600 / 12, so it must be 9,600 / 6. Only 1,600 fits.
**IBPS trap warning.** Do not compute both shares. Go straight to the difference in parts. Option (E) 800 is one part.

body.x: A started a business with Rs 12,000. After 4 months B joined with Rs 15,000, and after 2 more months C joined with Rs 18,000. If the total profit at the end of the year is Rs 18,600, find C’s share of the profit (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Weights 12,000 x 12, 15,000 x 8 and 18,000 x 6; C’s share = 18,600 x 108,000 / 372,000.
**30-second exam method.** Months are 12, 8 and 6. Weights 12 x 12 : 15 x 8 : 18 x 6 = 144 : 120 : 108 = 12 : 10 : 9, total 31. One part = 18,600 / 31 = 600. C = 9 parts = 5,400. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** C has 9 parts, so the answer must divide by 9. Only 5,400 does. Back-check: 7,200 + 6,000 + 5,400 = 18,600. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** “After 2 more months” means 6 months from the start, so C stays 6 months. Sharing by capital alone (4 : 5 : 6) gives option (D) 7,440.

body.x: The investments of A and B in a business are in the ratio 5 : 6 and their profits are in the ratio 3 : 4. If B invested for 10 months, for how many months did A invest?

items.x: **Conventional method.** (5 x a) / (6 x 10) = 3/4, so a = 9.
**30-second exam method.** Time = profit / capital, term by term: 3/5 : 4/6 = 18 : 20 = 9 : 10. B’s 10 parts are 10 months, so A invested 9 months. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** Test 9: A’s weight 5 x 9 = 45, B’s 6 x 10 = 60, and 45 : 60 = 3 : 4. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Profit is a product (capital x time). To get time you must divide the ratios. Multiplying them (3 x 5 : 4 x 6) is the usual mistake.

body.x: P and Q started a business with Rs 16,000 and Rs 20,000 respectively. Q left the business 4 months before the end of the year. If the total profit for the year is Rs 17,600, find Q’s share (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** Q’s share = 17,600 x (20,000 x 8) / (16,000 x 12 + 20,000 x 8).
**30-second exam method.** Q stayed 12 - 4 = 8 months. Weights 16 x 12 : 20 x 8 = 192 : 160 = 6 : 5. One part = 17,600 / 11 = 1,600. Q = 5 parts = 8,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** Q has 5 parts of 11, so the answer is 17,600 x 5 / 11. Only 8,000 fits.

**IBPS trap warning.** “Left 4 months before the end” is 8 months of investment. “Left after 4 months” would be 4 months. Using 4 here gives a share that is not a whole number, which is a signal to re-read.

body.x: A and B started a business with Rs 9,000 and Rs 12,000 respectively. After 8 months A invested Rs 3,000 more and B withdrew Rs 3,000. If the total profit at the end of the year is Rs 25,200, find A’s share (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** A = 9,000 x 8 + 12,000 x 4; B = 12,000 x 8 + 9,000 x 4; share in that ratio.
**30-second exam method.** In thousands: A = 9 x 8 + 12 x 4 = 120. B = 12 x 8 + 9 x 4 = 132. Ratio 10 : 11. One part = 25,200 / 21 = 1,200. A = 12,000. **Answer (B).**
**Option elimination hack.** A has 10 parts of 21, so the answer is 25,200 x 10 / 21. Back-check: 12,000 + 13,200 = 25,200. Correct.
**IBPS trap warning.** Option (D) 13,200 is B’s share. Option (C) 12,600 is an equal split.

items.title: Drill 6. Changed capital with an unknown (T5)

body.x: A started a business with Rs X and B with Rs (X + 2,000). After 6 months A doubled his investment. If A’s share is Rs 5,400 out of a total profit of Rs 9,600 at the end of the year, find X.

items.x: **Conventional method.** (6X + 12X) / (12X + 24,000) = 5,400 / 4,200. Solve.

**30-second exam method.** A’s weight = 6X + 6 x 2X = 18X. B’s weight = 12(X + 2,000). Profits 5,400 : 4,200 = 9 : 7. One line: 7 x 18X = 9 x 12(X + 2,000), so 126X = 108X + 2,16,000 and X = 12,000. **Answer (C).** One line with X is used because the unknown sits inside a sum of blocks.
**Option elimination hack.** Plug in the middle option: X = 12,000 gives weights 216 and 168 (thousands), which is 9 : 7. Correct at the first try.
**IBPS trap warning.** B’s share is not given; subtract first (9,600 - 5,400 = 4,200). Using 5,400 : 9,600 as the ratio is wrong.

body.x: A and B invested in a business in the ratio 5 : 3. 10% of the total profit goes to charity. A, being the working partner, gets 20% of the remaining profit, and the rest is shared in the ratio of their investments. If A receives Rs 6,300 in all, find the total profit (in Rs).

items.x: **Conventional method.** 0.2 x 0.9P + (5/8) x 0.8 x 0.9P = 6,300.
**30-second exam method.** Take profit 100. Charity 10, leaving 90. Salary = 20% of 90 = 18, leaving 72. A’s 5/8 of 72 = 45. A’s total = 63. So 63% = 6,300 and the profit is 10,000. **Answer (C).**
**Option elimination hack.** None needed.
**IBPS trap warning.** The salary is 20% of the remaining 90, not of the full 100. Taking it from 100 gives a total that is not a round option.

blocks.x: Universal fallback

When a question fits no engine, build the **weight table**. One row per partner; one column per stretch of time between changes. Fill each cell with capital x months (keep any unknown as it is), add across each row, and write the row totals as a ratio. That ratio equals the profit ratio, whatever the story. Compare it with the profit data given and solve the one balance that results.

blocks.x: Red flags

items.x: **Capital-only split.** If any partner joined late or left early, the capital ratio is not the profit ratio.
**Counting months.** “After 4 months” is 8 months of investment in a year; “for 4 months” is 4.
**Business longer than a year.** Check for “at the end of 2 years” or “20 months” before using 12.
**Share against total.** A share “out of” a total is not the ratio of the two partners. Subtract first.
**Order of a ratio.** “Ratio of Kavin to Sandy” after naming Sandy first reverses the order.
**Whose share.** The other partner’s share is always among the options.

intro.x: When people run a business together, the profit is shared by a simple rule of fairness: **more money, and money left in for longer, earns more.**

These nine short lessons build that one idea step by step. The first two share by money alone, the third brings in time, and the rest are the ways the exam turns the same idea around. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the month table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
If one thing stays with you, let it be this: write each partner's **capital x months**, make it a ratio, and the rest is the ratio work you already know.

lessons.title: Sharing a profit when everyone invests for the same time
lessons.plain: The starting point: partners put in money for the same period, and the profit is shared in the ratio of their money.

teach.x: A **partnership** is a business that two or more people put money into. The money each one puts in is called their **capital** or **investment**. At the end, the profit is shared out fairly.

What is fair? If everyone's money stayed in the business for the same length of time, the answer is simple: **the profit is shared in the same ratio as the money.** Someone who put in twice as much gets twice as much.
So this first kind is a ratio question, exactly like the ones in the Basics.

items.x: Write the capitals as a ratio and make it as small as you can. Rs 15,000 and Rs 25,000 is 15 : 25, which is 3 : 5. Always strike off the zeros first.

The question then gives one real number about the profit. Match it to parts, the same three ways as always: the **total** profit matches the parts added; a **difference** between two shares matches the parts subtracted; **one person's share** matches that person's parts.
Find one part, and read off whatever is asked.
