example.q: A and B invest Rs 12,000 and Rs 18,000 in a business for one year. The profit is Rs 10,000. Find A's share.
steps: Capitals: 12,000 : 18,000. Strike off the zeros and divide by 6: 2 : 3.
Same time for both, so the profit is shared 2 : 3.
The real number is the total profit, so add the parts: 2 + 3 = 5 parts = 10,000.
One part = 2,000. A has 2 parts: Rs 4,000.

checks.q: P and Q invest in the ratio 3 : 5 for the same period. Q's share of the profit is Rs 4,500. What is the total profit?
checks.why: Q has 5 parts and they are worth 4,500, so one part is 900. The total is 3 + 5 = 8 parts = 7,200. (2,700 is P's share.)

checks.tag: Three partners, and one share is known
checks.q: A, B and C invest Rs 2,000, Rs 3,000 and Rs 5,000 for a year. B's share of the profit is Rs 1,200. What is C's share?
checks.why: The ratio is 2 : 3 : 5. B's 3 parts are 1,200, so one part is 400. C has 5 parts: 2,000.

lessons.title: When the capitals are described, not given
lessons.plain: New: same time for everyone still, but the money is described with fractions, "twice", percents or linked ratios.

teach.x: The method has not changed: same time, so the profit ratio is the capital ratio. What changes is that the paper does not hand you the capitals as plain numbers. Your first job is to **turn the description into a clean ratio**. There are five common descriptions.
**Fractions.** "They invest in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4." Multiply every fraction by a number all the bottoms go into. Here that is 12: the ratio becomes 6 : 4 : 3.
**"Twice" and "three times".** "A's capital is twice B's, and B's is three times C's." Start from the smallest: C is 1, so B is 3 and A is 6.
**Two ratios sharing a name.** "A : B = 5 : 6 and B : C = 3 : 4." Make B the same in both, as in the Basics: 5 : 6 : 8.

**Percent words.** "A invests 50% more than B, and B invests 20% less than C." Start from the one the others are described against. C is 100, B is 80, A is 120. The ratio A : B : C is 120 : 80 : 100 = 6 : 4 : 5.

**"Rs 5,000 more than".** This one is not a ratio yet. Write the smallest as a base, the others as base plus extra, and use the total capital to find the base. Then you have real capitals and can make the ratio.
Once the ratio is clean, finish exactly as in the last lesson.

tags: "Twice" and "three times".
Fractions.
Two ratios that share a name.
Percent words in a chain.
"Rs 5,000 more than", with the total capital.

example.q: A invests 25% more than B, and C invests half of what B invests. The profit at the end of the year is Rs 11,000. Find A's share.
steps: Both are described against B, so call B 100.
A is 25% more: 125. C is half of B: 50.
Ratio A : B : C = 125 : 100 : 50. Divide by 25: 5 : 4 : 2.
Parts added: 11 parts = 11,000, so one part = 1,000.
A has 5 parts: Rs 5,000.

checks.q: Two partners invest in the ratio 1/3 : 1/4. What is this as a ratio of whole numbers?
checks.why: Multiply both by 12: 12/3 = 4 and 12/4 = 3. The ratio is 4 : 3. A third is bigger than a quarter, so the first partner has the bigger number.

lessons.title: When the money stays for different lengths of time
lessons.plain: New: someone joins late or leaves early. Now time matters as much as money.

teach.x: Suppose A puts in Rs 20,000 for the whole year, and B puts in the same Rs 20,000 but only for the last six months. Sharing the profit equally would not be fair: A's money worked twice as long.
So a partner's claim on the profit depends on two things: **how much money**, and **for how long**. Multiply them together. We will call the result the partner's **weight**.
**weight = capital x months**
The profit is shared in the ratio of the weights. That is the only new idea in this lesson, and it is the heart of the whole topic.
The care needed is in counting the months. Read the phrase slowly:

rows: Months to use, in a 12-month year

teach.x: "After 4 months B joined" means B missed the first 4 months, so B's money worked for 8. "After 4 months B left" means B's money worked for only 4. The same three words lead to opposite answers.
Also check how long the business ran. It is usually a year, but if the question says "at the end of 2 years", the full period is 24 months.
A tip that saves a lot of arithmetic: you only need the weights as a **ratio**, so strike off zeros and common factors before you multiply.

tags: Both invest for part of the year.
One joins late.
One leaves early.
The business runs for two years.
Three partners, two of them leaving at different times.

example.q: A starts a business with Rs 20,000. After 3 months B joins with Rs 40,000. The profit at the end of the year is Rs 25,000. Find B's share.
steps: Months: A is there all year, 12 months. B joins after 3 months, so 9 months.
Weights, in thousands: A = 20 x 12 = 240. B = 40 x 9 = 360.
Parts added: 5 parts = 25,000, so one part = 5,000.
B has 3 parts: Rs 15,000.

checks.q: A invests Rs 10,000 for 12 months and B invests Rs 15,000 for 8 months. In what ratio is the profit shared?
checks.why: Weights: 10 x 12 = 120 and 15 x 8 = 120. They are equal, so the profit is shared 1 : 1. B put in more money, but for a shorter time. (2 : 3 uses the capitals alone and forgets the months.)

checks.q: A and B start a business with Rs 30,000 each. B leaves 4 months before the end of the year. In what ratio is the profit shared between A and B?
checks.why: "4 months before the end" means B stayed for 12 - 4 = 8 months. Weights: 30 x 12 = 360 and 30 x 8 = 240, which is 3 : 2. (3 : 1 would be right if B had stayed only 4 months.)

lessons.title: Weights without real rupees
lessons.plain: New: the capitals and the months are themselves given as ratios, multiples or letters.

teach.x: Last lesson you multiplied real capitals by real months. The exam often removes the real numbers and gives ratios instead. Nothing changes: **weight is still capital x time**, and you can multiply the ratio numbers just as you multiplied rupees.
**Ratios of both.** "They invest in the ratio 2 : 3, for periods in the ratio 9 : 4." Multiply partner by partner: 2 x 9 = 18 and 3 x 4 = 12. The profit ratio is 18 : 12 = 3 : 2.

**Multiples of an unknown sum.** "A invests a sum at the start. B invests double that sum after 6 months." Call A's sum 1. Then B's is 2. Weights: 1 x 12 = 12 and 2 x 6 = 12. You never need to know the sum.

**A letter.** "They invest Rs 1.2p and Rs p." The p will cancel, so treat the capitals as 1.2 and 1. If the first invests for 8 months and the second for 12: 1.2 x 8 = 9.6 and 1 x 12 = 12, which is 4 : 5.
After that, match the real number in the question to the parts, as always. Remember that the real number may be a difference between two shares.

tags: Three partners: a ratio of capitals and a ratio of times.
Multiples of one unknown sum, joining at different times.
A letter in the capitals, and a difference between the shares.

example.q: A and B invest in the ratio 2 : 3. A's money is used for 9 months and B's for 4 months. The profit is Rs 6,000. Find A's share.
steps: Weight = capital x time, partner by partner.
Profit ratio 18 : 12 = 3 : 2.
Parts added: 5 parts = 6,000, so one part = 1,200.
A has 3 parts: Rs 3,600.

checks.q: Two partners invest in the ratio 3 : 4, for periods in the ratio 2 : 1. In what ratio do they share the profit?
checks.why: Multiply partner by partner: 3 x 2 = 6 and 4 x 1 = 4. 6 : 4 = 3 : 2.

lessons.title: Working backwards from the profit
lessons.plain: New: the profit ratio is known. A capital, or a number of months, is what is missing.

teach.x: So far you knew the money and the months and found the profit. The Clerk paper's favourite form turns this round: it **tells you how the profit was shared** and asks for a missing capital or a missing time.
The rule is the same one, read from the other side. Since weight = capital x months, and the profit ratio equals the weight ratio:

items.x: missing **capital** = that partner's weight / months;
missing **months** = that partner's weight / capital.

teach.x: The steady way to do it:

items.x: Work out the weight of the partner you know everything about.
Use the profit ratio to find the other partner's weight. If the profit is shared 3 : 2 and the first weight is 360, the second weight is 240.
Divide that weight by whatever you know about the second partner, months or capital, to get the missing one.

teach.x: When the question has **no real numbers**, only ratios, do the division partner by partner. "Capitals are in the ratio 2 : 3 and profits in the ratio 4 : 3. Find the ratio of their times." Times = profit / capital: 4/2 and 3/3, which is 2 : 1.
One warning. In the last lessons you multiplied ratios. Going backwards you **divide** them. Multiplying here is the most common mistake in the topic.

tags: Find a missing capital.
Find when the second partner joined.
Only ratios: find the ratio of times.
Only ratios, with months given: find the ratio of capitals.
A real paper: one leaves early, find the ratio of capitals.

example.q: A starts a business with Rs 30,000. After 4 months B joins with Rs X. At the end of the year the profit is shared between A and B in the ratio 3 : 2. Find X.
steps: A's weight, in thousands: 30 x 12 = 360.
The profit ratio is 3 : 2, so the weights are 3 : 2. A's 360 is 3 parts, so one part is 120 and B's weight is 240.
B joined after 4 months, so B's money worked for 8 months.
B's capital = weight / months = 240 / 8 = 30.

checks.q: The capitals of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3 and their profits are in the ratio 4 : 3. What is the ratio of the periods for which they invested?
checks.why: Time = profit / capital, partner by partner: 4 / 2 = 2 and 3 / 3 = 1. The ratio is 2 : 1. (8 : 9 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.)

text.x: If two partners end up with **equal** profit, their weights are equal. So the one whose money stayed longer must have put in less, and by exactly the opposite ratio:
**capitals are in the opposite ratio of the months** (and months in the opposite ratio of the capitals).
A's money is used for 8 months and B's for 10, with equal profit: A : B capitals = 10 : 8 = 5 : 4.
A invests Rs 40,000 for 12 months and B invests Rs 60,000, with equal profit: the capitals are 2 : 3, so the months are 3 : 2. B's money worked for 8 months, which means B joined after 4.

lessons.title: Working backwards, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: the same method. The profit ratio is hidden behind "his share out of the total", a percent, or a letter.

teach.x: Recent papers rarely state the profit ratio plainly. You have to dig it out first. After that, everything is last lesson.

**"B's share is Rs 21,000 out of a total profit of Rs 49,000."** This is not the ratio 21 : 49. That would compare B with the whole. Subtract to get A's share first: 49,000 - 21,000 = 28,000. Now the ratio A : B is 28 : 21, which is 4 : 3.
**The missing capital is asked as a percent.** "B joined with x% of A's capital." Find B's capital in rupees as usual, and only at the end turn it into a percent of A's.

**The total capital is given, not each one.** "P and Q invested a total of Rs 6,400 for 12 months and 9 months." Find the ratio of the capitals by dividing profit by months, partner by partner, and then split the total in that ratio.
**Letters, such as x and (x + 4,000).** Write each weight with the letter, set the weight ratio equal to the profit ratio, and cross-multiply. It is one line.
In every case the order of work is: **profit ratio first, then weights, then the missing piece.**

tags: A share "out of" the total.
The same, and the answer is wanted as a percent.
Only the total capital is known.
Three partners, ratios only.
Letters: x and (x + 4,000).

example.q: A started a business with Rs 12,000. After 4 months B joined with Rs X. At the end of the year B's share is Rs 8,000 out of a total profit of Rs 20,000. Find X.
steps: Dig out the profit ratio. A's share = 20,000 - 8,000 = 12,000. So A : B = 12 : 8 = 3 : 2.
A's weight, in thousands: 12 x 12 = 144. That is 3 parts, so one part is 48 and B's weight is 96.
B's money worked for 12 - 4 = 8 months.
B's capital = 96 / 8 = 12.

checks.q: B's share is Rs 6,000 out of a total profit of Rs 15,000 in a business with A. What is the ratio of A's share to B's share?
checks.why: A's share = 15,000 - 6,000 = 9,000. A : B = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2. (5 : 2 compares the total with B, which is not what a profit ratio means.)

lessons.title: When someone adds or withdraws money midway
lessons.plain: New: a partner's capital changes during the year. Cut their time into stretches and add the pieces.

teach.x: "A starts with Rs 10,000. After 4 months he adds Rs 5,000." Now A's capital is not one number for the whole year, so capital x months cannot be done in one step.
The fix is natural: **cut that partner's time into stretches, one for each amount of money, and add the weights of the stretches.**

items.x: First 4 months at 10,000: 10 x 4 = 40.
Remaining 8 months at 15,000: 15 x 8 = 120.
A's weight for the year: 40 + 120 = 160.

teach.x: A partner whose money never changed still has a single stretch, as before. Then share the profit in the ratio of the total weights.
The words to read carefully:

rows: the capital goes up by 5,000 for the rest of the time
twice the capital for the rest of the time
half, or three-fourths, of it remains

teach.x: If only ratios are given, such as capitals of 4 : 5, use those numbers as the capitals. One-fourth withdrawn from 4 leaves 3; one-fifth withdrawn from 5 leaves 4.
A neat way to keep your working tidy is a small table: one row per partner, one column per stretch.

tags: One partner adds money.
One withdraws at the moment the other joins.
Doubling, with letters instead of rupees.
Both withdraw a fraction; only ratios are given.
Withdraws half, and half again, over two years.

example.q: A and B start a business with Rs 10,000 each. After 4 months A adds Rs 5,000. The profit at the end of the year is Rs 14,000. Find A's share.
steps: A has two stretches. First 4 months at 10 (thousand): 10 x 4 = 40.
Next 8 months at 15: 15 x 8 = 120. A's weight = 160.
B has one stretch: 10 x 12 = 120.
Parts added: 7 parts = 14,000, so one part = 2,000. A gets Rs 8,000.

checks.q: A invests Rs 6,000 and doubles his investment after 6 months. What is his weight for the year, in thousand-months?
checks.why: Two stretches: 6 x 6 = 36, then 12 x 6 = 72. Together 108. (144 would be right only if the money had been doubled from the first day.)

lessons.title: A changed capital with something to find
lessons.plain: New: lessons 5 and 7 together. The capital changes midway, and a letter or a month is missing.

teach.x: This is the hardest form in the topic, and it has appeared in the Clerk paper once. It joins two things you can already do: stretches of time, and working backwards.
There is no clever trick here, and it is better to know that than to hunt for one. The honest method is short:

items.x: Build each partner's weight with stretches, **keeping the unknown as a letter**.
Dig out the profit ratio (subtract if it is given as a share out of a total).
Say the two things are equal: weight ratio = profit ratio. Cross-multiply and solve the one line.

teach.x: When the unknown is a **month** ("after how many months should A add money?"), call it m. The first stretch lasts m months and the second lasts 12 - m.
Keep the numbers small by working in thousands and by cancelling before you multiply.

tags: A letter in the capitals, a withdrawal, and a share out of the total.
The missing piece is the month in which money was added.

example.q: A and B invest Rs X and Rs (X + 2,000). After 6 months A withdraws half of his money. At the end of the year the profit is shared between A and B in the ratio 1 : 2. Find X.
steps: A's stretches: X for 6 months is 6X. Half of X for the next 6 months is 3X. A's weight = 9X.
B's weight: (X + 2,000) for 12 months = 12X + 24,000.
Weight ratio = profit ratio: 9X : (12X + 24,000) = 1 : 2.
Cross-multiply: 2 x 9X = 12X + 24,000, so 18X = 12X + 24,000.
Check: A's weight 36,000; B's 72,000. That is 1 : 2.

checks.q: A invests Rs 8,000 and adds another Rs 8,000 after m months. B invests Rs 12,000 for the whole year. If they share the profit equally, what is m?
checks.why: In thousands: A's weight = 8 x m + 16 x (12 - m) = 192 - 8m. B's weight = 12 x 12 = 144. Equal profit means equal weights: 192 - 8m = 144, so m = 6.

lessons.title: When something is taken out before sharing
lessons.plain: New: a salary for the working partner, a gift to charity, or a part shared equally comes off the profit first.

teach.x: Sometimes the whole profit is not shared by weights. A slice is dealt with first, and only the rest is shared in the usual ratio. This kind has not appeared in the Clerk papers we checked, but it is common in practice sets and uses nothing new.

**A working partner's salary.** "A, the working partner, gets 10% of the profit for managing the business. The rest is shared in the ratio of their capitals." Take the 10% out and give it to A. Share the other 90% in the capital ratio. A's total is his salary plus his share.
**Charity.** "5% of the profit goes to charity." That 5% leaves the business. The remaining 95% is shared.

**A part shared equally.** "40% of the profit is shared equally and the rest in the ratio of capitals." Do the two parts separately. Notice that the equal part gives both partners the same, so it creates no difference between them. Any difference in what they receive comes from the other part alone.

A good habit for these: **write each person's total as a percent of the whole profit.** If A gets 10% as salary and then three-fifths of the remaining 90%, that is 10 + 54 = 64% of the profit. Then one real number gives you everything.
The same weight idea also shares a **rent**. If three people graze cows on one field, each one's weight is cows x months, and the rent is split in that ratio, just like a profit.

tags: A salary, then the rest: find what the working partner receives.
Charity first; work back from one share to the profit.
Salary and share together are given: find the profit.
A part shared equally, and a difference between the two partners.
Not a profit at all: sharing a rent by cows and months.

example.q: A and B invest in the ratio 3 : 1. A is the working partner and gets 20% of the profit as salary. The rest is shared in the ratio of their capitals. If the profit is Rs 20,000, how much does A receive in all?
steps: Salary first: 20% of 20,000 = 4,000, to A.
Left to share: 16,000, in the ratio 3 : 1.
4 parts = 16,000, so one part = 4,000. A's share is 3 parts = 12,000.
As a percent of the profit: 20 + three-quarters of 80 = 80%, and 80% of 20,000 is 16,000.

checks.q: 10% of the profit of a business goes to charity. The rest is shared between A and B in the ratio 2 : 1. If B gets Rs 1,500, what is the total profit?
checks.why: 90% is shared, and B gets one third of it: 30% of the profit. 30% = 1,500, so 1% = 50 and the profit is 5,000. (4,500 is the amount that was shared.)

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: turn the job into chocolates.** Never work with fractions like 1/12 + 1/18. Make the total work a number of units (the LCM of the given days), then everybody eats a whole number of units per day.
**The LCM-unit algorithm (use it on every question):**

items.x: Total work = LCM of all the “days” (or hours) given.
Each person’s daily units = Total ÷ their days. A group’s daily units = Total ÷ the group’s days.
Add units for people working together. Subtract for an outlet pipe or a leak.
Time = Work left ÷ units per day of whoever is working.

blocks.x: Example: A 10 days, B 15 days. Total = 30 units. A = 3 a day, B = 2 a day. Together 5 a day, so 6 days.
**Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **Efficiency and time are upside-down partners.** Efficiency 3 : 2 means time 2 : 3. Flip the ratio, never the percentage.
**Men-days.** Men × Days (× Hours) = Work. Same work on both sides, so 12 men × 15 days = 20 men × 9 days.
**“6 men or 9 women”** means 6 men = 9 women, so 2 men = 3 women. Convert everybody into one type, then use men-days.
**Pipes.** Filling pipe = plus units. Emptying pipe or leak = minus units.
**Part of the work.** “60% of the work” means 60% of the total units, so 60% of the full time for that person.
**Wages** are shared in the ratio of work done (units per day × days worked), not in the ratio of days.

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: “more efficient” to “less time”**
**Non-linear warning.** “25% more efficient” is not “25% less time”; it is 20% less time. And days never add: 10 days and 15 days together is not 25 days and not 12.5 days. Only units per day add.
**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** LCM units, then write one line: *units done by each phase add up to the total*. If you are stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Counts are out of the 495 bank questions; the PYQ figure is IBPS Clerk Prelims questions; sister figure is from the 12 sister questions.

rows: Combine known rates (work or pipes, with or without an outlet)
Group minus sub-group (find the missing person, pipe or leak)
Efficiency given as ratio, percent or “times”
Phased work (someone leaves or joins after a stated time)
Men-days, chain rule, men and women

lead.x: Two bank questions fit no archetype and are left out (CON-TNW-30, G-cap-7).

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** every person’s or pipe’s own time is given; asks the time together.
**Shortcut engine.** LCM units, add fillers, subtract emptiers, divide.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** A fills in 10 h, B in 15 h, C empties in 20 h. Tank = 60 units. A +6, B +4, C −3. Net 7 an hour. Time = 60/7 hours.

items.title: Group minus sub-group

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “A, B and C together… B and C together… find A”, or “pipe takes 12 h, with a leak 18 h”.
**Shortcut engine.** LCM units for the two group times. Big group’s units minus small group’s units = the missing one’s units. A leak is just the missing “minus” pipe.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** All three 12 days, B and C 20 days. Work = 60. All = 5 a day, B+C = 3 a day, so A = 2 a day. A alone = 30 days.
**Leak example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023).** Pipe 12 h, with leak 18 h. Tank = 36. Pipe +3, pipe with leak +2, so leak = −1. Leak empties in 36 hours.

items.label: Confirmed (the single most repeated Clerk pattern here)

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “50% more efficient”, “1.5 times as efficient”, “time ratio 4 : 6 : 3”.

**Shortcut engine.** write the efficiency ratio as whole numbers (use the grid). Those numbers are the units per day. Total work = (sum of units of whoever worked) × days. Then divide by whoever is asked.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Dec 2020).** Times are 4 : 6 : 3, so units per day are 3 : 2 : 4 (divide 12 by each). Together 9 a day for 8 days = 72 units. A alone = 72 ÷ 3 = 24 days. Three-fourths of the work = 18 days.
**Pattern clues.** “worked for 5 days then left”, “B joins after 8 days”, “pipe A is closed after 2 hours”.
**Shortcut engine.** LCM units. Units done in phase 1 = rate × days. Units left ÷ new rate = phase 2 time.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2024).** A 15 days, B 18 days. Work = 90. A = 6, B = 5. A works 5 days = 30 units. Left 60. B needs 60 ÷ 5 = 12 days.

items.title: Men-days, chain rule, men and women

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** numbers of men, women, days, hours; “some more join”; “6 men or 9 women”.
**Shortcut engine.** Work = Men × Days. Find the work, subtract what is done, divide the rest. For men and women, convert all to one type first.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2018).** 20 women, 12 days = 240 woman-days. First 3 days use 60. Left 180 to be done in 6 days needs 30 women. So 10 joined.

items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** nobody’s time is given outright; “B takes 6 days more than twice the time taken together”.

**Shortcut engine.** this is the one place where the honest route is a quadratic, which is too slow. So **test the options**: together time of two people = product ÷ sum of their days. Start with the middle option.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2018).** A takes 20 days. B = 6 more than twice the together time. Try B = 30: together = 20 × 30 ÷ 50 = 12. Twice 12 plus 6 = 30. Fits. Answer 30 days.

items.title: Alternate days

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “work on alternate days starting with A”.
**Shortcut engine.** units in one 2-day cycle = A + B. Take as many full cycles as fit, then finish the leftover day by day in the starting order.
**Worked example (that PO paper).** A and B together 15 days, A alone 40 days. Work = 120. Pair = 8 a day, A = 3, so B = 5. One 2-day cycle = 8 units. 15 cycles = 120. Time = 30 days.

items.label: Seen once (IBPS PO Prelims 22 Aug 2026 Shift 2)

items.title: Leaves some days before completion

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “B left 6 days before the work was finished”.
**Shortcut engine.** work backwards. The last stretch is done by the one who stayed: take those units off first. The rest was done by both together. Add the two times.

**Worked example (that RRB paper).** A and B together 15 days, B alone 36 days, B leaves 6 days before the end. Work = 180. Pair = 12, B = 5, so A = 7. Last 6 days A alone = 42. Rest 138 ÷ 12 = 11.5 days. Total 17.5 days.

items.label: Seen once (IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims 6 Dec 2025 Shift 2)

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** share money in the ratio of units done. If all work the same days, that is just the efficiency ratio.
**Worked example (bank CON-TNW-08).** A 10 days, B 15 days, paid ₹3,000. Units per day 3 : 2. A gets 3/5 of 3,000 = ₹1,800.
**Shortcut engine.** the litres given match a fraction of the tank. Find that fraction, then scale up.
**Worked example (bank G-cap-2).** 3/5 full, add 28 litres, becomes 5/6 full. 5/6 − 3/5 = 7/30 of the tank = 28 litres. So 1/30 = 4 litres and the tank = 120 litres.

tail.x: Note: one Clerk PYQ (2016, pipes 16 h and 12 h, tank 240 litres) is a W1 question with a litres step at the end, so the litres idea has appeared, but only as a finishing step.

lead.x: All eight questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was checked by script. One drill per Core archetype.

body.x: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours. Pipe C empties the full tank in 36 hours. All three are opened together. In how many hours is the tank full?

method.x: **30-Second Exam Method:** Tank = 36 units. A +3, B +2, C −1. Net 4 an hour. 36 ÷ 4 = 9. **Answer (B).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** all three rates are whole units, so the net rate is whole and the answer must divide 36. That removes 8 and 10. Six hours would need 6 units an hour, more than both fillers give (5), so 6 goes. Twelve hours is A alone, but B adds more than C removes, so it must be faster than 12. Only 9 is left. Back-check: 9 × 4 = 36.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding the emptying pipe instead of subtracting gives 6, which is option (E).

body.x: A, B and C together finish a work in 8 days. B and C together finish it in 12 days. In how many days can A alone finish 75% of the work?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** A’s one-day work = 1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24. A alone takes 24 days; 75% of the work takes 18 days.
**30-Second Exam Method:** Work = 24 units. All three 3 a day, B and C 2 a day, so A does 1 a day. 75% of 24 = 18 units, so 18 days. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** no safe one here; the direct route is already two steps. Back-check: 18 days × 1 unit = 18 = three-quarters of 24.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 24 is sitting in the options for people who stop at “A alone”. The Clerk papers of 24 Aug 2024 and 2025 both asked for 60% of the work, not the whole work. Read the last line.

body.x: A is 25% more efficient than B. A takes 6 days less than B to finish a work alone. In how many days can B alone finish it?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let B’s days be b; A’s days are b ÷ 1.25 = 0.8b; b − 0.8b = 6, so b = 30.
**30-Second Exam Method:** efficiency A : B = 5 : 4, so time A : B = 4 : 5. The gap of 1 part = 6 days. B = 5 parts = 30 days. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** B’s time is 5 parts, so it must be a multiple of 5. Only 30 qualifies. Back-check: A = 24, and 30 − 24 = 6.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “25% more efficient” does not mean “25% less time”. Taking 6 days as 25% of B’s time gives 24, which is option (B) (and is actually A’s time).

body.x: A can finish a work in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work together for 6 days, then A leaves. In how many more days does B finish the remaining work?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** work done in 6 days = 6 × (1/20 + 1/30) = 6 × 1/12 = 1/2. B does the other half in 30 × 1/2 = 15 days.
**30-Second Exam Method:** Work = 60 units. A 3, B 2, together 5. Six days = 30 units. Left 30 ÷ 2 = 15 days. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** B alone does 2 units a day and 30 units are left, so no trick is needed. Back-check: 6 × 5 + 15 × 2 = 60.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** “how many more days” is 15; “in how many days in total” would be 21. Both are in the options. The Clerk paper of 4 Oct 2025 Shift 4 asked for the total, the Shift 3 pipes question asked for the additional time.

body.x: 6 men or 9 women can finish a work in 12 days. In how many days can 4 men and 12 women finish it?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** 6 men = 9 women, so 1 man = 1.5 women. 4 men + 12 women = 6 + 12 = 18 women. 9 women take 12 days, so 18 women take 6 days.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 2 men = 3 women, so 4 men = 6 women. Team = 18 women, which is double 9 women. Double the people, half the days: 6. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the work is 9 × 12 = 108 woman-days, and the team is a whole number of women, so the answer must divide 108. That removes 8 and 7. Back-check: 18 × 6 = 108.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “6 men **or** 9 women” is an equation between men and women. Reading it as “6 men **and** 9 women” makes the question unsolvable or wrong.

body.x: A and B together finish a work in 6 days. Working alone, A takes 5 days less than B. In how many days can B alone finish the work?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** 1/(b − 5) + 1/b = 1/6 leads to a quadratic, b² − 17b + 30 = 0, so b = 15. Too slow for the exam.
**30-Second Exam Method:** test options with product ÷ sum. B = 15 means A = 10. 15 × 10 ÷ 25 = 6. Fits. **Answer (A).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** the slower worker always takes more than twice the together time, so B is more than 12. That removes 10 and 12 before you test anything. Back-check: 10 and 15 give 150 ÷ 25 = 6.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 10 is A’s time and it is in the options. Check whose time is asked.

body.x: A can finish a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. In how many days is the work finished?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** two days’ work = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. After 14 days, 35/36 is done. The 15th day is A’s: 1/36 left ÷ 1/12 = 1/3 day. Total 14⅓ days.
**30-Second Exam Method:** Work = 36. A 3, B 2, cycle of 2 days = 5 units. Seven cycles (14 days) = 35. One unit left, A’s turn, A does 3 a day, so one-third of a day. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** options are not whole numbers, so do not try one. Do it directly.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** doubling the together time (7.2 × 2 = 14.4) is option (C) and it is wrong, because the last bit is done at A’s speed, not at the average speed. Also check whose turn the leftover falls on.

body.x: A can finish a work in 20 days and B in 30 days. They start together, but A leaves 5 days before the work is finished. In how many days in total is the work finished?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let the total be T days. B works T days, A works T − 5: T/30 + (T − 5)/20 = 1, so T = 15.
**30-Second Exam Method:** Work = 60. A 3, B 2. Last 5 days B alone = 10 units. The other 50 units at 5 a day = 10 days. Total 10 + 5 = 15. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** together all the way would take 12 days; A leaving early can only make it longer. That removes 10 and 12. Back-check: 10 × 5 + 5 × 2 = 60.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “leaves 5 days before completion” is not “leaves after 5 days”. And 10 (the together part only) is in the options for those who forget to add the last 5 days.

intro.x: This topic covers people doing a job and pipes filling a tank. They are the same thing, and one idea handles both: **give the job a number of units, and count how many units each worker does in a day.**

There are twelve short lessons. The first four build that idea for workers and for pipes. The rest are the ways the exam varies it. Go in order the first time; the later lessons lean on the earlier ones.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the efficiency table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
Whatever the story, begin the same way: units for the job, units per day for each worker. If you can write those down, the question is already half done.

lessons.title: Turning a job into units
lessons.plain: The starting point: give the whole job a number of units, and see how many each person finishes in a day.

teach.x: "A can do a piece of work in 10 days and B can do it in 15 days. How long will they take together?" The answer is not 25, and it is not 12.5. Days cannot be added or averaged, because two people working together are **faster**, not slower.
What you can add is **how much each one gets done in a day**. To make that easy, give the whole job a size.

items.x: **Pick a number of units for the whole job** that all the given days go into. 10 and 15 both go into 30, so call the job 30 units. (Think of it as 30 bricks to lay.)
**Find each person's units per day.** A finishes 30 units in 10 days, so A does 3 a day. B finishes 30 in 15 days, so B does 2 a day.
**Add the daily units** of everyone working together: 3 + 2 = 5 a day.
**Time = units to be done / units per day.** 30 / 5 = 6 days.

teach.x: That is the whole method, and almost every question in this topic is these four steps with a small twist. The number you pick in step 1 can be any number the days go into; the smallest such number keeps the arithmetic light.
If the question tells you about **part** of the job ("A does one-fourth of the work in 6 days"), first work out the time for the whole job: four quarters take 4 x 6 = 24 days.

tags: The plain form: two people, find the time together.
Three people instead of two.
It asks what fraction is left, not how long.
Each person's time is hidden in a part of the job.
Not work at all: money that pays wages.

example.q: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B can do it in 24 days. In how many days can they do it together?
steps: Pick the units: 12 and 24 both go into 24. Call the job 24 units.
A does 24 / 12 = 2 units a day. B does 24 / 24 = 1 unit a day.
Together they do 2 + 1 = 3 units a day.
Time = 24 / 3 = 8 days.

checks.q: A can do a job in 6 days and B can do it in 12 days. In how many days can they do it together?
checks.why: Call the job 12 units. A does 2 a day and B does 1 a day, so together 3 a day. 12 / 3 = 4 days. (9 is the average and 18 is the sum; neither means anything here.)

shortcut.title: Product over sum, for two workers

text.x: For exactly **two** people who take **a** days and **b** days alone, the time together is:
10 days and 15 days: 150 / 25 = 6 days. 12 and 24: 288 / 36 = 8 days.
It is the units method done in one line. It works only for two workers doing the whole job together, so keep the units method for everything else.

lessons.title: Pipes and tanks: the same idea
lessons.plain: New: pipes filling a tank are workers. A pipe that empties the tank is a worker who undoes the work.

teach.x: A pipe that fills a tank in 20 minutes is just a worker who finishes a job in 20 minutes. So everything from the last lesson carries over: give the tank a number of units, find each pipe's units per minute (or per hour), and add.
There is one new thing. Some pipes **empty** the tank. An emptying pipe, an outlet, a drain or a leak takes water away, so its units are **subtracted**.
Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours. Pipe B empties it in 10 hours. Both are open.

items.x: Call the tank 30 units.
A adds 5 units an hour. B removes 3 units an hour.
Each hour the tank gains 5 - 3 = 2 units.
Time to fill = 30 / 2 = 15 hours.

teach.x: If the tank's size is given in **litres**, you do not need to invent units: the litres are the units. A 240-litre tank filled by a pipe in 16 hours gets 240 / 16 = 15 litres an hour from it.
And if the tank is **already partly full**, only the empty part is the job. A half-full tank of 30 units has 15 units left to fill.

tags: The plain form: two filling pipes.
One pipe fills while the other empties.
Two fill and one empties, as a real paper asked it.
It asks for the fraction filled in a few minutes.
The tank is given in litres, and it asks how much is still needed.

example.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours. Pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. If all three are opened together, how long will the empty tank take to fill?
steps: Call the tank 60 units: 12, 15 and 20 all go into 60.
A adds 5 an hour, B adds 4 an hour, and C removes 3 an hour.
Each hour the tank gains 5 + 4 - 3 = 6 units.
Time = 60 / 6 = 10 hours.

checks.q: A pipe can fill a tank in 8 hours and an outlet can empty it in 24 hours. If both are open, in how many hours will the empty tank be full?
checks.why: Call the tank 24 units. The pipe adds 3 an hour and the outlet removes 1, so the tank gains 2 an hour. 24 / 2 = 12 hours. (6 hours would be right if both pipes were filling.)

lessons.title: A group, minus part of the group
lessons.plain: New: you know how fast a group works and how fast part of it works. Subtract to find the one who is missing.

teach.x: This is the single most repeated pattern in the Clerk papers for this topic, and it is one subtraction.
"A, B and C together can finish a job in 12 days. B and C together can finish it in 20 days. How long would A take alone?"
Nobody's own time is given. But units per day can be added, so they can also be **subtracted**.

items.x: Call the job 60 units.
All three together do 60 / 12 = 5 units a day.
B and C together do 60 / 20 = 3 units a day.
The difference is what A does: 5 - 3 = 2 units a day.
A alone takes 60 / 2 = 30 days.

teach.x: The same subtraction works for two people: "A and B together take 8 days and A alone takes 12 days" gives B's units as the difference.

**The pairs form.** "A and B take 12 days, B and C take 15 days, C and A take 20 days." Add all three pairs. Each person has been counted twice, so the sum is two lots of A + B + C. Halve it to get what all three do in a day.
Finish by reading the last line. It may ask for only part of the job: if A takes 10 days for the whole job, A takes 6 days for 60% of it.

tags: Two people: the pair and one of them.
Three people: the group and a pair.
A fraction for the days, and it asks for part of the job.
The pair's time is hidden in a percent.
Three pairs, and no single person.

example.q: A and B together can do a piece of work in 6 days. A alone can do it in 10 days. In how many days can B alone do it?
steps: Call the job 30 units.
A and B together do 30 / 6 = 5 units a day.
A alone does 30 / 10 = 3 units a day.
So B does 5 - 3 = 2 units a day.
B alone takes 30 / 2 = 15 days.

checks.q: A, B and C together can finish a job in 6 days. A and B together can finish it in 9 days. In how many days can C alone finish it?
checks.why: Call the job 18 units. All three do 3 a day; A and B do 2 a day. So C does 1 a day and takes 18 days. (3 comes from subtracting the days, which has no meaning.)

text.x: If a group finishes in **t** days and part of the group alone would take **a** days (a is the bigger number), the missing worker takes:
Together 6 days, A alone 10 days: 60 / 4 = 15 days for B.
It is the cousin of "product over sum" from lesson 1: product over **difference**. The same line finds a leak in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Leaks and drain pipes
lessons.plain: New: last lesson's subtraction, with tanks. The missing one is a leak or a drain.

teach.x: "A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. Because of a leak, it takes 18 hours." The leak is a hidden worker who undoes some of the pipe's work. You find it exactly as you found the missing person in the last lesson.

items.x: Call the tank 36 units.
The pipe alone adds 36 / 12 = 3 units an hour.
With the leak, the tank gains only 36 / 18 = 2 units an hour.
So the leak removes 3 - 2 = 1 unit an hour.
A full tank of 36 units would drain through the leak in 36 hours.

teach.x: Read these questions as "what the pipes should add" against "what the tank actually gains". The gap is the drain.
The disguises are the same as for people:

items.x: a third pipe C that is "also open", where the tank fills more slowly than A and B alone would manage, so C must be emptying;
two outlets, one of them known;
three pairs of pipes;
a last line that asks about **half** the tank or some other part.

tags: A leak slows one pipe down.
A third pipe that turns out to be emptying.
The same, and it asks about half the tank.
Two outlets, one of them known.
Three pairs of pipes.

example.q: A pipe can fill a tank in 10 hours. Because of a leak in the bottom, it takes 15 hours. If the tank is full, how long will the leak take to empty it?
steps: Call the tank 30 units.
The pipe alone adds 3 units an hour.
With the leak the tank gains 30 / 15 = 2 units an hour.
So the leak removes 3 - 2 = 1 unit an hour.
A full tank is 30 units: the leak empties it in 30 hours.

checks.q: Pipes A and B together can fill a tank in 4 hours. When a drain pipe C is also open, the tank fills in 6 hours. In how many hours can C alone empty the full tank?
checks.why: Call the tank 12 units. A and B add 3 an hour; with C open the tank gains 2. So C removes 1 an hour and empties 12 units in 12 hours.

lessons.title: Faster workers take less time
lessons.plain: New: workers are compared by how good they are: "twice as efficient", "50% more efficient".

teach.x: **Efficiency** means how much work someone does in a day. It is exactly the "units per day" you have been using. So a sentence about efficiency hands you the daily units directly.
"A is twice as efficient as B." Give B 1 unit a day; then A does 2. That is all the sentence says.
Percent words work as in the Basics. "B is 50% more efficient than A": A is 100 and B is 150, so their daily units are in the ratio 2 : 3.
The one fact to hold on to: **efficiency and time run in opposite directions.** The better worker takes fewer days. If the efficiencies are 2 : 3, the times are 3 : 2.
Two kinds of question follow.

**The total time together is given.** "A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish in 14 days." Together they do 2 + 1 = 3 units a day, so the job is 3 x 14 = 42 units. A alone takes 42 / 2 = 21 days.
**One person's time is given.** "A takes 30 minutes; B is 50% more efficient." Efficiencies 2 : 3 mean times 3 : 2. A's 30 minutes is 3 parts, so B takes 20 minutes.
If the question gives a ratio of **times** for three people, such as 4 : 6 : 3, turn each into units per day by dividing a common number by it. Using 12: the daily units are 3, 2 and 4.

tags: "Twice as efficient", with the time together.
The same with pipes: "three times as fast".
Percent words, and one time is given.
A chain: A to B by efficiency, B to C by days.
A ratio of times for three people.

example.q: A is three times as efficient as B. Working together they finish a job in 9 days. In how many days can A alone finish it?
steps: Give B 1 unit a day. Then A does 3 units a day.
Together they do 4 units a day.
They take 9 days, so the job is 4 x 9 = 36 units.
A alone: 36 / 3 = 12 days.

checks.q: A can do a job in 20 days. B is 25% more efficient than A. In how many days can B do the same job?
checks.why: A is 100 and B is 125, so their efficiencies are 4 : 5 and their times are 5 : 4. A's 20 days is 5 parts, so one part is 4 and B takes 16 days. (15 comes from taking 25% off the days, which is the common mistake.)

checks.q: B is 20% less efficient than A. A can finish a job in 12 days. In how many days can B finish it?
checks.why: A is 100 and B is 80, so efficiencies are 5 : 4 and times are 4 : 5. A's 12 days is 4 parts, so one part is 3 and B takes 15 days. (14.4 adds 20% to the days; the time goes up by a quarter, not a fifth.)

text.x: If someone is **1/n more efficient**, they take **1/(n + 1) less time**. It is the same turn-around you met in Percentages.
25% more efficient is 1/4 more, so 1/5 less time: 20 days becomes 16.
50% more efficient is 1/2 more, so 1/3 less time: 30 minutes becomes 20.
Twice as efficient is 100% more, so half the time.

lessons.title: Efficiency, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the idea. The efficiency is tied to "takes 60 days less", a part of the job, or a third worker.

teach.x: Real papers combine the efficiency sentence with something else. There are two combinations worth knowing well.

**"...and therefore takes 60 days less."** "A is three times as good a workman as B and takes 60 days less." Turn the efficiencies round to get the times: 1 : 3. The difference between the times is 3 - 1 = 2 parts, and that is the 60 days. So one part is 30: A takes 30 days and B takes 90. Now it is lesson 1.

This is the same "match the real number to the parts" move you know from ratios. Here the real number is a difference in **days**, so it must be matched to the parts of the **time** ratio, not the efficiency ratio.
**A group's time, with efficiencies inside it.** "A and B together finish two-thirds of a job in 20 days, and A is 50% more efficient than B." Take it in order:

items.x: Get the time for the **whole** job: two-thirds in 20 days means the whole in 30 days.
Give the job units and find the group's units per day.
Split the group's daily units between its members in the ratio of their efficiencies.

teach.x: After that every person has their own units per day, and any question about any combination of them is an addition and a division.
A sentence like "C takes half the time taken by A" is efficiency in disguise: half the time means twice the daily units.

tags: "Thrice as good" and "60 days less".
The same with a decimal multiple, and an awkward answer.
A part of the job, an efficiency, and a third worker.
"100% more efficient", and it asks for the part done.
"Half the time" as an efficiency.

example.q: A is twice as good a workman as B and takes 15 days less than B to do a job. In how many days can they do it working together?
steps: Efficiencies are 2 : 1, so times are 1 : 2.
The difference in time is 2 - 1 = 1 part, and it is 15 days.
So A takes 15 days and B takes 30 days.
Call the job 30 units. A does 2 a day and B does 1: together 3.

checks.q: A is 50% more efficient than B and takes 10 days less than B to finish a job. In how many days can B alone finish it?
checks.why: Efficiencies are 3 : 2, so times are 2 : 3. The difference is 1 part = 10 days. B has 3 parts: 30 days. (20 is A.)

lessons.title: Work done in stages
lessons.plain: New: the team changes partway through. Someone leaves, or someone joins.

teach.x: "A and B work together for 4 days, and then A leaves. How long will B take to finish?" The job is now done in **stages**, with a different team in each stage.
The units method was made for this. Units already done can simply be taken away from the total.

items.x: Give the job units and find each person's units per day, as always.
**Stage one:** units done = team's units per day x days worked.
**Subtract** to find the units left.
**Stage two:** time = units left / units per day of whoever is working now.

teach.x: If there are more stages, repeat steps 2 and 3. A quick sketch helps: write the total at the top and subtract each stage beneath it.
The questions are turned around in two ways.

**Find the newcomer.** "A works alone for 10 days, then B joins and they finish in 8 more days." Work out the units left and divide by the 8 days. That gives what A and B do in a day together; take A's units away and you have B's.
**A percent of the job.** "A completes 60% of a work in 15 days." Calling the job 100 units makes this easy: A does 60 units in 15 days, which is 4 a day, and 40 units are left.
Then check the last line. "How many more days" is the second stage only. "In how many days is the work completed" is all the stages added.

tags: Together first, then one leaves.
One starts alone and the other takes over.
Find the one who joined.
A percent of the job comes first.
Three people; one leaves as another joins; it asks for the total time.

example.q: A can do a job in 10 days and B can do it in 15 days. They work together for 3 days and then B leaves. In how many more days will A finish the job?
steps: Call the job 30 units. A does 3 a day and B does 2.
Stage one: together they do 5 a day for 3 days = 15 units.
Units left: 30 - 15 = 15.
Stage two: A alone does 3 a day. 15 / 3 = 5 days.

checks.q: A can do a job in 20 days. He works alone for 5 days, and then B finishes the rest alone in 12 days. In how many days could B do the whole job alone?
checks.why: Call the job 20 units; A does 1 a day. In 5 days A does 5, leaving 15. B does those 15 in 12 days, which is 1.25 a day. Whole job: 20 / 1.25 = 16 days.

lessons.title: Pipes opened and closed at different times
lessons.plain: New: the stages idea with tanks. A pipe is closed early, or opened late.

teach.x: Stages work the same way for tanks. A pipe being **closed** is a worker leaving; a pipe being **opened later** is a worker joining. Find the units added in each stage and subtract from the tank.
Two forms are particular to pipes.

**"After how many minutes should B be closed so that the tank is full in exactly 9 minutes?"** Look at it from pipe A's side. A is open for all 9 minutes, so you know exactly how much A adds. Whatever is still missing must come from B, and B's units per minute tell you how long B needs to be open.
**A drain that is closed, or opened, partway.** While the drain is open its units are subtracted; once it is closed, they are not. Treat the two stretches as two stages with different net units.
Pipe questions more often ask for the **total** time than work questions do, so remember to add the first stage back at the end when the question says "in how many hours in total".

tags: Both open, then one is closed.
The same, with an answer that is not a whole number.
One pipe is opened late, and it asks for the total time.
When should a pipe be closed?
A drain that is closed partway.

example.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 minutes and 18 minutes. Both are opened together, and after 4 minutes A is closed. In how many more minutes will B fill the tank?
steps: Call the tank 36 units. A adds 3 a minute and B adds 2.
Stage one: 5 a minute for 4 minutes = 20 units.
Units left: 36 - 20 = 16.
Stage two: B alone adds 2 a minute. 16 / 2 = 8 minutes.

checks.q: Pipe A can fill a tank in 10 hours and pipe B in 15 hours. A is opened first, and after 5 hours B is also opened. In how many hours in total is the tank full?
checks.why: Call the tank 30 units. A adds 3 an hour: 15 units in 5 hours. The other 15 are filled by both at 5 an hour, which takes 3 hours. Total 5 + 3 = 8 hours. (3 is only the second stage.)

lessons.title: Many workers: men and days
lessons.plain: New: teams of equal workers. More people means fewer days, and the work is people multiplied by days.

teach.x: When a question talks about "12 men" or "20 women", every worker in the group is taken to be equally good. Then there is a very simple way to measure a job: **how many days of one person's work it needs.**
12 men working for 15 days put in 12 x 15 = 180 days of one man's work. We call that 180 **man-days**. The job needs 180 man-days however they are arranged, so 20 men would need 180 / 20 = 9 days.
**work = workers x days**
If hours per day are mentioned, they multiply in too: workers x days x hours.
This one line handles all the usual stories.
**Some workers leave partway.** Find the total man-days. Subtract the man-days already done. Divide what is left by the workers who remain.
**Some workers join partway.** Find the man-days left and the days allowed. Dividing gives the number of workers needed; subtract those already there.
**Only part of the job is done.** "40 men did one-third of the work in 30 days." That third cost 40 x 30 = 1,200 man-days, so the remaining two-thirds needs 2,400.
**The job itself changes size.** A wall twice as long needs twice the man-days. Work out the man-days for one metre, or simply scale the total.
Notice the direction: more workers, fewer days. If your answer has more workers taking longer, something has been divided the wrong way round.

tags: The plain form: more men, fewer days.
Hours per day are part of the work.
Some men leave partway.
Some join partway: how many?
Only part of the job is done, and there is a deadline.

example.q: 16 men can finish a job in 9 days. In how many days can 12 men finish the same job?
steps: Total work = 16 x 9 = 144 man-days.
With 12 men: 144 / 12 = 12 days.
Fewer men, more days. That is the right direction.

checks.q: 10 men working 6 hours a day can finish a job in 12 days. In how many days can 8 men working 9 hours a day finish it?
checks.why: Work = 10 x 6 x 12 = 720 man-hours. The new team does 8 x 9 = 72 man-hours a day. 720 / 72 = 10 days.

checks.q: 8 men can build a wall 40 metres long in 5 days. In how many days can 10 men build a similar wall 80 metres long?
checks.why: 40 metres needs 8 x 5 = 40 man-days, which is 1 man-day a metre. So 80 metres needs 80 man-days. With 10 men: 8 days.

text.x: When a question compares two teams, you can write both sides at once:
**(men x days x hours) / work  is the same on both sides**
10 men build 100 metres in 6 days; how long for 15 men to build 200 metres? (10 x 6) / 100 = (15 x days) / 200. So 15 x days = 120, and days = 8.
Leave out anything the question does not mention. It is the man-days idea, written so that nothing gets forgotten.

lessons.title: Two kinds of workers
lessons.plain: New: men and women, or men and boys, who do not work at the same speed. Turn everyone into one kind.

teach.x: "3 men **or** 5 women can do a job in 12 days." The little word "or" is the key. It says that 3 men do the same as 5 women. So you can **swap one for the other**: 3 men = 5 women.
Use that to turn the whole team into one kind of worker, and the question becomes last lesson.
"How long will 6 men and 5 women take?" 6 men is two lots of 3 men, so it equals 10 women. The team is worth 10 + 5 = 15 women. The job is 5 women x 12 days = 60 woman-days, so 15 women take 4 days.

If the question says "**and**" instead of "or", you are not told the swap directly. "4 men and 6 women finish in 8 days; 3 men and 7 women finish in 10 days." Both teams do the same job, so their man-days are equal:

items.x: (4 men + 6 women) x 8 = (3 men + 7 women) x 10
32 men + 48 women = 30 men + 70 women
2 men = 22 women, so 1 man = 11 women.

teach.x: Now you have the swap, and can carry on.
**Identical pipes** are the same idea in a tank. "12 identical pipes fill a tank in 40 minutes" means the tank needs 12 x 40 = 480 pipe-minutes.

tags: "Or" gives the swap directly.
"And": the swap has to be worked out.
It asks only for the swap, as a ratio.
Identical pipes, some out of order.
Identical pipes, with more opened halfway.

example.q: 2 men or 3 women can do a job in 10 days. In how many days can 4 men and 9 women do it?
steps: "Or" gives the swap: 2 men = 3 women.
So 4 men = 6 women. The team is worth 6 + 9 = 15 women.
The job is 3 women x 10 days = 30 woman-days.
15 women take 30 / 15 = 2 days.

checks.q: 6 identical pipes can fill a tank in 30 minutes. In how many minutes can 9 such pipes fill it?
checks.why: The tank needs 6 x 30 = 180 pipe-minutes. With 9 pipes: 180 / 9 = 20 minutes.

lessons.title: Taking turns, and leaving before the end
lessons.plain: New: two patterns of who works when. They work on alternate days, or one stops a few days before the finish.

teach.x: Two more arrangements of the stages idea. Each has appeared once in the papers we checked, and each has a neat way in.
**Alternate days.** "A and B work on alternate days, starting with A." Think in **rounds**. One round is one day of A and one day of B.

items.x: Find the units done in one round.
See how many **whole** rounds fit into the job.
Finish the last few units by hand, one day at a time, in the right order: A's day first, then B's.

teach.x: Step 3 matters. The last day is often only part of a day, and it is done at the speed of whoever's turn it is, not at the average speed.
The same works for pipes opened alternately for an hour each, and for "A is helped by B and C every third day": a round is three days, and on the third day all three work.

**Leaving before the end.** "A and B start together, but A leaves 5 days before the work is completed." You do not know how long they worked together, but you do know how the job **ended**: the last 5 days were B alone. So work backwards.

items.x: Units done in the last stretch = B's units per day x 5.
Take those off the total. Everything else was done by both together.
Divide by their combined units for the days together, and add the 5 days back.

teach.x: Compare the wording with lesson 7. "A leaves **after** 5 days" tells you the first stage. "A leaves 5 days **before the end**" tells you the last stage.

tags: Alternate days, with part of a day at the end.
Pipes opened alternately.
Help arrives every third day.
One leaves a few days before the finish.

example.q: A can do a job in 10 days and B can do it in 15 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. In how many days will the job be finished?
steps: Call the job 30 units. A does 3 a day and B does 2.
One round (A's day, then B's day) = 5 units in 2 days.
30 / 5 = 6 whole rounds, with nothing left over.
6 rounds x 2 days = 12 days.

checks.q: A and B can do a job in 20 days and 30 days. They start together, but B leaves 5 days before the job is completed. In how many days is the whole job completed?
checks.why: Call the job 60 units; A does 3 a day and B does 2. The last 5 days are A alone: 15 units. The other 45 were done together at 5 a day: 9 days. Total 9 + 5 = 14 days.

lessons.title: Sharing the pay, and when no one's time is given
lessons.plain: New: two last settings. Wages follow the work done; and some questions are best solved from the options.

teach.x: **Sharing the pay.** When people are paid for a job done together, the fair rule is: **money follows work**. Each person's share is in the ratio of the units they did.

If everyone works for the same number of days, the units done are in the ratio of their units per day. "A takes 10 days and B takes 15 days; together they earn Rs 3,000." Call the job 30 units: A does 3 a day and B does 2. The pay is shared 3 : 2, so A gets Rs 1,800.
Notice it is **not** shared in the ratio of the days, 10 : 15. The one who needs fewer days is the better worker and earns more.
If a helper C joins so that the job is done faster, find C's units per day by subtraction (lesson 3), and then share in the ratio of all three.
**When nobody's time is given.** A few questions give no one's days outright: "A takes 10 days less than B. Together they take 12 days. How long does A take?"
Solving this properly needs a heavier equation than anything else in the topic. It is fair to say so, and it is fair not to use it. **The options are part of the question.** Try them.

items.x: Take an option for A, say 20 days. Then B takes 30.
Check with the units method: job 60 units, A does 3 a day, B does 2, together 5 a day, 12 days. It matches.

teach.x: Start with a middle option. If the time together comes out too long, the true answer is a smaller number; if too short, a larger one. Two tries are usually enough.

tags: Two workers share the pay.
A helper joins: find the helper's share.
No one's time is given: try the options.
The same puzzle with pipes.
A real paper's version: "6 days more than twice the time together".

example.q: A can do a job in 6 days and B can do it in 12 days. They do it together and are paid Rs 900. What is B's share?
steps: Call the job 12 units. A does 2 a day and B does 1.
They work the same days, so the work done is in the ratio 2 : 1.
Money follows work: 3 parts = 900, so one part = 300.
B has 1 part: Rs 300.

checks.q: A takes 5 days less than B to do a job. Working together they take 6 days. In how many days can A alone do it?
checks.why: Try 10 for A, so B takes 15. Job 30 units: A does 3 a day and B does 2, together 5 a day, which is 6 days. It matches. (15 is B.)

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: Distance = Speed × Time, and one of the three is always fixed.** Find which one is fixed and the other two become a simple ratio.

rows: Speed and time are upside-down partners
Twice the time, twice the distance

blocks.x: **The ratio-parts algorithm (use it on most questions):**

items.x: Write the speed ratio in small whole numbers.
Same distance? Flip it to get the time ratio.
The question gives a gap (“30 minutes more”, “15 minutes late and early”). That gap = the difference in parts.
Find one part, then the part asked.

blocks.x: **Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **Units.** km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5. Minutes to hours: divide by 60.
**Two bodies.** Towards each other: add the speeds. Same direction: subtract the speeds. Time = gap ÷ that combined speed.
**Train passing something.** Distance = train’s own length + length of the thing passed. A pole or a man has zero length. A platform, bridge or other train has length.
**Train passing a moving man or another train.** Use add or subtract speeds as above, with the distance from the line before.
**Average speed** = total distance ÷ total time. Never the plain average of the speeds, unless the times are equal.
**Head start.** First move the early starter alone, then treat what is left as a fresh two-body question.

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: km/h to m/s (worth memorising)**
**Speed change to time change (same distance)**
**Non-linear warning.** Going at 40 and returning at 60 does not average 50; it averages 48. And 25% more speed does not save 25% of the time; it saves 20%.

**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** convert everything to the same units, then write Distance = Speed × Time for each leg or each body and line them up. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Counts are out of the 394 bank questions; the PYQ figure is IBPS Clerk Prelims questions; the sister figure is from the 17 sister questions.

rows: One train passes a pole, platform or bridge
Ratio of speeds, times or distances
Average speed and journeys in parts
Two bodies meeting or chasing (no lengths)
Plain distance = speed × time, unit change
Speed change gives time change (late/early, usual time)

lead.x: Seven bank questions fit no archetype (races, circular track, right-angle directions, a sum of hourly distances) and none of those ideas appeared in any paper opened. They are left out.
What stands out: 13 of the 20 Clerk PYQs and 9 of the 17 sister questions are train questions. Trains is where this topic’s marks are.

items.title: One train passes a pole, platform or bridge

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “crosses a pole in…, crosses a platform in…”.

**Shortcut engine.** pole time covers the train’s length. Platform time covers train + platform. So the **extra seconds cover exactly the platform**. Speed = platform length ÷ extra seconds. Train length = speed × pole time.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 2).** bridge 240 m in 28 s, pole in 16 s. Extra 12 s covers 240 m, so speed 20 m/s = 72 km/h. Length = 20 × 16 = 320 m.

items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** two trains, “opposite direction” or “same direction” or “overtakes”.
**Shortcut engine.** distance = sum of both lengths. Speed = sum of speeds (opposite) or difference (same direction). Work in m/s.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Dec 2020).** lengths add to 600 m, crossed in 20 s in opposite directions, so combined speed 30 m/s = 108 km/h. A does 36, so B does 72 km/h.

items.title: Ratio of speeds, times or distances

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “speeds in the ratio 3 : 4”, “A takes 30 minutes more than B”.
**Shortcut engine.** the ratio-parts algorithm from section 1.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017 model paper).** speeds A : B = 3 : 4, same distance, so times 4 : 3. One part = 30 minutes. A = 4 parts = 2 hours.

items.label: Confirmed

items.title: Average speed and journeys in parts

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “goes at… returns at…”, “first part by bus, rest by car”.
**Shortcut engine.** for a go-and-return, pick the distance as the LCM of the two speeds, find each time, then total distance ÷ total time. For parts, find each leg’s time and add.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** 60 km/h out, 90 km/h back. Take 180 km each way: 3 h + 2 h = 5 h for 360 km. Average 72 km/h.

items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** two towns, two start times, “when do they meet”, “how far from A”.
**Shortcut engine.** if one starts early, move it alone first. Then time to meet = remaining gap ÷ sum of speeds (or ÷ difference if chasing).

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017 model paper).** 330 km apart. First train leaves at 7 a.m. at 60 km/h; second leaves the other end at 8 a.m. at 75 km/h. By 8 a.m. the gap is 270. Closing speed 135, so 2 hours. They meet at 10 a.m.
**Pattern clues.** one body, or two bodies with a simple link between their speeds; often a unit change.
**Shortcut engine.** find the one speed you can, apply the link, multiply.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 3 Sep 2022 Slot 2).** car does D km in 50 minutes at 36 km/h, so D = 30 km. Bike must do 60 km in 40% less time, which is 30 minutes. Speed = 120 km/h.
**Pattern clues.** “late by… early by…”, “usual time”, “by what percent should he increase his speed”.
**Shortcut engine.** same distance, so time ratio is the speed ratio flipped. The minutes gained or lost = the difference in parts.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2021).** he wants to cut the time by three-fifths, so the new time is 2/5 of the old. Speed must become 5/2 of the old, which is 150% more. The 20 km and the 5 km/h are not needed.
**Pattern clues.** “a man walking in the same/opposite direction”.
**Shortcut engine.** distance = train length only. Speed = add (opposite) or subtract (same direction).

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** 300 m train crosses a 190 m platform in 14 s, so speed = 490 ÷ 14 = 35 m/s. Raised 20% = 42 m/s. Man at 10.8 km/h = 3 m/s, opposite direction, so 45 m/s. Time = 300 ÷ 45 = 6.67 s.
**Shortcut engine.** minutes stopped per hour = (speed lost ÷ speed without stops) × 60.
**Worked example (bank CON-TSD-11).** 60 km/h without stops, 48 km/h with stops. Lost 12 out of 60, so the bus stops 12 minutes in every hour.

lead.x: All eight questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was checked by script. One drill per Core archetype.

body.x: A train crosses a pole in 12 seconds and a 180 m long platform in 21 seconds. What is the length of the train (in metres)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let the length be L and speed S. L = 12S and L + 180 = 21S. Subtract: 180 = 9S, S = 20 m/s, L = 240 m.
**30-Second Exam Method:** extra 9 seconds cover the 180 m platform, so speed = 20 m/s. Length = 20 × 12 = 240. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none that finishes it; the direct route is two divisions. Back-check: 240 + 180 = 420 m in 21 s is 20 m/s, same as 240 m in 12 s.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** dividing 180 by 21 instead of by the extra 9 seconds. The platform time includes the train’s own length.

body.x: A man rides to his office at 40 km/h and returns by the same road at 60 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole trip (in km/h)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** average speed = 2 × 40 × 60 ÷ (40 + 60) = 4,800 ÷ 100 = 48.
**30-Second Exam Method:** take the road as 120 km. Going takes 3 h, returning 2 h. 240 km in 5 h = 48. **Answer (C).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** he spends more time at the slower speed, so the average sits below the middle value 50. That removes 50 and 52. Back-check: 120 ÷ 40 + 120 ÷ 60 = 5 hours, and 240 ÷ 5 = 48.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 50, the plain average of 40 and 60, is option (A). The same question came in IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 (60 and 90) and SBI Clerk Prelims 20 Sep 2025 (20 and 30).

body.x: Riding his scooter at 30 km/h, Ravi reaches office 10 minutes late. At 40 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early. How far is the office (in km)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let the distance be d. d/30 − d/40 = 15/60, so d/120 = 1/4 and d = 30.
**30-Second Exam Method:** speeds 3 : 4, so times 4 : 3. The gap of 1 part = 10 + 5 = 15 minutes. Time at 30 km/h = 4 parts = 60 minutes. Distance = 30 km. **Answer (D).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** test an option: the two travel times must differ by exactly 15 minutes. 20 km gives 40 and 30 minutes (gap 10), out. 30 km gives 60 and 45 minutes (gap 15), fits. Back-check done in the same step.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** late and early are on opposite sides of the right time, so the gap is 10 + 5, not 10 − 5.

body.x: The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 6. For the same journey A takes 20 minutes more than B. How many minutes does A take?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let B’s time be t minutes; A’s is t + 20. Same distance: 5(t + 20) = 6t, so t = 100 and A takes 120.
**30-Second Exam Method:** speeds 5 : 6, so times 6 : 5. One part = 20 minutes. A = 6 parts = 120. **Answer (E).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** A’s time is 6 parts, so it must be a multiple of 6. That leaves 90 and 120. With 90 one part would be 15, not 20. Back-check: 120 and 100 are 6 : 5 and differ by 20.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 100 is B’s time and it is option (A). Also, forgetting to flip the ratio gives A the smaller time, which contradicts “A takes more”.

body.x: Towns X and Y are 350 km apart. A car leaves X for Y at 8:00 a.m. at 50 km/h. Another car leaves Y for X at 9:00 a.m. at 70 km/h. At what time do they meet?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let them meet t hours after 9:00. 50(t + 1) + 70t = 350, so 120t = 300 and t = 2.5.
**30-Second Exam Method:** by 9:00 the first car has done 50 km, so the gap is 300 km. Closing speed 50 + 70 = 120. 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 hours after 9:00 = 11:30. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** options are clock times, so do not try one. Back-check: first car 3.5 h × 50 = 175, second 2.5 h × 70 = 175, total 350.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** ignoring the head start (350 ÷ 120 hours after 8:00) gives 10:55, which is option (A).

body.x: Two trains, 220 m and 180 m long, run in the same direction on parallel tracks at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. How many seconds does the faster train take to pass the slower one completely?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** relative speed = 54 − 36 = 18 km/h = 18 × 5/18 = 5 m/s. Distance = 220 + 180 = 400 m. Time = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 s.
**30-Second Exam Method:** same direction, so subtract: 15 − 10 = 5 m/s. Lengths add: 400 m. 400 ÷ 5 = 80. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** overtaking is slow. Even at the faster train’s full 15 m/s, 400 m takes about 27 s, so anything at or below that (16) is impossible. Back-check: 80 × 5 = 400.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding the speeds (the opposite-direction rule) gives 16, option (B). Using only one length gives 44 or 36.

body.x: A 240 m long train runs at 63 km/h. How many seconds does it take to pass a man walking at 9 km/h in the same direction?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** relative speed = 63 − 9 = 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Time = 240 ÷ 15 = 16 s.
**30-Second Exam Method:** subtract speeds: 54 km/h is 15 m/s from the grid. 240 ÷ 15 = 16. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed. Back-check: 16 × 15 = 240.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** if the man walked the opposite way the answer would be 240 ÷ 20 = 12, which is option (A). The Clerk paper of 5 Oct 2025 used the opposite direction. Read the direction word.

body.x: A covers 96 km in 3 hours. A’s speed is 20% less than B’s speed. How many km does B cover in 5 hours?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** A’s speed = 32 km/h. 32 = 0.8 × B’s speed, so B = 40 km/h. In 5 hours B covers 200 km.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 20% less means A : B = 4 : 5. A is 32, so one part is 8 and B is 40. 40 × 5 = 200. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** B is faster than A, and A would do 160 km in 5 hours, so the answer is above 160. That removes 160. Back-check: 40 less 20% is 32.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “A is 20% less than B” is not “B is 20% more than A”. Adding 20% to 32 gives 38.4 and then 192, which is option (A).

rows: Extra seconds cover the platform; speed, then length
Lengths add; speeds add (opposite) or subtract (same)
Speeds in a ratio, “takes t more”
Flip to time ratio; gap = difference in parts
Goes at a, returns at b
LCM distance, total distance ÷ total time
Percent of distance, not of time
Move the early one first; gap ÷ closing speed
One body, a link between two speeds
Find one speed, apply the link, multiply
Time ratio = flipped speed ratio; minutes = parts gap
Train length only; add or subtract speeds

blocks.x: **Five facts to carry in:**

items.x: Same distance: speed ratio flipped = time ratio.
Towards each other add speeds; same direction subtract.
Crossing distance = own length + length of the thing crossed (zero for a pole or a man).
Average speed for equal distances is always below the plain average.
