intro.x: Everything in this topic comes from one relation: **distance = speed x time**. The questions differ only in which of the three is the same for both parts of the story.

There are eight short lessons, about people and vehicles on the move. Go in order the first time. **Trains** now have a topic of their own, which adds one idea (a train has length); it is the natural one to do straight after this.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the km/h to m/s table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
When a question looks tangled, come back to two plain checks: are my units the same, and what exactly is the distance being covered?

lessons.title: Distance, speed and time
lessons.plain: The starting point: one small relation, and the habit of keeping the units the same.

teach.x: **Speed** tells you how much distance is covered in each unit of time. 60 km/h means 60 kilometres in every hour. From that one sentence you get the only relation this topic needs:
**distance = speed x time**
Know any two and you have the third: speed = distance / time, and time = distance / speed.
Nearly every slip in the early questions is a **units** slip. Before you multiply or divide, make sure the units agree.

items.x: If the speed is in km/h, the time must be in hours and the distance in km.
If the speed is in m/s (metres per second), the time must be in seconds and the distance in metres.

teach.x: To change between the two kinds of speed:

items.x: **km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18.** 72 km/h is 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s.
**m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5.** 10 m/s is 36 km/h.

teach.x: Where does 5/18 come from? One kilometre is 1,000 metres and one hour is 3,600 seconds, and 1,000 / 3,600 = 5/18. A handy anchor: **18 km/h is 5 m/s**, so 36 is 10, 54 is 15, 72 is 20 and 90 is 25.
For minutes, remember that 30 minutes is half an hour and 50 minutes is 50/60 = 5/6 of an hour.

tags: km/h and seconds: change the speed first.
Find a speed, and give it in km/h.
Two speeds to compare.
One speed found from another through a ratio.
A letter for the distance, and a percent cut in the time.

example.q: A bus is moving at 54 km/h. How many metres does it cover in 20 seconds?
steps: The time is in seconds and the answer is wanted in metres, so change the speed to m/s.
Distance = speed x time = 15 x 20 = 300 metres.

checks.q: A man walks 900 metres in 10 minutes. What is his speed in km/h?
checks.why: 10 minutes is 600 seconds, so his speed is 900 / 600 = 1.5 m/s. In km/h: 1.5 x 18/5 = 5.4. (1.5 is the speed in m/s.)

lessons.title: The same distance at two speeds
lessons.plain: New: two people, or one person on two days, cover the same distance. Faster means less time, in the opposite ratio.

teach.x: When the **distance is the same**, speed and time pull in opposite directions. Go twice as fast and you need half the time.
So if two speeds are in the ratio 3 : 4, the times for the same distance are in the ratio **4 : 3**. Just turn the ratio round.
This turns a whole family of questions into ratio questions. They never tell you the distance; they tell you a **gap in time**.
"The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3. A takes 15 minutes more than B for the same distance."

items.x: Times are 3 : 2.
The gap in time is 3 - 2 = 1 part, and it is 15 minutes.
So A takes 45 minutes and B takes 30.

teach.x: The same idea covers one person changing speed. "Walking at three-fourths of his usual speed, a man is 20 minutes late." His speed is 3/4 of usual, so his time is **4/3** of usual. The extra one-third of his usual time is the 20 minutes, so his usual time is 60 minutes.
Words such as "twice as fast" are a speed ratio in disguise: 2 : 1. A chain of them ("A is twice as fast as B, and B is thrice as fast as C") is built up from the slowest: C is 1, B is 3, A is 6.

tags: A speed ratio and a gap in time.
The same, as a real paper asked it, in hours.
A chain of "twice" and "thrice".
One person, slower than usual.
A train below its usual speed: how much time would be saved?

example.q: The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3. To cover the same distance, A takes 15 minutes more than B. How long does B take?
steps: Same distance, so turn the speed ratio round: times are 3 : 2.
The gap in time is 3 - 2 = 1 part = 15 minutes.
B has 2 parts: 30 minutes.

checks.q: Walking at four-fifths of his usual speed, a man reaches his office 10 minutes late. What is his usual time?
checks.why: Speed is 4/5 of usual, so time is 5/4 of usual. The extra quarter is 10 minutes, so the usual time is 40 minutes. (50 is today's time.)

shortcut.title: A change in speed as a fraction

text.x: If the speed goes up by **1/n**, the time comes down by **1/(n + 1)**. If the speed comes down by 1/n, the time goes up by 1/(n - 1). It is the turn-around from Percentages once more.
Speed up by 1/4 (25% faster): time is 1/5 less. Speed down by 1/4: time is 1/3 more.
So "at three-fourths of his speed he is 20 minutes late": the speed is down by 1/4, the time is up by 1/3, and 1/3 of the usual time is 20 minutes.

lessons.title: Late, early, and changing the speed
lessons.plain: New: the gap in time comes from being late one day and early another, or the speed must change to save time.

teach.x: "At 40 km/h he reaches office 10 minutes late. At 50 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early." This is last lesson's question with the gap in time hidden.
Late on one day and early on the other: the two journeys differ by 10 + 5 = **15 minutes**. (If he were late on both days, by 10 and by 4 minutes, the gap would be the difference, 6 minutes.)
Now proceed as before.

items.x: Speeds 40 : 50 = 4 : 5, so times are 5 : 4.
The gap is 1 part = 15 minutes.
At 40 km/h he takes 5 parts = 75 minutes, which is 1.25 hours.
Distance = 40 x 1.25 = 50 km.

teach.x: **Changing the speed to save time.** "A car covers 450 km in 9 hours. By how much must its speed rise to do it in 7.5 hours?" Find both speeds and subtract. Present speed 50, needed speed 60: a rise of 10 km/h. Read whether the question wants the **new speed** or the **increase**.
If the time is to be cut by a fraction, think of what is **left**. Cutting the time by three-fifths leaves two-fifths of it, so the speed must become 5/2 of what it was, which is 150% more.

**When only a difference in speed and a difference in time are given**, such as "10 km/h faster would save 1 hour over 200 km", the proper method is a heavier equation. Test the options instead: try a speed, work out both times, and see whether they differ by an hour.

tags: Late at one speed, early at another.
How much faster to save time?
The time is cut by a fraction; it asks for a percent.
Only differences are given: test the options.
Walking and riding, both ways.

example.q: Travelling at 30 km/h a man reaches his office 10 minutes late. Travelling at 40 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early. Find the distance to his office.
steps: Late one day, early the other: the journeys differ by 10 + 5 = 15 minutes.
Speeds 30 : 40 = 3 : 4, so times are 4 : 3.
The gap is 1 part = 15 minutes.
At 30 km/h he takes 4 parts = 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Distance = 30 x 1 = 30 km.

checks.q: A car covers a certain distance in 6 hours at 50 km/h. At what speed must it travel to cover the same distance in 5 hours?
checks.why: Distance = 50 x 6 = 300 km. In 5 hours: 300 / 5 = 60 km/h.

shortcut.title: Late and early in one line

text.x: For two speeds **a** and **b** over the same distance, with a time gap **t** between the journeys:
**distance = (a x b x t) / (b - a)**
Use hours for t. With 40 km/h and 50 km/h and a gap of 15 minutes (1/4 hour): (40 x 50 x 1/4) / 10 = 50 km.
It is the ratio method with the steps folded together. If you forget it, the ratio method is always there.

lessons.title: Average speed
lessons.plain: New: a journey at two or more speeds. The average speed is total distance over total time, never the average of the speeds.

teach.x: "A man goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. What is his average speed?" The tempting answer is 50. It is wrong, and seeing why is the lesson.
He spends **more time** on the slow leg than on the fast one, so the slow speed counts for more. The honest definition is:
**average speed = total distance / total time**
When the distance is not given, **choose one that suits you**. Pick a number both speeds go into: 120 km each way.

items.x: Going: 120 / 40 = 3 hours. Returning: 120 / 60 = 2 hours.
Total distance 240 km, total time 5 hours.
Average speed = 240 / 5 = 48 km/h.

teach.x: Any distance you choose gives 48. It is a little below 50, as it should be.
First check **what is equal** in the question.

items.x: **Equal distances** (there and back, or "one-third of the way at each speed"): choose a convenient distance, as above.
**Times are given** ("5 km/h for 2 hours, then 15 km/h for 3 hours"): simply add up the distances and divide by the total time.

teach.x: Average speed also works backwards. If the average speed for a return trip is 48 km/h and the trip takes 5 hours, the total distance is 240 km, so one way is 120 km.

tags: There and back.
The same, as a real paper asked it.
Times are given, not distances.
Three equal parts.
Backwards: the total time is given, find the distance.

example.q: A man goes to a town at 30 km/h and comes back at 20 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole journey?
steps: Equal distances, so choose one that both speeds go into: 60 km each way.
Going: 60 / 30 = 2 hours. Returning: 60 / 20 = 3 hours.
Total distance 120 km, total time 5 hours.
Average speed = 120 / 5 = 24 km/h.

checks.q: A car travels at 30 km/h for 2 hours and then at 60 km/h for 1 hour. What is its average speed?
checks.why: Here the times are given, so add the distances: 60 + 60 = 120 km in 3 hours. 120 / 3 = 40 km/h. (45 is the plain average of the speeds.)

text.x: For two **equal distances** at speeds **a** and **b**, the average speed is:
Use it only when the two distances are equal. If the two **times** are equal instead, the average speed really is the plain average of the two speeds.

lessons.title: A journey in parts
lessons.plain: New: the journey is split into stretches, and the question asks about one stretch, the total time, or the speed still needed.

teach.x: Longer journey questions break the trip into stretches. The method is bookkeeping: **for each stretch, write its distance, its speed and its time.** Two of the three are usually given, and the third is one division away. Then add up what the question asks for.
A small table keeps it tidy.
Three forms come up.
**What speed is needed for the rest?** "He must cover 120 km in 4 hours. He does the first 60 km at 20 km/h." That stretch took 3 hours. So 60 km remain and only 1 hour is left: he needs 60 km/h.

**Two speeds, total distance and total time given.** "400 km in 6 hours, partly at 80 km/h and partly at 60 km/h." Use the "pretend" idea you have met before. Pretend the whole 6 hours was at the slower speed: 360 km. The real distance is 40 km more. Each hour at the faster speed adds 20 km extra, so 2 hours were at 80 km/h, which is 160 km.

**Equal distances, total time given.** "Three equal distances at 3, 4 and 5 km/h take 47 minutes in all." Choose a convenient distance for each part, find the time that would take, and scale to the real time.

tags: Two speeds, total distance and total time.
What speed is needed for the rest?
Two equal halves, and the total time is given.
Three equal distances, total time in minutes.
Four stretches given as percents of the distance.

example.q: A man travels 300 km in 5 hours, partly at 50 km/h and partly at 70 km/h. What distance does he cover at 70 km/h?
steps: Pretend all 5 hours were at the slower speed: 50 x 5 = 250 km.
The real distance is 300 km, which is 50 km more.
Each hour at 70 km/h adds 70 - 50 = 20 km extra.
So the time at 70 km/h is 50 / 20 = 2.5 hours.
Distance at 70 km/h = 70 x 2.5 = 175 km.

checks.q: A man has to cover 120 km in 4 hours. He covers the first 60 km at 20 km/h. At what speed must he cover the rest to arrive on time?
checks.why: The first 60 km takes 3 hours. That leaves 60 km and 1 hour: 60 km/h. (30 km/h is the speed for the whole trip, which is no longer enough.)

lessons.title: Two people moving at once
lessons.plain: New: two moving people or vehicles. What matters is how fast the gap between them shrinks.

teach.x: When two things move at the same time, stop watching each one and **watch the gap between them**.
**Moving towards each other.** If A walks at 25 km/h and B at 35 km/h towards each other, every hour the gap shrinks by 25 + 35 = 60 km. So when they approach, **add the speeds**.
**One chasing the other.** If a policeman runs at 12 km/h after a thief running at 10 km/h, every hour the gap shrinks by only 12 - 10 = 2 km. So when they move the same way, **subtract the speeds**.
Either way:
**time to meet = gap between them / speed at which the gap shrinks**
The speed at which the gap changes is called the **relative speed**. It is not a new kind of speed; it is just how the two speeds combine.
Once you know **when** they meet, anything else follows from the first lesson. How far has A gone? A's speed x that time. How far has A still to go? The total minus that.
Two neat disguises:

items.x: **On a circular track**, going opposite ways, they first meet when they have covered one full lap between them. The gap is the length of the track.
**One reaches the end and turns back.** By the time they meet, the two together have covered **twice** the distance between the ends. Divide that by the sum of their speeds.

teach.x: Keep the units the same here too. A gap of 500 metres with speeds in km/h should be written as 0.5 km.

tags: Towards each other.
A chase, with the gap in metres.
After they meet: how far has one still to go?
A circular track, opposite directions.
One reaches the end and turns back.

example.q: Two cyclists are 90 km apart and ride towards each other at 12 km/h and 18 km/h. After how long do they meet?
steps: They are approaching, so add the speeds: the gap shrinks by 12 + 18 = 30 km every hour.
Time = gap / that speed = 90 / 30 = 3 hours.
Check: in 3 hours they ride 36 km and 54 km, which is 90 km together.

checks.q: A is 200 metres behind B. A runs at 6 m/s and B runs at 4 m/s in the same direction. After how many seconds will A catch B?
checks.why: Same direction, so subtract: the gap shrinks by 2 metres each second. 200 / 2 = 100 seconds. (20 seconds comes from adding the speeds, which is for approaching.)

lessons.title: When one starts earlier
lessons.plain: New: the two do not start together. Let the early one move alone first, then it is last lesson.

teach.x: "A train leaves A at 7 am. Another leaves B at 8 am towards it." The two-body method needs both to be moving. So deal with the lonely stretch first.

items.x: **Let the early starter travel alone** until the other one starts. Work out how far it goes.

**Find the gap at that moment.** If they are approaching, the gap is the distance between the towns **minus** what the early one has covered. If one is chasing the other, the gap **is** what the early one has covered: that is its lead.
**Now both are moving.** Time to meet = gap / speed at which it shrinks (add for approaching, subtract for chasing).
**Count that time from the later start**, and give the answer as a clock time or a distance, whichever is asked.

teach.x: Step 4 is where marks are lost. If the second train left at 8 am and they meet 2 hours after that, the answer is 10 am, not 9 am.
If the question asks **how far from the start** the faster one overtakes, multiply the faster one's speed by the time it has been moving.

tags: Approaching, one hour apart.
The same with trains, from a real paper.
The same again, and the answer is not among the times.
A chase with a half-hour lead.
A chase, and it asks how far from the start.

example.q: A leaves a town at 9 am at 30 km/h. B leaves the same town at 11 am at 50 km/h in the same direction. At what time does B overtake A?
steps: A travels alone from 9 to 11: 30 x 2 = 60 km. That is A's lead.
From 11 am both are moving the same way, so subtract: the gap shrinks by 50 - 30 = 20 km an hour.
Time to close 60 km = 60 / 20 = 3 hours.
Count from 11 am: B overtakes A at 2 pm.

checks.q: Towns X and Y are 200 km apart. A train leaves X at 8 am towards Y at 40 km/h. Another leaves Y at 9 am towards X at 40 km/h. At what time do they meet?
checks.why: By 9 am the first train has covered 40 km, so 160 km separate them. They approach at 80 km an hour: 2 hours. Counting from 9 am, they meet at 11 am.

lessons.title: Two last settings: stoppages, and what happens after they meet
lessons.plain: New: a bus that stops along the way, and two travellers who carry on after passing each other.

teach.x: Two smaller ideas to finish. They come up less often than the rest, and each is quick to learn.
**Stoppages.** "Without stops a bus averages 60 km/h. With stops it averages 48 km/h. How many minutes does it stop in each hour?"

Think about one hour of the journey. Without stopping the bus would cover 60 km. With stops it covers only 48 km, so it has **lost 12 km**. The time it stood still is the time it would have needed to drive those 12 km at its running speed: 12 / 60 of an hour, which is 12 minutes.
**minutes stopped per hour = (distance lost / running speed) x 60**
**After they meet.** "A and B start at the same time towards each other. After they meet, A takes 4 hours to reach the other end and B takes 9 hours. A's speed is 45 km/h; find B's."
There is a neat result for this exact situation. The two speeds are in the ratio of the **square roots of the two times, swapped over**:
**A's speed : B's speed = square root of B's time : square root of A's time**
Here that is the square root of 9 to the square root of 4, which is 3 : 2. A's 45 km/h is 3 parts, so B does 30 km/h.
The times in these questions are always chosen to be perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25), which is the clue that this result is wanted.

A related question gives two trains that each take the same number of hours for the journey but start at different times. That one is a head start in disguise (lesson 7): take each journey as a number of units, and let the early train go alone first.

tags: Stoppages.
After they meet.
Equal journey times, different starts: a head start in disguise.

example.q: Excluding stoppages the speed of a bus is 50 km/h, and including stoppages it is 40 km/h. For how many minutes does the bus stop per hour?
steps: In one hour without stops it would cover 50 km. With stops it covers 40 km.
It has lost 10 km.
At its running speed of 50 km/h, 10 km takes 10 / 50 of an hour.
That is 1/5 of an hour = 12 minutes.

checks.q: Two cars start at the same time towards each other. After they meet, the first takes 1 hour to finish its journey and the second takes 4 hours. If the first car's speed is 60 km/h, what is the second car's speed?
checks.why: Speeds are in the ratio of the square roots of the times, swapped: square root of 4 to square root of 1, which is 2 : 1. The first car's 60 km/h is 2 parts, so the second does 30 km/h.

sample.x: This topic was split out of **Speed, Time & Distance** so that trains could be taught on their own. The paper counts, the question types and the timed drills for trains are in that topic's Quick revision tab.

blocks.x: **One idea:** a train has length. Decide the distance, decide the speed, then distance = speed x time.

rows: a pole, a signal, a standing man
a platform, a bridge, a tunnel, a standing train
add if approaching, subtract if same way
add if opposite, subtract if same way
a man sitting in another train
add or subtract as for two trains

blocks.x: **Units.** Every 18 km/h is 5 m/s: 36 is 10, 54 is 15, 72 is 20, 90 is 25, 108 is 30.
**Pole and platform together.** Speed = platform / extra time. Train : platform = pole time : extra time.
**Completely inside a tunnel.** Distance = tunnel - train.
**Opposite and same direction both given.** One gives the speeds added, the other subtracted. Faster = half of (sum + difference).
**Traps.**

items.x: Leaving the speed in km/h when the lengths are in metres.
Giving the total distance when the platform or tunnel alone was asked.
Stopping at the combined speed when the train's own speed was asked.
Adding both lengths when a passenger, not a train, is being passed.
Treating a station-to-station question (km and hours) as a train-length question.

intro.x: A train question is a Speed, Time and Distance question with one extra thought: a train is long, so passing something means travelling its whole length past it.

There are nine short lessons. Each one changes just one thing: first what is being passed (a pole, a platform, a walking man, another train), then how the exam joins these together. Please go in order the first time. If distance = speed x time is not yet comfortable, do the first lesson of Speed, Time and Distance before this.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the table of who-passes-what on one page.

For any train question, ask yourself three things in order: are the units metres and seconds, whose lengths must go by, and are the speeds added or subtracted? With those answered, only one division is left.

lessons.title: A train has length: passing a pole
lessons.plain: The one new thought in this topic. To pass a pole, a train must move forward by its own length.

teach.x: Train questions are Speed, Time and Distance with one extra thought: **a train has length**. A car is treated as a dot. A train is not.

Picture a train passing a signal pole. The crossing begins when the **front** of the train reaches the pole, and ends when the **back** of the train goes by. In that time the train has moved forward by exactly **its own length**.
So for a pole, a signal, a tree or a man standing still:
**distance travelled = length of the train**
After that it is the usual relation, distance = speed x time. Three things can be asked: the time, the length, or the speed. Fill in the two you know.
**Please watch the units.** Lengths are in metres and times are in seconds, so the speed must be in **metres per second**. The question usually gives km/h.

items.x: km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. So 54 km/h = 15 m/s.
m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5. So 20 m/s = 72 km/h.

teach.x: Examiners put the unchanged number in the options on purpose. If a train's speed works out to 20 m/s and the options are in km/h, "20 km/h" will be sitting there waiting.

One more thing you already know from Speed, Time and Distance: for the same train (the same distance), a higher speed means less time, in the opposite ratio. If the speed becomes 3/2 times, the time becomes 2/3.

tags: Length and speed given: find the time.
Speed and time given: find the length.
Find the speed, with the unit trap waiting in the options.
No length at all: the speed changes, so use the ratio.
The speed changes, and the two speeds are in different units.

example.q: A train 240 metres long runs at 54 km/h. How long does it take to pass a signal pole?
steps: Change the speed: 54 x 5/18 = 15 m/s.
To pass a pole the train travels its own length: 240 metres.
Time = 240 / 15 = 16 seconds.

checks.q: A train running at 72 km/h crosses a pole in 9 seconds. What is the length of the train?
checks.why: 72 km/h is 20 m/s. Passing a pole, the train travels its own length: 20 x 9 = 180 metres. (648 comes from multiplying 72 by 9 without changing the units.)

text.x: Every **18 km/h is 5 m/s**. The exam uses the same few speeds again and again, so it is worth knowing them by sight:
For any other speed, break it up. 126 = 108 + 18, so 30 + 5 = 35 m/s.
If the speed is not a multiple of 18 (say 78 km/h), leave it as a fraction, 78 x 5/18 = 65/3 m/s. It nearly always cancels in the next step.

lessons.title: A platform, a bridge, a tunnel
lessons.plain: New: the thing being passed is long too. The train travels its own length plus the length of that thing.

teach.x: Last lesson the train passed a pole, which has no length. Now it passes something **long**: a platform, a bridge or a tunnel.

The crossing begins when the front of the train reaches the platform. It ends when the **back** of the train leaves the far end. Follow the front of the train: it runs the whole platform, and then one more train-length so that the back clears.
**distance travelled = length of the train + length of the platform**

rows: a pole, a signal, a standing man
a platform, a bridge, a tunnel
its own length + the length of that thing

teach.x: When the question asks for the platform or the tunnel, find the whole distance first (speed x time) and then **take away the train**. The whole distance is always in the options as a trap.
Two small variations appear now and then:

items.x: **"For how long is the train completely inside the tunnel?"** The train is fully inside from the moment its back enters until its front reaches the far end. The front travels the tunnel **minus** the train's length.
**A man crosses the platform.** A man has no length, so the distance is the platform alone. Always ask who is doing the crossing.

tags: Train and platform given: find the time.
Find the tunnel: take the train away from the total.
A pole first to get the speed, then a platform.
Train and platform are equally long.
Completely inside the tunnel: tunnel minus train.
It is a man who crosses the platform, not the train.

example.q: A train 120 metres long runs at 36 km/h. How long does it take to cross a platform 180 metres long?
steps: Change the speed: 36 km/h = 10 m/s.
The train travels its own length plus the platform: 120 + 180 = 300 metres.
Time = 300 / 10 = 30 seconds.

checks.q: A train 200 metres long running at 20 m/s crosses a bridge in 25 seconds. How long is the bridge?
checks.why: In 25 seconds the train travels 20 x 25 = 500 metres. That is the train and the bridge together, so the bridge is 500 - 200 = 300 metres. (500 forgets to take away the train.)

lessons.title: A pole and a platform in one question
lessons.plain: New: the same train passes a pole and a platform, and neither its length nor its speed is given. The extra time is spent on the platform alone.

teach.x: "A train crosses a pole in 24 seconds and a 200-metre platform in 36 seconds." Neither the train's length nor its speed is given. The Clerk papers come back to this form often, and it has a very pleasant way in. **Compare the two crossings.**

items.x: Passing the pole, the train travels its own length.
Passing the platform, it travels its own length **and** the platform.

teach.x: So the only difference between the two is the platform. The extra distance is 200 metres, and the extra time is 36 - 24 = 12 seconds.
**speed = length of the platform / extra time**
Here that is 200 / 12 = 50/3 m/s. And the train's length is what it travels while passing the pole: 50/3 x 24 = 400 metres.
The same comparison works whichever piece is missing.

items.x: If the **speed** is given and the platform is asked: platform = speed x extra time.
If there are **two platforms** and no pole: the extra distance is the difference between the platforms, and the extra time is the difference between the two times.
A **standing train** is just a platform. "Train A crosses a stationary train B" means A travels its own length plus B's length.

tags: Pole and platform: find the train.
The same, with the speed asked too.
The train is known this time: find the platform.
The speed is given: platform = speed x extra time.
Two platforms and no pole.
A standing train plays the part of the platform.

example.q: A train crosses a pole in 10 seconds and a platform 150 metres long in 25 seconds. Find the length of the train.
steps: Compare the two crossings. The extra distance is the platform: 150 metres.
The extra time is 25 - 10 = 15 seconds.
Passing the pole, the train travels its own length: 10 x 10 = 100 metres.

checks.q: A train crosses a pole in 8 seconds and a bridge 300 metres long in 20 seconds. What is the speed of the train?
checks.why: The extra distance is the bridge, 300 metres, covered in the extra 20 - 8 = 12 seconds. 300 / 12 = 25 m/s. (15 m/s divides 300 by the whole 20 seconds, forgetting the train's own length.)

shortcut.title: The train's length in one line

text.x: When a train passes a pole in **p** seconds and a platform in **t** seconds, the lengths are in the ratio of the times:
**train : platform = p : (t - p)**
Pole 24 seconds, 200-metre platform 36 seconds: train : platform = 24 : 12 = 2 : 1, so the train is 400 metres.
It is the lesson's idea with the speed skipped: at one speed, twice the time means twice the length.

lessons.title: A train passing someone who is walking
lessons.plain: New: the person moves too. The distance is still one train-length, but the speeds now combine: add if they approach, subtract if they go the same way.

teach.x: So far the thing being passed stood still. Now it is a **person who is walking**.
A person has no length. So the distance is still **the train's own length**, as with a pole.
What changes is the speed. What matters is how fast the train moves **compared with the person**:

items.x: walking **towards** the train: they close in on each other, so **add** the speeds;
walking **the same way** as the train: the train only gains slowly, so **subtract** the speeds.

teach.x: **time = length of the train / (speeds added or subtracted)**
It is easiest to add or subtract in km/h first, and change to m/s once.

When the **train's speed is asked**, work backwards in the same order. "A train 125 metres long passes a man running at 5 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds." The train gains on him at 125 / 10 = 12.5 m/s, which is 45 km/h. That 45 is the **difference** of the two speeds, so the train is doing 45 + 5 = 50 km/h.
Please do not stop at the 45. It is the speed of the train **as the man sees it**, not the train's real speed, and it is always among the options.

tags: The man comes towards the train: find the time.
The man goes the same way: find the train's speed.
Get the train's real speed from the man, then use it on a platform.
Two walkers, one train: its length is the same both times.
Exam wording: a platform gives the speed, the speed changes, then a man.

example.q: A train 200 metres long passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 12 seconds. Find the speed of the train.
steps: The man has no length, so the distance is the train's length: 200 metres.
The train gains on him at 200 / 12 = 50/3 m/s.
Same direction, so that is the difference of the speeds. Train = 60 + 6 = 66 km/h.

checks.q: A train 150 metres long runs at 50 km/h. How long does it take to pass a man running at 4 km/h in the opposite direction?
checks.why: Opposite directions: 50 + 4 = 54 km/h = 15 m/s. The distance is the train's length, 150 metres. 150 / 15 = 10 seconds.

lessons.title: Two trains passing each other
lessons.plain: New: the other thing is a moving train. Both lengths are added, and the speeds are added or subtracted as before.

teach.x: Now put the last two lessons together. The thing being passed is long (like a platform) **and** it is moving (like the walking man).
**The distance** is the sum of the two lengths. Each train has to get completely clear of the other.
**The speed** combines exactly as it did with the walking man:

items.x: running in **opposite** directions: **add** the speeds;
running in the **same** direction (one overtaking the other): **subtract** the speeds.

teach.x: **time = (length of one + length of the other) / (speeds added or subtracted)**
Combine the speeds in km/h first and change to m/s once. 40 km/h and 50 km/h in opposite directions give 90 km/h, which is 25 m/s.
Overtaking is slow, because the difference in speeds is small. If your answer for the same direction comes out shorter than for opposite directions, the speeds have been combined the wrong way round.
If the question asks for the **other train's speed**, find the combined speed first (total length / time), change it to km/h, and then take away, or add back, the speed you know.
If a train's speed is not given but its time to pass a pole is, that is lesson 1: speed = its length / that time.

tags: Opposite directions: add the speeds.
Same direction: subtract the speeds.
Equal trains: the distance is two lengths.
Find the other train's speed.
The same, with only the sum of the lengths given.
No speeds given: get each one from its pole time.

example.q: Two trains 100 metres and 200 metres long run in opposite directions at 36 km/h and 72 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other?
steps: Distance = both lengths: 100 + 200 = 300 metres.
Opposite directions, so add the speeds: 36 + 72 = 108 km/h.
Change to m/s: 108 km/h = 30 m/s.
Time = 300 / 30 = 10 seconds.

checks.q: The same two trains, 100 metres and 200 metres long, now run in the same direction at 36 km/h and 72 km/h. How long does the faster train take to pass the slower one?
checks.why: The distance is still 300 metres. Same direction, so subtract: 72 - 36 = 36 km/h, which is 10 m/s. 300 / 10 = 30 seconds, three times as long as before.

lessons.title: A person sitting in the other train
lessons.plain: New: two trains again, but the question is about a passenger. A passenger is a dot, so only one length counts.

teach.x: This is a short lesson about one trap that catches a great many people.
"A man sitting in a train sees a goods train pass him in 9 seconds." There are two trains in the story, so it is tempting to add both lengths. Please do not.
The man is a **dot**. He has no length, and the length of the train he is sitting in has nothing to do with it. The goods train has passed him once **its own length** has gone by his window.
But he is **moving**, at the speed of his own train. So the speeds combine as usual: add if the trains run in opposite directions, subtract if they run the same way.
So this is really lesson 4, a train passing a moving person. The person just happens to be travelling fast.
For every train question, these two checks are enough:

items.x: **Whose length must go by?** Only the thing doing the passing, plus the length of what is passed if that is a long thing. A person adds nothing.
**Are they approaching or going the same way?** Add or subtract.

tags: Opposite directions: find the other train's speed.
Same direction, with the slower train's length given only to mislead.

example.q: A man sitting in a train travelling at 40 km/h sees a train 250 metres long, coming the opposite way, pass him in 9 seconds. Find the speed of that train.
steps: The man is a dot. The distance is the other train's length: 250 metres.
Combined speed = 250 / 9 m/s. In km/h: 250/9 x 18/5 = 100 km/h.
Opposite directions, so that is the two speeds added.
Other train = 100 - 40 = 60 km/h.

checks.q: Two trains, 200 metres and 300 metres long, run in the same direction at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. How long does the faster train (200 m) take to pass a man sitting in the slower train?
checks.why: Only the faster train's 200 metres must go by the man. Same direction: 72 - 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. 200 / 5 = 40 seconds. (100 seconds uses both lengths.)

lessons.title: Opposite and same direction in one question
lessons.plain: New: the same two trains are described twice. One sentence gives the speeds added, the other gives them subtracted.

teach.x: Here the question gives the same two trains crossing **twice**, or ties their speeds together with a ratio. Each sentence gives you one fact about the two speeds.
"Two trains, each 100 metres long, cross in 8 seconds going opposite ways and in 40 seconds going the same way."

items.x: Opposite: 200 / 8 = 25 m/s. That is the two speeds **added**.
Same way: 200 / 40 = 5 m/s. That is the two speeds **subtracted**.

teach.x: When you know the sum and the difference of two numbers, the bigger one is half of (sum + difference) and the smaller one is half of (sum - difference). So the faster train does (25 + 5) / 2 = 15 m/s and the slower does 10 m/s.
If you have done Boat and Stream, this is the same step as finding the boat and the stream from the downstream and upstream speeds.

**Speeds tied by a ratio or a percent.** "B is 20% faster than A; they cross in opposite directions in 24 seconds." Find the speeds added together from total length / time. Then share that sum in the ratio of the speeds, here 5 : 6.
In both forms the first step is the same: turn each crossing into one combined speed.

tags: Two crossings: the sum and the difference of the speeds.
One crossing, and the speeds tied by a percent.
Only times are given: write each length as speed x time.

example.q: Two trains, each 150 metres long, cross each other in 6 seconds when running in opposite directions and in 30 seconds when running in the same direction. Find the speed of the faster train.
steps: Distance each time = 150 + 150 = 300 metres.
Opposite: 300 / 6 = 50 m/s, the speeds added.
Same way: 300 / 30 = 10 m/s, the speeds subtracted.
Faster = (50 + 10) / 2 = 30 m/s, which is 108 km/h.

checks.q: Two trains, each 120 metres long, cross in 8 seconds when running in opposite directions and in 24 seconds when running in the same direction. What is the speed of the faster train?
checks.why: Distance = 240 metres. Added: 240 / 8 = 30 m/s. Subtracted: 240 / 24 = 10 m/s. Faster = (30 + 10) / 2 = 20 m/s.

text.x: Two trains pass a standing man in **t1** and **t2** seconds, and pass each other (opposite directions) in **t** seconds. Then:
**speed of first : speed of second = (t - t2) : (t1 - t)**
It is the swap from alligation: 23 is the mixture of 27 and 17, and each train gets the other one's distance from 23.
This form comes up only now and then, so learn it only if the lesson's own way feels slow to you.

lessons.title: Two sentences, two trains: exam wording
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the ideas. Each sentence is a small train question of its own; solve the one with a single unknown first.

teach.x: The newest papers take the ideas you now have and link several of them in one long question. No new formula is needed. The method is to **take one sentence at a time**.
**Write one line for each crossing**, always in the same shape:
**distance to be covered = speed x time**
Then look for the line that has only **one** thing missing. Solve it, and carry its answer into the next line.
"Train A, 200 metres long, crosses train B in the same direction in 100 seconds. The difference of their speeds is 6 m/s. B crosses a 480-metre platform in 40 seconds."

items.x: First sentence: (200 + B's length) = 6 x 100. Only B's length is missing: 400 metres.
Last sentence: (400 + 480) = B's speed x 40. So B does 22 m/s.
A is the one overtaking, so A is faster: 22 + 6 = 28 m/s.

teach.x: **Lengths in a ratio, speeds in a ratio.** "A is half as long as B; their speeds are 4 : 3; they cross the same 100-metre platform in 5 and 10 seconds." Call the lengths L and 2L and the speeds 4v and 3v. The two lines are L + 100 = 20v and 2L + 100 = 30v. Double the first and compare it with the second, and one letter drops out.
These questions are long, not hard. In the exam, if one looks like it will take more than a minute and a half, it is quite all right to mark it and come back.

tags: Overtaking gives a length, a platform gives a speed.
Lengths in a ratio and speeds in a ratio.
The same shape with different numbers: do not reuse the last answer.
Three sentences: find B's speed, write A's, then the overtaking.

example.q: Train A is 150 metres long and overtakes train B, running in the same direction, in 50 seconds. A is 7 m/s faster than B. Train B crosses a 400-metre platform in 30 seconds. Find the speed of train A.
steps: Overtaking: 150 + B's length = 7 x 50 = 350, so B is 200 metres long.
B and the platform: 200 + 400 = 600 metres in 30 seconds, so B does 20 m/s.
A is 7 m/s faster: 27 m/s.

checks.q: Train P is twice as long as train Q, and both run at the same speed. Q passes a pole in 6 seconds. How long does P take to pass a pole?
checks.why: Passing a pole, each train travels its own length. At the same speed, twice the length takes twice the time: 12 seconds.

lessons.title: Station to station: when the length does not matter
lessons.plain: New: a way to recognise the train questions that are not train questions. Over kilometres, a train is a dot again.

teach.x: One last thing, and it is about **recognising** rather than calculating.

Some questions mention trains but give **no lengths in metres and no seconds**. They speak of stations, kilometres, hours and clock times: "A train leaves A at 7 am at 60 km/h. Another leaves B at 8 am..."

Over 300 km, a train a few hundred metres long is a dot. So these are **not** train-length questions. They are the two-travellers questions from Speed, Time and Distance, and everything stays in km and hours.
A short reminder of how those go:

items.x: **Towards each other:** the gap closes at the two speeds **added**. Time to meet = gap / sum of speeds.
**One chasing the other:** the gap closes at the speeds **subtracted**.
**One starts earlier:** let the early train run alone first. See how far it gets, and what gap is left. From then on it is one of the two cases above.

teach.x: So the first thing to do with any train question is to look at the units. **Metres and seconds: lengths matter. Kilometres and hours: they do not.**
These ideas are taught slowly in Speed, Time and Distance, lessons 6 to 8. The questions below are the same ones you will find there.

tags: Start together, towards each other.
One starts an hour earlier.
The same with other numbers, and an answer not in the options.
Same direction: the later train chases.
No speeds at all: only how long each journey takes.

example.q: Stations A and B are 300 km apart. A train leaves A at 6 am at 50 km/h towards B. Another leaves B at 7 am at 75 km/h towards A. When do they meet?
steps: From 6 am to 7 am the first train runs alone: 50 km.
At 7 am the gap is 300 - 50 = 250 km.
Now they approach each other: 50 + 75 = 125 km/h.
250 / 125 = 2 hours after 7 am, which is 9 am.

checks.q: Two trains start at the same time from stations 240 km apart and run towards each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. After how long do they meet?
checks.why: They approach at 50 + 70 = 120 km/h. 240 / 120 = 2 hours. (12 hours comes from subtracting the speeds, which is for chasing.)

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: put the cost price at 100 and walk along the chain.**
Cost Price (CP) → mark up → Marked Price (MP) → discount → Selling Price (SP).

items.x: Profit and loss percent are always measured on **CP**.
Discount percent is always measured on **MP**.
Markup percent is measured on **CP**.

blocks.x: **The CP = 100 algorithm (use it on almost every question):**

items.x: Let CP = 100 units (not rupees).
Apply the markup to get MP in units. Apply the discount to MP to get SP in units.
Whatever rupee figure the question gives (a profit, a discount, a difference) matches some number of units.
Find 1 unit in rupees, then the thing asked.

blocks.x: Example: marked 25% above cost, 20% discount, discount is Rs 50. CP 100, MP 125, SP 100. Discount = 25 units = Rs 50, so 1 unit = Rs 2 and CP = Rs 200.
**Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **Multiplying factors.** 20% profit means × 1.2. 25% discount means × 0.75. Chain them: SP = CP × markup factor × discount factor.
**Successive discounts multiply, they do not add.** 20% then 15% = 0.8 × 0.85 = 0.68, a 32% discount, not 35%.
**Two scenarios, one cost.** “Sold at 25% loss; for Rs 378 more, 20% profit”: the rupee gap equals the percent gap of CP.
**Equal cost prices, two articles.** Take each CP as 100; add the two results; compare with 200.
**Equal selling prices, one at x% profit and one at x% loss:** always an overall loss of x²/100 percent.
**Dishonest dealer selling “at cost”:** gain % = weight cheated ÷ weight actually given × 100.

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: percent to fraction and factor**
**Non-linear warning.** Mark up 40% and discount 25% is not a 15% profit; it is 1.4 × 0.75 = 1.05, a 5% profit. Percentages on different bases never add or subtract.
**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** CP = 100 units, walk the chain, match the rupee figure to units. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Counts are out of the 293 bank questions; the PYQ figure is IBPS Clerk Prelims questions; the sister figure is from the 13 sister questions.

rows: Marked price, discount and profit together
Two articles, overall profit or loss
CP of x articles = SP of y articles
Chain sale (A to B to C)

lead.x: Eleven bank questions are not really profit and loss (plain percentage, linear equations, one partnership question, one caselet that cannot be solved from its text) and are left out.

What stands out: the marked-price chain (P2) is 6 of the 19 Clerk PYQs and 10 of the 13 sister questions. With P3 and P10, which are the same chain in other clothes, it is 12 of 19. No paper opened asked a plain “CP and SP, find profit %” question on its own; that skill only appears as a step inside the others.

items.title: Marked price, discount and profit together

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “marked x% above cost”, “allows a discount of”, a rupee figure for profit or discount.
**Shortcut engine.** CP = 100 units, walk the chain, match rupees to units. If MP is given in rupees, walk it directly.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3).** MP Rs 180, discount 25%, loss 10%. SP = three-quarters of 180 = 135. That is 90% of CP, so CP = 135 ÷ 0.9 = Rs 150.

items.label: Confirmed

items.title: Two articles, overall profit or loss

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “two articles”, “same cost price” or “same selling price”, “overall loss of Rs”.
**Shortcut engine.** equal CPs: take 100 each, add the two results, the net units = the rupee figure. Equal SPs: find each CP by dividing SP by its factor.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 24 Aug 2024 Shift 1).** equal CPs, A at +20%, B at −30%, overall loss Rs 50. On 100 each: +20 − 30 = −10 units = Rs 50, so 1 unit = Rs 5 and each CP = Rs 500. B at 40% profit = Rs 700.

items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “two successive discounts”, “first discount is 10%, find the second”.
**Shortcut engine.** multiply the factors; or peel one discount off and see what factor is left.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 2).** MP Rs 1,050, bought for Rs 756, first discount 10%. After the first: 945. 756 ÷ 945 = 0.8, so the second discount is 20%.
**Pattern clues.** “ratio of marked price to cost price is 5 : 3”.
**Shortcut engine.** use the ratio numbers as the units directly; bring in the third price with its factor.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 12 Dec 2021 Set 2).** MP : CP = 5 : 3, profit 20%. SP = 3 × 1.2 = 3.6. Discount = 5 − 3.6 = 1.4 on 5, which is 28%.
**Pattern clues.** “had he sold it for Rs … more, he would have gained”.
**Shortcut engine.** percent gap between the two scenarios = the rupee gap. Loss to profit: add the two percents. Profit to bigger profit: subtract.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 12 Dec 2021 Set 1).** 25% loss; Rs 378 more gives 20% profit. Gap = 25 + 20 = 45% of CP = 378. CP = Rs 840.
**Pattern clues.** “professes to sell at cost price but uses a weight of”.
**Shortcut engine.** gain % = grams cheated ÷ grams actually given × 100.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** gives 800 g for 1 kg. Cheats 200 on 800 given: 25%.
Profit % = profit ÷ CP × 100. SP = CP × factor. CP = SP ÷ factor.

items.title: CP of x articles = SP of y articles

blocks.x: Profit % = (x − y) ÷ y × 100; negative means loss.
**Example (bank S-MT70-51).** CP of 16 = SP of 12. Gain = 4 on 12 = 33 1/3%.

items.label: Bank only

blocks.x: Multiply every factor along the chain.
**Example.** A sells to B at 20% profit, B to C at 25% profit, C pays Rs 600. A’s cost = 600 ÷ (1.2 × 1.25) = Rs 400.
Find the cost of the whole mixture and the money received for the whole mixture, then treat as P1.
**Example.** 2 kg at Rs 30 and 3 kg at Rs 40 cost Rs 180 for 5 kg; sold at Rs 45 a kg gives Rs 225; profit 45 on 180 = 25%.

lead.x: All seven questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was recomputed. Four cover the required types; the rest give every Core archetype a drill.

body.x: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and allows a 25% discount. What is his profit percent?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let CP = 100. MP = 140. SP = 140 − 25% of 140 = 105. Profit = 5%.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 1.4 × 0.75 = 1.05. Profit 5%. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the discount is taken on a bigger number than the markup, so the profit must be below 40 − 25 = 15. That removes 15. Back-check: three-quarters of 140 is 105.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 40 − 25 = 15 is option (A). RRB Clerk Prelims 13 Dec 2025 Shift 1 asked this exact form with 40% and 20%.

body.x: An article is marked 60% above its cost price and sold at a 25% discount. If the profit is Rs 90, find the marked price (in Rs).

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let CP = c. MP = 1.6c, SP = 1.2c, profit = 0.2c = 90, so c = 450 and MP = 720.
**30-Second Exam Method:** CP 100, MP 160, SP 120. Profit 20 units = Rs 90, so 1 unit = Rs 4.5. MP = 160 units = 720. **Answer (D).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** MP is 160 units and CP is 100 units, so MP must be 8/5 of a whole rupee cost and larger than both CP and SP. 450 is the CP and 540 is the SP of the same article; the largest of that family, 720, is the MP. Back-check: 720 less 25% = 540; 540 − 450 = 90.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** the CP (450) and SP (540) are both in the options. Read which price is asked.

body.x: A jacket marked at Rs 2,500 is sold after two successive discounts of 20% and 15%. What is its selling price (in Rs)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** after 20%: 2,000. After 15% of 2,000 (300): 1,700.

**Option Elimination Hack:** the second discount is taken on a smaller price, so the total discount is less than 35% and SP is more than 1,625. That removes 1,625. Back-check: 2,500 − 500 − 300 = 1,700.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding the discounts (35%) gives 1,625, option (A).

body.x: A trader sells two watches at Rs 1,200 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is his overall result?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** CP of first = 1,200 ÷ 1.2 = 1,000. CP of second = 1,200 ÷ 0.8 = 1,500. Total CP 2,500, total SP 2,400. Loss Rs 100.
**30-Second Exam Method:** same SP, same percent up and down: always a loss of 20 × 20 ÷ 100 = 4% of total CP. Total SP 2,400 is 96% of CP, so CP = 2,500 and loss = 100. **Answer (E).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** equal selling prices with equal gain and loss percent can never break even or give a profit, so (A) and (C) go at once. Back-check: 1,000 + 1,500 = 2,500.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** “same selling price” and “same cost price” behave differently. With the same cost price, +20% and −20% do cancel. Also, 4% of the SP total (Rs 96) is option (B); the 4% is on CP.

body.x: An article is sold at a loss of 12%. Had it been sold for Rs 360 more, there would have been a profit of 8%. Find the cost price (in Rs).

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let CP = c. 1.08c − 0.88c = 360, so 0.2c = 360 and c = 1,800.
**30-Second Exam Method:** from 12% below cost to 8% above cost is a 20% swing = Rs 360. CP = 360 × 5 = 1,800. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** 20% of the answer must be 360; test: 20% of 1,800 = 360. Back-check: 88% of 1,800 = 1,584; add 360 = 1,944 = 108% of 1,800.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** loss and profit sit on opposite sides of cost, so the percents add (12 + 8), not subtract. SBI Clerk Prelims 21 Sep 2025 used profit to bigger profit (20% to 30%), where they subtract.

body.x: The ratio of the marked price to the cost price of an article is 8 : 5. If a discount of 25% is allowed, what is the profit percent?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let MP = 8k and CP = 5k. SP = 75% of 8k = 6k. Profit = k on 5k = 20%.
**30-Second Exam Method:** MP 8, CP 5. Three-quarters of 8 = 6. Profit 1 on 5 = 20%. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** markup is 60% (3 on 5); profit must be less than 60 − 25 = 35. That removes 35. Back-check: 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 60 − 25 = 35 is option (A). And profit is 1 on 5 (CP), not 1 on 6 or 1 on 8.

body.x: A dishonest shopkeeper claims to sell rice at cost price but uses a 900 g weight in place of 1 kg. What is his gain percent?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** he charges for 1,000 g and gives 900 g. Gain = 100 g on a cost of 900 g = 100/900 × 100 = 11 1/9%.
**30-Second Exam Method:** cheated 100, given 900. 100 ÷ 900 = 1/9 = 11 1/9%. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** options are not whole numbers, so do not try one. Back-check: 1/9 is in the grid as 11 1/9%.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** dividing by 1,000 (what he pretends to give) gives 10%, option (A). Divide by what he actually gives.
