intro.x: A shopkeeper buys, puts a price on the tag, gives a discount and sells. This topic is those three prices in a row, and one habit handles nearly all of it: **call the cost price 100 and walk along the row.**
There are twelve short lessons. The first four build the row and are where most exam questions come from. The rest take one variation each. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the fraction table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
When a question feels crowded, ask the same question of every percent in it: percent of what? Profit and mark-up are on the cost; discount is on the marked price.

lessons.title: Cost price, selling price and profit percent
lessons.plain: The starting point: three words, and the rule that profit and loss are always measured on what the thing cost.

teach.x: A shopkeeper buys something and sells it. Three words describe what happens.

items.x: **Cost price (CP)**: what he paid for it. If he also pays for repairs or transport, those are part of the cost.
**Selling price (SP)**: what he sells it for.
**Profit** if he sells for more than it cost; **loss** if he sells for less. Profit = SP - CP.

teach.x: The one rule to fix in your mind: **profit percent and loss percent are always measured on the cost price.** The cost is the 100.
So the easiest way to think is: **call the cost price 100%.**

items.x: A profit of 16% means the selling price is 116% of the cost.
A loss of 8% means the selling price is 92% of the cost.

teach.x: With that, the three basic questions are the three percent questions you already know.
**Find the profit percent.** Bought for 800, sold for 920: profit 120, measured on the cost. 120 / 800 = 15%.
**Find the selling price.** Cost 1,250, profit 16%: 116% of 1,250 = 1,450.

**Find the cost price.** "Sold for 780 at a gain of 30%." The 780 is 130% of the cost. So 1% is 6 and the cost is 600. Going backwards like this is the one that needs care: never take 30% of the selling price.

tags: Find the profit percent.
Find the selling price.
Backwards from a loss: find the cost.
Repairs are part of the cost.
Some of the goods are spoiled.

example.q: By selling an article for Rs 780, a man gains 30%. What is the cost price?
steps: Call the cost 100%. A gain of 30% makes the selling price 130%.
130% of the cost is Rs 780.
Cost price = 100 x 6 = Rs 600.

checks.q: An article bought for Rs 400 is sold for Rs 500. What is the profit percent?
checks.why: Profit = 100, measured on the cost: 100 / 400 = 25%. (20% measures it on the selling price, which is the common slip.)

lessons.title: One article, two selling prices
lessons.plain: New: the same article is imagined sold at two different prices. The gap in rupees is the gap in percent.

teach.x: "An article is sold at a loss of 10%. Had it been sold for Rs 60 more, there would have been a gain of 5%." The cost has not changed. Only the selling price has moved.
Keep the cost at 100%.

items.x: At a loss of 10%, the selling price is 90%.
At a gain of 5%, the selling price is 105%.

teach.x: The two selling prices are 15% of the cost apart, and the question says they are Rs 60 apart. So 15% of the cost is Rs 60, 1% is Rs 4, and the cost is Rs 400.
This is the "what is the only thing that changed?" idea again. **The gap in rupees matches the gap in percent.**
When one is a loss and the other a gain, the gap is the two percents **added** (10 + 5). When both are gains, or both losses, it is their difference.

A close relative: "He sells for Rs 450 at a loss of 10%. At what price should he sell to gain 20%?" Here 90% is 450, so 1% is 5, and 120% is 600. You never need to stop at the cost; go straight from one percent to the other.
And one disguise worth knowing: "The profit on selling at Rs 832 equals the loss on selling at Rs 448." If the profit and the loss are equal, the cost sits exactly **halfway** between the two prices.

tags: From a loss to a gain: find the new price.
A loss and a gain, and the rupee gap between them.
The same, as a real paper asked it.
The profit at one price equals the loss at another.
No rupees at all: the price doubles and the profit trebles.

example.q: An article is sold at a loss of 10%. Had it been sold for Rs 60 more, there would have been a gain of 5%. Find the cost price.
steps: Cost = 100%. First selling price: 90%. Second selling price: 105%.
The gap is 105 - 90 = 15% of the cost.
15% of the cost = Rs 60, so 1% = Rs 4.
Cost price = Rs 400.

checks.q: A man sells an article for Rs 450 at a loss of 10%. At what price should he sell it to gain 20%?
checks.why: 90% of the cost is 450, so 1% is 5. A gain of 20% needs 120%: 120 x 5 = 600. (540 adds 20% to the selling price instead of working from the cost.)

lessons.title: Marked price and discount
lessons.plain: New: a third price, the one on the tag. Discount is measured on the tag; profit is still measured on the cost.

teach.x: Shops rarely sell at the price on the tag. That tag price is the **marked price (MP)**. The shopkeeper takes a **discount** off it, and what is left is the selling price.
So there are now three prices in a row:
**cost price, then marked price, then selling price**
And two different percents, each with its own base. This is the heart of the whole topic:

items.x: **Mark-up** and **profit** are measured on the **cost price**.
**Discount** is measured on the **marked price**.

teach.x: Keep the cost at 100 and walk along the row.
"A shopkeeper marks an article 50% above cost and allows a discount of 20%."

items.x: Cost: 100.
Marked price: 50% above cost, so 150.
Discount: 20% **of 150**, which is 30. Selling price: 120.
Profit: 120 - 100 = 20 on a cost of 100, so 20%.

teach.x: Notice the answer is not 50 - 20 = 30%. The discount was 20% of the bigger number, 150, so it took away more than 20.
You can walk the row in either direction. If you know the selling price and the discount, go back to the marked price by dividing: a 10% discount leaves 90%, so marked price = selling price / 0.9.

tags: Marked price and discount only: find the selling price.
Walk the whole row: mark-up, discount, profit.
Backwards: discount and profit are known, find the mark-up.
A loss instead of a profit, in rupees.
The same goods at two different discounts.

example.q: A shopkeeper marks an article 50% above its cost price and allows a discount of 20%. What is his profit percent?
steps: Call the cost 100.
Marked 50% above cost: marked price = 150.
Discount is 20% of the marked price: 20% of 150 = 30.
Selling price = 150 - 30 = 120.
Profit = 20 on a cost of 100: 20%.

checks.q: The marked price of an article is Rs 800 and a discount of 15% is allowed. What is the selling price?
checks.why: 15% of 800 is 120. Selling price = 800 - 120 = 680. (120 is the discount itself.)

shortcut.title: Mark-up, discount and profit in one line

text.x: With the cost as 100, a mark-up of **m%**, a discount of **d%** and a profit of **p%** are tied together by:
Marked 40% up with a 25% discount: 140 x 75 = 10,500, so 100 + p = 105 and the profit is 5%.
Discount 10% and profit 20%: (100 + m) x 90 = 12,000, so 100 + m = 133 1/3 and the mark-up is 33 1/3%.
It is the walk along the row written as one multiplication.

lessons.title: Marked price questions, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: the same row of three prices, with one rupee figure to match and often a second article or a second scenario.

teach.x: The Clerk papers set this form more than any other in the topic. It is the walk along the row from the last lesson, plus one step you know from every earlier topic: **match the rupee figure to units.**

items.x: Call the cost 100 units. Walk to the marked price and the selling price in units.
The question gives one rupee figure: the profit, the discount, or a difference between two selling prices. Find how many **units** that same thing is.
Rupees / units gives the value of one unit. The cost is 100 of them.

teach.x: "Marked 30% above cost, 10% discount, and the profit is Rs 68." Cost 100, marked price 130, selling price 117. Profit is 17 units, and it is Rs 68. One unit is Rs 4, so the cost is Rs 400.
The disguises:

items.x: **The rupee figure is the discount**, not the profit. The discount in units is marked price minus selling price.
**Two scenarios for the same article** ("had he marked it 50% above and given 12% discount..."). Work out the selling price in units for each, and match the rupee gap to the gap in units.
**A second article** whose cost is described from the first ("the cost of B is 40% more than that of A"). Finish article A completely first; B is then a fresh, short question.
**The discount percent changes** ("from 5% to 10%"). The change in profit is simply that extra slice of the marked price.

tags: The profit in rupees, then a second article.
Two ways of pricing the same article.
The discount percent changes.
Two articles tied by ratios, with equal discounts in rupees.
No rupees: the discount percent equals the profit percent.

example.q: A shopkeeper marks an article 30% above its cost price and allows a discount of 10%. If his profit is Rs 68, find the cost price.
steps: Call the cost 100 units. Marked price = 130 units.
Discount = 10% of 130 = 13 units. Selling price = 117 units.
Profit = 17 units, and the question says it is Rs 68.
One unit = 68 / 17 = Rs 4.
Cost = 100 units = Rs 400.

checks.q: A shopkeeper marks an article 20% above its cost price and allows a discount of 5%. If the discount is Rs 30, what is the cost price?
checks.why: Cost 100 units, marked price 120 units. The discount is 5% of 120 = 6 units. 6 units = Rs 30, so one unit is Rs 5 and the cost is Rs 500. (600 is the marked price.)

lessons.title: When the prices are given as a ratio
lessons.plain: New: instead of percents, the three prices are compared as a ratio. Turn the percent into the same ratio and line them up.

teach.x: "The ratio of the marked price to the selling price is 8 : 7, and the article is sold at a 40% profit." Two facts, in two different languages. Put them into one.
A 40% profit is itself a ratio: selling price to cost price = 140 : 100 = 7 : 5.
Now you have two ratios that share the selling price:

items.x: marked price : selling price = 8 : 7
selling price : cost price = 7 : 5

teach.x: The selling price is 7 in both, so they join at once: **marked : selling : cost = 8 : 7 : 5**. If the shared number were different in the two ratios, you would first make it the same, as in the Basics lesson on joining ratios.
After that it is a plain ratio question. The real number in the question (a difference between two of the prices, usually) matches a number of parts.
This lesson is also the place to settle a small trap. **A percent means nothing until you know what it is a percent of.**

items.x: "A profit of 20%" means 20% of the **cost**, by default.
"A profit of 20% **calculated on the selling price**" is different: selling price 100, profit 20, so the cost is 80, and the profit on cost is 20 / 80 = 25%.
"He gains the selling price of 9 metres" means the profit is described in units of selling price. Write everything in those units before you compare.

tags: Marked to selling as a ratio, with a profit percent.
The same, where the shared number has to be made equal first.
Marked to cost as a ratio: find the discount.
A profit measured on the selling price.
A profit described as "the selling price of 9 metres".

example.q: The ratio of the marked price to the cost price of an article is 3 : 2. A discount of 20% is allowed. What is the profit percent?
steps: Take the marked price as 3 parts and the cost as 2 parts.
A 20% discount leaves 80% of the marked price: 80% of 3 = 2.4 parts. That is the selling price.
Profit = 2.4 - 2 = 0.4 parts, measured on a cost of 2 parts.

checks.q: The profit on an article is 25% of its selling price. What is the profit percent on the cost price?
checks.why: Take the selling price as 100. The profit is 25, so the cost is 75. Profit on cost = 25 / 75 = 33 1/3%.

lessons.title: One discount after another
lessons.plain: New: two discounts in a row. The second is taken on the already reduced price, so they do not simply add.

teach.x: "Two successive discounts of 20% and 10%." **Successive** means one after the other. The second discount is taken on what is left after the first, not on the original price.
You met this idea in Percentages (one change after another). The safe method is the same: **go one step at a time.**

On a marked price of 100: the first discount takes 20, leaving 80. The second takes 10% **of 80**, which is 8, leaving 72. Altogether 28 has come off, so the two discounts are worth a single discount of **28%**, not 30%.
As multipliers: 0.8 x 0.9 = 0.72.
Two successive discounts are always worth a little **less** than their sum, because the second one bites on a smaller price. The order does not matter: 10% then 20% also leaves 72.
Once you have the single discount, the question is an ordinary marked-price question, and the whole of the last two lessons applies:

items.x: find the selling price;
find a missing second discount (divide what he actually paid by the price after the first discount);
carry on to the cost using the profit percent.

tags: Find the single equivalent discount.
A single discount against two successive ones, in rupees.
The second discount is the missing one.
Two discounts, then on to the cost.
The total discount in rupees, and a small profit.

example.q: An article marked at Rs 1,000 is sold after two successive discounts of 20% and 5%. What is the selling price?
steps: First discount: 20% of 1,000 = 200. Price now 800.
Second discount: 5% of 800 = 40. Price now 760.

checks.q: Two successive discounts of 10% and 10% are equivalent to a single discount of:
checks.why: On 100: the first discount leaves 90. The second takes 10% of 90 = 9, leaving 81. Altogether 19 has come off.

text.x: Two successive discounts of **a%** and **b%** equal a single discount of:
It is the "two changes in one line" rule from Percentages with both changes negative.

lessons.title: Offers that are discounts in disguise
lessons.plain: New: "buy 4, get 1 free", and a discount given as a fraction. Turn each into an ordinary discount percent.

teach.x: Shops do not always state a discount as a percent. Two disguises are common.
**"Buy 4, get 1 free."** The customer takes home 5 articles and pays for 4. So 1 out of every 5 is given away: a discount of 1/5, which is 20%.
Be careful which number goes underneath. It is the number **taken home** (5), not the number paid for (4). "Buy 3, get 1 free" is 1 out of 4, a 25% discount.
After that, an offer behaves exactly like a discount. "He marks his goods 50% above cost and offers buy 3, get 1 free": cost 100, marked price 150, a 25% discount leaves 112.5. Profit 12.5%.

**Discounts written as fraction-percents.** A paper may write 11 1/9% or 16 2/3%. These are 1/9 and 1/6 (the Basics lesson on percents that are simple fractions has the list). Treat them as fractions and the arithmetic is light: a discount of 11 1/9% leaves 8/9 of the price.

**Discount compared with profit.** A favourite last line is "the difference between the discount and the profit is Rs 200". Write both in units of the cost and subtract. Discount = marked price - selling price. Profit = selling price - cost price.

tags: Turn an offer into a discount percent.
A mark-up followed by an offer.
Fraction discounts, and discount compared with profit.

example.q: A shop offers "Buy 2, get 1 free". What is the effective discount percent?
steps: The customer takes home 3 articles and pays for 2.
1 out of 3 is free: a discount of 1/3.
1/3 as a percent is 33 1/3%.

checks.q: A shopkeeper marks his goods 60% above the cost price and offers "Buy 3, get 1 free". What is his profit percent?
checks.why: Buy 3, get 1 free is 1 out of 4: a 25% discount. Cost 100, marked price 160, selling price 75% of 160 = 120. Profit 20%.

lessons.title: Two articles with the same cost
lessons.plain: New: two things bought at the same price, sold at different profit or loss percents. Find the overall result.

teach.x: "Two articles have the same cost price. One is sold at a 25% profit and the other at a 15% loss." What happened overall?
Because the costs are equal, give **each** a cost of 100.

items.x: The first sells for 125. The second sells for 85.
Together they cost 200 and sold for 210.
Overall profit: 10 on 200, which is **5%**.

teach.x: The step people forget is that the total cost is **200**, not 100. A gain of 10 units on two articles is 5%, not 10%.
With equal costs, the overall percent is simply the average of the two percents: (25 - 15) / 2 = 5%. Count a loss as negative.
If the question gives the overall profit or loss **in rupees**, match it to units as usual. An overall gain of 10 units that is worth Rs 60 makes one unit Rs 6, so each article cost Rs 600.

**Unequal amounts of goods.** "He sells two-thirds of his goods at 15% profit and the rest at 6% loss." Now the two parts are different sizes, so weight them: two-thirds of 15 is 10, and one-third of 6 is 2. Overall 10 - 2 = 8% profit.

Finally, read on after the overall result. Papers like to finish with a fresh small question about one of the articles ("at what price should B be sold to gain 40%?"), which uses the cost you have just found.

tags: Equal costs, the same percent up and down.
An overall loss in rupees, then a new question about A.
The same pattern, then a new question about B.
The second selling price is described from the first.
Unequal parts of the goods.

example.q: Two articles have the same cost price. One is sold at a 25% profit and the other at a 15% loss, giving an overall profit of Rs 60. Find the cost price of each.
steps: Give each a cost of 100 units. Total cost 200 units.
Selling prices: 125 and 85. Total 210 units.
Overall profit = 10 units, and the question says it is Rs 60.
One unit = Rs 6.
Each article cost 100 units = Rs 600.

checks.q: Two articles are bought at the same price. One is sold at a 30% profit and the other at a 10% loss. What is the overall profit percent?
checks.why: Costs 100 each: 200 in all. Selling prices 130 and 90: 220. Profit 20 on 200 = 10%. (20% forgets that the total cost is 200.)

lessons.title: Two articles sold at the same price, and break-even pairs
lessons.plain: New: this time the selling prices are equal, not the costs. One gains x% and the other loses x%, and the result is always a loss.

teach.x: "A man sells two articles for Rs 1,980 each. On one he gains 10% and on the other he loses 10%." It sounds as if he breaks even. He does not.
The two articles did **not** cost the same. The one sold at a loss cost more (1,980 is only 90% of its cost), so 10% of it is a bigger amount than 10% of the cheaper one. The loss outweighs the gain.
There is a tidy result for exactly this situation. When two articles are sold at the **same price**, one at a gain of **x%** and the other at a loss of **x%**:
**there is always an overall loss, of (x times x) / 100 percent.**
At 10%: a loss of 1%. At 20%: a loss of 4%. At 25%: a loss of 6.25%.

To turn that into rupees: the total selling price is (100 minus that loss) percent of the total cost. With two articles at Rs 1,980 the total is 3,960, which is 99% of the cost. So the cost was 4,000 and the loss is Rs 40.
The rule also runs backwards. If you are told the overall loss is 6.25%, then x times x is 625, so x is 25.

**Break-even pairs.** A different question with a similar look: "He sells one article at a 20% profit and the other at a 10% loss, and on the whole neither gains nor loses." Here the rupees gained on one equal the rupees lost on the other. So 20% of the first cost = 10% of the second cost. You know this form from Percentages: swap the percents to get the ratio. The costs are in the ratio 10 : 20 = 1 : 2.

tags: The rule, turned into rupees.
The rule backwards: the overall loss is given.
A break-even pair.

example.q: A man sells two fans for Rs 1,200 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. Find his overall loss in rupees.
steps: Same selling price, 20% up and 20% down: an overall loss of (20 x 20) / 100 = 4%.
Total selling price = 2,400, which is 96% of the total cost.
1% = 25, so the total cost is Rs 2,500.

checks.q: Two articles are sold at the same price. One is sold at a gain of 10% and the other at a loss of 10%. What is the overall result?
checks.why: Same selling price, x% up and x% down: always a loss of (x times x) / 100 = 1%.

lessons.title: "Had he bought it for less..."
lessons.plain: New: the imagined scenario changes the cost as well as the selling price. Build both scenarios side by side.

teach.x: In lesson 2 only the selling price moved. Here the question imagines a different **cost** too: "He sold it at a 25% profit. Had he bought it for 20% less and sold it for Rs 30 more, he would have gained 75%."
It reads like a tangle, but it unties in the same way as everything else: **call the real cost 100 units, and build the two scenarios side by side.**
The imagined selling price is 140 - 125 = 15 units higher, and the question says that is Rs 30. So one unit is Rs 2 and the real cost is Rs 200.
The one place to slow down: the imagined profit percent is measured on the **imagined cost** (80), not on the original 100. Profit always follows its own cost.

tags: The plain form.
The same, as a real paper asked it.

example.q: A man sold an article at a profit of 25%. Had he bought it for 20% less and sold it for Rs 30 more, he would have gained 75%. Find the cost price.
steps: Real: cost 100 units, profit 25%, selling price 125.
Imagined: cost 20% less = 80 units. Profit 75% of 80 = 60. Selling price 140.
The imagined selling price is 140 - 125 = 15 units more.
15 units = Rs 30, so one unit = Rs 2.
Real cost = 100 units = Rs 200.

checks.q: A man sold an article at a profit of 10%. Had he bought it for 10% less and sold it for Rs 8 more, he would have gained 40%. What is the cost price?
checks.why: Real: cost 100 units, selling price 110. Imagined: cost 90, selling price 140% of 90 = 126. The gap is 16 units = Rs 8, so one unit is Rs 0.50 and the cost is Rs 50.

lessons.title: Counting articles, and sales passed along a chain
lessons.plain: New: "the cost of 20 articles equals the selling price of 16", and an article sold from A to B to C.

teach.x: Two settings that have not appeared in the Clerk papers we checked but are regulars in practice sets.
**Counting articles.** "The cost price of 20 articles is equal to the selling price of 16 articles." No rupees are given, so choose your own. Say each article **costs Re 1**.

items.x: Then 20 articles cost Rs 20.
That same Rs 20 is what he gets for selling 16. So he sells 16 articles, which cost him Rs 16, for Rs 20.
Profit of 4 on a cost of 16: 25%.

teach.x: The same trick handles "he buys 11 for Rs 10 and sells 10 for Rs 11". Work out the cost of one and the selling price of one, or better, choose a number of articles that suits both: 110. He buys 110 for Rs 100 and sells 110 for Rs 121. Profit 21%.
**A chain of sales.** "A sells to B at a 20% profit, and B sells to C at a 25% profit. C pays Rs 1,500." Each seller's profit is on what **they** paid, so the prices multiply along the chain:

items.x: A's cost x 1.2 = what B paid;
what B paid x 1.25 = what C paid.

teach.x: Going forwards, multiply. Here the end is known and the start is wanted, so **divide your way back**: 1,500 / 1.25 = 1,200, and 1,200 / 1.2 = 1,000.

tags: Cost of 20 = selling price of 16.
Bought at 11 for Rs 10, sold at 10 for Rs 11.
A chain of two sales, worked backwards.

example.q: The cost price of 18 articles is equal to the selling price of 15 articles. What is the profit percent?
steps: Say each article costs Re 1. Then 18 articles cost Rs 18.
He receives that same Rs 18 for selling 15 articles.
Those 15 articles cost him Rs 15. Profit = 3.

checks.q: The cost price of 10 articles is equal to the selling price of 8 articles. What is the profit percent?
checks.why: Say each costs Re 1. He sells 8 articles, costing Rs 8, for Rs 10. Profit 2 on 8 = 25%. (20% divides by 10, the wrong number.)

shortcut.title: Cost of x = selling price of y

text.x: If the cost price of **x** articles equals the selling price of **y** articles:
**profit percent = (x - y) / y x 100**
If y is the bigger number the answer comes out negative, which means a loss. The number underneath is always the number **sold**.

lessons.title: The dishonest dealer
lessons.plain: New: a dealer who claims to sell at cost but gives less than a full kilogram. His profit is hidden in the weight.

teach.x: "A dealer says he sells at cost price, but uses a weight of 900 grams in place of 1 kilogram." He charges the customer for 1,000 grams and hands over 900. Where is his profit?
Think about what he **gives** and what he **gets paid for**.

items.x: He gives 900 grams. That is what the goods cost him: the value of 900 grams.
He is paid the price of 1,000 grams.
So on goods costing "900", he receives "1,000". His gain is 100, on a cost of 900.

teach.x: The cost is what he actually parts with, so the number underneath is the weight he **gives**, not the full kilogram.
**gain percent = weight he keeps back / weight he actually gives x 100**
With 800 grams for a kilogram: 200 / 800 = 25%.

**If he also raises the price.** "He sells at 10% above cost and also uses 800 grams for a kilogram." For every kilogram he claims to sell he is paid 110% of the price of 1,000 grams, which is the price of 1,100 grams. He gives 800 grams. So on a cost of 800 he receives 1,100: 1,100 / 800 = 1.375, a gain of 37.5%.

tags: 900 grams for a kilogram.
800 grams for a kilogram, from a real paper.
A false weight and a raised price together.

example.q: A dishonest dealer professes to sell his goods at cost price but uses a weight of 750 grams in place of 1 kilogram. What is his gain percent?
steps: He is paid for 1,000 grams and gives 750 grams.
His cost is the 750 grams he gives. His gain is the 250 grams he keeps back.
As a percent: 33 1/3%.

checks.q: A dealer claims to sell at cost price but uses a weight of 960 grams for a kilogram. What is his gain percent?
checks.why: He keeps back 40 grams and gives 960. 40 / 960 = 1/24, which is 4 1/6%. (4% divides by the full 1,000 grams.)

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: there are only four speeds, and they sit on a number line with equal gaps.**
Upstream (U) … Boat in still water (B) … Downstream (D), and the gap on each side is the Stream (S).

items.x: D = B + S
U = B − S
B is the middle of D and U: B = (D + U) ÷ 2
S is half the gap: S = (D − U) ÷ 2

blocks.x: Give me any two of the four and the other two follow. Every question in this topic is: find two of the four, get the rest, then use Distance = Speed × Time.
**The four-box algorithm (use it on every question):**

items.x: Draw four boxes: U, B, D, S.
Fill what the question gives. A trip (“60 km downstream in 2.5 hours”) fills D or U directly. A ratio fills boxes in parts.
Complete the boxes with the number-line rules.
Answer with distance ÷ the right box.

blocks.x: **Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **Ratio B : S = a : b** means D = a + b parts and U = a − b parts.
**Ratio D : U = p : q** means B = (p + q)/2 parts and S = (p − q)/2 parts.
**Same distance, times in ratio** means speeds in the flipped ratio (times D : U = 3 : 5 means speeds D : U = 5 : 3).
**“Stream is 20% of boat”** is the ratio B : S = 5 : 1.
**Still-water trip:** use B, not D or U.
**Round trip time** = distance ÷ D + distance ÷ U. Never total distance ÷ B.
**Two boats moving towards each other on the same river:** the stream cancels; closing speed = sum of their still-water speeds.

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: ratio to the four boxes (in parts)**
(For D : U rows the parts are doubled where needed so that B and S come out whole.)

**Non-linear warning.** A boat at 10 km/h in a 2 km/h stream does not average 10 km/h over a round trip. It goes 12 one way and 8 the other, and the slow leg takes longer, so the round trip is slower than in still water.
**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** four boxes, fill, complete, divide. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Counts are out of the 247 bank questions; the PYQ figure is IBPS Clerk Prelims questions; the sister figure is from the 11 sister questions.

lead.x: Sorting rule used: if a ratio or percent links the speeds, the question is B4 even when it also has a round trip, because the ratio is what unlocks it.
What stands out: half of the Clerk PYQs (11 of 22) hand you a ratio or a percent between the speeds. Learn the grid in section 1 and half this topic is done.

items.title: A ratio or percent links the speeds

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “ratio of boat to stream is 7 : 2”, “stream is 20% of boat”, “ratio of downstream to upstream speed”.
**Shortcut engine.** write all four boxes in parts. One real number in the question (a trip or a speed) gives the size of a part.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 12 Dec 2021 Set 1).** B : S = 7 : 2, so D = 9 parts and U = 5 parts. 432 km downstream in 6 h means D = 72, so 1 part = 8 and U = 40. Time for 280 km upstream = 7 hours.

items.label: Confirmed

items.title: Two trips give D and U

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “covers x km downstream in t₁ and y km upstream in t₂”; or “sum of upstream and downstream speeds”.
**Shortcut engine.** divide to get D and U. B = middle, S = half the gap.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** 32 km downstream in 240 minutes: D = 8. 48 km upstream in 1,440 minutes: U = 2. Stream = (8 − 2) ÷ 2 = 3 km/h.

items.label: Confirmed

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “goes and comes back in 18 hours”, “takes 4 hours more upstream than downstream”.
**Shortcut engine.** find D and U. Take a trial distance equal to the LCM of D and U, find its time (total or difference), then scale to the time given.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017 model paper).** B = 6, S = 4, so D = 10 and U = 2. Trial distance 10 km each way: 1 h + 5 h = 6 h. Given 18 h is three times that, so 30 km each way. Total distance 60 km.
**Pattern clues.** “if the speed of the boat is decreased by 20%”, “stream speed increased by 80%”.
**Shortcut engine.** fill the four boxes first. Change only the box named. Rebuild D or U. Then do the new trip.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** 192 km downstream in 4 h: D = 48. 210 km upstream in 5 h: U = 42. B = 45. Cut 20%: 36. In still water for 3 h: 108 km.
**Pattern clues.** “upstream speed is 6 km/h and stream is 2 km/h”.
**Shortcut engine.** complete the boxes, divide.
**Worked example (IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims 6 Dec 2025 Shift 2).** U = 6, S = 2, so B = 8 and D = 10. Time for 80 km downstream = 8 hours.
Towards each other on the same river: time = gap ÷ sum of still-water speeds; the stream cancels. Same direction: gap ÷ difference of still-water speeds.
**Example (bank CON-BOT-15).** 108 km apart, still-water speeds 12 and 15, stream 3. They meet in 108 ÷ 27 = 4 hours.

This is the one place the honest route is two equations, which is too slow. Test the options: pick the option’s D and U and see if both trips give the stated times. Only 2 of 247 bank questions are of this kind and no paper opened had one.

lead.x: All five questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was recomputed. One drill per Core archetype; between them they cover the easy, two-step, non-linear and phrasing types.

body.x: The upstream speed of a boat is 9 km/h and the speed of the stream is 3 km/h. How many hours does the boat take to cover 60 km downstream?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** B = U + S = 12. D = B + S = 15. Time = 60 ÷ 15 = 4.
**30-Second Exam Method:** downstream is two stream-steps above upstream: 9 + 3 + 3 = 15. 60 ÷ 15 = 4. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** downstream speed must be above 12 (the still-water speed), so the time must be under 5. That removes 5, 6 and 10. Back-check: 4 × 15 = 60.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding the stream only once gives 12, which is the still-water speed, and 60 ÷ 12 = 5 is option (A). IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims 6 Dec 2025 Shift 2 asked this exact form.

body.x: A boat covers 84 km downstream in 3 hours and 60 km upstream in 3 hours. What is the speed of the stream (in km/h)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** D = 28, U = 20. S = (28 − 20) ÷ 2 = 4.
**30-Second Exam Method:** D 28, U 20, gap 8, half the gap = 4. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed. Back-check: B = 24; 24 + 4 = 28 and 24 − 4 = 20.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** forgetting to halve the gap gives 8, option (A). The still-water speed, 24, is option (B).

body.x: A boat’s speed in still water is 10 km/h and the stream flows at 2 km/h. The boat goes 48 km downstream and returns to the start. What is the total time taken (in hours)?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** D = 12, U = 8. Time = 48/12 + 48/8 = 4 + 6 = 10.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 48 ÷ 12 = 4, 48 ÷ 8 = 6, total 10. **Answer (D).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** in still water the 96 km would take 9.6 h, and a stream always makes a round trip slower, so the answer is above 9.6. That removes 9.6, 9 and 8. Back-check: 4 × 12 = 48 and 6 × 8 = 48.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 96 ÷ 10 = 9.6 is option (A). The stream does not cancel over a round trip.

body.x: The speed of the stream is 25% of the speed of a boat in still water. The boat covers 90 km upstream in 6 hours. How many hours will it take to cover 100 km downstream?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let B = b, S = b/4. U = 3b/4 = 15, so b = 20 and S = 5. D = 25. Time = 100 ÷ 25 = 4.
**30-Second Exam Method:** B : S = 4 : 1, so U = 3 parts and D = 5 parts. U = 90 ÷ 6 = 15, so 1 part = 5 and D = 25. 100 ÷ 25 = 4. **Answer (E).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** downstream is faster than upstream (15), so 100 km takes less than 6.67 h; and faster than still water (20), so less than 5 h. That leaves 3 and 4. Back-check: 25 − 5 − 5 = 15.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “25% of the boat’s speed in still water”, not 25% of the upstream speed. And using the still-water speed 20 for the downstream trip gives 5, option (A).

body.x: A boat covers 96 km downstream in 4 hours. The ratio of the boat’s speed in still water to the stream’s speed is 5 : 1. If the stream’s speed increases by 50%, how many hours will the boat take to cover 70 km upstream?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** D = 24 = 6 parts, so B = 20 and S = 4. New S = 6. New U = 14. Time = 70 ÷ 14 = 5.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 24 ÷ 6 parts = 4 a part. B 20, S 4. Stream becomes 6, upstream becomes 14. 70 ÷ 14 = 5. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** new upstream speed is below the old one (16), so the time is above 70 ÷ 16, about 4.4. That removes 4. Back-check: 5 × 14 = 70.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** only the stream changes; the boat’s own speed stays 20. Raising the boat by 50% instead, or using the old upstream speed, gives a wrong time. IBPS PO Prelims 23 Aug 2025 Shift 2 used the same build with an 80% rise.

intro.x: A boat on a river is helped along when it goes with the flow and held back when it goes against it. This topic is Speed, Time and Distance with that one extra thought.

There are ten short lessons. The first three set up the four speeds and how any two of them give the rest. The others are the ways the exam uses them: round trips, ratios, and a speed that changes. Go in order the first time, and if distance = speed x time is not yet comfortable, do the first lesson of Speed, Time and Distance before this.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the ratio table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
Whatever the wording, begin by asking which two facts about the four speeds you have been given. Once the four are filled in, the rest is a single division.

lessons.title: With the stream and against it
lessons.plain: The starting point: a river pushes a boat along one way and holds it back the other. That gives four speeds.

teach.x: A river flows. So a boat on it never moves at just its own speed: the water carries it along or holds it back. That is the whole topic, and it comes down to four speeds.

items.x: **Speed of the boat in still water**: how fast the boat goes on a lake, with no current. We will call it the **boat speed**.
**Speed of the stream** (or current): how fast the river itself flows.
**Downstream speed**: going **with** the flow. The river helps, so the speeds add.
**Upstream speed**: going **against** the flow. The river hinders, so the stream is taken away.

teach.x: **downstream = boat + stream**
**upstream = boat - stream**
A boat that does 12 km/h in still water, on a stream of 3 km/h, goes downstream at 15 and upstream at 9.
Once you have the right one of these, the question is the first lesson of Speed, Time and Distance: distance = speed x time. So the routine is always two steps.

items.x: Decide the direction, and work out the downstream or upstream speed.
Use distance = speed x time.

teach.x: Words to know: "with the stream" or "along the current" means downstream; "against the stream" means upstream. And when a boat goes somewhere downstream and then **returns**, the return is upstream.

tags: Downstream: find the time.
Upstream: find the time.
Downstream: find the distance, with the time in minutes.
Both directions compared.
A trip one way, then the return.

example.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 12 km/h and the speed of the stream is 3 km/h. How long will the boat take to cover 45 km downstream?
steps: Downstream, the stream helps: 12 + 3 = 15 km/h.
Time = distance / speed = 45 / 15 = 3 hours.

checks.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 9 km/h and the speed of the stream is 3 km/h. How long will it take to cover 24 km upstream?
checks.why: Upstream, the stream hinders: 9 - 3 = 6 km/h. 24 / 6 = 4 hours. (2 hours uses the downstream speed, 12.)

lessons.title: Finding the boat and the stream from two trips
lessons.plain: New: the question gives the downstream and upstream speeds. The boat is halfway between them; the stream is half the gap.

teach.x: Last lesson you were given the boat and the stream and built the other two. More often it is the other way round: you learn the **downstream** and **upstream** speeds, and must find the boat and the stream.
Picture the four speeds on a line. The boat speed sits in the middle. Going downstream adds the stream; going upstream takes the same amount away.
**upstream ... boat ... downstream**, with one stream-sized step on each side.
So:

items.x: **boat speed = halfway between the two = (downstream + upstream) / 2**
**stream speed = half the gap between them = (downstream - upstream) / 2**

teach.x: Downstream 20 and upstream 12: the boat is (20 + 12) / 2 = 16, and the stream is (20 - 12) / 2 = 4. Check: 16 + 4 = 20 and 16 - 4 = 12.

The question may not hand you the two speeds directly. It may describe two **trips**: "36 km downstream in 3 hours and 24 km upstream in 4 hours". Turn each trip into a speed first (12 and 6), then use the line.
The slip to avoid is forgetting to halve. The gap between downstream and upstream is **two** streams, not one.

tags: Two speeds given: find the boat.
Two speeds given: find the stream.
Two trips: find the boat.
The same, with a real paper's bigger numbers.
Times in minutes: find the stream.

example.q: A boat covers 40 km downstream in 2 hours and 36 km upstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the boat in still water and the speed of the stream.
steps: Downstream speed = 40 / 2 = 20 km/h. Upstream speed = 36 / 3 = 12 km/h.
Boat = halfway between: (20 + 12) / 2 = 16 km/h.
Stream = half the gap: (20 - 12) / 2 = 4 km/h.

checks.q: A boat goes downstream at 14 km/h and upstream at 8 km/h. What is the speed of the stream?
checks.why: The stream is half the gap: (14 - 8) / 2 = 3 km/h. (6 is the whole gap, which is two streams. 11 is the boat.)

lessons.title: Any two of the four give the rest
lessons.plain: New: the two facts come in less obvious forms: a sum, a time in still water, even a floating log.

teach.x: There are four speeds, tied together by two simple relations. So **any two of them, or any two facts about them, fix all four.** Every question in this topic is a hunt for two facts.
Here are the less obvious ways the two facts arrive.

**The sum of the two trip speeds.** Downstream + upstream = (boat + stream) + (boat - stream) = **twice the boat**. So "the sum of the upstream and downstream speeds is 36" tells you the boat does 18.

**One speed described through another.** "The upstream speed is 12 more than the stream." Upstream is boat minus stream, so boat - stream = stream + 12, which means the boat is twice the stream plus 12. Use that with the second fact.

**Times for the same distance, instead of speeds.** "A boat takes 8 hours in still water and 6 hours downstream for the same distance." No distance is given, so choose one that both times go into: 24 km. Then the boat does 3 km/h and downstream is 4 km/h, so the stream is 1 and upstream is 2.
**A floating log.** A log, a raft or anything that simply drifts has no speed of its own. It moves at the **speed of the stream**. So "how long will a log take" is asking for distance / stream speed.
**A trip in still water** uses the boat speed alone, with no stream added or taken away.

tags: Two trips, and the answer is a ratio.
The sum of the two trip speeds.
One speed is described through another.
Times for the same distance, with still water as one of them.
A floating log.

example.q: A boat takes 4 hours to cover a certain distance downstream and 6 hours to cover the same distance in still water. How long will it take to cover the same distance upstream?
steps: Choose a distance both times go into: 12 km.
Downstream speed = 12 / 4 = 3 km/h. Boat speed = 12 / 6 = 2 km/h.
Stream = 3 - 2 = 1 km/h, so upstream speed = 2 - 1 = 1 km/h.
Time upstream = 12 / 1 = 12 hours.

checks.q: The sum of the downstream and upstream speeds of a boat is 30 km/h, and the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. What is the downstream speed?
checks.why: The sum of the two is twice the boat, so the boat does 15 km/h. Downstream = 15 + 2 = 17 km/h. (15 is the boat itself.)

lessons.title: There and back
lessons.plain: New: the boat goes somewhere and returns. Add the two times; never use the still-water speed for the whole trip.

teach.x: "A boat goes 30 km downstream and comes back." The two legs are at different speeds, so they take different times. Work them out separately and add.
**total time = distance / downstream speed + distance / upstream speed**

It is tempting to say the stream "cancels out" over a round trip, and to divide the total distance by the boat's still-water speed. It does not cancel. The boat spends **longer** on the slow upstream leg, so the stream costs more time than it saves. You met the same thing with average speed.
**When the distance is the unknown.** "The boat goes to a place and comes back in 5 hours. How far is the place?" Use the trick of choosing a convenient distance.

items.x: Say the speeds are 12 downstream and 8 upstream. Choose a distance both go into: 24 km.
For 24 km: 2 hours down and 3 hours back, 5 hours in all.
Compare with the real time and scale. Here the real time is also 5 hours, so the place is 24 km away. Had it been 10 hours, the place would be 48 km away.

teach.x: **Not all the way back.** If the boat returns only to a point halfway, the upstream leg is half the distance. Write each leg with its own distance.
Read carefully whether the question wants the distance to the place or the **total** distance travelled (which is twice as much).

tags: Find the total time.
Find how far the place is.
It asks for the total distance travelled.
The average speed for the whole trip.
The boat comes only halfway back.

example.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 6 km/h and the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. How long will it take to go 16 km downstream and come back?
steps: Downstream speed = 8 km/h. Upstream speed = 4 km/h.
Going: 16 / 8 = 2 hours. Returning: 16 / 4 = 4 hours.
Total = 6 hours.
(Dividing 32 km by the still-water speed, 6, would give 5 1/3 hours, which is too little.)

checks.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 5 km/h and the speed of the stream is 1 km/h. The boat goes to a place and comes back in 5 hours. How far is the place?
checks.why: Speeds are 6 downstream and 4 upstream. Try 12 km: 2 hours down and 3 hours back, 5 hours. That matches, so the place is 12 km away. (12.5 km uses the still-water speed for the whole trip.)

shortcut.title: Average speed for a round trip

text.x: For going somewhere and coming straight back, the average speed over the whole trip is:
**downstream speed x upstream speed / boat speed**
Boat 10, stream 2: 12 x 8 / 10 = 9.6 km/h. It is always a little less than the boat's own speed.

From that, total time = total distance / this average, and total distance = this average x total time. With boat 10, stream 2 and 5 hours in all: 9.6 x 5 = 48 km there and back, so the place is 24 km away.

lessons.title: "Takes 2 hours more upstream", and a missing speed
lessons.plain: New: the question gives the difference between the two times, or hides one of the speeds inside a round trip.

teach.x: Two more forms of the there-and-back question.

**The difference in time is given.** "The boat takes 2 hours more to cover a distance upstream than downstream." Use the same trial-distance idea, but look at the **gap** between the two times instead of their total.

items.x: Speeds 15 downstream and 9 upstream. Choose 45 km.
That takes 3 hours down and 5 hours up: a gap of 2 hours.
Compare with the real gap and scale. If the real gap is 2 hours, the distance is 45 km; if it were 4 hours, 90 km.

teach.x: **One of the speeds is missing.** "The boat does 9 km/h in still water. It goes 36 km downstream and comes back in 9 hours. Find the speed of the stream."

Here you cannot build the two speeds, because the stream is the unknown. Solving it properly leads to an equation with the unknown squared, which is slow and easy to get wrong. The sensible route is to **test the options**.

items.x: Try a stream of 3: downstream 12, upstream 6. Times 3 hours and 6 hours, total 9. It fits.

teach.x: A good first guess saves time. The stream is usually a small whole number, and it should make both speeds divide the distance neatly. Start with the option that does.
Testing options is not a lesser method here. It is the fastest correct one, and it checks the answer as you go.

tags: A time gap: find the distance.
A time gap, then a still-water trip.
A round trip with the stream missing: test the options.
A time gap with the stream missing: test the options.
A round trip with the boat missing, then a further trip.

example.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 8 km/h and the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. The boat takes 4 hours more to cover a certain distance upstream than downstream. Find the distance.
steps: Downstream 10 km/h, upstream 6 km/h.
Choose a distance both go into: 30 km. Times: 3 hours down, 5 hours up.
That is a gap of 2 hours for 30 km.
The real gap is 4 hours, twice as much, so the distance is 60 km.

checks.q: A boat does 7 km/h in still water. It goes 24 km downstream and comes back in a total of 7 hours. What is the speed of the stream?
checks.why: Test the options. Stream 1: downstream 8, upstream 6. Times 3 hours and 4 hours, total 7. It fits.

shortcut.title: The time gap in one line

text.x: If going upstream takes **t** hours longer than going downstream over the same distance:
**distance = t x downstream speed x upstream speed / (downstream speed - upstream speed)**
Speeds 15 and 9 with a gap of 2 hours: 2 x 15 x 9 / 6 = 45 km.
It is the cousin of the late-and-early line from Speed, Time and Distance. The bottom number is twice the stream.

lessons.title: When a ratio links the speeds
lessons.plain: New: the boat and stream are given as a ratio or a percent. Write all four speeds in parts, then match one real number.

teach.x: The Clerk papers set this form more than any other in the topic. Instead of speeds, you are told how two of them compare: "the ratio of the boat to the stream is 7 : 2".
Treat the ratio as **parts**, and build all four speeds in parts with the two relations you know.

Then the question gives one real number, usually a trip. "432 km downstream in 6 hours" means the downstream speed is 72 km/h. Downstream is 9 parts, so one part is 8 km/h. Now every speed is known: upstream is 5 x 8 = 40 km/h.
This is the "match the real number to the parts" step from every earlier topic.
The ratio can link **any** two of the four, and it may be given as a percent.

items.x: "The stream is 20% of the boat": stream 1, boat 5.
"Upstream to stream is 4 : 1": upstream 4, stream 1, so boat = 4 + 1 = 5 and downstream = 6.
"Downstream to stream is 9 : 1": downstream 9, stream 1, so boat = 8 and upstream = 7.
"Upstream to downstream is 3 : 5": boat is halfway, 4; stream is half the gap, 1.

teach.x: Whichever two you are given, fill in the other two using: downstream = boat + stream, upstream = boat - stream.

tags: Boat to stream, and a downstream trip.
The link is a percent.
Upstream to stream.
Downstream to stream, with the stream given.
Upstream to downstream, with the stream given.

example.q: The ratio of the speed of a boat in still water to the speed of the stream is 5 : 1. The boat covers 36 km downstream in 2 hours. How long will it take to cover 48 km upstream?
steps: In parts: boat 5, stream 1, downstream 6, upstream 4.
Real number: downstream speed = 36 / 2 = 18 km/h. That is 6 parts, so one part is 3 km/h.
Upstream = 4 parts = 12 km/h.
Time = 48 / 12 = 4 hours.

checks.q: The speed of the stream is 25% of the speed of a boat in still water. If the downstream speed is 20 km/h, what is the upstream speed?
checks.why: 25% means stream 1, boat 4. Downstream is 5 parts and upstream is 3 parts. 5 parts = 20, so one part is 4 and upstream is 12 km/h. (16 is the boat.)

lessons.title: The ratio hidden in times and distances
lessons.plain: New: no ratio is stated. "Twice as long upstream" or "20 km up in the time of 30 km down" is one in disguise.

teach.x: Sometimes the ratio of downstream to upstream speed is not stated but is sitting in the sentence. Two disguises cover almost all cases, and both come from Speed, Time and Distance.

**Same distance, times compared.** "He takes twice as long to row upstream as downstream." For the same distance, speed and time are opposite. Twice the time means half the speed. So **downstream : upstream = 2 : 1**.
Likewise "downstream in 2 hours, back in 3 hours" gives times 2 : 3, so the speeds are 3 : 2.

**Same time, distances compared.** "In the time it covers 20 km upstream it covers 30 km downstream." In the same time, a faster boat goes further in direct proportion. So **upstream : downstream = 20 : 30 = 2 : 3**.
Once you have downstream : upstream, the other two follow as in the last lesson:

items.x: the **boat** is halfway between the two numbers;
the **stream** is half the gap.

teach.x: With downstream 3 and upstream 2: boat 2.5 parts, stream 0.5 part. If halves bother you, double everything: 6, 4, 5 and 1.
Then match the one real number. "The stream is 2 km/h" makes 0.5 part equal to 2, so one part is 4.

tags: "Twice as long upstream", with the boat given.
Distances in the same time, with the stream given.
Two times for the same distance: find the distance.
A percent between the two trip speeds.
A ratio of trip speeds and a total time; find the still-water time.

example.q: A man takes three times as long to row a distance upstream as to row the same distance downstream. His speed in still water is 8 km/h. Find the speed of the stream.
steps: Three times the time means one third of the speed: downstream : upstream = 3 : 1.
Boat = halfway between 3 and 1 = 2 parts. Stream = half the gap = 1 part.
The boat is 8 km/h, so one part is 4 km/h.
Stream = 1 part = 4 km/h.

checks.q: In the time a boat covers 15 km upstream, it covers 25 km downstream. If the speed of the stream is 3 km/h, what is the speed of the boat in still water?
checks.why: Same time, so upstream : downstream = 15 : 25 = 3 : 5. Boat = 4 parts, stream = 1 part. The stream is 3 km/h, so the boat is 12 km/h.

lessons.title: Ratios, in exam wording
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the idea. The real number arrives as a difference between two speeds, a round-trip time, or a letter.

teach.x: Recent papers keep the ratio but change what the real number is. Here are the forms, each with the one thought that opens it.

**"Downstream is 5 km/h more than upstream."** The gap between downstream and upstream is always **twice the stream**. So a gap of 5 means the stream is 2.5 km/h. That is a real speed, and with a boat-to-stream ratio you have everything.
**Speeds written with a letter**: "downstream is x and upstream is x - 15". The same thought: the gap is 15, so the stream is 7.5.

**A round-trip time.** "120 km down and back in 24 hours; stream to boat is 2 : 3." Build the two trip speeds in parts (5 and 1 here). Write the total time with one part as the unknown: 120 / 5 parts + 120 / 1 part. That is 24 + 120, all divided by the size of one part, and it must equal 24 hours.

**Two trips whose times are tied by a letter**: "32 km downstream in (t + 1) hours and 12 km upstream in t hours, with downstream twice upstream". Write each speed as distance over time and use the ratio between them.
In each case the order of work is the same as before: **parts first, then find the real size of one part, then answer.**

tags: The gap between the two trip speeds, written with a letter.
The gap in km/h, then a two-leg trip.
A round-trip time with a ratio.
The ratio is hidden in equal times, with a round-trip time.
Two trips tied by a letter in the times.

example.q: The downstream speed of a boat is 6 km/h more than its upstream speed. The ratio of the speed of the boat in still water to the speed of the stream is 5 : 1. How long will the boat take to cover 36 km downstream?
steps: The gap between downstream and upstream is twice the stream. So the stream is 3 km/h.
Boat : stream = 5 : 1, so the boat does 15 km/h.
Downstream = 15 + 3 = 18 km/h.
Time = 36 / 18 = 2 hours.

checks.q: The downstream speed of a boat is x km/h and its upstream speed is (x - 8) km/h. The ratio of the boat's speed in still water to the speed of the stream is 3 : 1. What is x?
checks.why: The gap is 8, so the stream is 4 km/h. Boat : stream = 3 : 1, so the boat does 12. Downstream, x = 12 + 4 = 16.

lessons.title: When one of the speeds changes
lessons.plain: New: the boat's speed is cut, or the stream rises after rain. Change only that one, then rebuild the trip speed.

teach.x: "If its speed in still water is decreased by 20%..." or "after rain the speed of the stream doubles". One of the two basic speeds, the boat or the stream, is altered, and the question asks about a trip afterwards.
The danger is changing the wrong thing. A cut of 20% in the **boat's** speed is not a cut of 20% in the downstream speed. So keep to this order:

items.x: **Find the boat speed and the stream speed as they are now**, using whatever the first part of the question gives.
**Change only the one the question names.**
**Rebuild** the downstream or upstream speed from the new pair.
Do the new trip.

teach.x: "A boat covers 30 km upstream in 5 hours when the stream is 2 km/h. The stream rises by 2 km/h." Now: upstream 6, so the boat does 8. Change the stream to 4. Rebuild: upstream = 8 - 4 = 4. New time for 30 km: 7.5 hours.
Notice how hard a stronger stream hits an upstream trip: the stream only doubled, but the trip takes half as long again.

A different twist puts **letters in the distances**: "(X + 50) km downstream in 5 hours". Find the trip speed from the boat and stream first, multiply by the time to get the real distance, and read off the letter.

tags: The stream changes.
The boat's speed is cut, then a still-water trip.
The boat's speed is raised, with a ratio and a letter.
Letters in the distances.

example.q: A boat covers 30 km upstream in 5 hours when the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. If the speed of the stream increases by 2 km/h, how long will the boat take to cover 30 km upstream?
steps: Now: upstream speed = 30 / 5 = 6 km/h. The stream is 2, so the boat does 8 km/h.
Change only the stream: it becomes 4 km/h.
Rebuild: upstream = 8 - 4 = 4 km/h.
New time = 30 / 4 = 7.5 hours.

checks.q: A boat goes downstream at 20 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h. If its speed in still water is increased by 25%, what is its new downstream speed?
checks.why: Now: boat 16, stream 4. Raise only the boat by 25%: 20. New downstream = 20 + 4 = 24 km/h. (25 raises the downstream speed itself by 25%, which is not what changed.)

lessons.title: Two boats, and two mixed trips
lessons.plain: New: two boats on the same river, where the stream cancels; and a pair of mixed trips that is best solved from the options.

teach.x: Two settings to finish. Neither has appeared in the papers we checked, but both sit in practice sets.

**Two boats moving towards each other.** One is going downstream and the other upstream, on the same river. The stream helps one and hinders the other by exactly the same amount, so in the gap between them **the stream cancels out**.

items.x: First boat, downstream: its still-water speed + stream.
Second boat, upstream: its still-water speed - stream.
Add them to see how fast the gap closes: the stream drops away, leaving the **sum of the two still-water speeds**.

teach.x: So time to meet = distance between them / (sum of the still-water speeds). The speed of the stream in the question is there to distract. (It does matter if the question asks **where** they meet.)
If the two boats move in the same direction, the stream carries both along equally, and the gap closes at the difference of their still-water speeds.

**Two mixed trips.** "A boat goes 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours, and 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours." Each trip mixes the two directions, so neither speed can be read off. The proper method is a pair of equations with the unknowns underneath, which is slow.
Test the options instead. Take an option for the boat speed and look for an upstream and downstream speed around it that divide the distances neatly. Check both trips.

tags: Two boats approaching each other.
Two mixed trips: test the options.

example.q: Two boats start at the same time from points 90 km apart on a river and move towards each other. Their speeds in still water are 10 km/h and 8 km/h, and the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. After how long do they meet?
steps: One boat goes downstream: 10 + 2 = 12 km/h. The other goes upstream: 8 - 2 = 6 km/h.
The gap closes at 12 + 6 = 18 km/h. That is just 10 + 8: the stream has cancelled.
Time = 90 / 18 = 5 hours.

checks.q: In the example above, suppose the speed of the stream were 4 km/h instead of 2 km/h. After how long would the two boats meet?
checks.why: The stream cancels when two boats approach each other: 14 + 4 = 18 km/h, the same as before. They still meet after 5 hours.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: follow the ingredient that does not change.**
In almost every exam question, something is added or removed, and one ingredient is left untouched. Fix your eyes on that one.

items.x: **Add water:** milk does not change.
**Add milk:** water does not change.
**Take out some mixture:** both go down, but the ratio does not change.

blocks.x: **The litres-table algorithm (use it on every question):**

items.x: Turn the starting ratio or percent into litres of each ingredient.
If mixture is removed, shrink both by the same fraction (the ratio stays).
Add what is added, to the right ingredient only.
Read off the answer, or match the final ratio to find the unknown.

blocks.x: Example: 56 litres, milk : water = 4 : 3, so 32 and 24. Water is added until the ratio is 8 : 7. Milk is still 32 = 8 parts, so a part is 4 and water is 28. Added: 4 litres.

**When litres are not given, use the unchanged ingredient to line up the two ratios.** Before 5 : 4, after adding 2 litres of water 10 : 9. Milk is unchanged, so write the first ratio as 10 : 8. Water went from 8 parts to 9 parts: 1 part = 2 litres. New water = 9 parts = 18 litres.
**Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **“Water is 25% of milk”** means milk : water = 4 : 1. It does not mean water is 25% of the mixture.
**Removing mixture never changes the ratio.** Only the amounts shrink.
**Remove then replace with water:** milk left = milk before × (fraction of mixture kept).
**Mixing two vessels:** add the milk litres, add the total litres. Never average the two percents unless the volumes are equal.
**Repeated replacement (same amount each time):** milk left = milk at start × (fraction kept) × (fraction kept) …
**Alligation cross (prices or percents):** cheaper : dearer = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper).

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: ratio to share of the mixture**
**Non-linear warning.** 20 litres at 70% milk mixed with 30 litres at 60% milk is not 65% milk. It is (14 + 18) ÷ 50 = 64%. The bigger vessel pulls the answer towards itself.
**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** litres table with two columns (milk, water) and one row per step. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: All six questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was recomputed. Four cover the required types; the rest give every Core archetype a drill.

body.x: A 60-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How many litres of water must be added so that the ratio becomes 3 : 2?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** milk 45, water 15. Let w be added: 45 : (15 + w) = 3 : 2, so 15 + w = 30 and w = 15.
**30-Second Exam Method:** milk is unchanged and is 3 parts both times, so a part stays 15 litres. Water goes from 1 part to 2 parts: add 15. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** one part is 15 litres and water rises by a whole number of parts, so the answer is a multiple of 15. That leaves 15 and 30. Back-check: 45 : 30 = 3 : 2.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** 30 is the final water, not the water added. It is option (B).

body.x: An 80-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 5 : 3. 16 litres of the mixture is taken out and replaced with 16 litres of water. How many litres of water are in the final mixture?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** milk 50, water 30. 16 litres out is one-fifth: milk 40, water 24. Add 16 water: 40.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 64 litres left at 5 : 3 is 40 and 24. Water 24 + 16 = 40. **Answer (C).**

**Option Elimination Hack:** the final total is 80 again and milk can only have gone down from 50, so water is above 30. And water is at most 30 + 16 = 46 only if no water left with the removed mixture, which it did, so below 46. That leaves 40 and 36. Back-check: milk 40 + water 40 = 80.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding 16 to the original 30 gives 46, option (A). The 16 litres taken out carried 6 litres of water with it.

body.x: Jar A has 30 litres of a mixture that is 40% milk. Jar B has 20 litres of a mixture that is 60% milk. Both are poured into one jar. What percent of the new mixture is milk?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** milk = 40% of 30 + 60% of 20 = 12 + 12 = 24. Total 50 litres. 24/50 = 48%.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 12 + 12 = 24 in 50, double it: 48%. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the bigger jar is the weaker one, so the answer sits below the midpoint 50 and above 40. That removes 50 and 52. Back-check: water 18 + 8 = 26, and 24 + 26 = 50.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** averaging 40 and 60 gives 50, option (A). That is right only when the two jars are the same size.

body.x: In a 100-litre mixture of milk and water, the water is 25% of the milk. If 20 litres of water is added, what is the ratio of water to milk in the new mixture?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** milk : water = 4 : 1, so milk 80 and water 20. New water 40. Water : milk = 40 : 80 = 1 : 2.
**30-Second Exam Method:** “25% of the milk” is 4 : 1. 100 litres gives 80 and 20. Water becomes 40. 40 : 80 = 1 : 2. **Answer (E).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** options are ratios, so do not try one. Back-check: 20 is 25% of 80.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** reading it as “water is 25% of the mixture” gives 75 and 25, then 45 : 75 = 3 : 5, option (A). Also the question asks water to milk, not milk to water. IBPS Clerk Prelims 24 Aug 2024 Shift 1 used exactly this phrasing.

body.x: A 90-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. 30 litres of the mixture is taken out, and then 5 litres of milk and 15 litres of water are added. What is the new ratio of milk to water?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** milk 60, water 30. Remove one-third: 40 and 20. Add: 45 and 35. Ratio 9 : 7.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 60 litres left at 2 : 1 = 40 and 20. Plus 5 and 15 = 45 and 35 = 9 : 7. **Answer (A).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** options are ratios, so do not try one. Back-check: 45 + 35 = 80 = 90 − 30 + 20.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** skipping the removal gives 65 : 45 = 13 : 9, option (C). Writing water first gives 7 : 9, option (B).

body.x: Rice costing Rs 40 a kg is mixed with rice costing Rs 55 a kg so that the mixture costs Rs 46 a kg. In what ratio (cheaper : dearer) are they mixed?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** let c kg of cheaper and d kg of dearer: 40c + 55d = 46(c + d), so 9d = 6c and c : d = 3 : 2.
**30-Second Exam Method:** cross: (55 − 46) : (46 − 40) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the mean, 46, is nearer to 40 than to 55, so there is more of the cheaper rice. That removes 2 : 3 and 3 : 5. Back-check: 3 × 40 + 2 × 55 = 230 for 5 kg = 46.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** the cross is upside-down: the cheaper one gets the gap from the dearer side. Writing it straight gives 2 : 3, option (A).
