intro.x: A mixture question is about two things in one vessel, usually milk and water, and what happens when you add something, take something out, or pour two vessels together.

There are eleven short lessons. The first seven stay with one vessel: reading it, adding to it, and replacing part of it. The last four mix two different lots and bring in the method called alligation. Please go in order the first time, because each lesson uses the one before it.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has every rule on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more questions.
Whatever the wording, begin with one question to yourself: what did **not** change? In one vessel, it is the liquid that was not added. Follow that, and the rest is small arithmetic.

lessons.title: Reading what is in the vessel
lessons.plain: A mixture is a total split into shares. Turn the ratio or the percent into litres before doing anything else.

teach.x: A mixture question always starts by telling you what is in the vessel, either as a **ratio** or as a **percent**. Your first job is to turn that into actual amounts.
**From a ratio.** Milk and water are in the ratio 7 : 2 and there are 54 litres. Add the ratio numbers: 7 + 2 = 9 parts. One part is 54 / 9 = 6 litres. So milk is 7 x 6 = 42 and water is 2 x 6 = 12.
**From a percent.** 40 litres with 10% water means 4 litres of water and 36 litres of milk.
Two things to keep in mind from the very first day:

items.x: A percent in a mixture is **out of the whole mixture**, not out of the other liquid. 5 litres of water added to 20 litres of milk is 5 out of 25, which is 20%, not 25%.
When you **take some mixture out**, you take milk and water together, in the same ratio they were in. So the ratio left behind does not change; only the total gets smaller.

teach.x: That second point is used in almost every exam question later, so let it settle now: after removing 20 litres from 60 litres of a 3 : 2 mixture, the 40 litres left is still 3 : 2.

tags: Ratio and total: turn it into litres.
A percent is out of the whole mixture.
Some mixture is taken out: what happens to the ratio?
Take mixture out, then put one thing in.
The same reading, done backwards from the final mixture.

example.q: A vessel has 36 litres of milk and water in the ratio 5 : 4. If 9 litres of the mixture is taken out, how much milk is left?
steps: Taking mixture out does not change the ratio. It is still 5 : 4.
What is left is 36 - 9 = 27 litres.
5 + 4 = 9 parts, so one part is 27 / 9 = 3 litres.
Milk = 5 x 3 = 15 litres.

checks.q: 40 litres of mixture has milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. If 8 litres of the mixture is taken out, how much milk is left?
checks.why: 32 litres are left, still 3 : 1. One part is 8, so milk is 24. (22 comes from taking all 8 litres out of the milk, but what you remove is a mixture.)

lessons.title: Adding one thing: the other does not move
lessons.plain: New: something is added. Whatever you did not add stays exactly as it was, and that fixed amount gives you the answer.

teach.x: Last lesson you learned to read what is in the vessel. Now something is **poured in**.
The idea that solves every question of this kind is very simple: **if you add only water, the milk does not change.** If you add only milk, the water does not change.
So the method is always the same three steps:

items.x: Work out the two amounts at the start.
Hold on to the one that was **not** added. Use the new ratio to find what the other must become.
Subtract to see how much was added.

teach.x: For example: 60 litres in the ratio 2 : 1 is 40 milk and 20 water. To make it 1 : 2 by adding water, the milk stays 40. In 1 : 2, milk is 1 part, so one part is 40 and water must be 80. Water added = 80 - 20 = 60 litres.

The exam likes to describe the mixture in words instead of a ratio. Change the words to a ratio first: "water is 25% of the milk" means water : milk = 1 : 4, and "milk is 75% more than water" means milk = 1.75 times the water.

tags: Water is added: milk stays fixed.
Milk is added instead: now water stays fixed.
The same thing with a real paper's ratios.
The mixture is described in words, not as a ratio.
The target is in words: "75% more than".
Two things are added: fix the one you know, then find the other.

example.q: 35 litres of mixture has milk and water in the ratio 4 : 3. How much water must be added to make the ratio 2 : 3?
steps: 7 parts = 35, so one part = 5. Milk = 20 litres and water = 15 litres.
Only water is added, so milk stays 20.
In the new ratio 2 : 3, milk is 2 parts. So one part = 10 and water must be 30 litres.
Water added = 30 - 15 = 15 litres.

checks.q: 30 litres of mixture has milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 1 : 1?
checks.why: Milk is 20 and water is 10. Milk stays 20, so for 1 : 1 the water must be 20. Add 10 litres.

lessons.title: The same idea when the question speaks in percent
lessons.plain: New: the mixture is given in percent. Follow the thing that did not change, and ask what percent it is now.

teach.x: This is the last lesson's idea again, with percent in place of a ratio. There is one small trap in it, and once you see it you will not fall in.
40 litres of mixture has 10% water. How much water must be added to make it 20% water?
The tempting answer is "10% more, so 4 litres". That is wrong, because when you pour water in, the **total grows too**.

Follow the thing that did **not** change instead. Milk is 36 litres before and after. At the end water is 20%, so milk is **80%** of the new mixture. If 36 litres is 80%, the whole mixture is 36 / 0.8 = 45 litres. So 45 - 40 = 5 litres were added.
So the steps are:

items.x: Find the amount of the thing that is **not** added or removed.
Work out what percent it is at the end.
Amount / percent gives the new total. Compare the new total with the old one.

teach.x: The same steps work when water is **boiled away**: then the salt is the thing that does not change, and the total gets smaller.

tags: Water is added: milk is the fixed thing.
The strong thing is added: now the rest is fixed.
Water is removed instead of added: the salt is fixed.

example.q: 30 litres of a solution has 20% acid. How much water must be added so that acid becomes 15% of the solution?
steps: Acid = 20% of 30 = 6 litres. Adding water does not change it.
At the end, 6 litres is 15% of the solution.
New total = 6 / 0.15 = 40 litres.
Water added = 40 - 30 = 10 litres.

checks.q: 50 litres of mixture has 20% water. How much water must be added to make water 50% of the mixture?
checks.why: Milk is 40 litres and does not change. At the end milk is 50%, so the total is 80 litres. 80 - 50 = 30 litres. (15 is 30% of the old 50, which forgets that the total grows.)

lessons.title: When no total is given: let the fixed side match
lessons.plain: New: you are not told how many litres there are. Make the unchanged side the same number in both ratios, and the change is worth one clear number of parts.

teach.x: So far the question gave you the total. Often it does not. It only says how the **ratio changed** when something was added.
Milk and water are 5 : 1. After adding 5 litres of water the ratio is 5 : 2. How much milk is there?

Only water was added, so milk is the same before and after. Look at the two ratios: milk is 5 in both. So the parts are the same size in both, and water went from 1 part to 2 parts. That one extra part is the 5 litres you added. So one part = 5 litres and milk = 5 parts = 25 litres.
Sometimes the unchanged side does **not** show the same number. Then make it the same first.

Milk and water are 3 : 2. After adding milk the ratio is 2 : 1. Water did not change, but it shows as 2 and then as 1. Write 2 : 1 as **4 : 2**. Now water is 2 in both, and milk went from 3 to 4: one part was added.
So: **find the side that did not change, make its number equal in both ratios, then see how many parts the other side moved.** Those parts equal the litres added.
If the new mixture is given as a percent, turn it into a ratio first. "Milk is 80%" is milk : water = 4 : 1.

tags: The fixed side already matches.
The fixed side has to be made to match first.
The new mixture is given as a percent.
The same vessel, with a different thing asked.

example.q: Milk and water are in the ratio 3 : 2. When 10 litres of milk is added, the ratio becomes 2 : 1. How much milk was there at first?
steps: Only milk was added, so water did not change.
Water shows as 2 and then 1. Write the new ratio 2 : 1 as 4 : 2.
Now it is 3 : 2 before and 4 : 2 after. Milk grew by 1 part, and that is the 10 litres.
Milk at first = 3 parts = 30 litres.

checks.q: Milk and water are in the ratio 3 : 1. After adding 4 litres of water, the ratio becomes 3 : 2. How much milk is there?
checks.why: Milk is 3 in both ratios, so water went from 1 part to 2 parts. One part = 4 litres, and milk = 3 parts = 12 litres.

lessons.title: Take some out, then pour something in
lessons.plain: New: two moves in a row. Taking out shrinks both liquids in the same ratio; pouring in changes only one. Do them one at a time.

teach.x: Now the two things you know are joined into one question. Some mixture is **taken out**, and then something is **poured in**. When the same amount of water is poured back, this is called **replacing**.
Do not try to do both at once. Take them in order:

items.x: **Step 1, take out.** Both liquids go down, and the ratio stays the same (lesson 1). Work out what is left of each.
**Step 2, pour in.** Only one liquid goes up (lesson 2). Add it on.

teach.x: 60 litres at 3 : 1 is 45 milk and 15 water. Take out 12 litres: 48 litres are left, still 3 : 1, so 36 milk and 12 water. Now pour in 12 litres of water: 36 milk and 24 water, which is 3 : 2.
The mistake to avoid is taking the 12 litres out of the milk only, or out of the water only. What leaves the vessel is always **mixture**.
If the amount taken out is given as a percent, such as "20% of the mixture is removed", simply keep 80% of each liquid.

tags: Replace with water.
Replace with milk instead.
The amount removed is a percent, and you choose how much to pour in.
The start is told in words, and what is poured in is unknown.

example.q: 50 litres of mixture has milk and water in the ratio 4 : 1. 10 litres is taken out and replaced with water. What is the new ratio of milk to water?
steps: At first: milk 40, water 10.
Take out 10 litres. 40 litres are left, still 4 : 1: milk 32, water 8.
Pour in 10 litres of water: milk 32, water 18.

checks.q: 20 litres of mixture has milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. 4 litres is taken out and replaced with water. What is the new ratio of milk to water?
checks.why: 16 litres are left at 3 : 1, so 12 milk and 4 water. Add 4 water: 12 : 8 = 3 : 2. (11 : 9 comes from taking all 4 litres out of the milk.)

lessons.title: Working backwards from a replacement
lessons.plain: New: the result is given and you must find how much was replaced, or how much there was. Watch the liquid that was not poured back.

teach.x: In the last lesson you were told how much was replaced and found the result. The exam often turns this round: it tells you the **result** and asks how much was replaced, or how big the vessel was.
Look at the liquid that is **not** poured back. It only goes through one change: some of it leaves with the mixture. Pouring the other liquid in does not touch it.
And when mixture is taken out, every liquid in it loses the **same fraction**. Take out a quarter of the mixture and you take out a quarter of the milk.

A can has 60 litres at milk : water = 2 : 1, so 40 litres of milk. Some mixture is replaced with water and the ratio becomes 1 : 1, so milk is now 30 litres. Milk went from 40 to 30: a **quarter** of it left. So a quarter of the mixture was taken out: 60 / 4 = 15 litres.

Some questions pour in a **different** amount from what was taken out. Then the fraction idea does not apply directly. Use the slower, safe way: call what is left after the removal 5k and 2k (in the old ratio), add what was poured in, and set up the new ratio.

tags: How much to replace: the total is known.
The amount replaced is known: find the vessel.
The same, then one more step to the liquid asked for.
A different amount is poured back: use the safe way.
Two different things are poured back.

example.q: A vessel has 60 litres of milk and water in the ratio 3 : 2. How many litres of the mixture must be replaced with water to make the ratio 1 : 1?
steps: Milk now = 3/5 of 60 = 36 litres. Water is poured back, so milk only loses what is taken out.
At 1 : 1, milk must be 30 litres.
Milk goes from 36 to 30: it loses 6 out of 36, which is one-sixth.
So one-sixth of the mixture is taken out: 60 / 6 = 10 litres.

checks.q: Milk is 80% of a vessel. Some of the mixture is replaced with water and milk becomes 60%. What fraction of the mixture was replaced?
checks.why: Milk left is 60 out of 80, which is 3/4 of what it was. So 1/4 was taken out. (3/4 is the part that stayed.)

shortcut.title: One line for "how much was replaced"

text.x: When the amount taken out and the amount poured back are equal, and the liquid poured back is the **other** one:
**fraction left = new share / old share** of the liquid that was not poured back.
Milk share goes from 5/8 to 1/2: fraction left = (1/2) / (5/8) = 4/5, so 1/5 of the vessel was replaced.
It works with percents too: 40% falling to 30% means 3/4 is left and 1/4 was replaced.
Do not use it when the amounts out and in are different. Use the 5k and 2k way from the lesson there.

lessons.title: Replacing again and again
lessons.plain: New: the same replacement is done two or three times. Each round keeps the same fraction of the milk, so you multiply by that fraction each time.

teach.x: Here the replacement from the last two lessons is done **more than once**. It looks long, but it becomes one short multiplication.
A vessel has 50 litres of pure milk. 10 litres is taken out and replaced with water. Each time, 10 out of 50 leaves: one-fifth goes, so **four-fifths of the milk stays**.

items.x: After the first round: 50 x 4/5 = 40 litres of milk.
After the second round: 40 x 4/5 = 32 litres of milk.

teach.x: Notice that the second round does not remove 10 litres of milk. It removes 10 litres of **mixture**, which is only 8 litres of milk. That is why the answer is 32 and not 30.
So: **milk left = milk at the start x (fraction kept) x (fraction kept) ...**, once for each round. The fraction kept is 1 - (amount taken out / vessel size).
Going backwards: if after two rounds milk : water is 16 : 9, milk is 16/25 of the vessel. 16/25 is 4/5 x 4/5, so 4/5 is kept each round, and one-fifth of the vessel is taken out each time.

tags: Two rounds: find the milk left.
The result is given: find the size of the vessel.

example.q: A vessel has 80 litres of pure milk. 20 litres is taken out and replaced with water, and this is done once more. How much milk is left?
steps: Each round removes 20 out of 80, one-fourth. So three-fourths of the milk stays each time.
After round one: 80 x 3/4 = 60 litres.
After round two: 60 x 3/4 = 45 litres.

checks.q: A vessel has 40 litres of pure milk. 4 litres is taken out and replaced with water, and this is done once more. How much milk is left?
checks.why: Nine-tenths stays each round: 40 x 0.9 = 36, then 36 x 0.9 = 32.4. (32 comes from taking 4 litres of milk both times, but the second 4 litres is mixture.)

lessons.title: Mixing two lots: what the mixture is worth
lessons.plain: New: two different things are mixed. Add up the totals and divide. The answer leans towards the bigger lot.

teach.x: Until now there was one mixture. From here, **two different lots are mixed together**, and the question asks about the result: its price per kg, or its strength.
There is nothing new to learn for this, only care. **Add up the total value, add up the total quantity, and divide.**
3 kg of tea at 200 with 2 kg at 250: the total cost is 600 + 500 = 1100, the total weight is 5 kg, so the mixture costs 220 per kg.

It is not 225, the plain middle of 200 and 250. There is more of the cheaper tea, so the answer sits **closer to 200**. This is worth remembering as a quick check: the mixture always leans towards the bigger lot.
The same works for strength. 10 litres at 20% alcohol holds 2 litres of alcohol. 20 litres at 50% holds 10 litres. Together: 12 litres of alcohol in 30 litres = 40%.
When two vessels are given as **ratios**, change each ratio into "what fraction is milk" first. 3 : 1 means 3/4 is milk. 2 : 3 means 2/5 is milk. Then mix as above.

tags: Two prices, two quantities.
The same with strength in percent.
One jar in percent, the other as a ratio.
Two ratios, equal quantities.
Three ratios, equal quantities.
The mixture's price is known: find a missing price.

example.q: 4 litres of a 30% acid solution is mixed with 6 litres of a 50% acid solution. What is the strength of the mixture?
steps: Acid in the first = 30% of 4 = 1.2 litres.
Acid in the second = 50% of 6 = 3 litres.
Total acid = 4.2 litres in 10 litres.

checks.q: 2 kg of rice at ₹30 per kg is mixed with 3 kg at ₹40 per kg. What is the price of the mixture per kg?
checks.why: Total cost = 60 + 120 = 180 for 5 kg, so ₹36. (35 is the plain middle. There is more of the ₹40 rice, so the answer leans that way.)

lessons.title: Alligation: in what ratio should they be mixed?
lessons.plain: New: the mixture you want is given, and the ratio is asked. Each lot is taken in proportion to how far the other one is from the target.

teach.x: The last lesson went from quantities to the mixture. This lesson goes the other way: you know the mixture you **want**, and must find the **ratio** to mix in. The method has a name, **alligation**, and it is one small picture.
Rice at 40 and rice at 55 should give a mixture worth 46.
Write the two prices on the left and right, and the target in the middle. Then find how far each one is from the target:

items.x: 40 is **6** away from 46.
55 is **9** away from 46.

teach.x: Now **swap them**: the cheap rice gets the 9 and the dear rice gets the 6. So cheap : dear = 9 : 6 = **3 : 2**.

Why swap? Because the target 46 is nearer to 40, so there must be **more of the 40 rice**. The lot that is closer to the target is always the bigger one. Use this to check you have the ratio the right way round.
Three notes for the exam:

items.x: Always write the ratio in the order the question asks.
It works for prices, percentages and "fraction that is milk" alike.
**Water costs 0** and has 0% milk. Pure milk is 100% milk. Put those numbers in like any other.

tags: Two prices and a target: the plain case.
The same with strengths in percent.
Vessels given as ratios: use the fraction that is milk.
After the ratio, one quantity is given.
One of the two is water, which costs nothing.

example.q: In what ratio should tea at ₹60 per kg be mixed with tea at ₹90 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹72 per kg?
steps: 60 is 12 away from 72. 90 is 18 away from 72.
Swap: the ₹60 tea gets 18 and the ₹90 tea gets 12.
Check: 72 is nearer to 60, so there should be more of the ₹60 tea. Yes.

checks.q: In what ratio should sugar at ₹20 per kg be mixed with sugar at ₹30 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹24 per kg?
checks.why: 20 is 4 away and 30 is 6 away. Swap: 6 : 4 = 3 : 2. 24 is nearer to 20, so there is more of the ₹20 sugar. (2 : 3 is the same sum without the swap.)

lessons.title: Alligation where nothing is being mixed
lessons.plain: New: no liquids at all, but still two rates and one overall rate. The same picture gives the split.

teach.x: This lesson has no new method. Its purpose is to help you **recognise** alligation when the question does not look like a mixture.
The sign to look for: **two rates, and one overall rate that lies between them.** Whenever you see that, the swap picture tells you how the whole is split.

items.x: A trader sells part of his rice at 10% profit and the rest at 25% profit, and makes 16% overall. The two rates are 10 and 25; the overall is 16.
A man lends part of his money at 6% and the rest at 10%, and earns 7.4% overall.
A jar at 40% alcohol is partly replaced with 19% alcohol and ends at 26%. The part kept is at 40, the part poured in is at 19, and the result is 26.

teach.x: In each one: find how far each rate is from the overall, swap, and you have the ratio of the two parts. Then share the total in that ratio.
If the overall rate is not given directly, find it first. Interest of 1,480 on 20,000 is 7.4%.

tags: Two profit rates and an overall profit.
Two interest rates: find the overall rate first.
A replacement seen as mixing two strengths.

example.q: A shopkeeper has 60 kg of sugar. He sells part at 8% profit and the rest at 18% profit, and gains 14% on the whole. How much did he sell at 18% profit?
steps: Two rates, 8 and 18. Overall 14.
8 is 6 away from 14. 18 is 4 away from 14.
Swap: the 8% part : the 18% part = 4 : 6 = 2 : 3.
The 18% part = 3/5 of 60 = 36 kg.

checks.q: A class of 30 students has an average mark of 60. The boys average 55 and the girls average 70. How many girls are there?
checks.why: 55 is 5 away and 70 is 10 away. Swap: boys : girls = 10 : 5 = 2 : 1. Girls = 1/3 of 30 = 10. The average 60 is nearer the boys' 55, so there are more boys.

lessons.title: Mixtures that end in a profit
lessons.plain: New: the mixture is sold. Find what one kg of the mixture cost first, then it is an ordinary profit question.

teach.x: This last lesson joins mixtures to Profit and Loss. There is always one extra step, and it comes either at the end or at the start.
**Profit asked at the end.** Two lots are mixed and sold. Find the total cost and the total selling price, and compare them. Profit percent is always measured **on the cost**.
26 kg at 20 and 30 kg at 36 cost 520 + 1080 = 1600. Sold as 56 kg at 30, that brings in 1680. Profit is 80 on 1600, which is 5%.

**Profit given at the start.** The question tells you the selling price and the gain, and asks for the mixing ratio. First **undo the profit** to find what the mixture must cost. Selling at 44 with a 10% gain means the mixture costs 44 / 1.1 = 40. Now it is a plain alligation with 40 as the target.
**Water sold as milk.** Water is free, so whatever a milkman is paid for the water is pure profit. Count only what he paid for the milk as his cost.
If Profit and Loss itself feels unsure, its first two lessons are enough for this one.

tags: Mix, sell, find the profit.
The lots are given as a ratio instead of in kg.
One of the lots is water, which costs nothing.
Water and milk sold at milk's price: find the ratio.
The profit is given first: undo it, then alligate.

example.q: A shopkeeper mixes 20 kg of rice at ₹30 per kg with 30 kg at ₹40 per kg and sells the mixture at ₹45 per kg. What is his profit percent?
steps: So the mixture costs 1800 / 50 = ₹36 per kg.
He sells at ₹45, so the profit is ₹9 on ₹36.

checks.q: A milkman adds 1 litre of water to every 5 litres of milk and sells the mixture at the cost price of milk. What is his gain percent?
checks.why: He pays for 5 litres and is paid for 6. The extra 1 litre is profit on a cost of 5 litres: 1/5 = 20%. (16⅔% is 1 out of 6, which measures on the selling side.)

shortcut.title: Water sold at the price of milk

text.x: When a milkman sells the mixture at the **cost price of milk**, all of his gain is the water:
**gain % = water / milk x 100**
1 litre of water to every 4 litres of milk gives 25%. 1 to every 5 gives 20%.
Going the other way, a gain of 25% means water : milk = 25 : 100 = 1 : 4.
This is only for selling at milk's own cost price. If he also raises or lowers the price, work it out fully as in the lesson.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: never calculate what you can look up, cancel, or split.** Every question here is plain arithmetic. Speed comes from three habits: know the tables below by heart, cancel before you multiply, and split awkward numbers into easy pieces.
**The order rule (BODMAS, with “of” promoted):**

items.x: Brackets, innermost first.
Roots and powers.
**“of”** (it binds tighter than ÷ and ×). “1/2 of 90” is one lump, 45.
÷ and ×, strictly left to right.
+ and −, left to right.

blocks.x: **When the question mark is buried** (it is, in most Clerk questions): finish the side that has no question mark, then undo the other side one step at a time, outermost step first. Example: 35% of 480 + 15% of ? = 204. Known part 168. So 15% of ? = 36. So ? = 36 ÷ 15 × 100 = 240.
**Mechanics you must know cold:**

items.x: **Percent as a fraction.** 25% of 480 is 480 ÷ 4. Use the grid.
**Swap rule.** a% of b = b% of a. So 48% of 250 = 250% of 48 = 120.
**Multiplying by 25, 125, 11.** × 25 is × 100 ÷ 4. × 125 is × 1000 ÷ 8. × 11: write the number, add neighbours (47 × 11 = 4 \| 4+7 \| 7 = 517).
**Fractions chained with “of”.** Cancel across all of them before multiplying.
**Mixed numbers.** Add the whole parts and the fraction parts separately.

**Same base powers.** Multiply: add the powers. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply. First rewrite everything in one base (4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 16 = 2⁴, 32 = 2⁵, 64 = 2⁶; 9 = 3², 27 = 3³, 81 = 3⁴; 25 = 5², 125 = 5³; 49 = 7², 343 = 7³).
**Difference of squares.** a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). 140² − 60² = 200 × 80 = 16,000.

blocks.x: **Grid 1: percent to fraction**
**Grid 2: squares 11 to 30**
**Grid 3: cubes 1 to 20**

**Reading a big root without the table.** Square root of 4489: it ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7; 60² = 3600 and 70² = 4900, so it is sixty-something; 65² = 4225 is below 4489, so it is 67. Cube root of 6859: ends in 9, so the root ends in 9; 6 is between 1³ and 2³, so 19.
**Non-linear warning.** The root of a sum is not the sum of the roots: √(225 + 400) = √625 = 25, not 15 + 20. And ÷ then × goes left to right: 144 ÷ 12 × 3 is 36, not 4.
**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** BODMAS in the order above, one line per step, known side first. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Each question was sorted by its hardest ingredient, checked in this order: unusual powers, then fractions, then percent, then roots and squares, then decimals, then plain. Counts are out of the 1,791 readable bank questions; the PYQ figure is IBPS Clerk Prelims questions (and the number of papers they came from); the sister figure is from the 88 sister questions.

rows: Powers with the unknown in the exponent, or large powers

lead.x: What stands out:

items.x: Percent questions lead: 76 of the 227 Clerk PYQs, and in every one of the 22 papers.
In 155 of the 227 Clerk PYQs the question mark is buried inside the expression, not sitting alone after the equals sign. Practise undoing, not just computing.

Approximation is close to absent in Clerk Prelims: 4 questions, all from one 2017 model paper. In the sister papers it appeared only in IBPS PO Prelims, never in SBI Clerk or RRB Clerk. Your bank has 453 approximation questions; do not let that share set your practice time for Prelims.

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** one or more “a% of b” terms.
**Shortcut engine.** grid fraction if there is one; otherwise split the percent, or use 1% and 10% of the number.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3).** 23% of 600 + 33% of 800 = ? + 53% of 400. 1% of each is 6, 8 and 4, so 138 + 264 = ? + 212. 402 − 212 = 190.
**Pattern clues.** √, ∛, ² or ³.
**Shortcut engine.** replace each from the grids first, then it is a plain question.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3).** √784 ÷ ∛343 × √625 − ∛1728 = 28 ÷ 7 × 25 − 12 = 100 − 12 = 88.
**Pattern clues.** only whole numbers and + − × ÷.
**Shortcut engine.** ÷ and × left to right, cancelling as you go; then + and −.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** ? = 225 ÷ 45 ÷ 5 × 75. 225 ÷ 45 = 5; 5 ÷ 5 = 1; 1 × 75 = 75.
**One identity that has come (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2016).** (854³ − 276³) ÷ (854² + 854 × 276 + 276²) is the pattern (a³ − b³) ÷ (a² + ab + b²) = a − b = 578.
**Pattern clues.** “a/b of”, mixed numbers such as 7 1/2.
**Shortcut engine.** chain of “of”: cancel across, then multiply once. Mixed numbers: wholes and fractions separately.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 4).** 3/4 of 8/9 of 27/32 of 4608. Cancel: 3 × 8 × 27 over 4 × 9 × 32 comes down to 9/16. 4608 ÷ 16 = 288; × 9 = 2592.
**Mixed numbers (same paper).** 7 1/2 + 6 2/3 − 5 1/6 + 3 1/3. Wholes: 7 + 6 − 5 + 3 = 11. Fractions in sixths: 3 + 4 − 1 + 2 = 8 sixths = 1 1/3. Answer 12 1/3.
**Pattern clues.** decimal points, exact answer wanted.
**Shortcut engine.** turn the decimal into a fraction you know (12.5 = 100/8, 0.75 = 3/4, 2.5 = 10/4), or shift the point on both numbers.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 2).** 3750 ÷ 12.5 + 180. 3750 × 8 ÷ 100 = 300. Answer 480.
**Pattern clues.** 2\^? or 7\^?, or powers above the cube.
**Shortcut engine.** rewrite everything in one base, then only add and subtract the powers.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 5 Oct 2025 Shift 1).** 2⁴ × 2\^? = 32 × 64 = 2⁵ × 2⁶ = 2¹¹. So ? = 11 − 4 = 7.

items.title: Approximation

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “approximate value”, numbers like 31.98 or 499.99.
**Shortcut engine.** round every number to the nearest friendly whole number first (and percents to grid fractions), then solve as an exact question. Pick the nearest option.

items.label: Seen once (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2017 model paper)

tail.x: There is no Insurance group in this topic: every archetype has appeared in a paper.

lead.x: All seven questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was checked by script. One drill per archetype; between them they cover the easy, two-step, non-linear and phrasing types.

method.x: **30-Second Exam Method:** 36 + 90 = 126; minus 26 = 100. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** unit digits only: 6 + 0 − 6 = 0, so the answer ends in 0. That leaves 100 and 110. Back-check: 126 − 26 = 100.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** doing 12 × 3 first gives 144 ÷ 36 = 4, then 68, option (A). ÷ and × go left to right.
**Conventional Method:** 35% of 480 = 168. Right side = 144 + 60 = 204. So 15% of ? = 36 and ? = 36 × 100 ÷ 15 = 240.
**Option Elimination Hack:** test the middle option: 15% of 240 = 24 + 12 = 36. It fits, so stop. Back-check: 168 + 36 = 204.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** stopping at 36 (the value of the percent term) and hunting for it in the options. The question mark is the number the percent is taken of.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 25 + 216 = 241; minus 141 = 100. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** unit digits: 5 + 6 − 1 = 0, so it ends in 0. That removes 105 and 95. Back-check: 241 − 141 = 100.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** taking √225 + √400 = 15 + 20 = 35 gives 110, option (A). Add inside the root first.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 360 ÷ 45 = 8; add 2 1/2. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the first part is a whole number (8) and 2 1/2 is added, so the answer ends in a half. That removes 8 and 18. Back-check: 45 × 8 = 360.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “of” is done before ÷. Going left to right (360 ÷ 1/2 = 720, then × 90) gives a huge number. IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 1 used this exact shape with roots.
**Conventional Method:** 512 × 256 ÷ 256 = 512 = 2⁹.
**30-Second Exam Method:** in base 2: 8³ = 2⁹, 4⁴ = 2⁸, 16² = 2⁸. 9 + 8 − 8 = 9. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed once the bases match. Back-check: 2⁹ = 512.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding the written powers (3 + 4 − 2 = 5) without first changing 8, 4 and 16 into powers of 2.
**30-Second Exam Method:** ÷ 12.5 is × 8 ÷ 100: 300. Three-quarters of 64: 48. 348 − 148 = 200. **Answer (E).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** unit digits: 0 + 8 − 8 = 0, so it ends in 0. That leaves 180 and 200. Back-check: 12.5 × 300 = 3750.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** misplacing the decimal: 3750 ÷ 12.5 is 300, not 30 or 3000. Quick sense check: 12.5 × 100 is 1250, so the answer is a few hundred.

body.x: What approximate value comes in place of the question mark? 24.98% of 639.97 + (17.02)² − √323.9 = ?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** exact working gives about 159.86 + 289.68 − 18.00 = 431.5.
**Option Elimination Hack:** not needed; the options are 20 apart and the rounding moves the answer by less than 1. Back-check: 449 − 18 = 431.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** rounding 24.98% to 25% is safe; rounding 17.02 to 20 is not. Round to the nearest whole number, or to the nearest value in your tables, never further.

rows: Grid fraction, or split the percent, or swap a and b
Root of a sum is not the sum of roots

blocks.x: **Three checks that kill options (use only when options are whole numbers):**

items.x: **Unit digit.** Work only the last digits through + − ×. Does not work through ÷ or roots.
**Size.** A rough round-number version tells you the hundred the answer lives in.
**Multiple.** If the answer is something × 9, its digits add to a multiple of 9; if something × 5, it ends in 0 or 5.

The rungs are faster here than in other topics (40 and 25 seconds, not 60 and 45) because these questions have to pay for the time the word problems take. **How this topic was checked (different from the other modules).** These questions are bare expressions, so I wrote one evaluator that reads each expression, tries every option in place of the question mark, and reports which option makes the two sides equal. No question was encoded by hand and no helper runs were used. For approximation questions the evaluator first rounds every decimal to the nearest whole number and looks for an exact fit; if there is none, it solves exactly and takes the nearest option.

Bank questions used: 2,227 (227 PYQ + 2,000 practice), of which 436 are printed as images and could not be read. The floor of 8 target-exam shifts and 6 to 10 sister questions is met many times over. Memory-based papers are reconstructions, not official papers.
This is the largest block in the paper: the four 4 Oct 2025 Clerk shifts in your bank carry 10 to 12 of these each. It deserves the most practice time of any topic in this file.

intro.x: Simplification is plain arithmetic: one line of numbers and signs, and one value to find. There are no stories to untangle. What it asks for is a fixed **order** of working and a few tables known well enough that you do not have to stop and calculate.

There are fourteen short lessons. The first two set up the order and the working-backwards habit. Then each lesson adds one kind of term: percents, squares and roots, fractions, decimals, powers. The last two cover approximation and full exam-style lines. Go in order the first time.

after.x: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has all the tables on one page, and the Course in the Clerk Quant bank has over two hundred real paper questions to practise on.
This topic rewards a little daily practice more than any other. Ten questions a day, with the tables beside you until you no longer need them, is the surest way to make it fast.

lessons.title: Which step comes first
lessons.plain: The starting point: a fixed order for doing the operations, so that everyone reaches the same answer.

teach.x: "48 x 15 ÷ 12 + 140". Simplification questions are plain arithmetic, but one line can hold several operations. If you did them in any order you liked, different people would get different answers. So there is an agreed order, and the whole topic rests on it.

items.x: **Brackets** first. If there are brackets inside brackets, start with the innermost.
**Roots and powers** next (square roots, squares, cubes).
**"Of"**. In these questions "of" means multiply, and it is done before ordinary dividing and multiplying. "1/2 of 90" is treated as one lump, 45.
**Divide and multiply**, strictly from left to right, whichever comes first.
**Add and subtract**, from left to right.

teach.x: This is often remembered as **BODMAS**. The two places people slip are both in step 4.

items.x: Division and multiplication have **equal rank**. In 225 ÷ 45 ÷ 5 x 75 you do not multiply first. You go left to right: 225 ÷ 45 = 5, then 5 ÷ 5 = 1, then 1 x 75 = 75.
Adding never jumps ahead of multiplying. In 120 + 17 x 8, the 17 x 8 is done first.

teach.x: A good working habit: **underline the multiplying and dividing lumps first**, finish each lump, and only then do the adding and subtracting between them.

tags: Multiply and divide, then add.
Two divisions in a row: strictly left to right.
Two lumps with adding and subtracting between them.
Brackets inside brackets, and an "of".
"Of" is done before dividing.

steps: Find the lumps joined by ÷ and x: "72 ÷ 8 x 5" and "3 x 4".
First lump, left to right: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, then 9 x 5 = 45.
Second lump: 3 x 4 = 12.
Now add and subtract, left to right: 45 - 12 + 6 = 39.

checks.why: Left to right: 36 ÷ 6 = 6, then 6 x 3 = 18. Then add: 18 + 2 = 20. (4 comes from doing 6 x 3 first, which is not allowed: ÷ and x go in the order they appear.)

lessons.title: When the question mark is in the middle
lessons.plain: New: the blank is not at the end. Finish everything you can, then undo the steps around the blank one at a time.

teach.x: In most Clerk questions the question mark is not sitting alone on one side. It is buried: "(? + 24) ÷ 6 x 5 = 60". You cannot simply calculate. You have to **work backwards**.

items.x: **Finish every part that has no question mark in it.** That usually leaves one side as a plain number.
**Undo the steps around the question mark, starting from the outside.** The last thing done to the blank is the first thing you undo.

teach.x: Undoing means doing the opposite:

rows: What was done to the blank

teach.x: Take "? ÷ 12 + 15 = 40". The blank was divided by 12, and then 15 was added. Undo in the reverse order: take away the 15 first (25), then multiply by 12 (300).
One arrangement needs a little care: when the blank is what you **divide by** or **subtract**. In "9240 ÷ ? = 330", the blank is 9240 ÷ 330. In "336 - ? = 108", the blank is 336 - 108.
Sometimes the blank appears **twice**, as in "3 x ? ÷ 8 = 54 ÷ ?". Bring both to one side by multiplying: ? x ? = 54 x 8 ÷ 3 = 144, so ? = 12.

tags: The blank is one of the numbers added.
The blank is what you divide by.
Finish both sides first.
Several steps to undo.
The blank appears on both sides.

steps: The right side is already a plain number: 60.
The last thing done on the left was "x 5". Undo it: 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
Before that came "÷ 6". Undo it: 12 x 6 = 72.

checks.why: Undo from the outside. Take away the 15: 25. Then undo "÷ 12" by multiplying: 25 x 12 = 300. (25 stops one step too early.)

lessons.title: Percent of a number
lessons.plain: New: terms such as "35% of 480". Find each one quickly by splitting the percent into easy pieces.

teach.x: "a% of b" terms are in most Clerk simplification questions. Each one is a lump: work it out first, then add and subtract the lumps.
You know the basic method: 1% is the number divided by 100. Two stepping stones make it quicker.

items.x: **50%, 25%**: a half, a quarter. 25% of 480 is 120.

teach.x: Then **split** any percent into pieces you can do in your head.
35% of 480: a quarter is 120, 10% is 48, together 168.
When the number is a round hundred, go straight through 1%. "23% of 600": 1% is 6, so 23 x 6 = 138.

If the question mark is itself a percent ("... = ?% of 930"), find the left side as a number first, then ask what percent of 930 it is: divide by 930 and multiply by 100, or more simply, divide by the 1% (9.3).

tags: Round percents of round numbers.
Split the percent.
One term is easier swapped.
Three terms, with the blank on the right.
The blank is the percent.

steps: First lump, split 35% as 25% + 10%: a quarter of 480 is 120, and 10% is 48. Together 168.
Second lump: 10% of 200 is 20, and half of that is 10. Together 30.
Add the lumps: 168 + 30 = 198.

text.x: **a% of b is the same as b% of a.** When a percent is awkward but the other number is friendly, swap them.
48% of 250 is fiddly. But 250% of 48 is two and a half times 48: 96 + 24 = 120.
Look for 25, 50, 125 or 250 as the second number; those are the ones worth swapping.

lessons.title: Percent terms with the blank inside
lessons.plain: New: lessons 2 and 3 together. The number you take the percent of is the unknown.

teach.x: "35% of 480 + 15% of ? = 204." The blank is inside a percent term. Nothing new is needed; combine the last two lessons.

items.x: Finish the terms that have no blank: 35% of 480 = 168.
Undo the adding: 15% of ? = 204 - 168 = 36.
Now you know a **part** and want the **whole**. Go through 1%: 36 ÷ 15 = 2.4, so the whole is 240.

teach.x: Step 3 is the "find the whole from a part" move from the Basics. When the percent is a simple fraction, use that instead: if 25% of something is 150, the something is 4 x 150 = 600; if 75% is 375, a quarter is 125 and the whole is 500.
Two arrangements to recognise.

items.x: **The blank is inside a bracket**: "25% of (? + 360) = 150". Treat the bracket as one thing first. The bracket is 600, so ? is 240.
**The blank is the percent**: "?% of 120 + 45 = 57". Then ?% of 120 is 12, and 12 out of 120 is 10%.

tags: The blank is a plain number subtracted.
The blank is the whole.
The blank is inside a bracket.
The blank is the percent.
A percent above 100, and a plain multiplication.

steps: Finish the known term: 35% of 480 = 120 + 48 = 168.
Undo the adding: 15% of ? = 204 - 168 = 36.
Part to whole: 1% = 36 ÷ 15 = 2.4.

checks.why: Undo the adding: 20% of ? = 60. 20% is one fifth, so the whole is 5 x 60 = 300. (12 takes 20% of 60 instead of going back to the whole.)

lessons.title: Percents that are fractions in disguise
lessons.plain: New: 12.5%, 37.5%, 16 2/3% and percents above 100. Replace each with its fraction and divide.

teach.x: Some percents look unpleasant as numbers but are simple fractions underneath. Examiners use them on purpose, and the numbers they attach are chosen to divide exactly.
"12.5% of 968" is one eighth of 968: 121. "37.5% of 256" is three eighths: 256 ÷ 8 = 32, and 3 x 32 = 96.
The eighths are worth knowing as a family: 12.5, 25, 37.5, 50, 62.5, 75, 87.5 are 1/8 to 7/8.
**Percents above 100** split the same way. 150% is the number plus half of it. 130% is the number plus 30% of it. 225% is twice the number plus a quarter of it.
**A percent of a percent.** "60% of 50% of 650": do one at a time. Half of 650 is 325, and 60% of 325 is 195.

lessons.title: Squares and square roots
lessons.plain: New: the signs for squaring and square root. Replace each from memory, and the question becomes plain arithmetic.

teach.x: A small raised 2 means **squared**: the number multiplied by itself. 14 squared is 14 x 14 = 196.
The sign √ means **square root**: the number that was squared to give this one. √196 is 14, because 14 x 14 = 196.

In the order of operations these come early, straight after brackets. So the first move in any such question is to **replace every square and every square root with its value**. What remains is the plain arithmetic of lesson 1.
That is why this lesson is mostly about recognising numbers. The squares up to 30 appear constantly, in both directions. They are worth learning the way you learned multiplication tables.
For a bigger root, a little reasoning finds it. √1764: it lies between 40 squared (1600) and 50 squared (2500), and it ends in 4, so the root ends in 2 or 8. It must be 42.
The last digit is a useful check both ways: a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square.

tags: Two square roots.
Two squares.
Three square roots.
Roots mixed with dividing and multiplying.

steps: Replace each one. √1296 = 36 (it lies between 30 squared and 40 squared, and ends in 6).
17 squared = 289. 15 squared = 225.

text.x: To square a number ending in 5: take the part before the 5, **multiply it by the next number up**, and write 25 after the result.
35 squared: 3 x 4 = 12, then 25. So 1225.
65 squared: 6 x 7 = 42, then 25. So 4225. And 105 squared: 10 x 11 = 110, then 25: 11,025.
It also runs backwards: √5625 ends in 25, and 56 = 7 x 8, so the root is 75.

lessons.title: Cubes, cube roots and roots inside roots
lessons.plain: New: the cube (a number times itself twice) and its root, and how to open a root that sits inside another root.

teach.x: A small raised 3 means **cubed**: 5 cubed is 5 x 5 x 5 = 125. The sign ∛ is the **cube root**: ∛125 = 5.
As with squares, the first move is to replace each one with its value. The cubes that come up are these.
Some papers write a cube root as a power of one-third: (729) to the power 1/3 means ∛729. Likewise a power of one-half means a square root.
**A root inside a root.** "√(157 + √(130 + √196))". Work from the **inside out**, exactly as with brackets.

items.x: Innermost: √196 = 14.

teach.x: The same goes for a root of a root. √(√6561): the inner root is 81, and the root of 81 is 9.

tags: A cube root and a square root.
Cube roots written as a power of one-third.
Roots inside a bracket.
A root inside a root inside a root.
A root of a root, twice.

steps: ∛4913 = 17 (from the table).
Inside out: √256 = 16, and √16 = 4.

checks.why: The number ends in 4, and the only digit whose cube ends in 4 is 4. Between 10 cubed (1000) and 20 cubed (8000), that makes it 14. Check: 14 x 14 = 196, and 196 x 14 = 2744.

shortcut.title: Reading a cube root from its last digit

text.x: For a perfect cube, the last digit of the root is fixed by the last digit of the number. Most digits stay the same; only four swap.
Then drop the last three digits and see which cube the rest sits just above. That gives the first digit.
∛6859: it ends in 9, so the root ends in 9. Drop "859" and 6 remains; 1 cubed is 1 and 2 cubed is 8, so the first digit is 1. The root is 19.

lessons.title: Squares with a blank, and a pattern that saves work
lessons.plain: New: the blank is itself squared; and a difference of two squares can be done without squaring anything.

teach.x: Two things in this lesson.

**When the blank is squared.** "2500 + 24² - 51 = ?² - 111." Treat "? squared" as the unknown first. Finish the known side, undo the steps, and you will have "? squared = some number". Then take the square root as the very last step.
This is where knowing the squares table backwards pays off: 3136 is 56 squared, 676 is 26 squared, 2809 is 53 squared.
**A difference of two squares.** Whenever you see one square minus another, there is a pattern that avoids squaring at all:
**a squared minus b squared = (a + b) x (a - b)**
Use it when the two numbers add or subtract to something round. If they do not, just use the table.
Be careful that it is a **difference**. There is no such shortcut for a sum of two squares: 14² + 16² simply has to be 196 + 256.

tags: A difference of squares, then a division.
A difference of squares inside a longer line.
Three squares, and the answer side has one too.
The blank is squared.

steps: A difference of two squares: (73 + 27) x (73 - 27).

checks.why: (65 + 35) x (65 - 35) = 100 x 30 = 3,000. (900 is 30 squared: the difference must not be squared.)

text.x: A pattern that has appeared in the Clerk paper once, in a frightening-looking form:
**(a cubed - b cubed) ÷ (a squared + a x b + b squared) = a - b**
When a question repeats the same two numbers in this exact arrangement, it is asking you to notice the pattern, not to multiply.

lessons.title: Fractions of a number
lessons.plain: New: "3/7 of 2/5 of 1050". Cancel across the fractions before you multiply anything.

teach.x: "3/7 of 1050" means divide 1050 by 7 and multiply by 3. Always **divide first**: 1050 ÷ 7 = 150, then 3 x 150 = 450. Dividing first keeps the numbers small.
When several fractions are chained with "of", they are all being multiplied. The golden rule is: **cancel before you multiply.**
"3/4 of 8/9 of 27/32 of 4608". Write all the tops together and all the bottoms together:

items.x: tops: 3 x 8 x 27
bottoms: 4 x 9 x 32

teach.x: Now cancel any top with any bottom. 8 goes into 32 four times. 27 and 9 leave 3. The chain shrinks to 3 x 3 on top and 4 x 4 underneath: 9/16.
You may also cancel a bottom number straight against the big number at the end, if it divides exactly. Cancel in whatever order looks easiest; the answer is the same.
If the question has two fraction terms joined by plus or minus, each is its own lump: work out each, then add or subtract.
A top-heavy fraction such as 23/19 behaves the same way: "23/19 of 684" is 684 ÷ 19 = 36, then 23 x 36.

tags: Two fractions in a chain.
Three fractions in a chain.
Awkward numbers that cancel completely.
Two fraction lumps added.
A top-heavy fraction, and a blank.

steps: Tops: 4 x 3 x 5. Bottoms: 9 x 8 x 6.
Cancel: 4 into 8 leaves 2 underneath. 3 into 9 leaves 3 underneath. Now 5 on top, and 3 x 2 x 6 = 36 underneath.
So the chain is 5/36.

checks.why: The 3s cancel, leaving 2/4, which is a half. Half of 480 is 240.

lessons.title: Mixed numbers
lessons.plain: New: numbers such as 7 1/2. Add and subtract the whole parts and the fraction parts separately.

teach.x: A **mixed number** is a whole number with a fraction beside it: 7 1/2 means seven and a half.
**Adding and subtracting.** Do not turn them into top-heavy fractions. Handle the two parts separately.

items.x: Add and subtract the **whole parts**.
Add and subtract the **fraction parts**. To do that, give them all the same bottom number: one that all the bottoms go into (the Basics lesson on this is "A number that several numbers go into").
Put the two results together. If the fractions come to more than 1, carry the extra to the whole part. If they come out negative, borrow 1 from the whole part.

teach.x: "4 3/4 + 2 5/6 - 3 1/3": the whole parts give 4 + 2 - 3 = 3. For the fractions, 4, 6 and 3 all go into 12: 9/12 + 10/12 - 4/12 = 15/12, which is 1 3/12 = 1 1/4. Together: 4 1/4.
**Multiplying and dividing.** Here you **do** turn each into a top-heavy fraction first, because the parts cannot be multiplied separately. 4 2/5 is (4 x 5 + 2) over 5 = 22/5.
Then multiply as in the last lesson, cancelling across. To divide by a fraction, turn it upside down and multiply.
A mixed number times a whole number is a useful special case: 3 1/13 x 65 is 40/13 x 65 = 40 x 5 = 200.

tags: Adding and subtracting, with a carry.
Adding and subtracting, with a borrow.

steps: Whole parts: 4 + 2 - 3 = 3.
Fractions, with 12 underneath: 9/12 + 10/12 - 4/12 = 15/12.
15/12 is 1 and 3/12, which is 1 1/4.

checks.why: Whole parts: 2 + 3 - 1 = 4. Fractions with 6 underneath: 3/6 + 2/6 - 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. Together 4 2/3.

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.plain: New: numbers with a decimal point. Line them up to add; turn awkward ones into fractions to multiply or divide.

teach.x: **Adding and subtracting decimals.** Line up the decimal points and work as with whole numbers. It often helps to add the easy pairs first: in 45.6 + 124.75 - 68.35, notice that 124.75 - 68.35 = 56.4, and 56.4 + 45.6 = 102.

**Multiplying.** Ignore the points, multiply, then put the point back so that the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers had together. 2.4 x 1.5: 24 x 15 = 360, two decimal places, so 3.60.
**Dividing by a decimal.** Move the point the same number of places in **both** numbers until the divisor is whole. 15.6 ÷ 0.13 becomes 1560 ÷ 13 = 120.
The real time-saver is recognising decimals that are simple fractions. Dividing by them turns into multiplying by something easy.
So 3750 ÷ 12.5 = 3750 x 8 ÷ 100 = 300. And multiplying by 12.5 goes the other way: x 100 ÷ 8.
Watch for squares hiding behind a decimal point: 1.44 is 1.2 squared and 2.56 is 1.6 squared, so 36 ÷ 1.44 is 3600 ÷ 144 = 25.

tags: Adding and subtracting.

steps: 8.4 x 2.5: multiplying by 2.5 is x 10 ÷ 4. 84 ÷ 4 = 21.

lessons.title: Powers
lessons.plain: New: a small raised number counts how many times a number is multiplied by itself. With one base, you only add and subtract those counts.

teach.x: 2⁵ means 2 multiplied by itself five times: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32. The 2 is the **base** and the 5 is the **power**.
Questions on powers look heavy but are among the lightest, because of three rules. They work only when the **base is the same**.

rows: You do this to the powers
take a power of a power

teach.x: So the method is always:

items.x: **Rewrite every number as a power of one base.** This is the real work.
Add, subtract or multiply the powers.

teach.x: The numbers to recognise:

items.x: powers of 3: 9, 27, 81, 243 are 3², 3³, 3⁴, 3⁵;
powers of 5 and 7: 25, 125 are 5², 5³; and 49, 343 are 7², 7³.

teach.x: "2⁴ x 2^? = 32 x 64." The right side is 2⁵ x 2⁶ = 2¹¹. So 4 + ? = 11, and ? = 7.
Decimals can share a base too: 0.49 is 0.7 squared and 0.343 is 0.7 cubed.
If two numbers have the **same power** but different bases, divide the bases instead: 64⁵ ÷ 32⁵ = (64 ÷ 32)⁵ = 2⁵.

steps: Rewrite in base 2. 4 is 2², so 4³ = 2⁶. 8 is 2³, so 8² = 2⁶. 16 is 2⁴.
Multiplying adds the powers: 6 + 6 = 12.
Dividing subtracts: 12 - 4 = 8.

checks.why: In base 3: 27 is 3³, 81 is 3⁴ and 9 is 3². So 3 + 4 - 2 = 5.

lessons.title: Approximation
lessons.plain: New: the numbers are ugly on purpose, such as 24.98 and 119.97. Round each to a friendly number first, then solve.

teach.x: Some questions ask for the **approximate** value. You can tell them by the numbers: 24.98, 16.02, 119.97. Each is a whisker away from a round number, and that is the hint. Nobody is expected to multiply 24.98 by 16.02.
The method is one step added to everything you already know:

items.x: **Round every number to the nearest friendly value.** 24.98 becomes 25. 16.02 becomes 16. 119.97 becomes 120.
**Solve the tidy question** exactly as usual.
**Choose the option nearest to your answer.** It will usually match exactly.

teach.x: A few things to round with care.

items.x: **Percents**: round to one you can do. 34.98% is 35%. 33.32% is one third. 16.67% is one sixth.
**Roots**: round the number under the root to the nearest perfect square or cube. √624.9 is √625 = 25. ∛342.9 is ∛343 = 7.
**A root that is not a perfect square**, such as √255: use the nearest one, √256 = 16.

teach.x: Do not round too early or too roughly. Change each number by a tiny amount only; if you find yourself turning 31.98 into 30, you have gone too far. It should become 32.
One oddity: if the blank is squared, a paper may give the answer as ± 12, meaning 12 or minus 12, since both give 144 when squared.

lessons.title: Everything in one line
lessons.plain: New: nothing new. A real Clerk question mixes three or four of these ideas, so practise taking it one lump at a time.

teach.x: A typical Clerk question does not test one idea. It puts a percent, a square, a fraction and a blank into a single line: "55% of 1400 + ?² + 282 = 12³".
You already have every piece. What is left is a calm routine for long lines.

items.x: **Mark the lumps.** Each percent term, each fraction term, each square or root is a lump.
**Replace every lump that has no blank with its value.** Write the line again with plain numbers. It will be much shorter.
**Follow the order of operations** on what is left, or **undo towards the blank**.
**Glance at the options** before the last step. If they are all whole numbers and you are heading for a decimal, something has slipped.

teach.x: Writing the line out again after step 2 is not wasted time. It is where most errors are caught.

A final word on speed. It comes from the tables (squares, cubes, fraction percents) far more than from tricks. If one of those tables still feels slow, a few minutes on it every day will do more for this topic than anything else.

sections.title: Core Mental Model, Mechanics and Conversion Grid

blocks.x: **The one idea: put numbers on the page and let the pencil count, not your head.** Every question here is mechanical. Nobody gets these wrong for lack of logic; they get them wrong by miscounting or misreading one word. So the method is always: mark, number, read off.
**Position rules (learn these five lines; they replace all counting back and forth):**

rows: nth to the **right** of mth from the **left**
nth to the **left** of mth from the **left**
nth to the **left** of mth from the **right**
nth to the **right** of mth from the **right**
mth from the right in a row of N

blocks.x: One way to remember it: if the movement takes you **away from** the end you are counting from, add. If it takes you **back towards** that end, subtract.
**The four habits:**

items.x: **Number the row once.** Write 5, 10, 15, 20 under every fifth element as soon as you see a row. All position questions on that row then take seconds.
**For “how many such…” questions, hunt the middle element.** If the question wants a digit with a letter before and a symbol after, look only at digits and check both neighbours. Tick each hit.
**For “if all symbols are dropped” questions, do not rewrite the row.** Count along it skipping the dropped kind. Rewrite only if three or more questions use the changed row.
**For letter questions, write alphabet numbers above the letters.** Use the grid and the anchors E J O T Y = 5 10 15 20 25.

blocks.x: **Conversion grid: alphabet positions**

items.x: Vowels: A E I O U (positions 1, 5, 9, 15, 21). Everything else is a consonant.
Next letter after Z is A; before A is Z, unless the question says otherwise.
Letter just after each vowel: B F J P V. Letter just before each vowel: Z D H N T. These are all consonants, so “vowels changed to the next letter” never creates a vowel.
Consonants that become vowels when moved one step forward: D H N T Z. One step back: B F J P V.

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** “Pairs of letters with as many letters between them as in the alphabet” must be counted in **both** directions when the question says “both forward and backward”. Counting only left to right gives a smaller, wrong number that is always among the options.

**Universal fallback (works on every question in this topic):** write the row or word out with numbers above it, do exactly what the sentence says one clause at a time, and read the answer off the page. If stuck, do that and nothing else.

lead.x: Bank counts are out of 933. The Clerk figure is questions seen in the 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers (and how many of the 12 papers had one); the sister figure is from the 12 sister papers.

rows: A row of letters, digits or symbols, 4 to 5 questions on it
Pairs of letters in a word, or digits in a number
One word or number changed by a rule, then a count

Odd one out among letter groups
Row of letters only (bank label; in papers it is counted in the first row)

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “how many such … each of which is immediately preceded by … and immediately followed by …”.
**Shortcut engine.** find every element of the kind asked for, check its left and right neighbour, tick.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3).** row 3 G 6 @ B K 9 # T \$ 2 E U Q € ★ 5 M F % L 8 R V © 7 W S 4 H A. Symbols preceded by a consonant and followed by a digit: go symbol by symbol. @ has 6 before, no. # has 9 before, no. \$ has T before and 2 after, yes. € has Q before, ★ after, no. ★ has € before, no. % has F before, L after, no. © has V before and 7 after, yes. Answer two.
**Pattern clues.** “which element is nth to the left of mth from the right end”.
**Shortcut engine.** turn it into one position with the five-line table, then count once.
**Worked example (same paper).** 3rd to the left of the 10th from the right = 13th from the right. Counting from the right end: A, H, 4, S, W, 7, ©, V, R, 8, L, %, F. Answer F.
**Pattern clues.** “if all the symbols are removed”, “if the second half is reversed”.
**Shortcut engine.** reduce to one position, then count along the row skipping what was removed.

**Worked example (same paper).** remove all symbols; 5th to the right of the 12th from the left = 17th from the left. Counting only letters and digits: 3, G, 6, B, K, 9, T, 2, E, U, Q, 5, M, F, L, 8, R. Answer R.

items.title: Row: pattern of groups

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** a line such as “RSD WKC VJE ?” built from the row.
**Shortcut engine.** write the row positions of each letter of each group; the positions move by a steady rule from group to group.

**Illustration on the 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3 row (my own example, not a paper question).** 3G6, BK9, T\$2, ? The groups sit at positions 1 to 3, 5 to 7, 9 to 11: three taken, one skipped. Next is positions 13 to 15 = U Q €. The 2021 paper’s question of this kind did not come through clearly enough for me to confirm its answer, so it is counted as a sighting only.

items.label: Confirmed (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2021 and 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3)

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “how many pairs of letters … as many letters between them in the word as in the alphabet”.

**Shortcut engine.** write alphabet numbers above the letters. A pair counts when the difference in alphabet numbers equals the difference in their places in the word, whichever of the two comes first. Go letter by letter and look only at later letters. For digits in a number, use the digits themselves.

**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 4 Oct 2025 Shift 2).** BUTTERFLY = 2, 21, 20, 20, 5, 18, 6, 12, 25. U (place 2) and T (place 3): one place apart, values 21 and 20, one apart: yes. T (place 4) and R (place 6): two places apart, values 20 and 18: yes. T (place 4) and Y (place 9): five places apart, values 20 and 25: yes. No other pair fits. Answer three.
**Pattern clues.** “each vowel is changed to the next letter and each consonant to the previous letter”; “digits arranged in ascending order, how many stay in place”.
**Shortcut engine.** write the new line directly under the old one, place by place, then count.

**Worked example (IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims 13 Dec 2025 Shift 1).** 589421367 in ascending order is 123456789. Place by place: 5 over 1, 8 over 2, 9 over 3, 4 over 4, 2 over 5, 1 over 6, 3 over 7, 6 over 8, 7 over 9. Only the 4th place is the same. Answer one.
**Pattern clues.** “if a meaningful word is formed using the 2nd, 5th, 8th and 9th letters of …”.

**Shortcut engine.** pull the letters out, try the consonant-vowel shapes. Then apply the question’s own rule: usually one word means give its nth letter, no word means X, more than one means Z. Read which letter stands for which case; papers change it.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2019).** TRANSLATION, letters 2, 5, 8, 9 are R, S, T, I. One common word: STIR. The key gives T, its second letter.
**Pattern clues.** five groups of three or four letters.
**Shortcut engine.** write the gaps between letters for each group; four share a gap pattern, one does not.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2019).** BEH, JMP, TWZ, CFI, KOP. Gaps: +3 +3 for the first four; KOP is +4 +1. Answer KOP.
**Pattern clues.** “TAP NOT MAT PQR STB” followed by five questions.
**Shortcut engine.** write the five words in a column once. Each question changes them in a different way and always starts again from the original words.
**Worked example (IBPS Clerk Prelims 2018).** TAP NOT MAT PQR STB. First and third letters interchanged: PAT, TON, TAM, RQP, BTS. Meaningful: PAT and TON. Answer two.
**Shortcut engine.** line the word up over its code and write the +1 or −1 for each letter; apply the same pattern.
**Worked example (that paper).** CIRCLE is DHSBMD: +1, −1, +1, −1, +1, −1. PUBLIC becomes Q, T, C, K, J, B = QTCKJB.

Same handling as R6: write them in a column, apply the change to each, read off. Typical asks: swap first and last digits then find the largest; add the digits; arrange digits within each number. Start again from the original numbers for every question.

lead.x: All nine questions are original, written for this module, and each answer was checked by script. Drills 1 to 4 use one row, as a paper does.
**Row for Drills 1 to 4:** K 7 # R 4 E @ 9 M \$ 2 U T 5 % A 8 W & 3 H 6 \* J

body.x: How many digits in the row are immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a symbol?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** read the row left to right testing every element.

**30-Second Exam Method:** look only at the nine digits. 7 (K before, # after) yes. 4 (R, E) no. 9 (@ before) no. 2 (\$ before) no. 5 (T, %) yes. 8 (A, W) no. 3 (& before) no. 6 (H, \*) yes. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none; a count has to be counted. Back-check: the three hits are K7#, T5%, H6\*.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “preceded by a letter and followed by a symbol” is not the same as “preceded by a symbol and followed by a letter”. Underline which side is which before you start.

body.x: Which element is 5th to the right of the 9th element from the right end?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** count 9 from the right end (A), then 5 steps to the right.
**30-Second Exam Method:** right of … from right: subtract. 9 − 5 = 4th from the right. J, \*, 6, H. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed. Back-check: 9th from the right is A; five steps right of A are 8, W, &, 3, H.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** adding instead of subtracting gives the 14th from the right, which is 2. Moving right while counting from the right end takes you back towards that end, so the number gets smaller.

body.x: If all the symbols are removed from the row, which element is 4th to the left of the 7th element from the right end?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** rewrite the row without symbols (18 elements), then count.
**30-Second Exam Method:** 7 + 4 = 11th from the right. Count from the right skipping symbols: J, 6, H, 3, W, 8, A, 5, T, U, 2. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed. Back-check: 7th from the right without symbols is A; four to its left are 5, T, U, 2.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** counting the symbols you were told to remove. Put a light stroke through them first if the row is on paper.

body.x: What comes in place of the question mark, based on the row? K#R [4@9](mailto:4@9) M2U ?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** find each group’s elements in the row and compare.
**30-Second Exam Method:** positions: K#R = 1, 3, 4. [4@9](mailto:4@9) = 5, 7, 8. M2U = 9, 11, 12. Each group moves on by four. Next = 13, 15, 16 = T, %, A. **Answer (B).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the first element moves 1, 5, 9, so the next is the 13th, T. That removes (C) and (E) at once. Back-check: 13th T, 15th %, 16th A.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** taking three in a row (T5%) because the group “looks” consecutive. Each group skips its second neighbour.

body.x: How many pairs of letters are there in the word MONSTER, each of which has as many letters between them in the word (in both forward and backward directions) as they have between them in the English alphabet?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** test all 21 pairs of letters.

**30-Second Exam Method:** M O N S T E R = 13, 15, 14, 19, 20, 5, 18. O and N: places 2 and 3, values 15 and 14: yes (backward). N and R: places 3 and 7, values 14 and 18: yes. S and T: places 4 and 5, values 19 and 20: yes. T and R: places 5 and 7, values 20 and 18: yes (backward). **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none; count them. Back-check: ON, NR, ST, TR.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** counting forward only gives NR and ST, two, which is option (A). “Both forward and backward” adds ON and TR.

body.x: In the word MARKETING, every vowel is changed to the next letter of the alphabet and every consonant to the previous letter. How many vowels are there in the new word?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** write the new word: L B Q J F S J M F. Count vowels: none.
**30-Second Exam Method:** a vowel moved forward is never a vowel. A consonant moved back becomes a vowel only if it is B, F, J, P or V. MARKETING has none of those. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** the shortcut above is the hack: check the word for B, F, J, P, V only. Back-check: LBQJFSJMF has no A, E, I, O, U.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** swapping the rule (vowel back, consonant forward). Then D, H, N, T become vowels and the answer changes. IBPS RRB Clerk Prelims 13 Dec 2025 Shift 1 asked this exact form with IMAGINED.

body.x: If it is possible to make only one meaningful English word with the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 9th letters of the word ORGANISED, the third letter of that word is your answer. If no such word can be made, mark X. If more than one such word can be made, mark Z.

method.x: **Conventional Method:** letters are R, A, I, D. Try arrangements: RAID, ARID.
**30-Second Exam Method:** R, A, I, D gives RAID at once; before marking its third letter, spend three seconds looking for a second word: ARID. Two words. **Answer (E).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none. Back-check: O R G A N I S E D, places 2, 4, 6, 9 are R, A, I, D.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** stopping at the first word and marking its third letter, I, option (B). Always look for a second word. The letters X and Z (or sometimes other letters) are defined in the question itself; read which is which.

body.x: Four of the following five are alike in a certain way. Find the odd one out.

method.x: **Conventional Method:** convert each to numbers and compare.
**30-Second Exam Method:** gaps: BDF +2 +2, KMO +2 +2, PRT +2 +2, HJM +2 +3, UWY +2 +2. **Answer (D).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** check only the last gap of each once you see the first gaps are all +2. Back-check: J to M skips K and L.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** looking for a meaning (vowels, word shapes) before checking the gaps. In the papers opened, every odd-one-out of this kind was a gap pattern.

body.x: TAP BIN GEM SUN ORE. If the letters within each word are arranged in alphabetical order, how many words remain unchanged?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** APT, BIN, EGM, NSU, EOR. Only BIN is unchanged.
**30-Second Exam Method:** a word is unchanged only if its letters already climb. T-A no. B-I-N yes. G-E no. S-U-N: U to N falls, no. O-R-E: R to E falls, no. **Answer (C).**
**Option Elimination Hack:** none needed. Back-check: B (2), I (9), N (14) climb.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “arranged within each word” is not “the words arranged in dictionary order”. The second moves whole words; the first moves letters.
