lessons.title: The alphabet as numbers
lessons.plain: The starting point. Almost every question in this topic needs a letter's place in the alphabet, from the left or from the right. Learn five anchors and one sum.

teach.x: This topic is a collection of short questions: pairs of letters in a word, a long row of letters, digits and symbols, a word changed by a rule, and a few others. They are not puzzles; each is a small routine. What they share is the alphabet, so that comes first.
**Five anchors.** You do not need all 26 places by heart. Learn every fifth letter:
Any other letter is one or two steps from an anchor. M is two before O: 13. R is two before T: 18. W is two before Y: 23.

**From the right end.** A letter's place from the right is **27 minus its place from the left**. T is 20th from the left, so 7th from the right. The 8th letter from the right is the 19th from the left: S.

**Opposite letters.** Two letters are opposite when their places add up to 27: A and Z, B and Y, G and T, M and N. Odd-one-out questions use this often. To find a letter's opposite, take its place away from 27.
**Letters between.** The number of letters between two letters is the difference of their places, minus 1. Between C (3) and I (9) there are 9 - 3 - 1 = 5 letters.
**Vowels** are A, E, I, O, U, at places 1, 5, 9, 15, 21. Everything else is a consonant. Many questions change vowels one way and consonants another, so it helps to notice two facts now:

items.x: the letter **after** a vowel is always a consonant (B, F, J, P, V);
the letter **before** A does not exist in these questions, and the letters before E, I, O, U are D, H, N, T, all consonants.

teach.x: So when a rule says "every vowel is changed to the next letter", no vowel survives. The only way a vowel can appear afterwards is from a consonant that turns into one.

example.q: (1) Which letter is 8th from the right end of the alphabet? (2) Which letter is opposite to G? (3) How many letters are there between D and M?
steps: (1) 27 - 8 = 19. The 19th letter is one before T (20): S.
(2) G is two after E (5), so 7. 27 - 7 = 20, which is T.
(3) D is 4 and M is 13. 13 - 4 - 1 = 8 letters.

checks.q: Which letter is 6th from the right end of the English alphabet?
checks.why: 27 - 6 = 21. The 21st letter is one after T (20): U.

checks.q: Which letter is opposite to K, in the sense that their places add up to 27?
checks.why: K is one after J (10): 11. 27 - 11 = 16, which is one after O (15): P.

checks.q: Every consonant in a word is changed to the next letter of the alphabet. Which of these consonants becomes a vowel?
checks.why: The letter after D is E. A consonant becomes a vowel only if it stands just before one: D, H, N or T.

lessons.title: Pairs of letters in a word
lessons.plain: New: the most regular question of all. For each letter, look only to its right, and walk the alphabet as you walk the word.

teach.x: "How many such pairs of letters are there in the word CHAMPION, each of which has as many letters between them in the word as they have between them in the English alphabet?"
In the earlier study of twelve IBPS Clerk papers, **eleven had exactly one question of this kind**. It is the surest two marks in the topic if you have a fixed routine, and a slow one if you do not.

**What a pair is.** Two letters of the word form a pair when the gap between them in the word equals the gap between them in the alphabet. O and N, side by side in CHAMPION, are also side by side in the alphabet: a pair. C and A have one letter between them in the word (H) and one between them in the alphabet (B): a pair.
**The routine.** Take each letter in turn, from the left, and look **only to its right**.

items.x: The letter 1 place to its right would have to be its alphabet neighbour (the next letter, or the one before).
The letter 2 places to its right would have to be 2 away in the alphabet.
The letter 3 places to its right would have to be 3 away, and so on.

teach.x: So you say the alphabet forwards and backwards from that letter while your finger moves along the word. From C: forwards D, E, F ... and backwards B, A. The word has H, A, M ...: at the second place you expect E or A, and there is an A. One pair.

**Forward and backward.** The pair C and A runs backwards (A comes before C in the alphabet but after it in the word). The question nearly always says "in both forward and backward directions", so both kinds count. If it says forward only, count only pairs that read left to right in alphabet order.

**What to expect.** I solved all 51 clean questions of this kind in your bank by script. The answer was **2 or 3 in 28 of them**, and between 1 and 5 in 47. More than half of all the pairs found were letters that are neighbours or next-but-one in the alphabet. So check the close letters with special care, and be a little suspicious of an answer of zero or of six.
The same question is asked about digits in a number. The routine is identical, with counting in place of the alphabet.

tags: A seven-letter word with a single pair.
Two pairs, both forwards, sharing a letter.
One letter in two pairs, forwards and backwards.
Pairs with one letter between.
The same question with digits.

example.q: How many such pairs of letters are there in the word CHAMPION, each of which has as many letters between them in the word (in both forward and backward directions) as they have between them in the English alphabet?
steps: C: to its right are H, A, M, P, I, O, N. Expected: D or B, then E or A, then F ... The second is A. Pair C-A.
H: expected I or G, J or F, K or E, L or D, M or C, N or B. The sixth letter to its right is N. Pair H-N.
A: nothing comes before A, so only forwards: B, C, D, E, F. The word has M, P, I, O, N. None.
M: expected N or L, O or K, P or J, Q or I. The word has P, I, O, N. None.
P and I: none. O: expected P or N, and the next letter is N. Pair O-N.
example.answer: Three pairs: C-A, H-N and O-N.

checks.q: How many such pairs of letters are there in the word BANKER, each of which has as many letters between them in the word (in both forward and backward directions) as in the English alphabet?
checks.why: B and A are neighbours in the word and in the alphabet. No other two letters match: for example K and E are two apart in the word but six apart in the alphabet. One pair.

shortcut.title: Say the alphabet with your finger on the word

text.x: Put a finger on the letter after the one you are testing, and say the alphabet from that letter, forwards: one letter per step of the finger. If the letter you say is ever the letter under your finger, that is a pair.
Then do it once more saying the alphabet backwards.
Two passes for each letter, and you only ever look to the right, so no pair is counted twice and none is missed.

lessons.title: A long row: finding a position
lessons.plain: New: a row of about 35 letters, digits and symbols, and a question such as "sixth to the left of the fifteenth from the right end". It is one addition or one subtraction.

teach.x: The second big family is the **row**: about 35 letters, digits and symbols in a line, with four or five questions on it. Half of the twelve Clerk papers studied had one. Your bank's rows are mostly between 33 and 40 long.
The questions on a row come in three kinds, one per lesson: find a position, count by neighbours, and do something to the row first. This lesson is the first kind.
"Which element is **sixth to the left of the fifteenth from the right end**?"
Do not count to the fifteenth and then count six more. Combine the two numbers first.

rows: Xth to the **left** of the Yth from the **right** end
Xth to the **right** of the Yth from the **left** end
Xth to the **right** of the Yth from the **right** end
Xth to the **left** of the Yth from the **left** end

teach.x: The rule behind the table: moving **away from** the end you are counting from **adds**; moving **towards** it **subtracts**.

Then count once, from whichever end is nearer. If the answer is "21st from the right" in a row of 34, it is quicker to count the 14th from the left, because **place from left + place from right = number of elements + 1**. To use that you need the length of the row, so count it once at the start and write it above the row. It pays for itself over five questions.
**"Exactly in the middle of Y and N."** Find the two places, add them and halve. If Y is 6th and N is 16th, the middle is the 11th.
**Mark every fifth element.** Put a small tick under the 5th, 10th, 15th ... element when you first read the row. After that every count is a short hop from a tick.

tags: Left of a place counted from the right: add.
Left of a place counted from the left: subtract.
Right of a place counted from the right: subtract.
The same with a longer row; count from the nearer end.
Exactly in the middle of two elements.

example.q: Row (20 elements): K 7 @ R 4 E # 9 M $ T 2 B % 5 W 8 & J 3. Which element is fourth to the left of the ninth from the right end?
steps: Left of something counted from the right moves away from the right end: add. 4 + 9 = 13th from the right end.
The row has 20 elements, so that is the 20 + 1 - 13 = 8th from the left.
Count eight from the left: K, 7, @, R, 4, E, #, 9.

checks.q: A row has 34 elements. The sixth to the left of the fifteenth from the right end is which element counted from the left end?
checks.why: 6 + 15 = 21st from the right. From the left that is 34 + 1 - 21 = 14th.

lessons.title: A long row: counting by neighbours
lessons.plain: New: "how many numbers are immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a symbol". Turn it into a pattern of three and scan once.

teach.x: This was the most frequent row question in the Clerk papers studied (9 of the 24 row questions).
"How many such **numbers** are there, each of which is immediately **preceded by a letter** and immediately **followed by a symbol**?"
**Turn the sentence into a pattern of three, in the order they sit in the row.** Preceded by means on its left; followed by means on its right. So the pattern is:
**letter - number - symbol**
Write that pattern above the row before you look at the row at all. The sentence gives the middle one first and the left one second, which is exactly how mistakes happen.

**Scan by the rarest kind.** A row has many letters and fewer digits and symbols. Do not check every element. Run along the row stopping only at the kind that is in the **middle** of your pattern (here, each number), and glance left and right. If the middle kind is "letter", stop instead at whichever of the two neighbours is rarer.
**The words that change the pattern.**

rows: the left neighbour is a letter that is not A, E, I, O, U
immediately followed by a symbol **but not** immediately preceded by a number
right neighbour a symbol; left neighbour anything except a number, or nothing at all
the middle one can be anything

teach.x: **The two ends.** The first element has nothing before it and the last has nothing after it. So neither can satisfy "preceded by ... and followed by ...". But the first element **does** satisfy "not preceded by a number".

Tick each hit under the row as you find it and count the ticks at the end. In the twenty bank questions of this kind that the script checked, the answer runs from none to six and is most often one, two or three.

tags: The plain pattern: letter - number - symbol.
'Elements': the middle can be anything.
Vowel and consonant instead of letter.
Only one side is mentioned.
'But not': one neighbour must fit and the other must not.

example.q: Row: K 7 @ R 4 E # 9 M $ T 2 B % 5 W 8 & J 3. How many such numbers are there, each of which is immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a symbol?
steps: Pattern, left to right: letter - number - symbol.
Stop at each number. 7: K before, @ after. Yes.
4: R before, E after. No. 9: # before. No. 2: T before, B after. No. 5: % before. No.
8: W before, & after. Yes. 3: nothing after it. No.

checks.q: Row: T 5 # A 9 L @ 2 K. How many numbers are immediately preceded by a letter and immediately followed by a symbol?
checks.why: Pattern: letter - number - symbol. T 5 # fits. A 9 L and @ 2 K do not. One.

lessons.title: A long row: something is done to it first
lessons.plain: New: "if all the symbols are dropped, which is the fourteenth from the right end". Do not rewrite the row. Count along the original and skip.

teach.x: The third kind of row question changes the row and then asks for a position or a count.
"If all the symbols are dropped from the arrangement, which will be the fourteenth element from the right end?"
**Do not write the new row out.** That costs half a minute and invites copying slips. Count along the **original** row from the end named, and simply **do not count** the elements that were dropped.
First combine the numbers exactly as in lesson 3 ("fourth to the left of the tenth from the right" is the fourteenth from the right). Then one pass with the finger, skipping.

rows: all symbols (or numbers, or letters) are dropped
count from the named end, skipping that kind
all symbols and numbers are dropped
count everything except consonants: vowels, digits and symbols
the 1st, 3rd, 5th ... stay; each step is two places in the original
the first half is reversed, or the last fifteen are reversed
work out where the asked place falls; inside the reversed part, count from its other end

teach.x: **Every second element dropped.** In a row of 36, the elements that stay are the 1st, 3rd, ... 35th. The last one that stays is the 35th. The 11th from the right among them is ten steps of two before that: the 35 - 20 = 15th element of the original row.

**When the question then asks for neighbours** ("if all the symbols are dropped, how many letters are immediately preceded by a number?"), the neighbours are the nearest surviving elements on each side. Look past the dropped ones.
Only when the operation rearranges things by value ("all the numbers are arranged in ascending order") is it worth writing a short part of the row again, and then only the part that moves.

tags: One kind dropped; count from the right and skip.
Two kinds dropped, and a position inside a position.
Counting from the left.
All consonants dropped: count everything else.
Every second element dropped: steps of two.

example.q: Row: K 7 @ R 4 E # 9 M $ T 2 B % 5 W 8 & J 3. If all the symbols are dropped, which element will be sixth from the right end?
steps: Count from the right end of the original row, skipping symbols.
3 (one), J (two), skip &, 8 (three), W (four), 5 (five), skip %, B (six).

checks.q: Row: H 3 @ P 6 # D 9 K. If all the numbers are dropped, which element is third from the right end?
checks.why: Count from the right, skipping numbers: K (one), skip 9, D (two), # (three).

lessons.title: A word or a number changed by a rule
lessons.plain: New: "each vowel is changed to the next letter and each consonant to the previous one, then the letters are arranged alphabetically". Write the new letters under the old ones, once, and only then answer.

teach.x: Seven of the twelve Clerk papers studied had a question of this kind. A word (or a number) is given, a rule changes it, and something is asked about the result.
There are two operations, used alone or one after the other.
**1. Arrange.** "The letters are arranged in alphabetical order from left to right." Write the word, and under it write the letters in order. For digits, ascending or descending.

items.x: If it asks **how many letters keep their position**, compare the two lines column by column.
If it asks for **the third from the right end**, you do not need the whole line. Find the three largest letters only.

teach.x: **2. Replace.** "Each vowel is changed to the next letter and each consonant to the previous letter." Write the new letter under each old one, working left to right. Use the anchors E 5, J 10, O 15, T 20, Y 25 to step one forward or one back without thinking.
For digits the same thing reads "1 is added to each even digit and 1 is subtracted from each odd digit".
**Then read the question's last words slowly.** After the same two operations the question may ask:

items.x: which letter is third from the right end;
how many letters appear more than once (count the letters that repeat, not the repeats);
how many letters lie between two of the new letters in the alphabet;
how many positions are unchanged compared with the **original** word.

teach.x: **"Arranged from right to left."** Ascending order from right to left is the same as descending order from left to right. Turn it into a left-to-right order before writing.

**Repeated letters.** If the word has a letter twice, both copies are changed and both are written. A rule that sends two different letters to the same one (G to F, and E to F) is how "appears more than once" questions are built.

tags: Arrange only, then a position.
Arrange, then count the letters that stay.
Replace, then arrange, then a position.
Replace, then find what repeats.
The digit version, with two different amounts.

example.q: Each vowel of the word PLANET is changed to the next letter of the alphabet and each consonant to the previous letter. The new letters are then arranged in alphabetical order from left to right. Which letter is second from the left end?
steps: Write the changes under the word: P becomes O, L becomes K, A becomes B, N becomes M, E becomes F, T becomes S.
The new letters are O, K, B, M, F, S.
In alphabetical order: B, F, K, M, O, S.
example.answer: The second from the left is F.

checks.q: The letters of the word BASKET are arranged in alphabetical order from left to right. How many letters remain in their original position?
checks.why: In order: A, B, E, K, S, T. Under B, A, S, K, E, T, the fourth (K) and the sixth (T) match. Two.

shortcut.title: Third from the right without sorting everything

text.x: When the question asks for a place near one end after arranging, find only that end.
"Third from the right end" after alphabetical order means the **third largest** letter. Pick out the largest, then the next, then the next, counting a repeated letter each time it appears.
For MEDIUM changed to L, F, C, J, V, L: largest V, then L, then the other L. The third from the right is L, and you never wrote the sorted word.

lessons.title: Making a word from chosen letters
lessons.plain: New: pick the named letters, then decide between one word, more than one, or none. The marks are in the instructions at the end of the question.

teach.x: "If it is possible to make only one meaningful four letter English word with the second, the fifth, the seventh and the eighth letters of the word FREQUENT, which will be the third letter of that word? If no such word can be formed give X as your answer. If more than one such word can be formed give Z."
Five of the twelve Clerk papers studied had one of these. The question is long, and has three parts that each need care.

**1. Pick the letters.** Number the letters of the long word with small figures above them (every fifth is enough) and write the chosen ones in a row. For FREQUENT, the 2nd, 5th, 7th and 8th are R, U, N, T.

**2. Try to make words.** Look for common, everyday words; the examiners do not expect rare ones. A quick way: place each vowel in the second or third place and try the consonants around it. From R, U, N, T: RUNT, TURN. Two already.
**3. Read the instructions for the three outcomes.** They change from question to question, and this is where marks are lost.

rows: What the question may ask for
its first, second or third letter, sometimes counted from the right end
a named letter, often X, Y, Z or P
another named letter, often Z, X or T

teach.x: The letter for "more than one" in one question is the letter for "none" in the next. Underline the two letters in the question before you start.
**Stop early.** As soon as you have two words, the answer is the "more than one" letter. You do not need to find them all.
**Before answering "none"**, try each letter as the first letter once. Four letters allow only 24 orders, and most can be dismissed at a glance.
In thirteen of your bank's questions of this kind, the keyed outcome is "more than one word" in eight, "exactly one" in three and "none" in two. So when a second word comes to mind quickly, trust it.

tags: Exactly one word.
No word.
More than one word.
One word, with the letter counted from the right end.
A different letter stands for 'more than one'.

example.q: If it is possible to make only one meaningful four letter English word with the first, the second, the third and the fourth letters of the word WONDERFUL, which will be the third letter of that word from the left? If no such word can be formed give X; if more than one can be formed give Z.
steps: The letters are W, O, N, D.
With the only vowel O in the second place: DOWN. Other orders (WOND, NOWD, ODWN ...) are not words.
Exactly one word: DOWN.
Its third letter from the left is W.

checks.q: The four letters picked are T, A, E and M. The question says: give the first letter if exactly one word can be made, X if none, Z if more than one. What is the answer?
checks.why: TEAM, MEAT, MATE and TAME are all common words. More than one word: Z.

lessons.title: Odd one out among letter groups
lessons.plain: New: five groups of three letters; four follow one rule. Write the steps between the letters, and the odd one shows itself.

teach.x: "Four of the following five are alike in a certain way based on their positions in the English alphabet. Which one does not belong?" followed by five groups such as FIM, PSW, LRU, GJN, JMQ. Five of the twelve Clerk papers studied had one.
**Write the step from the first letter to the second, and from the second to the third**, under each group. Use + for forwards and - for backwards.
FIM: F to I is +3, I to M is +4. PSW: +3, +4. LRU: +6, +3. GJN: +3, +4. JMQ: +3, +4. The odd one is LRU.
You rarely need to finish all five. Do the first two groups fully; they tell you the rule. Then check only the **first step** of the others; go on to the second step only if all first steps agree.
**If the steps do not settle it**, there are three other rules the bank uses.

items.x: **Opposite letters.** The first two letters add up to 27 (G and T, O and L, D and W), and the third is a fixed step from the second. A huge jump between the first two letters is the sign.
**Direction.** Four groups go forwards and one goes backwards with the same sizes: FHJ, NPR, ACE, KMO against XVT.
**Vowels.** Four groups contain exactly one vowel and one contains none or two. Try this last.

teach.x: **Speed with the anchors.** To get a step, turn the letters into numbers only when they are far apart. For close letters, count on your fingers: F, g, h, I is three.

The same question is also asked about a row ("based on their positions in the above arrangement") or about a finished puzzle. There the steps are counted along the row or the stack instead of along the alphabet, and the method is the same.

tags: Same sizes, one group reversed.
Two different steps.
A backward step then a forward one.
The same shape with other sizes.
Opposite letters, then a step.

example.q: Four of these five are alike in a certain way based on their positions in the English alphabet. Which one does not belong? CFI, MPS, TWZ, GJN, ADG
steps: CFI: C to F is +3, F to I is +3.
MPS: +3, +3. So the rule is two steps of three.
GJN: G to J is +3, but J to N is +4.

checks.q: Four of these five are alike. Which one does not belong? ACE, GIK, MOQ, SUX, PRT
checks.why: ACE, GIK, MOQ and PRT are two steps of +2. In SUX the second step, U to X, is +3.

lessons.title: Five three-letter words
lessons.plain: New: five short words and five questions, each applying a small rule to all five. One tidy table answers the whole set.

teach.x: "LED TIE ICE PAL ACE", followed by five questions. In the papers studied this set was more common in SBI and RRB Clerk and IBPS PO (15 questions in twelve papers) than in IBPS Clerk (one paper), and your bank has a great many. It is a full five marks for about three minutes, because every question is a rule you already know, applied five times.
**Write the five words in a column**, with space to the right. Each question adds one column beside them.
The rules that come up:

rows: What to write beside each word
the words are arranged as in a dictionary
the letters within each word are arranged alphabetically
the sorted word; tick the ones that did not change
each letter is changed to the next letter
the new word; circle any vowel
vowels to the next letter, consonants to the previous
the new word; circle any vowel
the first and third letters are interchanged
the new word; tick if it is a real word
a letter is added before each word
tick if it makes a real word
letters between the second letter of the second word and ...
pick the two letters, then difference of places minus 1

teach.x: **Dictionary order.** Compare first letters; where they are equal, compare second letters. ACE comes before ICE because A comes before I.
**Where can a vowel come from?** This is the quick way through the "how many words will have a vowel" questions (lesson 1).

items.x: If every letter moves **forward** one place, a vowel appears only from D, H, N or T (giving E, I, O, U).
If consonants move **back** one place, a vowel appears only from B, F, J, P or V (giving A, E, I, O, U).
A vowel that is itself moved never stays a vowel.

teach.x: So you do not need to change every letter. Look through the five words only for those few letters.
**"Meaningful word" questions** expect common words. RICE and RACE count; a word you have to argue for does not.

tags: Dictionary order.
Picking letters by position, then letters between.
A letter added in front.
Every letter moves forward one place.
Vowels forward, consonants back.

example.q: BAT HEN DIP MUG TOP. (1) If the letters within each word are arranged in alphabetical order, how many words remain unchanged? (2) If each letter of every word is changed to the next letter of the alphabet, how many of the new words contain a vowel?
steps: (1) BAT becomes ABT, HEN becomes EHN, MUG becomes GMU, TOP becomes OPT. DIP is already in order. One word is unchanged.
(2) Moving forward one place, a vowel appears only from D, H, N or T.
BAT has T (becomes U). HEN has H and N (become I and O). DIP has D (becomes E). MUG has none of them. TOP has T (becomes U).
Four of the new words contain a vowel.

checks.q: BAT HEN DIP MUG TOP. If the words are arranged as they appear in a dictionary, which word comes last?
checks.why: By first letter the order is BAT, DIP, HEN, MUG, TOP. The last is TOP.

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** A building has numbered floors, 1 at the bottom. In a **floor** puzzle one person lives on each floor. In a **floor-with-flat** puzzle each floor has two flats side by side (Flat A to the west, Flat B to the east; some papers call them P and Q or 1 and 2), and one person lives in each flat. Clues tell you who is above, below or beside whom. You have to rebuild the whole building.
**The one idea: draw the building first, then place the most fixed clue, and split into cases only when you must.**
**How to draw it**

items.x: Floor puzzle: one column of boxes, floor numbers written on the left, highest at the top.
Floor-with-flat: two columns, West (Flat A) on the left and East (Flat B) on the right, floor numbers on the left. It is a small map: up is north, right is east.

blocks.x: **The solving algorithm (use it on every set):**

items.x: Draw the grid. Write the names beside it and strike each one as you place it.

Sort the clues in your head into three kinds: **fixed** (“C lives on floor 4”, “only two persons live below M”), **linked** (“only two floors between K and N”, “A lives immediately above E”) and **loose** (“D lives above F”, “B is on an even floor”).
Place a fixed clue first. If there is none, start with the linked clue that has the biggest gap, because it fits in the fewest places.
A linked clue attached to something already placed gives one or two positions. If two, draw the grid twice side by side (Case 1, Case 2).
Use the remaining linked clues to kill cases. A case dies when a person needs a floor that does not exist or is already taken.
Use loose clues last. They usually settle the final two or three people.
Answer the questions from the finished grid.

blocks.x: **Grid: what the words mean**

rows: X is on the very next floor up
X is on any higher floor
Treating it as the next floor
Only two **floors** between X and Y
Only two **persons** live between X and Y
Two people in between; a vacant floor is not counted
Only two persons live below X
X is the 3rd person from the bottom
As many live above X as below Y
Count from the top for X, from the bottom for Y, same number
Using the same end for both
X lives to the west / east of Y
X lives to the north / south of Y
Same flat, a higher / lower floor
X lives to the north-east of Y
X in the east flat, Y in the west flat, X on a higher floor (any higher floor, unless it says immediately)
Using only the next floor up
X lives immediately below Y (flat puzzle)
Usually the next floor down in the same flat; some bank sets mean the next floor in either flat
Not trying the second meaning when the first fails

blocks.x: **Two free facts in every flat puzzle.** If someone lives to the west of X, then X is in the east flat (Flat B). If someone lives to the north-east of X, then X is in the west flat and is not on the top floor.

**Non-linear warning.** “Two floors between” and “two floors above” are different: the first is a difference of 3, the second a difference of 2. Write the difference as a number beside the clue before placing it.

**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** draw the grid once for each possible position of the most restricted person and test every clue in each grid. It is slower but it cannot fail.

lead.x: Bank counts are sets out of 108. Paper counts are sets seen in the 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers and in the 12 sister papers.

rows: Floors only, one person per floor (7 or 8 floors is usual)
Floor with two flats (4 floors × 2 flats = 8 persons is usual)
Either of the above with a second fact per person (age, city, item)
Either of the above with a vacant floor or flat

lead.x: F3 and F4 are counted inside F1 and F2 as well; they are features, not separate buildings.
Where they were seen:

items.x: Floors only: IBPS Clerk 4 Oct 2025 Shift 3 and 5 Oct 2025 Shift 1; SBI Clerk 20 Sep and 21 Sep 2025 Shift 1; IBPS PO 22 Aug 2026 Shift 2 (6 persons, with a dessert each).
Floor with flat: IBPS Clerk 4 Oct 2025 Shifts 2 and 3, and 2021; IBPS RRB Clerk 13 Dec 2025 Shift 2 (6 persons); IBPS PO 23 Aug 2025 Shift 2 and 24 Aug 2025 Shift 1.
Every set in the Clerk papers had 8 persons and 5 questions.

lead.x: What stands out: in the Clerk papers the plain forms are what appeared. No Clerk set had a vacant floor or a second fact per person. Practise those two after the plain forms are comfortable.

What the bank sets look like (from the 40 sets solved by script): 4 floors × 2 flats is the most common shape (12 of 40), then 8 floors with one person each (9), 7 floors (5), 3 floors × 2 flats (4) and 5 floors × 2 flats (3). In 32 of the 40, a good first clue leaves two cases; in 3 it leaves one; in 5 it leaves three.

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “eight persons live on eight different floors”, “lowermost floor is numbered 1”.
**Shortcut engine.** one column. Fixed clue first; biggest-gap linked clue next; two cases at most; loose clues last.
**Worked example.** Drill 1 below.
**Pattern clues.** “each floor has two flats”, “Flat A is to the west of Flat B”, compass words.

**Shortcut engine.** two columns. Turn every compass word into (which column, higher or lower). Use the two free facts to fix columns before floors. A pair on the same floor (“U is to the east of P”) needs a whole empty floor, which is often the strongest clue in the set.
**Worked example.** Drill 2 below.

items.title: With a second fact per person

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “each person likes a different colour”.

**Shortcut engine.** add one more column to the grid for the second fact. Solve the positions first using the clues that mention only people; then drop the facts in. A clue such as “the one who likes red lives immediately above K” places a fact on a floor even before you know who lives there.

items.label: Seen once (IBPS PO Prelims 22 Aug 2026 Shift 2)

items.title: With a vacant floor or flat

blocks.x: **Shortcut engine.** treat VACANT as one more name to place. Then re-read every counting clue: “floors between” counts the vacant floor, “persons between” does not.
**Worked example.** Drill 3 below.

items.label: Bank only

lead.x: Three original puzzles written for this module: basic, exam level, and one built around a wording trap. Each was checked by a brute-force script and has exactly one arrangement.

body.x: Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F live on six different floors of a six-storey building. The lowermost floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only one person lives on each floor.

items.x: C lives on floor number 4.
Only one person lives between C and E.
A lives immediately above E.
B lives on an even-numbered floor.
D lives on one of the floors above F.

qs.stem: Who lives on the topmost floor?
How many persons live between B and E?
Who lives immediately below D?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try each person on each floor and test all five clues until one arrangement survives.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Clue 1 is the only fixed clue: C on 4.
Clue 2 gives two cases: E on 2, or E on 6.
Clue 3: A is just above E. With E on 6 there is no floor above, so that case dies. E on 2, A on 3.
Clue 4: free floors are 1, 5, 6. The only even one is 6, so B on 6.
Clue 5: D and F take 5 and 1, D above F. D on 5, F on 1.

method.x: Arrangement, top to bottom: B, D, C, A, E, F.
**Answers:** Q1 (B). Q2 (D) Three. Q3 (A) C.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, clue 4 alone says B is on 2, 4 or 6 and clue 1 gives 4 to C; once E takes 2, B must be on 6. You can answer Q1 before finishing the grid.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** clue 5 says “one of the floors above”, not “immediately above”. D is four floors above F. Reading it as immediately above leaves no two neighbouring free floors and makes the puzzle look broken.

items.title: Drill 2 (Exam level, F2: floor with flat)

body.x: Eight persons P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W live in a four-storey building. The lowermost floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 4. Each floor has two flats, Flat A and Flat B. Flat A is to the west of Flat B. Flat A of floor 2 is immediately above Flat A of floor 1, Flat B of floor 2 is immediately above Flat B of floor 1 and so on. Only one person lives in each flat.

items.x: R lives on an odd-numbered floor.
T lives to the north-west of R.
U lives to the east of P on the same floor.
V lives immediately below U in the same flat.
S lives to the south-west of R.
Q lives on an even-numbered floor.

qs.stem: Who lives immediately above W in the same flat?
How many floors are there between Q and V?
In which floor and flat does S live?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** list all positions for R, then for each try T and S, and so on through every clue.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Clues 2 and 5 both put someone to the west of R, so R is in Flat B. Clue 1: floor 1 or 3.
Clue 5 needs a floor below R, so floor 1 dies. R is in Flat B of floor 3.
Clue 2: T is above R in Flat A, so T is in Flat A of floor 4. Clue 5: S is in Flat A of floor 1 or 2.

Clues 3 and 4: P and U need a whole empty floor, with a free Flat B just below U. Only floors 1 and 2 are fully free, so P and U take floor 2 (P in A, U in B) and V goes to Flat B of floor 1. S therefore goes to Flat A of floor 1.
Clue 6: the free flats are Flat A of floor 3 and Flat B of floor 4. Q needs an even floor: Flat B of floor 4. W takes Flat A of floor 3.

method.x: Arrangement: Floor 4: T, Q. Floor 3: W, R. Floor 2: P, U. Floor 1: S, V (Flat A first).
**Answers:** Q1 (C) T. Q2 (E) Two. Q3 (A).
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q3, S is to the south-west of R, so S is in Flat A. That removes (C) and (E) before you solve anything, and (D) goes because S is below R.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** “south-west” does not have to mean the very next floor down. Putting S in Flat A of floor 2 leaves no empty floor for P and U. In your bank, several sets only have a solution when north-east and south-west are read this wider way.

body.x: Seven persons H, J, K, L, M, N and O live on different floors of an eight-storey building. The lowermost floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 8. Only one person lives on each floor and exactly one floor is vacant.

items.x: K lives on floor number 5.
Only two floors are there between K and N.
As many persons live above J as live below N.
H lives immediately below O.
Only two floors are there between H and the vacant floor.
M lives on one of the floors above K.
Only one person lives between J and O.

qs.stem: Which of the following floors is vacant?
How many persons live between M and H?
Who lives immediately above K?

options.e: No one, the floor is vacant

method.x: **Conventional Method:** treat the vacant floor as an eighth name and test arrangements against all seven clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Clue 1: K on 5. Clue 2 (difference of 3): N on 2 or on 8.

N on 8: six persons are below N, so by clue 3 six are above J, making J the lowest person; clue 7 then makes O the third person from the bottom. Checking clue 5 against that leaves no place for the vacant floor. This case dies.
N on 2: if floor 1 were vacant, clue 5 would put H on 4 and O on 5, which is K’s floor. So floor 1 is occupied, one person is below N, and one person is above J.

Clue 6 puts M above K. J has exactly one person above it, so M and J are the top two persons and one of floors 6 to 8 is vacant. K is the third person from the top; clue 7 makes O the fourth: O on 4, H on 3.
Clue 5: the vacant floor is three floors from H: floor 6. So M on 8, J on 7, and L on 1.

method.x: Arrangement, top to bottom: M, J, vacant, K, O, H, N, L.
**Answers:** Q1 (B). Q2 (D) Three. Q3 (E).
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, clue 5 means the vacant floor is exactly three floors from H, and H sits just under O; once K is on 5, floors 4 and 5 cannot be vacant. That removes (C).

**IBPS Trap Warning:** a vacant floor is a floor but not a person. Between M (8) and H (3) there are four floors but only three persons; “Four” is option (B). Between J and O there are two floors but one person, which is what clue 7 counts.

rows: “X lives on floor n”, “only n persons below X”
“Only n floors between X and Y”
Difference = n + 1; one or two cases
Glue the two as a block
Top or bottom floor kills a case
“As many above X as below Y”
Count X from the top, Y from the bottom
Odd / even floor, “not on floor n”
Keep for the end; it picks between the last candidates
Same floor, fixes the column of both
Fixes both columns; any higher or lower floor
Two people on the same floor
They need a whole empty floor

blocks.x: **Order of work, in one line:** grid, fixed clue, biggest gap, two cases, kill one, loose clues, questions.

**When a set refuses to work:** re-read the three wordings that most often decide it in your bank: “immediately below” in a flat puzzle (same flat, or just the next floor), compass words (next floor, or any floor), and “persons between” when a floor is vacant.

These are Sreedhar mock sets from your bank that have exactly one solution on a plain reading and whose keys all agreed with the script. MT is the model test number; the range is the question numbers.
After these, work through the Guidely “floor-with-flat based puzzle, single variable” sets, then the “two variable” and “with vacant” sets.
**Built:** 6 Oct 2026.

items.x: 40 of the 108 bank sets (20 Sreedhar, 20 Guidely, spread across the sub-sections) were solved by brute force: a script tried every arrangement against every clue as worded, and the questions were then answered from what survived. The other 68 sets were sorted by section name and passage wording but not solved.
38 of the 40 have exactly one arrangement. For 26 of those the solver had to note a reading choice; the common ones are listed in the cheat sheet.
2 do not: FF120 (the ages of two persons can be swapped) and FF430 (one clue has slipped out of the passage into a question; with it restored the set is unique).
197 questions in those sets: 194 agree with the key, 3 do not (S-MT67-93, S-MT67-95, S-MT41-67).
The three drill puzzles each have exactly one arrangement by script, and their answers come from the script.

blocks.x: **Where the paper evidence comes from.** One helper run opened the 24 PDFs once each and listed the puzzle sets in each Reasoning section. I did not re-open them to cross-check, so a set may have been missed in a paper, and the 5 Oct 2025 paper was read in a Hindi version with partly garbled text. The counts are sightings, not frequencies.

**How the bank check was run.** The 40 sets were solved in helper runs, each writing its own solver script per puzzle. I merged and counted their results; I did not re-read each solver. The “cases” figures are the helpers’ estimate of a human path, not something computed.

**Data problems in the bank.** Several Guidely passages have lost their opening line (the list of persons or the number of floors), and a few carry part of the passage inside a question. Those sets were solved on the assumption that best fits, which the log above counts as a reading choice.
**Not verified:** the 68 unsolved bank sets; the paper inventory beyond a single reading; how often each form appears beyond these 24 papers. Memory-based papers are reconstructions.
**Corrections:** none so far.

sample.x: **Sample.** This module is built mainly from your question bank, as you asked. Bank: 108 puzzle sets with 530 questions (47 floor sets with one person per floor, 61 floor-with-flat sets; 69 sets from Guidely, 39 from Sreedhar). Your bank has no previous-year Reasoning questions, so what the exam asks comes from 24 memory-based papers opened on the web: 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers (2018 to Oct 2025) and 12 sister papers (SBI Clerk, IBPS RRB Clerk, IBPS PO Prelims). In the 12 Clerk papers there were 2 floor sets and 3 floor-with-flat sets; in the 12 sister papers, 3 and 3. Memory-based papers are reconstructions, not official papers.

**A note on time.** A puzzle set is one arrangement followed by about five questions. Nobody solves the arrangement in 45 seconds. The honest target is 4 to 5 minutes for the arrangement and 15 to 20 seconds for each question after it, which works out to about a minute per mark.

intro.x: Two puzzles share this name: people on floors, one to a floor; and people in flats, two to a floor. These lessons are built from the puzzles the clerk papers actually set, in the same way as the other reasoning topics.

**What I studied first.** Thirteen real clerk-level puzzles with their clues (IBPS Clerk 2025, SBI Clerk 2025, RRB Clerk 2024), a few officer-level ones for contrast, and 13 sets from your Sreedhar bank. Eleven of the paper puzzles and all 13 bank sets were written out as exact conditions and each has exactly one arrangement by script.

intro.x: **What this means.** The floors-only puzzle is the box puzzle with numbers printed, so two lessons are enough for it. The flat puzzle is where time is lost, because its clues are short and vague when read one at a time. The fix is to split each person into two facts, side and floor, and settle the sides first: four people in the west flats and four in the east. The IBPS Clerk puzzle of October 2025 goes from 52 open cases, read in printed order, to none.

A note on honesty: the paper puzzles are candidates' reconstructions, read through a summarising tool. Two of the thirteen were too condensed to use. One of the seven flat puzzles, with five floors, carries a shift label I could not confirm.

after.x: That covers both kinds as the clerk papers set them. The **Quick revision** tab keeps the older short notes.

For floors only: notes, block, count the fits, mirror, closers. For flats: the grid, the two teams, each column as four people on four floors, links across the columns, pairs and free floors, and the "not" clues last.

Still to come, as insurance: three flats on a floor, an empty flat or floor, five and six floors of flats, and a second fact per person. Your bank has these; none appeared in the clerk papers studied except the one five-floor set.

lessons.title: Floors only: a stack with the numbers already printed
lessons.plain: The starting point. One person per floor is the box puzzle again. Turn each clue into a floor number or a step, and join the exact clues into a block.

teach.x: There are two puzzles under this name. In the first, eight people live on eight floors, **one person per floor**. In the second, each floor has two flats. This lesson and the next deal with the first kind; the rest of the topic is about the second.

A floor puzzle with one person per floor is the **box puzzle with the numbers already written on the boxes**. The lowest floor is 1. Everything you learned for boxes applies without change, so this lesson is a short reminder and then practice.
**The words, as steps.**

rows: X lives three floors above Y
Only three persons live between X and Y; three floors between X and Y
As many persons live above X as below Y
the two floors add up to (number of floors + 1)

teach.x: Just as with boxes, "three **between**" is a step of 4, and "three floors **above**" is a step of 3. The real papers I checked agree: in the IBPS Clerk puzzle of 5 October 2025, "D lives four floor above A" has A on floor 2 and D on floor 6 in the answer key.
**How to solve.** Two of the four real floor puzzles I solved by script give no floor number and no even or odd clue at all. So do not wait for one.

items.x: Write each clue as a short note.
Join the notes that share a name into a **block**, measured from one person: G = A - 1, D = A + 4, and so on.
The block's height tells you how many ways it fits: floors minus height, plus one.
Draw a column for each fit, and use the other clues to remove columns. The mirror clue ("as many above X as below Y") is the first to try, because it places a new person in every column at once.

teach.x: A building of 8 floors is the IBPS and SBI Clerk size; RRB Clerk uses 7.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 5 October 2025, shift 1. Eight persons A to H live on eight floors, numbered 1 to 8 from the bottom. D lives four floors above A. G lives immediately below A. Two persons live between G and B. The number of floors above B and below C are the same. F lives immediately above H.
steps: Notes: D = A + 4. G = A - 1. G, B are 3 apart. Floor of B + floor of C = 9. F = H + 1.
Block from A: G is just below, D four above. B is 3 from G: that is A + 2, or A - 4. With A - 4 the block would run from A - 4 to A + 4, nine floors. So B = A + 2.
The block G, A, B, D covers six floors (A - 1 to A + 4). It fits three ways: A on floor 2, 3 or 4.
Mirror: A 2 puts B on 4, so C on 5. A 3 puts B on 5, so C on 4. A 4 puts B on 6, so C on 3, which is G's floor. Out.
A 3 (G 2, C 4, B 5, D 7): free floors 1, 6, 8. F and H need two floors in a row. Out.
A 2 (G 1, B 4, C 5, D 6): free floors 3, 7, 8. H 7, F 8, and E takes 3.
example.answer: From the top floor down: F, H, D, C, B, E, A, G.

checks.q: Eight floors. D lives four floors above A, and G lives immediately below A. On how many different floors can A live?
checks.why: G needs a floor below A, so A is at least 2. D needs floor A + 4, so A is at most 4. A can be 2, 3 or 4: three floors.

lessons.title: Floors: even, odd and "above the fifth"
lessons.plain: New: the clue that narrows one person to two floors. Join it to that person's next clue before drawing anything.

teach.x: When a floor puzzle does give a starting clue, it is nearly always a soft one about a single person:

items.x: "D lives on an even numbered floor above the 5th floor": floor 6 or 8.
"D lives on an odd numbered floor": 1, 3, 5 or 7.
"L lives on an even numbered floor but not on the 6th": 2 or 4 (in seven floors).

teach.x: Two of the four real floor puzzles open this way. Treat the clue as a short list of floors, and immediately **join it to the next clue about the same person**. Most of the list disappears.
"D is on 6 or 8, and three persons live between D and B": B is 4 below (4 above would be off the building). Two cases, each with two people placed.
"D is on an odd floor, and H lives three floors below D": D cannot be on 1 or 3. Two cases again: D 5 with H 2, or D 7 with H 4.

**Even and odd travel with the step.** An odd step (1, 3, 5) changes even to odd. An even step (2, 4) keeps it. So "N lives on an even floor, and J lives immediately above N" tells you J is on an odd floor without placing either. In a long bank set this check removes cases quickly.
**The order that works** in nearly every floor set, real or bank:

items.x: the soft clue plus its partner clue: two cases;
the mirror clue, as soon as one of its two people is in a case;
the remaining exact steps (immediately above, two between), looking at the free floors as numbers;
"more than three between", "not adjacent" and plain "above" for the last free floors.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 21 September 2025, shift 1. Eight persons A to H live on eight floors, numbered 1 to 8 from the bottom. D lives on an even numbered floor above the 5th floor. Three persons live between D and B. The number of floors above B is the same as the number of floors below E. Two persons live between E and G. C lives immediately above A. More than three persons live between A and H.
steps: D is on 6 or 8. B is 4 below: (D 6, B 2) or (D 8, B 4).
Mirror: floor of B + floor of E = 9. B 2 gives E 7; B 4 gives E 5.
G is 3 from E. E 7 gives G 4. E 5 gives G 2 (floor 8 is D's).
D 6, B 2, E 7, G 4: free floors 1, 3, 5, 8. C and A need two floors in a row. Out.
D 8, B 4, E 5, G 2: free floors 1, 3, 6, 7. A 6, C 7.
More than three between A and H: H on floor 1. F takes 3.
example.answer: From the top floor down: D, C, A, E, B, F, G, H.

items.x: a step of 1, 3 or 5 flips it;

text.x: "C is on an odd floor and B lives two floors above C": B is odd too. "Only two persons between F and H" is a step of 3: F and H are on floors of different kinds.

lessons.title: Two flats on each floor: what the words mean
lessons.plain: New: the building is now a grid, four floors high and two flats wide. Each person has two facts, a floor and a side. Learn exactly which clue speaks about which.

teach.x: Now each floor has **two flats**, a west one and an east one, and one person lives in each. In the clerk papers the building is four floors with eight people (IBPS and SBI Clerk) or three floors with six people (RRB Clerk). I found no real puzzle with three flats on a floor or with an empty flat.
**Draw a grid**: floors as rows with floor 1 at the bottom, two columns, west on your left. The puzzle always says which flat is west; write the flat names above the columns.
Every person now has **two separate facts**: which **floor**, and which **side**. The whole skill is knowing which of the two a clue is talking about.

rows: X is on a higher floor
X lives immediately above (just above) Y
There is one floor gap between X and Y
X and Y live on the same floor
so they are on opposite sides
X lives to the west of Y
X and Y live in the same named flat (same type of flat)
X lives immediately above Y in the same flat; X's flat is immediately above Y's flat

No one lives to the east of X
X is in the east flat

teach.x: **The line that matters most is the first.** A plain "X lives above Y" means **any higher floor, in either flat**. I did not assume this. In the IBPS Clerk puzzle of 4 October 2025 the clues say "E lives above G" and also "E and G do not live in the same type of flat"; and all seven real puzzles have exactly one arrangement when "above" is read this way. When the paper means the same column, it says so: "in the same named flat".

The compass words (north, south-west and so on) are common in your bank and rare in the papers, where two of the seven puzzles use one each. They are worth knowing because each one gives **both** facts at once.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 18 August 2024, shift 1. Six persons P to U live in a three-storey building with two flats on each floor; Flat X is to the west of Flat Y. P lives on the topmost floor. Q lives just below P, but not in the same named flat. R and S live on the same floor. U lives immediately above R but not in the same named flat. T does not live to the east of P.
steps: P is on floor 3. Q is on floor 2, on the other side from P.
R and S share a floor, so that floor must have both flats free: floor 1.
U is one floor above R: floor 2, in the flat Q did not take. That is the flat directly below P, so U is on P's side.
U and R are on different sides, so R is on Q's side and S is on P's side.
T takes the last flat, on floor 3 beside P. T is not east of P, so T is west and P is east.
So the east column is P, U, S and the west column is T, Q, R.
example.answer: Floor 3: T (X), P (Y). Floor 2: Q (X), U (Y). Floor 1: R (X), S (Y).

lessons.title: Two teams of four
lessons.plain: New: settle the sides first. Four people live in the west flats and four in the east. Once the teams are known, each team is just four people on four floors.

teach.x: A flat puzzle read clue by clue is slow. I measured the IBPS Clerk puzzle of 4 October 2025 that way: taken in printed order it reaches 52 open cases. Solved the way this lesson shows, it needs none.
The idea is to answer the two questions **one at a time**, and to take the easier one first.
**Step 1: sides.** Exactly four people live in west flats and four in east flats. Go through the clues and collect only what they say about sides.

items.x: "G lives in flat-B" puts G in a team.
"H lives to the west of F" puts H west and F east.
"same type of flat" ties two people to one team; "not the same type of flat" puts them in opposite teams.
"C and B live on the same floor" puts them in opposite teams.
Every compass word with east or west in it sorts two people at once.

teach.x: Write two short lists, West and East. **When one list reaches four names, everyone else belongs to the other.** When a tied pair would make a list five long, the pair goes to the other side. In most puzzles the teams are complete before you have thought about a single floor.

**Step 2: floors, one team at a time.** A team is four people in one column: **one on each floor**. That is a stack of four boxes. Clues about two people in the same team ("A lives above H", "D lives above B") order them directly.

**Step 3: across the teams.** Clues about people in different teams ("E lives above G", "C and B live on the same floor", "one floor gap between G and F") link the two columns. With only four floors, each of these has very few possibilities.
If the sides cannot be fully settled from the clues, sort as many as you can, and carry at most one unknown person into step 2.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 October 2025, shift 2. Eight persons A to H live in a four-floor building with flat-A to the west of flat-B on each floor. G lives in flat-B. H lives to the west of F. H and A live in the same type of flat. A lives above H. C and B live on the same floor. B lives below the floor of D, and both live in the same type of flat. E lives above G. E and G do not live in the same type of flat. There is one floor gap between G's floor and F's floor. E lives on an even-numbered floor.
steps: Sides. G is east. H is west and F is east. A is with H: west. E is opposite G: west.
So far, West: H, A, E. East: G, F. B and D are together; they cannot join West (that would make five), so they are East. East is full: G, F, B, D. So C is West.
East column, one per floor: G and F are two floors apart, so they hold floors 1 and 3. B and D get 2 and 4, with D above B: B 2, D 4.
C is on B's floor: C on floor 2, west.
West column has floors 1, 3, 4 left for H, A, E. E is on an even floor: E 4. A is above H: A 3, H 1.
H is west of F, so F is on floor 1, and G is on floor 3. E (floor 4) is above G.
example.answer: Floor 4: E, D. Floor 3: A, G. Floor 2: C, B. Floor 1: H, F. (West flat first.) No cases were needed.

lessons.title: Only four floors: gaps and parity
lessons.plain: New: with four floors, every floor clue has very few ways to be true. Learn the short list for each, and how even and odd pass through a gap.

teach.x: Four floors is a very small ladder. That makes floor clues far stronger than they are in an eight-floor building, and it pays to know exactly how strong.

rows: two floors gap between X and Y; three floors above
one floor gap between X and Y
X lives two floors above Y

teach.x: **Parity through a gap.** "One floor gap" means two floors apart, so both people are on odd floors or both on even floors. "Immediately above" switches between odd and even. So:

items.x: "D lives on an odd floor, two floors above H" is not two cases. It is one: D 3, H 1.
"One floor gap between Q and S, and S is on an odd floor": Q is on the other odd floor. Together they take floors 1 and 3 of their columns.
"Two floors gap between S and A, and S is on an even floor": S 4, A 1.

teach.x: **Chains of "above".** In one column there are four floors and four people. "K lives above P but below Y" is three people in order; if they are in the same column they fill three of its four floors in order.
**A whole floor is two people.** "R and V live on the same floor" fixes neither, but as soon as one of them has a floor, so has the other, in the opposite column.
Use these after the teams are sorted. A floor clue about two people in the same column is a direct order; about two people in different columns it is one of the short lists above.

steps: D is odd and two floors above H: D 3, H 1. F is above D: F 4.
Sides. C is south-west of F: C west, F east. A is opposite C: A east. E is directly below C: E west.
C has E below it, so C is not on floor 1, and it is below F, so not on 4. C and A are two floors apart: C 3 with A 1 (C 2 would need A on 4, where F already has the east flat).
So E is on floor 2, west. A is on floor 1, east, which means H takes floor 1 west, and D, on the other side from H, is floor 3 east.
Two flats are left: floor 4 west and floor 2 east. B is above G: B floor 4 west, G floor 2 east.

lessons.title: Floor-mates, and the clues that say "not"
lessons.plain: New: every person shares a floor with exactly one other. Count the four pairs, and use the "do not live on the same floor" clues to finish.

teach.x: One more way of looking at the grid, and then the closers.
**Four floors, four pairs.** Each floor holds exactly two people, so the eight people form four pairs of floor-mates. Clues hand you these pairs directly:

items.x: "X lives to the west of Y" and "X and Y live on the same floor" each name a pair.
"L lives to the west of the person who lives just below K in the same flat" names nobody new, but says a great deal: K is in the east column, not on floor 1, and L is west on the floor below K.

teach.x: When three pairs are known, the last two people are the fourth pair.

**Where a pair can go.** A pair needs a floor with **both** flats free. Late in the puzzle there is often only one such floor, and the pair is placed without any other clue. The RRB Clerk example in lesson 3 was solved exactly so.

**Two people who need two floors in a row in one column** ("R lives immediately above Q in the same flat") need that column to have two neighbouring floors free. If one column has floors 1 and 3 left and the other has 2 and 3, only the second will do.

**The clues that say "not".** Flat puzzles carry many of these: "K and X do not live on the same floor", "W and X do not live in the same named flat", "Z does not live on the first floor", "H does not live on the same floor as P".

items.x: "Not in the same flat" is a **side** clue and belongs in step 1 with the teams.
"Not on the same floor" and "not on floor 1" place nobody. Keep them for the end, when two people are left for two flats.

teach.x: So the full order of work for a flat puzzle is: teams, then exact floor clues inside each column, then links across the columns, then pairs and free floors, and finally the "not" clues.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 22 February 2025, shift 4. Eight persons G, K, L, M, W, X, Y, Z live in a four-storey building; flat-X is to the west of flat-Y. Y lives two floors above X in the same named flat. X does not live on an odd-numbered floor. L lives to the west of the person who lives just below K in the same named flat. K and X do not live on the same floor. There is one floor gap between W and Z. W and X do not live in the same named flat. Z does not live on the first floor. Z and K live on different floors. M lives above G.
steps: X is on an even floor with Y two floors above in the same column: X 2, Y 4.
K is in the east column, above floor 1, and not on X's floor: K is on 3 or 4. L is west, one floor below K.

Suppose X and Y are in the east column. Then K is east on floor 3 and L is west on floor 2. W must be opposite X: west. Z is not on floor 1 or on K's floor, so Z is on 2 or 4, and W two floors away needs floor 4 or 2 in the west column; with Z on 2 no flat is free for it, and with Z on 4 W would need L's flat. Out.
So X and Y are in the west column. K is east: on 3 it would need L in X's flat, so K is on floor 4 and L is west on floor 3.
W is opposite X: east. W and Z are two floors apart; Z is not on 1 and not on K's floor: Z 3, W 1. Z takes the east flat of floor 3.
Left: floor 2 east and floor 1 west. M is above G: M floor 2, G floor 1.
example.answer: Floor 4: Y, K. Floor 3: L, Z. Floor 2: X, M. Floor 1: G, W. (West flat first.)

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** Six to eight people sit around a round table, or around a square table with four at the corners and four at the middle of the sides. Clues say who is to the left or right of whom, who is opposite whom, and who is or is not a neighbour. You rebuild the seating.
**The one idea: a round table has no first seat, so you are free to put the first person anywhere. Put them at the bottom of your drawing and never move them.**
**How to draw it**

items.x: Circle: draw a circle with 8 short dashes (or 6, or 7). Number nothing.
Square: draw a square. Four seats at the corners, four at the middle of the sides. Going round, corners and middles alternate.

blocks.x: **Left and right: the only rule that matters**
Left and right always belong to the person named **after** the word “of”. “C sits to the immediate right of A” uses A’s right.
**The solving algorithm (use it on every set):**

items.x: Draw the table. If facing directions are given, write IN or OUT beside each name before anything else.
Pick the person who appears in the most clues and seat them at the bottom.
Use the clues measured from that person first (“second to the right of Q”, “third to the left of T”).
A clue such as “only one person sits between A and F” gives two seats: draw the table twice.
Kill a case with “immediate neighbour” and “not a neighbour” clues.
“Opposite” clues need a free pair of facing seats; count how many free pairs are left, often only one.
Fill the last seats, then answer.

blocks.x: **Grid: counting round a table of 8**

rows: Third to the left = fifth to the right
The two always add up to 8
Only two persons between X and Y

blocks.x: **Square-table facts**

items.x: Moving 2 or 4 seats keeps the seat type: a corner stays a corner, a middle stays a middle. Moving 1 or 3 seats changes it.
So “N sits in the middle of a side” and “N is second to the right of Q” together tell you Q is also in a middle.
The neighbours of a corner person are both middle persons, and the other way round.
A common exam form: corner persons face the centre and middle persons face outside, or the reverse. Then seat type decides left and right.

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** For a person facing outside, everything flips. If you solve a mixed-facing table as if all face the centre, you do not get a slightly wrong answer; you get a different arrangement or none at all.

**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** fix one person; for the next most connected person try each remaining seat in turn and run every clue. With 8 seats that is at most 7 small trials.

**Shortcut engine.** left is clockwise for everyone. Seat the most-mentioned person, chain the left/right clues, two cases, kill one with a neighbour clue.
**Worked example.** Drill 1 below.

**Shortcut engine.** write IN or OUT beside each name first. For every clue, look at the person after “of” and use that person’s left and right. When facing is not given but must be deduced, clues such as “X and Y face the same direction” or “both neighbours of X face opposite to X” do the deciding.

A vacant seat is a seat but not a person: “persons between” skips it. For a second fact, write it under the name; clues about “the one who likes red” seat a fact before a name.

items.title: Drill 1 (Basic, C1: circle facing the centre)

body.x: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F are sitting around a circular table facing the centre, with equal distance between adjacent persons, but not necessarily in the same order. C sits to the immediate right of A. Only one person sits between A and F. F sits to the immediate left of B. B is not an immediate neighbour of A. D is not an immediate neighbour of B.

qs.stem: Who sits opposite to D?
How many persons sit between A and B when counted from the left of A?
What is the position of F with respect to A?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** fix A and try every order of the other five against the clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Seat A at the bottom. C is on A’s immediate right (one seat anticlockwise).
One person between A and F: F is second to the left of A, or second to the right.
F is on B’s immediate left, so B is on F’s immediate right. If F is second to the left of A, B lands next to A, which is not allowed. So F is second to the right of A, and B is opposite A.
The two seats on A’s left are for D and E. D must not be next to B, so D is next to A and E is between D and B.

method.x: Clockwise from A: A, D, E, B, F, C.
**Answers:** Q1 (E) F. Q2 (C) Two. Q3 (A) Second to the right.

**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q3, C already holds A’s immediate right, so (D) is out; clue 2 says exactly one person is between A and F, so only “second to the left” or “second to the right” can be right.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “F sits to the immediate left of B” tells you where F is, measured from B. It means B is on F’s right. Reading it the other way round gives a different table.

body.x: Eight persons J, K, L, M, N, O, P and Q are sitting around a square table such that four of them sit at the corners and four of them sit in the middle of the sides. All of them are facing the centre, but not necessarily in the same order. N sits second to the right of Q. N sits in the middle of one of the sides. J sits third to the right of Q. L sits opposite to M. M sits to the immediate right of O. L sits second to the right of K.

qs.stem: Who sits third to the left of N?
How many persons sit between P and J when counted from the left of P?
Four of the following five are alike in a certain way based on their positions in the arrangement and hence form a group. Which one does not belong to that group?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** fix Q and try every order of the other seven.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: N is in a middle seat and is two seats from Q, so Q is in a middle seat too. Seat Q at the bottom middle; N is two seats to Q’s right.
J is third to the right of Q: the corner just beyond N.
L and M are opposite each other. Three of the four facing pairs already hold Q, N or J, so L and M take the seat between N and Q and the corner facing it.
M is on O’s immediate right, so O is on M’s immediate left. If M sat between N and Q, O would need Q’s seat. So L is between N and Q, M is opposite, and O is next to M on the J side.
L is second to the right of K, so K is second to the left of L: the corner on Q’s left. P takes the last seat.

method.x: Clockwise: J (corner), N, L (corner), Q, K (corner), P, M (corner), O.
**Answers:** Q1 (B) K. Q2 (D) Two. Q3 (E) P, the only one not at a corner.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, N is in a middle seat and three seats away is an odd move, so the answer is a corner person. P and O are middle persons, so (C) and (D) are out.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “second to the right” is not “immediate right”. Seating N next to Q puts Q on a corner and shifts the whole table by one seat.

body.x: Eight persons S, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z are sitting around a circular table with equal distance between adjacent persons. T, V and Y are facing outside (away from the centre) while the remaining five are facing the centre. S sits third to the left of T. Y sits to the immediate left of T. W sits to the immediate left of Y. W sits third to the left of X. Only one person sits between U and W. V is not an immediate neighbour of T.

qs.stem: Who sits second to the right of V?
How many persons sit between Y and Z when counted from the right of Y?
What is the position of S with respect to T?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** fix T and try every order of the other seven, taking each person’s own left and right.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Mark T, V, Y as OUT: their left is anticlockwise.
Seat T. From T: Y is one seat anticlockwise, S is three seats anticlockwise.
From Y (OUT): W is one seat anticlockwise of Y, between Y and S.
From X (IN): W is three seats clockwise of X, so X is three seats anticlockwise of W. That is the seat opposite Y.
U is two seats from W. One such seat is T’s, so U takes the other, between X and S.
Two seats are left for V and Z. V is not next to T, so Z is next to T and V is between Z and X.

method.x: Clockwise: S, W, Y, T, Z, V, X, U.
**Answers:** Q1 (C) U. Q2 (A) One. Q3 (D) Third to the left.
**Option Elimination Hack:** Q3 is given away by the first clue itself: “S sits third to the left of T”. Check the clues before you look at the drawing.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** for T, V and Y, left is anticlockwise. Treating everyone as facing the centre gives two possible tables instead of one, and Q1 and Q2 come out wrong. V also faces outside, so in Q1 V’s right is clockwise.

rows: IN or OUT beside each name first
“X is nth to the left of Y”
Count from Y, using Y’s left
“Only n persons between X and Y”
Square table, “sits at a corner / middle”
Even moves keep seat type, odd moves flip it

blocks.x: **Order of work, in one line:** table, IN/OUT marks, most-mentioned person at the bottom, clues from that person, two tables, neighbour clues kill one, opposite pairs, questions.

**Two checks before you answer.** For “who sits nth to the left of X”: is X facing in or out? For “how many persons between X and Y counted from the left of X”: go the way X’s left goes, and do not count X or Y.

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** Seven or eight people each do something (are born, attend a class, have an exam) at a different time. The times are either months, or dates in months (“the 10th and 25th of March, June, September and December”), or days of a week. Clues say who is before or after whom and how many people come between. You rebuild the timetable.
**The one idea: a calendar puzzle is a floor puzzle lying on its side. Write the time slots in a column in calendar order, number them, and it becomes a stack.**
**How to draw it**

items.x: Month puzzle: a column of the months given, earliest at the top. Write 30 or 31 beside each month.
Month-with-date: two rows per month (for example 10 March, 25 March, 10 June, 25 June…), so 4 months × 2 dates = 8 slots. Mark each slot odd or even date, and each month 30 or 31.
Day puzzle: a column Monday to Sunday (or Sunday to Saturday if the passage says the week starts on Sunday).

blocks.x: **The solving algorithm (use it on every set):**

items.x: Write the slots in calendar order and number them 1, 2, 3…
Beside the slots, mark what the clues can use: 30 or 31 days, odd or even date.
Place a fixed clue first: “born on 20 June”, “only three persons after T”, “in a month having 30 days” (this last one usually leaves two or three slots, which is a good start).
Attach linked clues: “only two persons between”, “immediately after”. Each gives one or two slots; draw a second column if two.
Kill cases when someone needs a slot that is taken or does not exist.
Loose clues (“C was born before F”) last.

blocks.x: **Grid 1: days in each month**

rows: January, March, May, July, August, October, December

blocks.x: Knuckle rule: make a fist and count months across the knuckles and the dips between them. Knuckles have 31 days; dips have 30 (February is the short dip). July and August both land on knuckles.
**Grid 2: what the words mean**

rows: X was born immediately after Y
X is in the very next slot
Only two persons between X and Y
Slot numbers differ by 3 (if no slot is empty)
X is the 4th person from the end
X is three persons after Y; “three persons before”
As many before X as after Y
X counted from the start equals Y counted from the end
In a month having 31 days / on an even date
X is older than Y (birth puzzles in one year)
X is in the first slot

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** In birth puzzles “older” means earlier in the year, so the oldest person is at the top of the column and the youngest at the bottom. Reversing this reverses the whole timetable.
**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** one column for each possible slot of the most restricted person, then run every clue down each column.

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try each of the six persons in each of the six slots against the clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Slots in order: 5 Mar, 20 Mar, 5 Jun, 20 Jun, 5 Sep, 20 Sep. Dev in slot 4.
Two persons between Dev and Anu: slot 7 does not exist, so Anu is in slot 1 (5 March).
30-day months here are June and September; odd date is the 5th. Bina is on 5 June or 5 September.
Esha is immediately after Bina. After 5 June comes 20 June, which is Dev’s. So Bina 5 September, Esha 20 September.
Slots 2 and 3 are left; Charu before Farid: Charu 20 March, Farid 5 June.

intro.x: **What this means.** Unlike box puzzles, these nearly always hand you a starting point, and it is very often a calendar clue ("a month having an even number of days", "an odd date"). The skill is turning calendar words into place numbers quickly and without slips. That is what the seven lessons train, one piece at a time, each with a real paper puzzle worked through and bank sets to practise on.

A note on honesty: memory-based papers are written down by candidates after the exam. Five of the twenty puzzles found were incomplete or did not give exactly one arrangement as remembered, so they are not used as examples.

lessons.title: One line, earliest on the left
lessons.plain: The starting point. Days, months and dates are all the same thing: a line of numbered places in time order. Learn to read every clue as a place or a step on that line.

teach.x: Day puzzles, month puzzles and month-with-date puzzles look like three topics. They are one. In each of them some people are put **in time order**, one after another, and the clues say who is earlier, who is later and how far apart.
So the first move is always the same: **draw one line of places, earliest on the left, and number them.** Monday to Sunday is places 1 to 7. Eight months in a list are places 1 to 8.
If you have done Box Puzzles, this is a stack lying on its side, and everything you learned there still works. If you have not, this lesson gives you all you need.
**Reading the clue words.** Call the number of places between two people their **step**.

Only two persons are between X and Y
X is three persons after Y; X is two days after Y

somewhere to the right, distance not known

X is third from the end

the two places add up to (number of places + 1)

teach.x: Two points that cost marks if you miss them:

items.x: **"Two between" is a step of 3; "two after" is a step of 2.** Add one only for "between".

In birth puzzles, **older means born earlier**, so older is to the **left**. "G is two months older than C" puts G to the left of C. "E is just younger than F" puts E immediately to the right of F. "The youngest" is the last place.

teach.x: **Start from what is fixed.** Here these puzzles differ from box puzzles in a helpful way. I solved 15 real clerk puzzles of this kind by script: **13 of the 15 tell you something definite about one person** (a named day, "after Thursday", "two persons before S", a month with 30 days). So look for that clue first, place it, and attach the others to it.
When a clue leaves two possible places, draw the line twice, one under the other, and carry both until a later clue removes one.

Q at 1: free places 2, 4, 5, 6. R and P are 3 apart: R 2, P 5. T must be before P: only place 4 is free, and that is Thursday. Out.

lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the ideas. Practise the plain day puzzle until fixing one person and chaining the rest feels automatic.

teach.x: The day puzzle is the plainest form: seven persons, Monday to Sunday, places 1 to 7. In the papers I studied it appeared in SBI Clerk and RRB Clerk, and it is the one to become quick at first.
**The fixed clue comes in four kinds.** Learn to spot each.

rows: L takes a class after Friday
B does not go on Thursday

teach.x: **Then chain.** Take the clue that mentions the person you have just placed. It gives the next person one or two places. Then the clue that mentions that person, and so on. You are following a chain of names through the clues, not reading them in printed order.

The edges do a great deal of work in a line of only 7. "Three persons between D and E" is a step of 4, and from place 4 that reaches neither end. From Saturday, a step of 4 can only go left. Before you write two cases, check whether one of them falls off the line.

**A pattern to recognise.** "As many persons between F and B as between D and F": F is named twice, so B and D are the same distance from F on **opposite sides**. If D is 3 to the right of F, B is 3 to the left.
Leave the plain "X is after Y" clues until the free places are few. With two free places and "G is after E", there is nothing to think about.
