teach.x: Two of the 15 real puzzles I solved fix nobody at all (SBI Clerk, 22 February 2025 shift 3 and 20 September 2025 shift 2). Both are day puzzles. There are two tools for these, and you already know the first.

**Tool 1: the block.** Join the clues that give an exact step. "Cricket is three days after Chess; Badminton is two days before Chess" locks three things together: Badminton, then Chess two later, then Cricket three after that. From first to last the block covers 6 places, so in a week of 7 it can sit in only **2** ways (7 - 6 + 1). Draw both and let the other clues decide.
**Tool 2: count the people who must be on each side.** A chain of plain "before" clues is stronger than it looks. Suppose F is before C, C is before G, G is before B and B is before E.

items.x: At least two people (F and C) are before G, so G is at place 3 or later.
At least two people (B and E) are after G, so G is at place 5 or earlier.

teach.x: Out of seven days, G has only three possible places, from clues that named no day. Add one exact clue about G ("G goes three persons after A") and it is nearly fixed: A is also before G, which makes three people before it.
So for any person in a chain, write two small numbers: **how many must come before, how many must come after.** The person's place is between (before + 1) and (7 - after).
Use whichever tool the puzzle offers. If there are two or three exact steps sharing a name, build the block. If the clues are mostly "before" and "after", count the sides.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 September 2025, shift 2. Seven persons A to G go to watch a show on different days from Monday to Sunday. G goes before B but after C. G goes three persons after A. B goes before E. Two persons go between E and D. C goes after F.
steps: Chain: F, then C, then G, then B, then E.
Before G: F, C and also A (A is three places before G). That is three people, so G is at place 4 or later. After G: B and E, so G is at place 5 or earlier.
G at 4: A is at 1, F and C take 2 and 3, and B, E, D share 5, 6, 7. E is after B, so E is 6 or 7, and D is 3 from E: place 3 or 4, both taken. Out.
G at 5: A is at 2. After G only 6 and 7 are left: B 6, E 7. D is 3 from E: place 4.
F and C take 1 and 3 in that order.
example.answer: Monday F, Tuesday A, Wednesday C, Thursday D, Friday G, Saturday B, Sunday E.

lessons.title: Months: mark the 30-day months first
lessons.plain: New: the places now carry a property. Write the month list, mark which months have 30 days, and a "month having an even number of days" clue becomes two or three places.

teach.x: A month puzzle gives seven or eight months, **usually with some missing**, and one person per month. According to the shift analyses it was in all four IBPS Clerk shifts on 4 October 2025, so it deserves care.
The line is the month list exactly as the puzzle gives it. If the list is January, March, April, June, then March is place 2 and June is place 4. Number them as listed.
**The new clue.** Month puzzles nearly always include one of these:

items.x: "A was born in a month having an **even number of days**" (or "having 30 days")
"B was born in a month having an **odd number of days**" (or "having 31 days")

teach.x: So before reading any clue, write the list and put a mark under each month with an even number of days.

rows: April, June, September, November (30 each), and February (28)
January, March, May, July, August, October, December

teach.x: Then the clue "A was born in a month having an even number of days" is no longer vague. With the list March to September it means April, June or September: places 2, 4 or 7. That is your fixed clue.

**Shrink it straight away.** Take the next clue about the same person and test each marked place against the edges. "Three persons between A and C" is a step of 4: from place 4 in a line of 7 that reaches neither end, so place 4 is gone before you have drawn anything.

In the two real month puzzles that use it and the nine bank sets I solved by script, the marked-month clue leaves **2 or 3 places** in every one, and one more clue about the same person usually brings it down to one or two.
Everything else is as before: older is left, younger is right, chain the clues, and keep plain "after" clues for the end.

steps: The list is places 1 to 7. Even-day months: April (2), June (4), September (7).
A is at 2, 4 or 7. C is 4 from A: from 2 it is 6; from 4 nothing fits; from 7 it is 3.
G is two places before C, and E is just after G.
A 2, C 6: G 4, E 5. B is 3 from E: place 2 (taken) or 8. Out.
A 7, C 3: G 1, E 2. B is 3 from E: place 5. D is younger than B, so later: place 6. F takes 4.
example.answer: March G, April E, May C, June F, July B, August D, September A.

checks.q: The months are January, March, April, June, July, August, November and December. H was born in a month having an even number of days, after April. Which months are possible for H?
checks.why: The even-day months in the list are April, June and November. After April leaves June and November.

text.x: Only four months have exactly 30 days: **April, June, September, November.** February has 28. Every other month has 31.
So "even number of days" means those four and February. "Odd number of days" means the other seven.

As soon as you copy the month list, put a small **E** under April, June, September, November and February wherever they appear. In the lists used by the real papers, between two and four months end up marked.

lessons.title: "Months after" is not "persons after"
lessons.plain: New: one wording trap, and puzzles with two calendar clues. A gap in months is counted on the calendar; a gap in persons is counted on your line.

teach.x: When months are missing from the list, two clues that sound alike mean different things.
Take the list January, April, May, August, September, October, November, December, and suppose Q was born in May.

items.x: "V was born three **persons** after Q": count places on your line. May is place 3, so V is at place 6, **October**.
"V was born three **months** after Q": count on the calendar. May plus three months is **August**, which is the very next place.

teach.x: The real IBPS Clerk puzzle of 24 August 2024 used exactly this, twice. Read as calendar months it has one arrangement; that is how I know which reading the paper intended.
So write the **calendar number** of each month under the list (January 1, April 4, May 5 ...). For a "months" clue, subtract calendar numbers. For a "persons" clue, subtract place numbers.
A "months" clue is also a strong filter, because many months have no partner in the list. "U was born one month before P": P cannot be April in that list, since March is not there.

**One wording I could not settle.** "There is a gap of three months between D and C" could mean the calendar numbers differ by 3, or that three months lie in between. The two papers that use it were not remembered clearly enough for the script to decide. Try the plain difference first, and if no arrangement survives, try the other.

**Two calendar clues in one puzzle.** Bank sets often give two: "D was born in a month with an even number of days" and "B was born in a month with an odd number of days". Write both lists of places, and look for the clue that connects the two people. Checking each pair of places against it is quicker than drawing cases.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 24 August 2024. Eight persons P to W were born in January, April, May, August, September, October, November and December. P was born in a month having an even number of days. U was born one month before P. As many persons were born before V as after W. V was born three months after Q. Two persons were born between R and S, who was born after R.
steps: Places 1 to 8. Even-day months: April (2), September (5), November (7).
U is one calendar month before P. April would need March, which is not in the list. So (P September, U August) or (P November, U October).
V is three calendar months after Q: the pairs in this list are January and April, May and August, August and November, September and December.
P 5, U 4: only (Q January, V April) is free. One person is before V, so one is after W: W 7. Free: 3, 6, 8. S is 3 after R: R 3, S 6. T takes 8. It works.
P 7, U 6: (Q 3, V 4) gives W 5 and leaves 1, 2, 8 with no pair 3 apart. (Q 5, V 8) gives W 1 and leaves 2, 3, 4. (Q 1, V 2) needs W at 7. All out.
example.answer: January Q, April V, May R, August U, September P, October S, November W, December T.

checks.q: The months are January, April, May, August, September, October, November and December. Q was born in May, and V was born three months after Q. In which month was V born?
checks.why: Three months after May on the calendar is August. (October would be three persons after Q, counted along the list.)

lessons.title: Month with two dates: a line of pairs
lessons.plain: New: each month now has two dates, so it has two places. It is still one line, and a month is a pair of neighbouring places.

teach.x: This was the most common kind in the real clerk papers I found: 8 of 20. "Eight persons were born on two dates, 8th and 27th, of four months." RRB Clerk uses three months (6 persons); SBI and IBPS Clerk use four (8 persons).
It is still one line in time order. Each month simply takes **two places**: its first date, then its second.
Draw the line with a small gap after every second place, so that the pairs are visible. Then the new clue words all become simple statements about pairs.

rows: X and Y were born in the same month
they are the two places of one pair: (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6) or (7, 8)
X and Y were born on the same date
both in odd places, or both in even places
X was born immediately before Y, and both in the same month
X is in an odd place, Y in the next one
X was born immediately before Y, but not in the same month
X is in an even place, Y in the next one
the two places of that pair

teach.x: **Careful with "same month" and neighbours.** Places 2 and 3 are next to each other on the line, but they are different months. Places 3 and 4 are the same month.
**"Persons between" counts along the whole line**, across months, exactly as before. "Two persons between C and A" is a step of 3.

**Odd and even dates.** "F was born on an even date" depends on the two dates in the puzzle. With 12th and 22nd both are even, and the clue tells you nothing. With 8th and 17th, the even date is the **first** of each pair, so it means places 1, 3, 5, 7. Always check which of the two dates is the even one before you write places.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 17 August 2024, shift 2. Six persons A to F were born on the 12th or 22nd of March, April and May. A was born in March. Two persons were born between C and A. B and C were born in the same month. F was born on the 22nd. E and F were not born in the same month. D was born before C.
steps: Places: 1 and 2 are March, 3 and 4 are April, 5 and 6 are May. The 22nd is the second place of each pair: 2, 4, 6.
A is at 1 or 2. C is 3 from A: place 4 or 5. B shares C's month: C 4 with B 3, or C 5 with B 6.
A 1, C 4, B 3: free 2, 5, 6. D is before C: place 2. F is on the 22nd: place 6. E gets 5, the same month as F. Out.
A 2, C 5, B 6: free 1, 3, 4. F is on the 22nd: place 4. E is not in April with F: E 1, D 3. D is before C.
example.answer: 12 March E, 22 March A, 12 April D, 22 April F, 12 May C, 22 May B.

checks.q: Eight persons were born on the 8th or 17th of April, May, August and November. N was born on an even date in a month having 30 days. Which dates are possible for N?
checks.why: The even date is the 8th. The 30-day months in the list are April and November. So 8 April or 8 November: places 1 and 7.

text.x: On the rough sheet, write the months across the top and the two dates down the side, and then number the eight boxes **across the dates first**: first month 1 and 2, second month 3 and 4, and so on.
From then on, think only in those numbers:

items.x: odd number = first date, even number = second date;
same month = an odd number and the number after it;
persons between = difference of the numbers, minus 1.

text.x: At the end, turn the numbers back into dates to answer the questions.

lessons.title: Two properties at once: the date and the month
lessons.plain: New: one clue names both the kind of date and the kind of month. It is the strongest clue in the puzzle, and leaves one or two places.

teach.x: The month-with-date puzzles in SBI Clerk like to open with a clue that has two halves:
"R attends on an **odd date** in a month having an **even number of days**."
Each half cuts the eight places down, and together they leave very few. Take the list September, October, November, December with dates 5 and 26.

items.x: Odd date: the 5th, which is the first of each pair: places 1, 3, 5, 7.
Month with an even number of days: September and November: places 1, 2, 5, 6.
Both together: **places 1 and 5** only.

teach.x: In the 13 bank sets of this kind that I solved, 9 contain a double clue like this. So the routine for a month-with-date puzzle is:

items.x: Number the pairs. Mark the 30-day months. Note which date is odd and which is even.
Find the double clue and write its one or two places.
Chain from that person, as in every lesson so far.

teach.x: **Negative wording.** The same clue is often written backwards: "on an odd date but **not** in a month having an odd number of days". Not odd means even. Turn it into the positive form before you look for places.

**A closer that belongs to this kind.** "No one is between S and W, and they are not in the same month." Neighbours on the line that are in different months must sit across a boundary: places 2 and 3, 4 and 5, or 6 and 7. That is only three possibilities out of seven neighbouring pairs.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 26 September 2026, shift 1. Eight persons R, S, T, U, V, W, X and Y attend events on the 5th or 26th of September, October, November and December. R attends on an odd date in a month having an even number of days. Two persons attend between S and R. No one attends between S and W, and they do not attend in the same month. As many persons attend before T as after Y. V attends just after Y, and not on an odd date. U does not attend after X.
steps: Places: September 1 and 2, October 3 and 4, November 5 and 6, December 7 and 8. Odd date (5th) is the first of each pair. Even-day months: September and November.
R is at 1 or 5.

R 5: S is 3 away, at 2 or 8. S 8 would need W at 7, the same month. S 2 gives W 3. V is in an even place just after Y: the only free fit is Y 7, V 8; then one person is after Y, so one is before T: T 2, which S has. Out.
R 1: S 4. W is next to S in another month: place 5.
Free: 2, 3, 6, 7, 8. V is in an even place just after Y: Y 7, V 8. One person is after Y, so one is before T: T 2.
U is not after X: U 3, X 6.
example.answer: 5 September R, 26 September T, 5 October U, 26 October S, 5 November W, 26 November X, 5 December Y, 26 December V.

checks.q: The dates are the 5th and 26th of September, October, November and December. S attends on 26 October. W attends immediately before or after S, but not in the same month. When does W attend?
checks.why: 26 October is place 4. Its neighbours are place 3 (5 October, the same month) and place 5 (5 November). So W attends on 5 November.

text.x: For a double clue, do not think in dates. Write two short lists of place numbers and keep what is in both.

items.x: Kind of date: all odd places, or all even places (after checking which date is which).
Kind of month: the two places of each marked month.

text.x: With four months, each list has four numbers, and they share at most two. With three months they often share one, and the person is placed outright.

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** Six to eight boxes, each with a letter name, are kept one above another. Clues say which box is above or below which, and how many boxes lie between. You rebuild the stack from top to bottom.
**The one idea: a box stack is a floor puzzle with no floor numbers printed. Number it yourself, from the bottom, before reading a single clue.**
**How to draw it.** One column of blank boxes. Write 1 at the bottom and the highest number at the top. Every clue then becomes a number.
**The solving algorithm (use it on every set):**

items.x: Draw the column and number it from the bottom.
Find a fixed clue: “third from the bottom”, “only two boxes below M”, “at the top”. Place it.
Attach linked clues to what is placed: “only three boxes between M and K”, “J is immediately above K”. Each gives one or two places.
If two places are possible, draw a second column (Case 2). Do not hold cases in your head.
Kill a case when a box needs a place that is taken or does not exist.
Use loose clues (“U is above P”) last.

blocks.x: **Grid: what the words mean, as numbers**

rows: As a number (stack of N, numbered from bottom)
Only three boxes between X and Y
X is three places above Y; “X is kept three boxes above Y”
As many boxes above X as below Y
More than two boxes between X and Y

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** “Three boxes between” (difference 4) and “three boxes above” (difference 3) look alike and are not. In your bank, five of the 40 sets checked by script have exactly one solution only when “n boxes above” is read as n places above.
**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** draw one column for each possible place of the most restricted box and run every clue down each column.

lead.x: Bank counts are sets out of 77. Paper counts are sets seen in the 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers and in the 12 sister papers.

rows: One stack, names only (7 or 8 boxes is usual)
One stack, each box also has a colour, item or weight
One stack with an empty shelf or a missing box
Two stacks side by side on shelves (“box with stack”)

lead.x: Where they were seen: IBPS Clerk 4 Oct 2025 Shifts 1 and 2 and 5 Dec 2020, each with 8 boxes; SBI Clerk 21 Sep 2025 Shift 1 (8 boxes); IBPS RRB Clerk 6 Dec 2025 Shift 2 and 13 Dec 2025 Shift 1 (7 boxes each); IBPS PO 22 Aug 2026 Shift 1 (6 boxes with an item in each).

What stands out: every box set in the Clerk and other clerk-level papers was the plain single stack. The two-stack form takes up a quarter of your bank’s box sets and appeared in none of the 24 papers.

What the bank sets look like (from the 40 sets solved by script): 7 boxes (11 sets) and 8 boxes (10) dominate; 6 boxes (3). After a good first clue, 22 sets leave two cases, 13 leave three, 3 leave four and 2 leave one. So expect one more case than in a floor puzzle, because box sets give fewer fixed clues.

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “eight boxes are kept one above another”.
**Shortcut engine.** number from the bottom; fixed clue; chain of linked clues; loose clues last.
**Worked examples.** Drills 1 and 2 below.

items.title: One stack with a second fact

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “each box is of a different colour”.

**Shortcut engine.** draw two columns side by side, one for the box name and one for the colour, sharing the same place numbers. A clue such as “the red box is immediately below J” fills the colour column even when the name is unknown.

items.label: Seen once (IBPS PO Prelims 22 Aug 2026 Shift 1)

blocks.x: Place EMPTY like a box. “Shelves between” counts it; “boxes between” does not.

It is a floor-with-flat puzzle: stack X on the west, stack Y on the east, shelves instead of floors. “To the west of” means the same shelf in the other stack. “Above” and “below” in your bank’s sets are sometimes meant within the same stack and sometimes across stacks; if one reading gives no arrangement, try the other.

lead.x: Three original puzzles written for this module. Each was checked by a brute-force script and has exactly one arrangement.

body.x: Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U are kept one above another in a stack, but not necessarily in the same order. Box R is kept at the third position from the bottom. Only two boxes are kept between box R and box T. Box S is kept immediately below box T. Only one box is kept between box Q and box R. Box U is kept above box P.

qs.stem: Which box is kept at the bottom of the stack?
How many boxes are kept between box U and box Q?
Which box is kept immediately above box R?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try each order of the six boxes against the five clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: R at place 3.
Two boxes between R and T: difference 3. Going down is impossible, so T at 6 (top).
S immediately below T: S at 5.
One box between Q and R: Q at 5 or 1. Place 5 is taken, so Q at 1.
Places 2 and 4 are left; U above P: U at 4, P at 2.

method.x: Stack, top to bottom: T, S, U, R, P, Q.
**Answers:** Q1 (C). Q2 (B) Two. Q3 (E) U.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, R is at place 3 so (E) is out at once; T and S end up at the top two places so (B) is out.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “U is kept above P” is not “immediately above”. U is two places higher than P.

body.x: Eight boxes J, K, L, M, N, P, Q and R are kept one above another in a stack, but not necessarily in the same order. Only two boxes are kept below box M. Only three boxes are kept between box M and box K. Box J is kept immediately above box K. Only one box is kept between box J and box N. Only two boxes are kept between box L and box Q, and box L is kept above box Q. Box R is kept below box Q.

qs.stem: Which box is kept immediately below box N?
How many boxes are kept above box P?
Which box is kept exactly between box K and box L?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** test orders of the eight boxes against all six clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Two boxes below M: M at 3.
Three boxes between M and K: difference 4, so K at 7.
J immediately above K: J at 8. One box between J and N: N at 6.
Places 1, 2, 4, 5 are left. L above Q with two between (difference 3): L at 5 and Q at 2, or L at 4 and Q at 1.
R is below Q, so Q cannot be at 1. Q at 2, L at 5, R at 1. P takes 4.

method.x: Stack, top to bottom: J, K, N, L, P, M, Q, R.
**Answers:** Q1 (D) L. Q2 (A) Four. Q3 (B) N.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q2, P is the last box placed and lands at 4 in a stack of 8, so 8 − 4 = 4 boxes above. No need to look at the drawing.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “only two boxes below M” puts M at place 3, not place 2. Starting one place off shifts K, J and N as well, and every answer changes.

body.x: Eight boxes S, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z are kept one above another in a stack, such that the bottommost box is numbered 1 and the topmost box is numbered 8. Box W is kept at the third position from the top. Box T is kept three places below box W. Only one box is kept between box T and box Y. Box X is kept immediately above box Y. Only one box is kept between box X and box Z. Box U is kept above box S, and more than one box is kept between them.

qs.stem: Which box is kept at the top of the stack?
How many boxes are kept between box W and box X?
Which box is kept immediately above box T?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** test orders of the eight boxes against all six clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Third from the top of 8 is place 6: W at 6.
Three places below: T at 3.
One box between T and Y: Y at 5 or 1. X is immediately above Y; with Y at 5, X needs place 6, which W holds. So Y at 1, X at 2.
One box between X and Z: Z at 4.
Places 5, 7, 8 are left for S, U, V. U above S with more than one box between: U at 8, S at 5. V takes 7.

method.x: Stack, top to bottom: U, V, W, S, Z, T, X, Y.
**Answers:** Q1 (B). Q2 (C) Three. Q3 (D) Z.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, W is third from the top, so (C) is out; S must have U well above it, so (D) is out.

**IBPS Trap Warning:** two traps in one set. “Third from the top” is place 6 here, not place 3. And “three places below” is a difference of 3; reading it as three boxes between puts T at 2 and the set no longer has a single arrangement.

rows: “nth from the bottom”, “only n boxes below”
“nth from the top”, “only n boxes above”
Convert to a bottom number first
Using the top number as a place
Difference n + 1; one or two places
Glue as a block of two
Top or bottom kills a case
“As many above X as below Y”
Mirror positions: X and Y add to N + 1
A colour or item per box

blocks.x: **Order of work, in one line:** number from the bottom, fixed clue, chain the linked clues, split into two columns, kill one, loose clues, questions.
**Useful fact.** If as many boxes are above X as below Y, then place of X + place of Y = N + 1. In a stack of 8, the pair is (1, 8), (2, 7), (3, 6) or (4, 5).

After these, work through the Guidely “box based puzzle, single variable” sets, then “two variable”. Leave the “box with stack” sets until last; no paper opened had one.

**What was checked by script**

items.x: 40 of the 77 bank sets (20 Sreedhar, 20 Guidely, spread across the sub-sections) were solved by brute force: a script tried every arrangement against every clue as worded, and the questions were answered from what survived. The other 37 sets were sorted by section name but not solved.

37 of the 40 have exactly one arrangement. For 22 of those the solver noted a reading choice, most often “n boxes above” meaning n places above, and “west of” meaning the same shelf in two-stack sets.

3 do not: BX189 (S-MT14-87 to 91) has five arrangements; BX205 (the set containing S-MT8-70) has two, with two boxes interchangeable; BX280 (a Guidely two-stack set) has four on a plain reading and part of a question merged into its passage.
198 questions in those sets: 194 agree with the key; 4 cannot be settled because their set (BX189) is not unique (S-MT14-88 to 91).
The three drill puzzles each have exactly one arrangement by script, and their answers come from the script.

**How the bank check was run.** The 40 sets were solved in helper runs, each writing its own solver script per puzzle. I merged and counted their results; I did not re-read each solver. The “cases” figures are the helpers’ estimate of a human path, not something computed.

**Data problems in the bank.** A few Guidely passages have lost their opening line (the list of boxes). Two Sreedhar “odd one out” questions say “based on positions in the English alphabetical order” when the key only works from the stack; treat that phrase as meaning the arrangement.
**Not verified:** the 37 unsolved bank sets; the paper inventory beyond a single reading; how often each form appears beyond these 24 papers. Memory-based papers are reconstructions.

sample.x: **Sample.** This module is built mainly from your question bank, as you asked. Bank: 77 puzzle sets with 376 questions (57 single-stack sets, 20 sets with two stacks side by side; 53 sets from Guidely, 24 from Sreedhar). Your bank has no previous-year Reasoning questions, so what the exam asks comes from 24 memory-based papers opened on the web: 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers (2018 to Oct 2025) and 12 sister papers (SBI Clerk, IBPS RRB Clerk, IBPS PO Prelims). Box sets seen: 3 in the Clerk papers, 4 in the sister papers. Memory-based papers are reconstructions, not official papers.

**A note on time.** A box set is one stack followed by about five questions. The honest target is 3 to 4 minutes for the stack and 15 to 20 seconds for each question after it. Box sets are usually the quickest puzzle in the paper, so do them early.

intro.x: A box puzzle is a stack of seven or eight boxes and about six clues. Most teaching for it stops at "find a fixed box, connect the clues, eliminate". That is true, but it is too general to make you fast. These lessons are built from the puzzles themselves.

**What I studied first.** Ten real clerk-level puzzles from memory-based papers (IBPS Clerk 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025; SBI Clerk 2022 and two from 2025; RRB Clerk 2021 and two from 2025), and 32 single-stack sets from your bank. Each was written out as exact conditions and solved by a script, so every number below was counted and none is a guess.

rows: 8 in IBPS and recent SBI Clerk, 7 in RRB Clerk
8 in 17 sets, 7 in 7, 9 or 10 in 7, 6 in 1
Puzzles that fix a box's place outright
Puzzles with no clue about a single box at all
Ways the main block fits, typically
Open cases when clues are taken in printed order
Open cases when the block is built first

intro.x: **What this means.** There is usually no fixed box to begin with, so the puzzle has to be started from the clues that lock boxes to each other. That is what the ten lessons teach, one piece at a time. Every worked example is a real paper puzzle, and every practice set comes from your bank with a full walk-through.

A note on honesty: memory-based papers are reconstructions by candidates. All ten puzzles used here have exactly one arrangement when checked by script, which is good evidence that they were remembered correctly, but the exact wording may differ slightly from the exam.

after.x: That is the single-stack box puzzle, which is the only kind found in the clerk-level papers studied. The **Quick revision** tab keeps the short tables.
For every set, the order is the same: short notes, hub, block, shapes, count the fits, columns, mirror and room clues, closers, then check one unused clue before answering.

Still to come for this topic, as insurance: boxes with a second fact (a colour or an item in each box), a vacant shelf, and two stacks side by side. None of the clerk papers studied had these, though your bank and the PO papers do.

lessons.title: Turn every clue into a number
lessons.plain: The starting point. Number the stack from the bottom, and read each clue as "so many places apart". Nothing is placed yet.

teach.x: A box puzzle gives you seven or eight boxes "kept one above another" and a handful of clues. Before any solving, there is a small language to learn. Each clue, however it is worded, says one of only a few things, and each of those is a **number**.

**Number the places from the bottom.** Place 1 is the lowest box. In a stack of 8, place 8 is the top. (If the puzzle itself says "the top box is numbered 1", follow the puzzle. One real paper did that.)
Now the clue words. Call the number of places between two boxes their **step**.

rows: X is immediately (or just) above Y
Only two boxes are between X and Y
two boxes sit in the middle
X is three boxes above Y
count three places up from Y

teach.x: Two of these are confused all the time, so please look at them once more:

items.x: **"Two boxes between"** is a step of **3**. Add one to the number in the clue.
**"Two boxes above"** is a step of **2**. Use the number as it is.

teach.x: You may wonder whether "three boxes above" could mean three boxes in between. I checked rather than guessed. In your bank, 14 single-stack sets use this wording. Read as a plain step, every one of them has exactly one arrangement, and in each set I checked against its answer key it is the keyed one; read the other way, most of them have no arrangement at all. In the three real papers where the final arrangement is known (IBPS Clerk 2024, SBI Clerk 20 and 21 September 2025), the same reading fits. So you can rely on it.
**Clues that count boxes above or below.** These give a place directly.

rows: Place, in a stack of N
Only two boxes are below X
Only two boxes are above X
As many boxes above X as below X
the middle place (only when N is odd)

teach.x: The habit this lesson is building: as you read each clue, write it in short form beside the puzzle, such as **T = R + 2** or **W, R: 4 apart**. From the next lesson on, you will solve from these short notes and hardly look at the sentences again.

example.q: Write each clue of this real puzzle as a number. (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 October 2025, shift 1, as candidates remembered it.) Three boxes are placed between W and R. T is placed two boxes above R. P is placed just below T but above W. Two boxes are placed between P and V. S is placed three boxes below V. Q is placed adjacent to W.
steps: Three boxes between W and R: **W, R are 4 apart** (which is higher is not said).
T two boxes above R: **T = R + 2**.
P just below T: **P = T - 1**. And P is above W: no number, keep it aside.
Two boxes between P and V: **P, V are 3 apart**.
S three boxes below V: **S = V - 3**.
Q adjacent to W: **Q, W are 1 apart**.
example.answer: Six short notes. You will solve this same puzzle from them in the next lesson.

checks.q: In a stack of 8 boxes numbered from the bottom, "only two boxes are kept above X". Where is X?
checks.why: Two boxes above X means places 7 and 8 are above it, so X is at place 6. (Place 3 would be "two boxes below X".)

checks.q: Only three boxes are kept between P and Q. P is at place 2. Where is Q?
checks.why: Three boxes between means a step of 4. 2 + 4 = 6. (Place 5 uses a step of 3, which would leave only two boxes between.)

checks.q: R is kept three boxes above S. S is at place 2. Where is R?
checks.why: "Three boxes above" is a step of 3, used as it is: 2 + 3 = 5.

checks.q: In a stack of 7 boxes, as many boxes are above M as below M. Where is M?
checks.why: Three above and three below: the middle, place 4. A real RRB Clerk paper (7 December 2025) opened with exactly this clue.

checks.q: In a stack of 7, more than two boxes are kept between X and Y, and X is at place 1. Where can Y be?
checks.why: More than two between means three or more between: a step of at least 4. From place 1 that is place 5, 6 or 7.

lessons.title: The block: join the clues before touching the stack
lessons.plain: New: do not look for a box to place. Join the clues that share a box into one rigid block, away from the stack.

teach.x: Most advice for puzzles begins with "find the fixed clue and place it first". For box puzzles at clerk level, that advice usually has nothing to work on.

I checked 10 real clerk-level puzzles (IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and RRB Clerk, 2020 to 2025) and 32 sets in your bank. **Only one paper puzzle in the 10, and three bank sets in the 32, tell you outright where a box is.** Six of the 10 paper puzzles give no clue at all about a single box's place.
So the puzzle has to be started another way. Here it is.

**Clues that share a box can be joined.** If T = R + 2 and P = T - 1, then all three are locked together: P = R + 1. You do not yet know where they are in the stack, but you know exactly how they sit **relative to each other**. That locked group is a **block**.
**How to build it.**

items.x: Pick the box that appears in the most clues. Call its place 0.
Take each clue that mentions a box already in the block, and write the new box as a number above (+) or below (-) the 0.
When a clue allows two ways ("4 apart" can be +4 or -4), see whether the block already rules one out: the spot may be taken, or a plain "above" clue may forbid it.
Keep going until no remaining clue touches the block.

teach.x: Then look at the **height** of the block: from its highest box to its lowest, counting both. If the height equals the number of boxes in the stack, the block **is** the stack, and the puzzle is finished without a single case.
This is not rare. In the 2025 IBPS Clerk puzzle below, seven of the eight boxes fall into one block that fills the stack.

example.q: Solve the IBPS Clerk Prelims puzzle of 4 October 2025 (eight boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W) from the notes of the last lesson: W, R are 4 apart. T = R + 2. P = T - 1, and P is above W. P, V are 3 apart. S = V - 3. Q, W are 1 apart.
steps: R is in two clues and T links to P, so start there. Let R = 0. Then T = +2 and P = +1.
W is 4 from R: +4 or -4. But P is above W, and P is at +1. So W cannot be at +4. **W = -4.**
V is 3 from P (+1): +4 or -2. S = V - 3. If V = +4, S = +1, which is P's spot. So **V = -2 and S = -5.**
The block now runs from T (+2) down to S (-5). That is 8 places: the whole stack. So T is at place 8 and S at place 1.
Fill in: T 8, P 7, R 6, V 4, W 2, S 1. Q is next to W: place 3 (place 1 is S). U takes place 5.
example.answer: Top to bottom: T, P, R, U, V, Q, W, S. No cases were needed.

checks.q: P is two boxes above Q. R is just below Q. Three boxes are between P and S, and S is below P. How many places does this block take, from its top box to its bottom box?
checks.why: Let Q = 0. P = +2, R = -1, S = P - 4 = -2. The block runs from +2 to -2: five places.

text.x: Start the block from the **hub**: the box named in the most clues that give an exact step (immediately, n between, n boxes above).
A quick way to find it: as you write the short notes, put a tick over a box's letter each time it appears. The letter with the most ticks is the hub.
In the 17 bank sets practised in these lessons, the main block holds about 4 of the boxes on average. That is half the puzzle done before the stack is drawn.

lessons.title: Sliding the block up and down
lessons.plain: New: the block is shorter than the stack. Count how many places it can sit in, draw one column for each, and let the other clues remove columns.

teach.x: Last lesson the block filled the whole stack. More often it is a little shorter, so it can **slide**.
**How many places can it sit in?** A block of height H in a stack of N boxes fits in
**N - H + 1 ways.**
A block 7 tall in a stack of 8 fits 2 ways: touching the top, or touching the bottom. A block 6 tall fits 3 ways.

This is the number of **cases** you face, and you know it before drawing anything. In the 32 bank sets and 10 real paper puzzles I worked through, the main block most often fits in **2 or 3 ways**. Working clue by clue in the order they are printed, the same puzzles typically reach about 8 open cases at their worst point. That difference is the time this method saves.
**What to do.**

items.x: Draw one column for each fit, side by side, with the block written in.
In each column, list the free places.
Take the remaining clues one at a time and ask of each column: can this clue still be satisfied with the free places left? Strike out a column the moment the answer is no.

teach.x: The best clues for striking out columns are the ones that need **room**: "U is immediately above Q" needs two free places next to each other; "two boxes between L and K" needs two free places 3 apart; "I is above F but below K" needs free places in a certain order. Look at the free places, not at the letters.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 September 2025, shift 2 (eight boxes F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M). J is three boxes above M. Two boxes are between L and K. G is just below J. Two boxes are between M and H. I is above F but below K. More than two boxes are between G and L.
steps: Block from J: G = J - 1, M = J - 3. H is 3 from M: that is J itself (taken) or J - 6. So H = J - 6.
Height from J down to H: 7 places. In a stack of 8 it fits 8 - 7 + 1 = 2 ways.
Fit 1, block touching the top: J 8, G 7, M 5, H 2. Fit 2, block touching the bottom: J 7, G 6, M 4, H 1.

Fit 2: free places 8, 5, 3, 2. L and K are 3 apart: (8, 5) or (5, 2). G is at 6 and L must be at least 4 away from it, so L = 2 and K = 5. Free: 8 and 3. I is below K, so I = 3, and F must be below I: nothing free. Fit 2 is out.
Fit 1: free places 6, 4, 3, 1. L and K 3 apart: (6, 3) or (4, 1). L is at least 4 from G (place 7): L = 3 with K = 6, or L = 1 with K = 4.
K = 4, L = 1 leaves 6 and 3; I must be below K, so I = 3, and F below I has no place. Out. So K = 6, L = 3, then I = 4 and F = 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: J, G, K, M, I, L, H, F.

checks.q: A block is 6 places tall. The stack has 8 boxes. In how many ways can the block sit in the stack?
checks.why: N - H + 1 = 8 - 6 + 1 = 3: with its top at place 8, 7 or 6.

shortcut.title: Read the free places, not the letters

text.x: After the block is in, write the free places of each column as plain numbers, for example **free: 6, 4, 3, 1**. Then test the remaining clues against those numbers:

items.x: "immediately above" needs two free numbers that differ by 1;
"two boxes between" needs two free numbers that differ by 3;
"X above Y above Z" needs three free numbers, and tells you which box gets the highest.

text.x: A column where the needed pair of numbers does not exist is dead at once. You do not have to try any letters in it.

lessons.title: When the block can take more than one shape
lessons.plain: New: a "between" clue does not say which box is higher, so the block may flip. Plain words like above, below and top settle it.

teach.x: A clue such as "three boxes between S and V" gives a step of 4 but not the **direction**. V may be 4 above S or 4 below. So a block with such a clue in it can have two shapes, and each shape slides on its own.
Before you draw columns for every shape, let the cheap clues work. Three kinds of clue choose the shape for you.
**1. A plain "above" or "below" about two boxes already in the block.** "P is above W", with P at +1: W cannot be at +4. These clues look weak, but inside a block they are exact.
**2. The edges of the stack.** A shape that is taller than the stack cannot exist. Work out the height of each shape; often one of them is 9 tall in a stack of 8.
**3. Clues about the top or bottom.** "At least two boxes are above C" or "D is not at the bottom" cut off the highest or lowest fits of a shape.
So the order of work is: build the block, write down each shape it can take, strike out shapes with rules 1 to 3, and only then slide what is left.
The real papers often give this partner clue in the very next sentence ("Two boxes are between B and G. G is below B."), so look for it straight away.

example.q: RRB Clerk (Office Assistant) Prelims, 8 August 2021 (seven boxes A to G). Two boxes are between B and G. G is below B. A is just below G. More than three boxes are between A and E. C is not above G. Two boxes are between F and C.
steps: B, G are 3 apart, and "G is below B" gives the direction at once: G = B - 3. Then A = G - 1 = B - 4. One shape only.
Height from B to A: 5 places. In a stack of 7 it fits 3 ways: A at place 3, 2 or 1.
"More than three between A and E" is a step of at least 5. With A at 3, E would need place 8. Out.
A at 1: then G is at 2, and C must be below G. Only place 1 is below, and A has it. Out.
A at 2: G 3, B 6, and E = 7. C is below G: place 1. F is 3 from C: place 4. D takes 5.
example.answer: Top to bottom: E, B, D, F, G, A, C.

checks.q: Three boxes are between K and L. M is immediately above K. M is above L. What do you know about L?

options.a: L is four places below K
options.b: L is four places above K
options.c: L may be four above or four below K
options.d: L is three places below K

checks.why: Let K = 0, so M = +1. L is at +4 or -4. If L were at +4 it would be above M. So L = -4: four places below K.

lessons.title: The mirror clue: as many above X as below Y
lessons.plain: New: one clue that looks vague and is in fact exact. The two places always add up to one more than the number of boxes.

teach.x: "As many boxes are kept above N as below G." This clue appears in more than half of the bank sets (18 of 32) and, in one form or another, in three of the ten real papers. It looks loose. It is one of the strongest clues in the puzzle.

Think of a stack of 7. If N is at the top, no box is above it, so no box is below G: G is at the bottom. If N is second from the top, G is second from the bottom. The two boxes sit at **mirror** places.
In numbers: **place of N + place of G = number of boxes + 1.**
Three things follow, and each one saves time.

items.x: **The moment one of the two is placed, the other is placed too.** So in every column of your block, the partner's place is forced. If that place is already taken by the block, the column is dead.
**In a stack of 7 they can never both be at place 4**, since they are different boxes. In a stack of 8 the pair 4 and 5 are neighbours.
The box named after "above" is the higher one whenever the count is less than half. "As many above N as below G" with only one or two boxes above N means N is near the top and G near the bottom.

teach.x: **Variations.** "The number of boxes above S is two more than the number below V": work out the count for one and add two. "As many boxes above M as below M" (the same box): M is exactly in the middle.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 6 December 2025, shift 2 (seven boxes A to G). Three boxes are between B and D. A is immediately below B. The number of boxes below A is the same as the number above G. One box is between G and C, and C is above G. E is not at the bottom.
steps: Mirror clue in a stack of 7: place of A + place of G = 8.
Short notes: B = A + 1. B, D are 4 apart. C = G + 2.
Run A through its places. A 6: G 2, B 7, D 3, C 4. All different. Keep.
A 5: G 3, B 6, C 5, which is A's place. Out. A 4: G would be 4 too. Out.
A 3: B 4, and D would need place 8 or 0. Out. A 2: G 6, C 8. Out. A 1: G 7, C 9. Out.
So B 7, A 6, C 4, D 3, G 2. Free: 5 and 1. E is not at the bottom: E 5, F 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: B, A, E, C, D, G, F.

checks.q: In a stack of 8 boxes, as many boxes are above X as below Y. X is at place 6. Where is Y?
checks.why: The places add up to 9. 9 - 6 = 3. (Check: two boxes are above place 6, and two are below place 3.)

shortcut.title: Use the mirror first when it touches the block

text.x: If one of the two mirror boxes is in your block, do not wait. As soon as the columns are drawn, write the partner's forced place in each one.
In all four practice sets of this lesson it removes at least one column on the spot, before any other clue is read.
To find the partner without thinking: partner's place = (number of boxes + 1) - this place. In 8 boxes: 9 minus. In 7 boxes: 8 minus.

lessons.title: Soft anchors: even, odd, prime, not at the top
lessons.plain: New: clues about one box that do not fix it but narrow it. Use them to cut the list of places for the block, before drawing columns.

teach.x: Clerk papers rarely say "T is at place 4". What they do say, quite often, is something softer about one box:

items.x: "T is at an even numbered place"
"A is kept in an odd numbered place"
"U is third from either of the ends"
"at least two boxes are above C"
"B is not at the top", "E is not at the bottom"

teach.x: None of these places a box. Each of them **cuts down the places the block can sit in**, and that is how to use them: join the soft clue to the block **before** counting the fits.

"S is at an even place but not below the fourth" leaves 4, 6 and 8. If the block also says V is 3 above S, then S = 8 is impossible (V would be at 11) and S = 6 too (V at 9). One place is left, and you never drew a column.
For quick use:

**Two soft clues on boxes of the same block multiply.** If Q is even and T, three places from Q, is also even, that cannot happen: an odd step changes even to odd. Checking **even against odd** like this is a very fast test. A step of 1 or 3 switches between even and odd; a step of 2 or 4 keeps it.
And the weakest ones, "not at the top" and "not at the bottom": keep them for the very end. In the real papers they are nearly always what decides between the last two boxes.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 19 November 2022, shift 1 (seven boxes P to V). U is third from either of the ends. P is adjacent to U. Three boxes are between P and S. The number of boxes above S is two more than the number below V. Q is above R, which is not below S.
steps: U is at place 3 or place 5.
P is next to U: 2 or 4 (with U at 3), or 4 or 6 (with U at 5). S is 4 from P.
P at 4 would put S at 8 or 0. So P is 2 or 6: either (U 3, P 2, S 6) or (U 5, P 6, S 2).
Count clue. S at 6: one box above it, so V would have minus one box below. Out.
S at 2: five boxes above, so three below V: V at 4.
Free: 7, 3, 1. Q is above R, and R is above S: R 3, Q 7. T takes 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: Q, P, U, V, R, S, T.

checks.q: Eight boxes. S is at an even numbered place, but not below the fourth. V is three boxes above S. Where is S?
checks.why: S can be 4, 6 or 8. V = S + 3 must exist in a stack of 8, so S cannot be 6 or 8. S is at place 4.

lessons.title: Start where the choices are fewest
lessons.plain: New: the biggest block is not always the best start. Count the places each group can take, and begin with the smallest count.

teach.x: So far the plan has been: build the biggest block, then slide it. In some puzzles the biggest block is small (two or three boxes) and slides in six or seven ways. Starting there would give you seven columns.
The better rule is the general one behind everything so far:
**Begin with the group of clues that leaves the fewest possible places.**
Three kinds of clue are much tighter than they look, and are worth checking before you choose where to begin.

**1. A wide gap.** "More than four boxes between M and T" in a stack of 8 means a step of at least 6. Only three pairs of places allow that: 1 and 7, 1 and 8, 2 and 8. A clue that sounded vague has pinned two boxes to the ends of the stack.

rows: Pairs of places that allow it

teach.x: **2. A mirror clue joined to an exact step.** "S is three above Y, and as many boxes are above S as below R": S can only be at 4, 5, 7 or 8, and each choice places three boxes at once.

**3. A chain of plain "above" clues.** "K is above R, and R is above V" is three boxes in a fixed order. If only three free places are left for them, they are placed with no thought at all. The more boxes in the chain, the earlier it helps.

And then the **closers**: "not adjacent" clues. They never help you start, but they are almost always what removes the last wrong column. Read them last, and check them against every column that is still alive.
In the IBPS Clerk puzzle of 2024 below, starting from the three-box block gives nine columns. Starting from the wide gap gives four, and each one closes quickly.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 25 August 2024, shift 3 (eight boxes A, B, F, K, M, P, T, V, numbered 1 at the bottom). P is three boxes above V. Only two boxes are between K and A. More than four boxes are between M and T. B is above F but not at an odd numbered place. T is just below A. F and M are not adjacent. B is not at the top.
steps: Wide gap first: M and T are at 1 and 7, 1 and 8, or 2 and 8.
T has A just above it, so T is not at 8. That leaves four columns: (T 1, M 7), (T 1, M 8), (T 2, M 8) and (T 7, M 1).
T 7, A 8, M 1: K is 3 from A, so K 5. P = V + 3 with free places 2, 3, 4, 6: V 3, P 6. Left: 2 and 4. B above F: B 4, F 2, but F is next to M. Out.
T 2, A 3, M 8: K 6. Free 1, 4, 5, 7: (V 1, P 4) leaves 5 and 7; (V 4, P 7) leaves 1 and 5. B must be even and not at 8: no even place in either. Out.
T 1, A 2, K 5, M 7: free 3, 4, 6, 8. V 3, P 6 only. Left: 4 and 8. B above F would put B at 8. Out.
T 1, A 2, K 5, M 8: free 3, 4, 6, 7. V 3, P 6 leaves 4 and 7: B would be 7, odd. Out. V 4, P 7 leaves 3 and 6: B 6, F 3. F is not next to M. It works.
example.answer: Top to bottom: M, P, B, K, V, F, A, T.

checks.q: In a stack of 7 boxes, more than three boxes are kept between A and E. How many pairs of places allow this?
checks.why: More than three between is a step of at least 5: places 1 and 6, 1 and 7, or 2 and 7. Three pairs.

lessons.title: Same-gap clues, and the midpoint
lessons.plain: New: "as many boxes between A and B as between C and D". Keep it for last, unless the two pairs share a box. Then it is a midpoint.

teach.x: "The number of boxes between K and M is the same as the number between L and P." This clue names four boxes and gives no step at all. On its own it cannot start anything.

**The usual case: use it last.** By the time the block is placed, one of the two pairs is normally already in the stack. Read off its step. The other pair must have the same step, and you look for two free places that far apart. It works exactly like a "between" clue whose number you find out late.
A very common result is a step of 1: if K and M turn out to be neighbours, there are no boxes between them, so L and P must be neighbours as well.
**The special case: the two pairs share a box.** "As many boxes between B and E as between E and C." Now E is named twice, and this is quite different:

items.x: B and C are different boxes, so they cannot both be on the same side of E at the same distance.
So E is **exactly halfway** between B and C. One is above E, the other the same number of places below.

teach.x: That is an exact clue, and it belongs **in the block**. If B is 4 above E, then C is 4 below E. In one of your bank's ten-box sets this single observation makes the block fill the whole stack, and a puzzle that looks like the hardest in the paper is done with no cases.
So when you see a same-gap clue, look first at one thing: is a box repeated? If yes, block. If no, last.

Three boxes are between S and K. The number of boxes between K and M equals the number between L and P. P is not at the bottom.
steps: M is in the middle of 7: place 4.
R is 2 from M: 6 or 2. S is just above R: 7 or 3. K is 4 from S: with S 7, K 3; with S 3, K 7.
Column 1: S 7, R 6, M 4, K 3. K and M are neighbours, so L and P must be neighbours. Free: 5, 2, 1. L and P take 2 and 1; P is not at the bottom, so P 2, L 1, and N takes 5.
Column 2: K 7, M 4, S 3, R 2. K and M have two boxes between them, so L and P must be 3 apart. Free: 6, 5, 1. No such pair. Out.

lessons.title: Putting it together: two blocks, and nine boxes
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the ideas. Two separate blocks have to fit around each other, and the stack may be longer. The same steps, with more care.

teach.x: Sometimes the exact clues do not all connect. You get **two blocks** of three boxes each, and neither is tied to the other. The SBI Clerk paper of 21 September 2025 was like this.
Do not try to slide both at once. The way through is:

items.x: Build both blocks on the side and note the height of each.
Place the **taller** one, or the one with a soft anchor or an "above" clue attached. It has fewer fits.

For each fit, write the free places as numbers, and ask whether the second block's pattern exists among them. A block needing places u, u - 1 and u - 3 either finds those three numbers free or it does not.
Then the closers.

teach.x: Most columns die at the third step without any further work, because a second rigid block is very hard to fit into scattered free places.
**Nine and ten boxes.** Your bank has several; the clerk papers I found had only 7 or 8, and the longer stacks appeared at PO level. If you meet one, the method does not change, but judge it first:

items.x: If the main block is 7 or more tall, the long stack is actually **easier**, because the block has very little room to slide.
If the biggest block is only 2 or 3 boxes and there are five or more loose boxes, it will take over five minutes. In the exam, do the other puzzles first and come back.

teach.x: A sensible target once the method is familiar: about 3 minutes for the stack and 15 to 20 seconds for each question.

Block 2: G, B (4 from G), D = B - 1.
E 2: A 7, F 6, so G 8, B 4, D 3. Free: 5 and 1. H is below A, C below H: H 5, C 1. It works.

lessons.title: The five questions: reading the answers off quickly
lessons.plain: New: the stack is built. A few habits make the five questions take seconds each.

teach.x: Once the stack is right, the five questions should be the quickest marks in the section. I sorted the 216 questions asked on single-stack sets in your bank, and the same few kinds keep returning. The real papers ask the same kinds.

rows: Which box is above, below or at a given place
How many boxes between, above or below
Four of the five are alike: find the odd one
Which statement is true or false
As many boxes above X as below which box
Rearranged alphabetically, or two boxes swapped

teach.x: **Write the place numbers beside the final stack.** Every one of these questions is then a small subtraction, not counting with a finger.

items.x: **Boxes between X and Y** = difference of the two places, minus 1.
**Boxes above X** = number of boxes minus X's place. **Boxes below X** = X's place minus 1.
**As many above X as below which box?** This is the mirror: the answer is the box at place (number of boxes + 1 - X's place).

**Odd one out, given as pairs.** Find the step for each pair. Four pairs share it; one does not. If the steps do not separate them, look at direction (first box above or below the second), and then at even and odd places.
**Odd one out, given as single boxes.** It is nearly always even places against odd places, or prime places against non-prime.
**Arranged in alphabetical order, how many stay unchanged?** Write the alphabetical column right beside your stack and compare row by row. Check whether it says from the top or from the bottom.
**Statements.** Check the shortest statement first; in "which is true" questions you can stop at the first true one unless an option says "both".

teach.x: One last habit: before answering, test your finished stack against the **one clue you used least**, usually a "not adjacent" one. It takes five seconds and protects all five answers.

example.q: The final stack, from top to bottom, is R, T, V, P, S, W, U, Q (eight boxes). Answer: (1) How many boxes are between T and W? (2) As many boxes are above V as below which box? (3) Which pair is the odd one: R-T, V-P, T-P, U-Q?
steps: Write the places: R 8, T 7, V 6, P 5, S 4, W 3, U 2, Q 1.
(1) T is 7 and W is 3. 7 - 3 - 1 = 3 boxes.
(2) Mirror of place 6 in 8 boxes: 9 - 6 = 3. The box at place 3 is W.
(3) Steps: R-T 1, V-P 1, T-P 2, U-Q 1. The odd one is T-P.

checks.q: The final stack, from top to bottom, is G, F, D, H, B, A, E, C (eight boxes). As many boxes are kept above F as below which box?
checks.why: F is at place 7. Its mirror in 8 boxes is 9 - 7 = 2, and the box at place 2 is E. (One box is above F, and one is below E.)

checks.q: The stack, top to bottom, is T, U, Q, S, P, W, R, V. Four of these are alike in their places: S, R, W, U, Q. Which is the odd one?
checks.why: Places: S 5, R 2, W 3, U 7, Q 6. Four are at prime places. Q, at place 6, is not.

checks.q: The stack, top to bottom, is X, S, V, T, Y, W, R, U. If the boxes are rearranged in alphabetical order from top to bottom, how many stay where they are?
checks.why: Alphabetical from the top: R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y. Compared row by row with X, S, V, T, Y, W, R, U, the second (S) and the sixth (W) match: two.

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** People sit in one straight row. In the basic form all face north and the number of people is given (6 to 8). Clues say who is to the left or right of whom and how many sit between. You rebuild the row.

**The form the Clerk papers actually use.** “A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north.” Only some of them are named. Clues chain the named people together with gaps, and one clue ties the chain to an end of the row. You find where each named person sits and how many people are in the row.
**The one idea: a row is a number line. Give every clue a number, and the row builds itself.**
**How to draw it**

items.x: Known number: a line of blanks, numbered 1, 2, 3… from the left.

Unknown number: do not draw the ends. Write the first named person in the middle of the page and grow the chain left and right, with dashes for unnamed seats. Add the ends only when a clue gives them.

blocks.x: **Left and right**
Left and right belong to the person named after “of”. When everyone faces north you can forget this table; when anyone faces south you cannot.
**The solving algorithm**

items.x: Draw the line. If people face different ways, write an up or down arrow under each name as you place it.
Known number: place the fixed clue (“third from the left end”, “at an extreme end”). Unknown number: start with the person who appears in the most clues.
Chain the gap clues. “Third to the right” is one seat. “Only two persons between” is two possible seats: two drawings.
Kill a drawing when a seat is taken twice, when someone falls off a known end, or when a “not a neighbour” clue is broken.

Unknown number: find the clue that mentions an end (“only two persons sit to the left of A”, “B is fourth from the right end”, “as many sit to the right of C as to the left of A”). It fixes the ends; count the seats.
Answer the questions.

blocks.x: **Grid: clues as numbers (row numbered from the left, everyone facing north)**

rows: X is third to the right of Y
X is third to the left of Y
Only two persons between X and Y
Only two persons sit to the left of X
X is fourth from the right end, row of N
X sits exactly between Y and Z
X is the midpoint of Y and Z
As many to the left of X as to the right of Y
X is nth from the left and mth from the right
More than three persons between X and Y

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** “Third to the right” (difference 3) and “three persons between” (difference 4) differ by one seat, and one seat off at the start moves the whole row and changes the total.
**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** number the seats, write each clue as a line of arithmetic from the grid, and try each possible seat for the first person.

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “a certain number of persons”, “not more than 20 persons”.
**Shortcut engine.** build the chain of named people with dashes for gaps; find the clue that touches an end; count.
**Worked example.** Drill 2 below.
**Pattern clues.** “eight persons sit in a straight row facing north”.
**Shortcut engine.** numbered blanks; fixed clue; gap clues give two drawings; neighbour clue kills one.
**Worked example.** Drill 1 below.
Draw the row as usual, then swap the words left and right in every clue. Or turn your page upside down in your head and solve it as a north row.
Arrow under every name. For each clue, use the arrow of the person after “of”.
**Worked example.** Drill 3 below.
A second line under the row for the fact. A vacant seat is a seat but not a person; in three of the bank sets solved, the clues only work when “persons between” skips the vacant seat.

items.title: Drill 1 (Basic, L2: known number, facing north)

body.x: Six persons D, E, F, G, H and J are sitting in a straight row, all facing north, but not necessarily in the same order. G sits third from the left end of the row. Only one person sits between G and J. E sits to the immediate right of J. H sits at one of the extreme ends of the row. D is not an immediate neighbour of G.

qs.stem: Who sits to the immediate left of D?
How many persons sit between J and H?
Who sits second to the right of G?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try every order of the six persons against the five clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: G at seat 3.
One person between G and J: J at 1 or at 5.
E is immediately right of J: J1 E2, or J5 E6.
H at an end: seat 6 in the first drawing, seat 1 in the second.
D is not next to G. In the second drawing the free seats are 2 and 4, both next to G: it dies. In the first, free seats are 4 and 5: D at 5, F at 4.

method.x: Row, left to right: J, E, G, F, D, H.
**Answers:** Q1 (C) F. Q2 (D) Four. Q3 (A) D.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q3, second to the right of G is seat 5, and D cannot be at seat 2 or 4, so once J and E take 1 and 2 the answer is forced before you place F.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “only one person between G and J” does not say which side. Trying only the right side leads to a dead end and a wrong left-end answer.

items.title: Drill 2 (Exam form, L1: unknown number of persons)

body.x: A certain number of persons are sitting in a straight row, all facing north. Only two persons sit to the left of A. B sits third to the right of A. Only four persons sit between B and C. D sits second to the left of C. As many persons sit to the right of C as to the left of A.

qs.stem: How many persons are sitting in the row?
How many persons sit between A and D?
What is the position of D from the right end of the row?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try each possible row length in turn and place the four people.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Two persons to the left of A: A is at seat 3.
B is third to the right: seat 6.
Four persons between B and C: C at 11 or at 1.
D is second to the left of C. With C at 1 there is no seat to its left. So C at 11, D at 9.
As many to the right of C as to the left of A: two. The row ends at seat 13.

method.x: Row: seats 1 to 13, with A at 3, B at 6, D at 9, C at 11.
**Answers:** Q1 (C) 13. Q2 (B) Five. Q3 (D) Fifth.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q3 use the rule N = left position + right position − 1: 13 = 9 + right − 1, so right = 5. No counting on the drawing.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** “only four persons between B and C” is a difference of 5, not 4. Using 4 puts C at 10, D at 8 and makes the row 12 long, which is option (B).

body.x: Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are sitting in a straight row which runs from west to east, but not necessarily in the same order. B, E and H face south, while all the others face north. D sits at one of the extreme ends of the row. Only two persons sit between D and E. H sits second to the left of E. Only one person sits between H and C. B sits to the immediate right of H. G sits second to the right of B. A is not an immediate neighbour of D.

qs.stem: Who sits to the immediate left of A?
How many persons sit between F and B?
Who sits second to the right of G?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try every order of the eight persons, using each person’s own left and right.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Arrows: B, E, H face south, so their left is east and their right is west.
D at an end with two between D and E: D at 1 and E at 4, or D at 8 and E at 5.
H is second to the left of E; E faces south, so go two seats east: H at 6, or H at 7.
One person between H and C. With H at 7, C needs seat 5 (taken by E) or seat 9 (does not exist): this drawing dies. With H at 6, seat 4 is E’s, so C at 8.
B is immediately right of H (H faces south: one seat west): B at 5. G is second to the right of B (two seats west): G at 3.
Seats 2 and 7 are left. A is not next to D: A at 7, F at 2.

method.x: Row, west to east: D, F, G, E, B, H, A, C.
**Answers:** Q1 (D) H. Q2 (B) Two. Q3 (C) B.
**Option Elimination Hack:** none worth using; the questions need the finished row. Check each answer against the arrow of the person named after “of”: A and G both face north.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** for a person facing south, left is towards the east. Solving as if all eight face north gives the mirror row, and then Q1 comes out as C and Q3 as D.

rows: Chain from the most-mentioned person; no ends yet
“Only n persons sit to the left of X”
X is at seat n + 1; this fixes the left end
“X is nth from the right end”
Right end is n − 1 seats beyond X
“As many to the left of X as to the right of Y”
Ends mirror each other; gives the total

blocks.x: **Order of work, in one line:** line, arrows if needed, anchor person, exact-gap clues, two drawings for “between” clues, kill one, end clue gives the total, questions.
**Three formulas for the unknown-number form**

items.x: Total = position from left + position from right − 1.
Persons between seats p and q = q − p − 1.
Persons to the right of seat p in a row of N = N − p.

lessons.title: A row is a number line
lessons.plain: The starting point. Give every seat a number from the left, and every clue becomes a small addition or subtraction.

teach.x: A single row is the simplest arrangement there is, and the clerk papers use it in two forms. In the older form, seven or eight named people fill the row. In the newer and far more common form, **the number of people is not given**, and finding it is one of the questions. This first lesson is the plain form; the rest of the topic is about the unknown number.
**Number the seats from the left: 1, 2, 3 ...** When everyone faces north, their left is your left and their right is your right, so "to the right" always means a **higher number**.

rows: X sits third to the right of Y
X sits second to the left of Y
X sits to the immediate left of Y
Only three persons sit between X and Y
X sits three places away from Y
X sits to the left of Y
X is a lower number; how much lower is not known
X sits at an extreme end
X sits third from one of the extreme ends
seat 3, or the third seat from the other end

teach.x: Notice the two different words. "Three persons **between**" is 4 apart. "Three **places away**" is 3 apart. The papers use both.

**If the row faces south**, the people are looking at you, and their right is your left. The simplest way to handle it: number the seats from **your right** instead, and then "to the right" is again a higher number. Nothing else changes.

**How to solve the plain form.** Start from a clue about an end, attach the people tied to that person by exact steps, and let the edges of the row remove cases. With only seven or eight seats, most clues can go only one way.
In the papers I found, the plain form with a fixed number appeared in only 4 clerk sets, against 20 of the unknown-number kind. So treat this lesson as the alphabet for what follows.

Three persons sit between F and E. C sits immediately to the left of E. E sits at an end of the row. A sits to the left of B.
steps: E is at an end and C is immediately on its left, so E is at the right end: E 7, C 6.
F is 4 from E: seat 3.
D is 2 from F: seat 1 or 5. B = D + 3: from 5 that would be seat 8, so D 1 and B 4.
Free seats: 2 and 5. A is to the left of B: A 2. G takes 5.
example.answer: From the left: D, A, F, B, G, C, E.

lessons.title: The number is not given: build a chain
lessons.plain: New: "a certain number of persons sit in a row". Do not draw seats. Write each person as a step from one chosen person, and the chain can be read before the total is known.

teach.x: "A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north." Five to nine people are named; the row is longer than that, usually 11 to 17 seats and sometimes 21; and one question is always "How many persons sit in the row?"

About half of all the clerk shift papers I could open for 2024 to 2026 had one of these, in IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and RRB Clerk alike. I found 20 real ones and solved 18 of them by script. They are the single most useful seating puzzle to be quick at.
The difficulty people feel is this: "I cannot draw the row because I do not know how long it is." The answer is that **you do not need the row**. You need a **chain**.
**Build the chain.** Pick the person who appears in the most clues and call that seat 0. Write every person tied to it by an exact step as a number, to the right as plus and to the left as minus.
"O sits second to the left of K. P sits fourth to the right of O. P sits third to the left of J. J sits third to the left of M." With O at 0: K is +2, P is +4, J is +7, M is +10.
On paper, write the letters along a line with the gaps between them: **O . K . P . . J . . M**. That is the row, apart from its two ends.
**The chain already answers most questions.**

items.x: "What is the position of J with respect to K?" 7 - 2 = 5: fifth to the right.
"How many persons sit between O and J?" 7 - 0 - 1 = 6.
"Who sits third to the left of M?" +7, which is J.

teach.x: None of these needs the total. In the real sets, two of the three questions are usually of this kind. So even if the total gives you trouble, the chain alone earns most of the marks.

**Clues with two possibilities.** "Only two persons sit between K and Q" puts Q at +5 or at -1. Write both, lightly. One of them nearly always turns out to be taken, or to fall off the row once an end is known.

**As soon as a left-end clue appears** ("D sits at the extreme left end", "M sits sixth from the left end", "no one sits to the left of F"), change the chain into real seat numbers by adding whatever makes that person's number right.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 17 August 2024, shift 4. A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north. Only two persons sit between K and Q. O sits second to the left of K. P sits fourth to the right of O. P sits third to the left of J. J sits third to the left of M. M sits at the extreme end of the row. The number of persons to the left of J is one more than the number of persons to the right of P. Without finding the total: how many persons sit between K and J, and who sits third to the left of M?
steps: Chain from O = 0: K is +2, P is +4, J is +7, M is +10.
Between K (+2) and J (+7): 7 - 2 - 1 = 4 persons.
Third to the left of M (+10) is +7: J.
Q is 3 from K: +5 or -1. This is left open for now.
example.answer: Four persons; J. (The next lesson finds the total of this same row.)

checks.q: In a row of unknown length, K sits second to the right of O, P sits fourth to the right of O, and J sits third to the right of P. How many persons sit between K and J?
checks.why: With O at 0: K is +2, P is +4, J is +7. Between K and J: 7 - 2 - 1 = 4.

shortcut.title: Write the gaps, not the seats

text.x: On the rough sheet, write the named people in order with a dot for each seat between them: **F . E A . . B . G**
Leave space at both ends of the line. People are often added to the left of your first letter, and the total is settled last.
Under each letter write its number in the chain. Every "position of X with respect to Y" and every "how many between" is then one subtraction.

lessons.title: Finding the total: the balance clue
lessons.plain: New: how the number of persons is actually fixed. One end is known; a clue compares the people on the left of one person with the people on the right of another; the total is one addition.

teach.x: Every unknown-number puzzle must contain something that fixes the length, or the first question would have no answer. In the 17 real puzzles that the script solved to a single arrangement, the length is fixed in one of only **two** ways:

rows: one end is known, and a **balance clue** compares left of X with right of Y
**both ends** are tied to named people

teach.x: This lesson is the first way. The next two lessons cover the awkward end clue and the second way.
**The balance clue.** "The number of persons sitting to the left of B is the same as the number of persons sitting to the right of A."
Once the left end is known, every named person has a real seat number. Then:

items.x: persons to the left of B = B's seat number minus 1;
persons to the right of A = total minus A's seat number.

teach.x: Put them equal and the total falls out:
**total = A's seat number + (B's seat number - 1)**
In words: **take the person on the "right of" side, and add the count from the "left of" side.**
If B is in seat 7 and A is in seat 10, six persons are to the left of B, so six are to the right of A, and the row has 10 + 6 = 16 seats.
**Variations that the papers use.**

rows: left of X is **one more than** right of Y
left of X is **one less than** right of Y
as many to the left of K as to the right of K; K sits exactly in the middle
persons between E and D equal persons to the right of D
count the first, add to D's seat
only one person sits to the right of D

teach.x: **When the left end is not known yet**, the balance clue still works on the chain: it gives one relation between the starting seat and the total, and the end clue gives the other. That is the next lesson.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 October 2025, shift 1. A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north. Two persons sit between B and E. C sits to the immediate right of E. Three persons sit between D and C. No one sits to the left of D. Four persons sit between A and C. The number of persons to the left of B is the same as the number of persons to the right of A. How many persons sit in the row?
steps: No one is to the left of D: D is in seat 1.
C is 4 from D: seat 5. E is immediately left of C: seat 4.
B is 3 from E: seat 7 (seat 1 is D's). A is 5 from C: seat 10 (seat 0 does not exist).
Six persons are to the left of B, so six are to the right of A.
example.answer: 16 persons. Six seats at the right end hold people who are never named.

checks.q: In a row facing north, B sits in the 7th seat from the left and A in the 10th. The number of persons to the left of B is the same as the number to the right of A. How many persons sit in the row?
checks.why: Six persons are to the left of B, so six are to the right of A. 10 + 6 = 16.

text.x: For "the number of persons to the left of X is the same as the number to the right of Y":
**total = seat of Y + seat of X - 1**
For "one more" or "one less", adjust that by one in the direction the words say, and check with a quick count.
For one person in the middle of the row: **total = twice that seat, minus 1**. The total is then always odd, which rules out even options at a glance.

lessons.title: "From one of the extreme ends"
lessons.plain: New: the end clue does not say which end. Try the end that leaves room for the chain; the other usually falls off the row.

teach.x: The papers seldom say "third from the left end". The usual wording is "sits third from **one of the** extreme ends of the row". Twelve of the real puzzles I found use it. It looks like two cases every time. In practice it is rarely more than one.
**Look at where the person sits in your chain.** The chain has a left part and a right part around that person.

items.x: If several named people must sit **more than two seats to their left**, the person cannot be third from the left end. They are third from the **right** end.
If the chain stretches far to their right, they are near the **left** end.

teach.x: "P sits fourth from one of the extreme ends. R sits ninth to the right of P." P cannot be fourth from the right end, because R needs nine seats beyond it. So P is in seat 4, and the chain becomes real numbers.

**Two such clues in one puzzle** give the total directly. "P is fourth from one end, and R, nine seats to its right, is third from one end": P is seat 4, R is seat 13, and R must be third from the right. Total = 13 + 2 = 15.
**When both ends really are possible**, write the two cases side by side:

items.x: Case L: the person is in seat k. The chain becomes numbers, and the balance clue gives the total.
Case R: the person is in seat (total - k + 1). The chain is then written as steps back from the right end, and the balance clue must still be satisfied.

teach.x: One of the two nearly always produces a seat number below 1, puts two people in one seat, or breaks a limit such as "not more than 15 persons". Check those three things in that order.
A plain "X sits at an extreme end" is the same idea with k = 1: see which side of X the chain lies on.
