example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 1 March 2025, shift 1. A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north. Four persons sit between S and T. P sits second to the left of T. P sits fourth from one of the extreme ends of the row. Five persons sit between P and V, and P sits to the left of V. R sits third to the right of V. R sits third from one of the extreme ends of the row. The number of persons to the right of R is the same as the number to the left of Q. M sits second to the left of Q. How many persons sit in the row?
steps: Chain from P = 0: T is +2, V is +6, R is +9.
P is fourth from one end. R sits nine seats to its right, so P cannot be near the right end: P is seat 4. Then T 6, V 10, R 13.
R is third from one end, and it is not seat 3: it is third from the right. Total = 13 + 2 = 15.
Two persons are to the right of R, so two are to the left of Q: Q is seat 3, and M is seat 1.
S is 5 from T: seat 11 (seat 1 is M's).
example.answer: 15 persons. From the left: M . Q P . T . . . V S . R . .

checks.q: In a row of unknown length facing north, P sits fourth from one of the extreme ends. R sits ninth to the right of P and third from one of the extreme ends. How many persons sit in the row?
checks.why: R needs nine seats to the right of P, so P is seat 4 and R is seat 13. R is third from the right end: 13 + 2 = 15.

lessons.title: Both ends pinned, and the limits
lessons.plain: New: the other way the total is fixed. One named person is tied to the left end and another to the right end, and the chain between them measures the row.

teach.x: In 5 of the 17 real puzzles there is no balance clue at all. Instead, **two different people are tied to the two ends**, and the chain between them gives the length.
The end-ties come in several wordings:

rows: No one sits to the left of F
No one sits to the right of G
Only one person sits to the right of R
R is the last seat but one
K sits fifth from the extreme right end
four persons to the right of K
Y is the only neighbour of P
P is at an end, with Y next to it
B sits at one of the ends, and G sits at the extreme end
if both are in one chain, they are the two ends

teach.x: **How to use them.** Fix the left one as a real number; run the chain to the right one; add what is beyond it.
"B sits at one end and G at the other. Four persons sit between B and K, and six between K and G." B 1, K 6, G 13. The row has 13 seats.
**The limits.** Some puzzles add a sentence about the total itself. These are not decoration; each one exists to remove the one extra case.

rows: Not more than 14 persons sit in the row
the case that gives 18 is out
At least nine persons sit in the row
Not more than seven persons sit to the left of M
limits M's seat, and with a middle clue limits the total
An odd number of persons sit in the row
someone can be exactly in the middle
Not more than two persons sit to the right of W
the total is at most W's seat + 2

teach.x: So when your working gives two possible totals, look for the limit sentence before doing anything else. If the options include "Cannot be determined", the limit is what makes the answer a number.

**The negative clues** ("G does not sit at an extreme end", "A and D are not immediate neighbours") do the same job for two possible seats of one person. Leave them for the end, as in every seating puzzle.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 26 September 2026, shift 1. An uncertain number of persons sit in a row facing north. Three persons sit between G and T. C sits second to the right of T. Four persons sit between C and N, and N sits to the left of C. Two persons sit between B and N. B sits fourth from one of the extreme ends. P sits two places away from B. The number of persons to the left of P is one less than the number to the right of C. G does not sit at an extreme end. Not more than 14 persons sit in the row. How many persons sit in the row?
steps: Chain from T = 0: C is +2, N is -3. B is 3 from N: that is 0 (T's seat) or -6. So B is -6.
B is fourth from one end. C sits eight seats to its right, so B is seat 4. Then N 7, T 10, C 12.
P is 2 from B: seat 2 or 6. G is 4 from T: seat 6 or 14.
P 6: five are to its left, so six are to the right of C, and the total would be 18. More than 14. Out.
P 2: one is to its left, so two are to the right of C. Total = 12 + 2 = 14.
G cannot be seat 14, the right end. So G is seat 6.
example.answer: 14 persons. From the left: . P . B . G N . . T . C . .

checks.q: In a row of unknown length, B sits at the left end and G at the right end. Four persons sit between B and K, and six persons sit between K and G. How many persons sit in the row?
checks.why: B is seat 1. K is 5 further on: seat 6. G is 7 further on: seat 13, the last seat.

lessons.title: Equal gaps and "exactly between" in a long row
lessons.plain: New: clues that compare two gaps. When the two pairs share a person, that person is a midpoint, and the clue becomes an exact step in the chain.

teach.x: Long rows are full of clues that compare distances:

items.x: "E sits exactly between J and H."
"As many persons sit between V and B as between B and R."
"The number of persons between O and S is half the number between K and S."

teach.x: They look like bookkeeping. Used properly they are among the strongest clues, because the row is long and a midpoint is exact.

**Exactly between.** The middle person's seat is the **average** of the other two. If J is 3 and H is 7, E is 5. For this to be a whole number, the two outer people must be an even number of seats apart; if they are not, the case is dead.

**As many between A and B as between B and C.** B is named twice. A and C are different people at the same distance from B, so they are on **opposite sides**, and B is exactly between them. If V is seat 1 and B is seat 9, R is seat 17.
This is how a row grows long. One midpoint clue can throw a person eight or ten seats beyond the rest of the chain, and that person is often the one tied to the far end.

**Twice, half, one more.** "The number between O and S is half the number between K and S": count the first gap, double it, and place K that many persons beyond S. Work with the number of persons **between**, then add 1 to turn it into a step.

**Two pairs with nobody in common** ("as many between P and X as between T and M"): keep this for last. When one pair is placed, count its gap and look for a free seat that gives the other pair the same gap.
**Order of work for a full unknown-number set**, now that all the pieces are here:

items.x: chain from the most-mentioned person, with midpoint clues included as exact steps;
the end clue, to turn the chain into seat numbers;
the balance clue or the second end, for the total;
limits and negative clues, to remove the last extra case.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 18 August 2024, shift 1. A certain number of persons sit in a row facing north. Exactly one person sits between J and L. L sits at an extreme end. Five persons sit between L and H. H sits immediately to the left of F. Two persons sit between F and B, and B is to the right of F. E sits exactly between J and H. The number of persons to the right of H is the same as the number to the left of E. How many persons sit in the row?
steps: L is at an end. Suppose it is seat 1: J is seat 3, H is seat 7, F is seat 8, B is seat 11.
E is exactly between J (3) and H (7): seat 5.
Four persons are to the left of E, so four are to the right of H. Total = 7 + 4 = 11, and B is in the last seat.
If L were the right end instead, J and B would both need the seat two to its left. Out.
example.answer: 11 persons. From the left: L . J . E . H F . . B

checks.q: In a row facing north, J is in the 3rd seat from the left and H in the 7th. E sits exactly between J and H. The number of persons to the right of H is the same as the number to the left of E. How many persons sit in the row?
checks.why: E is in seat (3 + 7) / 2 = 5. Four persons are to its left, so four are to the right of H. 7 + 4 = 11.

sections.title: Basic Type, Core Mental Model and Grid

blocks.x: **What the basic type looks like.** Ten or twelve people sit in two rows of five or six. Row 1 faces south and Row 2 faces north (or the other way round), so each person in one row faces one person in the other. Clues tell you positions within a row and who faces whom.
**The one idea: it is two linear rows joined by “faces”. Draw both rows, fix each row’s left and right once, and let every “faces” clue carry a position straight across.**

**How to draw it.** Two lines of blanks, one above the other, columns lined up. Put the south-facing row on top and the north-facing row at the bottom, so the two rows look at each other. Then write the four words on the page:
Write L and R at the two ends of each row before reading any clue. In the top row the R goes on your left.
**The solving algorithm (use it on every set):**

items.x: Draw the two rows, with the names of each row beside it. Mark L and R at the ends of each row.
Place a fixed clue: “sits at the extreme left end of row 1”, “sits third from the right end”.
Use “faces” clues to jump to the other row: the person faced is in the same column.
Gap clues inside a row (“only two persons between”) give two places: draw the pair of rows twice.
Long gaps are gifts: in a row of five, “three persons between S and R” puts them at the two ends; in a row of six, “four persons between” does the same.
Kill a drawing when someone falls off the row or a seat is used twice.
“Does not face”, “not at an end”, “not a neighbour” clues settle the last two people.

blocks.x: **Grid: counting in a row of 5 or 6**

rows: Three persons between X and Y
Four persons between X and Y
Third to the right of X
X at 1 or 2 (counting from that row’s left)
X faces the one who sits second to the left of Y
Find Y’s column, move two towards Y’s left, go straight across

blocks.x: **Non-linear warning.** The two rows have opposite lefts. A clue about a top-row person and a clue about a bottom-row person that both say “to the left” send you in opposite directions on the page.

**Universal fallback (works on every set in this topic):** solve the row with more fixed clues as a plain linear row first, listing its two or three possible orders; then test each order against the “faces” clues.

lead.x: Bank counts are sets out of 62. Paper counts are sets seen in the 12 IBPS Clerk Prelims papers and in the 12 sister papers.

rows: Two rows facing each other, 7 + 7 or more
With a vacant seat in each row, or a second fact per person

lead.x: The size figures come from the number word in each passage and are approximate; 12 passages did not state a size the script could read.
Where they were seen: IBPS Clerk 2019 and 2018 (12 persons, 5 questions each); SBI Clerk 20 Sep 2025 Shift 2 (10 persons); IBPS PO 22 Aug 2026 Shift 1 and 24 Aug 2025 Shift 1 (14 persons each).

What stands out: none of the six Clerk shifts from 2024 and 2025 had a parallel-row set; the two Clerk sightings are from 2018 and 2019. It is the least seen of the six puzzle topics in the Clerk papers opened. Learn it, because the same skill serves SBI Clerk and PO, but give it less practice time than month, box, circle or square.
What the bank sets look like (from the 40 sets solved by script): 5 + 5 is the most common (17 sets), then 6 + 6 (10). After a good first clue, 31 sets leave two cases, 5 leave one and 4 leave three.

blocks.x: **Pattern clues.** “twelve persons are sitting in two parallel rows containing six persons each”.
**Shortcut engine.** as the algorithm above. With six seats there is no middle seat, and “four persons between” means the two ends.

items.label: Bank only

lead.x: Three original puzzles written for this module. Each was checked by a brute-force script and has exactly one arrangement. Rows are written west to east, that is, left to right on your page.

body.x: Eight persons are sitting in two parallel rows containing four persons each, with equal distance between adjacent persons. In row 1, K, L, M and N are seated and all of them are facing north. In row 2, T, U, V and W are seated and all of them are facing south. Each person in row 1 faces exactly one person in row 2. L sits at the extreme right end of row 1. The one who faces L sits to the immediate left of W. Only one person sits between W and V. K faces T. M sits to the left of N.

qs.stem: Who faces N?
How many persons sit to the right of T?
Who sits second to the left of the one who faces W?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try every order of each row and test the clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Row 1 faces north: its right is east. L at the east end of row 1.
The person facing L is at the east end of row 2 and is on W’s immediate left. Row 2 faces south, so its left is east: W is one seat west of that person, second from the east.
One person between W and V: going east leaves the row, so V is at the west end.
T and U take the other two seats of row 2. K faces T, and the east-end seat faces L, so T is second from the west and U is at the east end. K is opposite T.
M is to the left of N in a north-facing row: M at the west end, N third from the west.

method.x: Row 1 (facing north): M, K, N, L. Row 2 (facing south): V, T, W, U.
**Answers:** Q1 (D) W. Q2 (B) One. Q3 (A) M.
**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, K faces T is given, so N cannot face T: (A) is out without solving.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** row 2 faces south, so its left is east. Using row 1’s sense of left for row 2 pushes W off the row. In Q2 the same slip counts two people to T’s right instead of one.

items.title: Drill 2 (Exam level, P1: five and five)

body.x: Ten persons are sitting in two parallel rows containing five persons each, with equal distance between adjacent persons. In row 1, G, H, J, K and L are seated and all of them are facing south. In row 2, P, Q, R, S and T are seated and all of them are facing north. Each person in row 1 faces exactly one person in row 2. L sits third to the right of H. Only one person sits between H and G. Q faces L. Three persons sit between S and R. K faces P. J does not face R.

qs.stem: Who faces G?
How many persons sit between Q and the one who faces H?
Who sits second to the right of K?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** try every order of each row and test the clues.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Row 1 faces south: its right is west. L is three seats west of H: H at the east end and L second from the west, or H second from the east and L at the west end.
One person between H and G: G in the middle (first drawing), or G second from the west (second drawing).
Three persons between S and R in a row of five: S and R are at the two ends of row 2. Q faces L, so L is not at an end. The second drawing dies.
J and K take the west end and the fourth seat of row 1. K faces P, and P is not at an end, so K is fourth from the west with P opposite; J is at the west end.
T takes the middle of row 2, facing G.
J does not face R: S is at the west end facing J, R at the east end facing H.

method.x: Row 1 (facing south): J, L, G, K, H. Row 2 (facing north): S, Q, T, P, R.
**Answers:** Q1 (E) T. Q2 (C) Two. Q3 (B) L.

**Option Elimination Hack:** for Q1, Q faces L and P faces K by the clues, so (A) and (B) are out; S and R are at the ends and G is in the middle, so (C) and (D) are out too. Q1 can be answered after step 3.
**IBPS Trap Warning:** the slip here comes at the question stage. K faces south, so K’s right is west on your page. Reading it as east finds only H on that side and gives “No one”.

items.title: Drill 3 (Trap, P5: a vacant seat in each row)

body.x: Ten persons are sitting in two parallel rows containing six seats each, with equal distance between adjacent seats. One seat is vacant in each row. In row 1, D, E, F, G and H are seated and all of them are facing south. In row 2, V, W, X, Y and Z are seated and all of them are facing north. Each seat in row 1 faces exactly one seat in row 2. F sits at the extreme left end of row 1. The seat to the immediate right of W is vacant. Z is an immediate neighbour of W and faces the vacant seat of row 1. Only one person sits between W and Y. V sits to the immediate left of Y. D faces Y. E sits second to the left of G.

qs.stem: Who faces the vacant seat of row 2?
How many persons sit between Z and V?
Who faces the one who sits second to the right of E?

method.x: **Conventional Method:** treat each vacant seat as a sixth name in its row and try every order.
**Fast Method:**

items.x: Row 1 faces south: its left is east. F at the east end of row 1.
Row 2 faces north: the seat just east of W is vacant, and Z, W’s neighbour, is just west of W. Block: Z, W, vacant.

lessons.title: One drawing, five columns, and whose left is it
lessons.plain: The starting point. Draw the two rows once, number the columns from your own left, and settle left and right for each row before reading a single clue.

teach.x: A parallel-rows puzzle seats ten people in two rows of five. One row faces north, the other faces south, so each person looks straight at one person of the other row. The clerk papers always tell you which five names are in which row.
Nearly every wrong answer in this topic comes from one thing: **mixing up left and right for the row that faces you.** So the drawing comes first, and it is always the same drawing.
**How to draw it.**

items.x: Draw two rows of five blanks, one above the other.
Put the row that faces **south on top**, and the row that faces **north at the bottom**. Now the two rows look at each other across the gap, just as the puzzle says.
Number the **columns 1 to 5 from your own left**. Column 1 is the left edge of your paper for both rows.

teach.x: **Whose left?** Left and right in a clue always belong to the **person sitting**, not to you.

So for the bottom row nothing changes. For the top row, everything flips. Write a small **R** at the left end of the top row and at the right end of the bottom row, as a reminder of where each row's right-hand side is.
**Facing.** Two people face each other when they are in the **same column**. That is the whole meaning of "faces" or "sits opposite".
**The step words** are the same as in every seating puzzle:

rows: X sits to the immediate right (or left) of Y
X sits second to the right of Y
X sits third to the left of Y
Only two persons sit between X and Y
X sits to the left of Y

teach.x: Write each clue as a short note with the direction already turned into columns. For a bottom-row pair, "B is third to the left of D" becomes **B = D - 3**. For a top-row pair, "S is second to the right of Q" becomes **S = Q - 2**, because their right is towards column 1.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 22 February 2025, shift 3. Row 1: A, B, C, D, E face north. Row 2: P, Q, R, S, T face south. B sits third to the left of D. The one who sits opposite D sits immediately to the left of R. Two persons sit between P and R. S sits second to the right of Q. A does not sit at an end. R does not face A. E and D are not immediate neighbours.
steps: Draw: P to T on top (facing south), A to E at the bottom (facing north). Columns 1 to 5 from your left.
Bottom row: B = D - 3. So B 1 with D 4, or B 2 with D 5.
The person in D's column is immediately left of R. In the top row, left is a higher column: so D's column = R + 1, or R = D - 1. D 4 gives R 3; D 5 gives R 4.
P and R are 3 apart. From column 3 that is impossible in five columns. So R 4, P 1, and D 5, B 2.
Top row: S = Q - 2. Free columns 2, 3, 5: Q 5, S 3. T takes 2.
Bottom row: free 1, 3, 4. A is not at an end and not facing R (column 4): A 3. E is not next to D: E 1, C 4.
example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: P, T, S, R, Q. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: E, B, A, C, D.

checks.q: P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row facing south. On your paper, from your left, the order is P, Q, R, S, T. Who sits to the immediate right of R?
checks.why: They face south, towards you, so their right is your left. The person on your left of R is Q.

checks.q: In the same row (facing south; from your left P, Q, R, S, T), who sits second to the left of Q?
checks.why: Their left is your right. Two places to your right of Q is S.

checks.q: The top row, from your left, is P, T, S, R, Q. The bottom row, from your left, is E, B, A, C, D. Who faces C?
checks.why: C is in column 4. The person in column 4 of the other row is R.

checks.q: Five persons sit in a row facing north. B sits third to the left of D. Which columns can D be in?
checks.why: Facing north, left is a lower column: B = D - 3. B must be at least 1, so D is 4 or 5.

lessons.title: Start with the widest step
lessons.plain: New: where to begin. In five seats a step of three fits only two ways, so that clue is the start of almost every clerk puzzle.

teach.x: These puzzles rarely fix anyone outright. Of the eight real clerk puzzles I solved by script, only one says "B sits at an end"; five give no clue about the ends at all. So, as with boxes, you start from a relative clue. But here there is a very reliable one.
**Count how many ways a pair can sit in five columns.**

rows: Ways, if the direction is given
fourth to the right; three between
third to the left; two between
second to the right; one between

teach.x: A clue such as "S sits third to the left of Q" leaves just **two** drawings. **Seven of the eight real puzzles contain a step of three**, and in seven of the eight the best opening clue leaves exactly two cases.
So the routine is:

items.x: Scan the clues for the widest step with a direction: "third to the left", "third to the right". Start there and draw the two cases side by side.
Take the next clue that names one of those two people. With only five columns, most second clues remove one case at once, because something falls off the end of the row.
Carry on along the chain of names.

teach.x: The step-three clue is sometimes wrapped in a facing clue: "A faces the one who sits third to the right of T". It is still a step of three, between A's column and T's column, and it still leaves two cases. The next lesson shows how to read those.

Starting anywhere else costs time. Taken in printed order, three of your bank's ten five-a-side sets reach 14, 52 and 78 open cases; started well and followed along the chain of names, those same three never go above 3.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims (2023 paper). Row 1: P, Q, R, S, T face north. Row 2: G, H, I, J, K face south. S sits third to the left of Q. One person sits between S and the one who faces H. I sits second to the right of J. Q does not face J. T faces the one who sits second to the right of K. P sits to the left of R.
steps: Draw G to K on top (south), P to T at the bottom (north).
Widest step: S = Q - 3. Two cases: (S 1, Q 4) or (S 2, Q 5).
H's column is 2 from S: with S 1, H is at 3; with S 2, H is at 4.
Top row: I = J - 2 (their right is a lower column). J must not be in Q's column.
Case S 1, Q 4, H 3: J can be 4 or 5. J 4 faces Q; J 5 needs I at 3, which H has. Out.
Case S 2, Q 5, H 4: J 3, I 1 (J 5 would face Q).
T's column = K - 2. K is at 2 or 5: K 5 gives T 3. G takes 2. P is left of R: P 1, R 4.
example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: I, G, J, H, K. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: P, S, T, R, Q.

text.x: Before reading the clues in order, run your eye down them for the numbers:

items.x: **"third"** with a direction: 2 cases. Start here.
**"two persons between"**: 4 cases alone, but usually 2 once the next clue is added.
**"second"**: 3 cases. Use it second, not first.
**"immediate"**: 4 cases. Never start here.

text.x: If two clues share a name, add their steps in your head: third to the left and then immediate left of the same person makes a block four columns wide, which fits only two ways.

lessons.title: Clues that cross the rows
lessons.plain: New: "the one who faces Q sits third to the right of E". Read it from the end, work inside one row, then drop straight across to the other.

teach.x: About three clues in every seven join the two rows. They look long, and they are the reason this puzzle feels harder than a single row. They are not harder once you see what they are.
A crossing clue is an ordinary step clue with one extra hop, and the hop costs nothing, because **facing means the same column**.
"The one who faces Q sits third to the right of E."

items.x: Start at the **end** of the sentence: E.
"Third to the right of E": stay in **E's row**, and use **E's row's** idea of right. That gives a column.
"The one who faces Q" is in that column. So **Q is in that column too**, in the other row.

teach.x: So the clue simply says: Q's column = E's column moved three to E's right. One short note: if E's row faces south, **Q = E - 3**.
The only care needed is this: **the direction always belongs to the row of the person named after "of"**. In "third to the right of E", it is E's right, whichever row Q is in.
The other common forms, all read the same way:

rows: The one who sits second to the left of D faces S
S = the column two to D's left
One person sits between A and the one who faces Q
A's column and Q's column are 2 apart
D faces one of the immediate neighbours of P
D's column and P's column are 1 apart
X and Y are at opposite ends, in different rows

teach.x: Once you write crossing clues as plain column notes, the two rows become one strip of five columns with two names in each, and you chain through it exactly as before.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 September 2025, shift 2. Row 1: A, B, C, D, E face south. Row 2: P, Q, R, S, T face north. The one who sits second to the left of D faces S. T sits to the immediate right of S. Two persons sit between T and Q. The one who faces Q sits third to the right of E. One person sits between E and C, who sits to the left of A. A does not face P.
steps: Draw A to E on top (south), P to T at the bottom (north).
Widest step, a crossing one: Q = the column three to E's right. E's row faces south, so Q = E - 3. Cases: (E 4, Q 1) or (E 5, Q 2).
T is 3 from Q: Q 1 gives T 4; Q 2 gives T 5. S is immediately left of T in the bottom row: S = T - 1.
S = the column two to D's left. D's row faces south, so that is D + 2: D = S - 2.
C is 2 from E, and C is to A's left, which in the top row means a higher column than A.
Case E 4, Q 1, T 4, S 3, D 1: C is at 2, and A would need a column lower than 2, but D has column 1. Out.
Case E 5, Q 2, T 5, S 4, D 2: C is at 3, A at 1, B at 4. A does not face P: P 3, R 1.
example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: A, D, C, B, E. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: R, Q, P, S, T.

checks.q: The top row faces south and the bottom row faces north. E sits in column 5 of the top row (the right edge of your paper). The one who faces Q sits third to the right of E. In which column is Q?
checks.why: E faces south, so E's right is towards column 1. Three to the right of column 5 is column 2, and Q is in that same column in the other row.

text.x: For any clue with "the one who", read from the last name towards the first, one hop at a time:
"R sits third to the right of the one who faces the one who sits second to the right of M."

items.x: M. Second to M's right: a column.
The one who faces that person: same column, other row.
Third to the right of that person (now using the other row's right): a column. R is there.

text.x: Each hop is either "move so many columns" or "same column, other row". Write the column number after each hop and the sentence cannot confuse you.

lessons.title: Ends, and the clues that say no
lessons.plain: New: "sits at an extreme end", "not at an end", "does not face", "not neighbours", "to the left of". Know which of these to use early and which to keep for last.

teach.x: Besides steps, the papers use a handful of other clues. Each has a best moment.
**Use early.**

items.x: **"X sits at an extreme end."** Two columns: 1 or 5. Combined with any step clue about X, it is as good as a step of three. "B is at an end, and one person sits between A and B" puts A in column 3 whichever end B is at.
**"X does not sit at an end", joined to a step.** "P is second to the left of R, and R is not at an end" leaves R in 3 or 4 only: two cases.
**"X sits diagonally opposite Y."** Both are at ends, at opposite corners. Two cases.

teach.x: **Use in the middle.**

items.x: **"X faces Y"** with no step: once either is placed, the other is placed.
**"X is an immediate neighbour of both E and A"**: X is in the middle of those two, so X is not at an end.

teach.x: **Keep for last.**

items.x: **"X sits to the left of Y"** with no number. It only orders two people. With two free columns left it decides them.

**"X does not face Y"** and **"X and Y are not immediate neighbours"**. These never place anyone. They exist to choose between the last two people for the last two columns. In the real papers, these are the final clues of the puzzle in almost every case.

teach.x: A warning about "to the left of" in the top row: left there is a **higher** column. "C sits to the left of A" in a south-facing row means C is nearer your right hand than A.
**Two free columns, two people.** When a row is down to its last two people, look straight for a "does not face" or "not neighbours" clue naming one of them. It will be there.

L sits opposite the one who sits second to the left of A. One person sits between L and M. F sits second to the right of E. J sits to the immediate right of N. D sits to the right of A.
steps: Draw J to N on top (south), A, B, F, D, E at the bottom (north).
B is at 1 or 5. A is 2 from B: column 3 either way.
F = E + 2. With A at 3, E and F can only be 2 and 4. That leaves D the remaining end. D is to the right of A, so D 5 and B 1.
L is opposite the person second to A's left: column 1. So L 1.
M is 2 from L: M 3.

example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: L, K, M, J, N. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: B, E, A, F, D.

lessons.title: Follow the names, not the printed order
lessons.plain: New: the order of attack. After the opening clue, always take the clue that shares a name with what is already drawn.

teach.x: You now have every piece. This lesson is about using them in the right order, because in this puzzle the order decides whether you carry two cases or twenty.
The rule is simple:
**After the opening clue, the next clue must mention someone who is already in your drawing.**

A clue about two people who are both still unplaced adds cases. A clue that touches the drawing removes them. So you move through the clues along a chain of shared names, jumping around the printed list as needed.

I measured this on your bank's ten five-a-side sets. Read strictly in printed order, the number of open cases at the worst moment was 78 in one set, 52 in another and 14 in a third. Followed along the chain of names, the worst moment in those same three sets was 2, 3 and 3.

**How to keep track.** As you write the short notes, number them. After placing someone, circle that name wherever it appears in the notes. The next clue to use is one with a circled name and one uncircled name.
**When two clues tie**, prefer:

items.x: the one with the wider step (fewer ways to fit);
then the one that crosses rows (it starts the second row moving);
then anything about an end.

teach.x: **A strong opener hiding in plain sight.** "More than two persons sit between T and R" in a row of five means a step of four: T and R are at the two ends. That is two cases, as good as any "third to the left".

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims (2022 paper). Row 1: P, Q, R, S, T face south. Row 2: A, B, C, D, E face north. A faces the one who sits third to the right of T. Two persons sit between A and B. The one who sits second to the left of B faces the one who sits to the immediate left of P. More than two persons sit between T and R. D sits second to the left of C, who does not face Q.
steps: Draw P to T on top (south), A to E at the bottom (north).
Opening: A's column = three to T's right. T's row faces south, so A = T - 3: (T 4, A 1) or (T 5, A 2).
Next clue with T in it: more than two between T and R means T and R are at the ends. So T 5, R 1, and A 2.
Next with A: B is 3 from A: B 5.
Next with B: the column two to B's left (bottom row: 5 - 2 = 3) is the column immediately left of P (top row: P + 1). So P 2.
D = C - 2 from the free columns 1, 3, 4: D 1, C 3. E takes 4.
C does not face Q: Q 4, S 3.
example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: R, P, S, Q, T. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: D, A, C, E, B.

checks.q: Five persons sit in each row. Which of these three clues leaves the fewest ways to place its two people? (1) D sits second to the left of C. (2) More than two persons sit between T and R. (3) Two persons sit between A and B.

lessons.title: Six in a row
lessons.plain: New: the same puzzle with six columns, as in your bank and in officer-level papers. Only the counting table changes.

teach.x: Every real clerk puzzle I found had five in a row. Rows of six and seven belong to the officer-level papers and to your bank (5 of its 15 standard sets have six). This lesson is insurance, and it is short, because nothing in the method changes.
**What changes is the table.** With six columns there is more room, so each step fits one more way.
So "third to the right" is no longer a two-case opener. In a row of six, look for one of these:

items.x: a step of **four** ("fourth to the left", "three persons between" with a direction);
an **end clue** joined to a step;
**"third from one of the ends"**, which in six columns means column 3 or column 4;
"more than three persons between", which forces the two ends.

teach.x: **There is no middle seat.** In five columns, "one person between A and B, and B is at an end" puts A in column 3 either way. In six it does not: A is at 3 or 4, and you carry both.

Everything else is the same: south-facing row on top, columns from your left, crossing clues read from the end, names followed along the chain, "does not face" kept for last. Expect one or two more cases than in a row of five, and about a minute longer.

example.q: RRB Officer Scale I Prelims, 4 August 2024, shift 2. Row 1: A, B, C, D, E, F face north. Row 2: P, Q, R, S, T, U face south. F sits at an end and faces T. One person sits between C and F. C sits to the immediate left of E. R faces an immediate neighbour of C. R sits second to the left of Q. Q does not sit at an end. B sits second to the right of A. The one who faces B sits to the immediate right of P. S sits exactly between Q and U.
steps: Draw P to U on top (south), A to F at the bottom (north). Columns 1 to 6.
F and T share column 1 or column 6. C is 2 from F and E = C + 1: (F 1, C 3, E 4) or (F 6, C 4, E 5).
R is second to the left of Q; in the top row that is R = Q + 2. Q is not at an end, so R is 4, 5 or 6. R's column is next to C's.
F 1, T 1, C 3: R 4, Q 2. S must sit between Q and U: S 3 needs U at 4, S 1 is T's seat. Out.
F 6, T 6, C 4: R 5, Q 3 (R 3 would put Q at an end). S between Q and U: S 2, U 1. P takes 4.
The person facing B is immediately right of P: in the top row that is column 3. So B 3. B = A + 2: A 1. D takes 2.
example.answer: Top row (facing south), from your left: U, S, Q, P, R, T. Bottom row (facing north), from your left: A, D, B, C, E, F.

checks.q: Six persons sit in a row. O sits third from one of the ends. Which columns can O be in?
checks.why: Third from the left end is column 3. Third from the right end of six is column 4.

intro.x: Nine small ideas that every arithmetic topic leans on. Each takes a few minutes.
If you already know one, answer its two quick questions and move on. If a lesson later feels hard, it will point you back to the idea it needs.

lessons.title: Now, ago and hence
lessons.plain: The words a question uses to move people forward and backward in time.

teach.x: Every age question talks about three kinds of moments:

items.x: **Present** or **now**: today.
**Ago** or **before**: in the past. "5 years ago" means take 5 away from today's age.
**Hence** or **after**: in the future. "5 years hence" means add 5 to today's age.

teach.x: "Hence" is an old word that exam papers still love. Whenever you see it, read it as "from now".
One more thing to notice early: when two moments are on opposite sides of today, the years between them **add up**. From "4 years ago" to "8 years hence" is 4 + 8 = 12 years.

example.q: Riya is 20 years old now. How old was she 6 years ago, and how old will she be 6 years hence?
steps: Ago means subtract: 20 - 6 = 14.
Hence means add: 20 + 6 = 26.

checks.q: Arun is 31 now. What will his age be 9 years hence?
checks.why: Hence means from now, so add: 31 + 9 = 40.

checks.q: How many years are there between "3 years ago" and "7 years hence"?
checks.why: The two moments are on opposite sides of today, so the gaps add: 3 + 7 = 10.

lessons.title: What a ratio really says
lessons.plain: A ratio counts equal parts. Find the size of one part and everything else follows.

teach.x: "The ages of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 5" does **not** say A is 3 and B is 5.
It says: cut both ages into equal **parts**. A has 3 of those parts and B has 5. We do not yet know how big one part is.
So the whole job is to find **the size of one part**. You need one real number to do that, and you match it to the right number of parts:

rows: B is 40, and B has 5 parts

teach.x: Then divide: real number / matching parts = one part.
In these lessons "one part" and "1 unit" mean the same thing.

example.q: A and B are in the ratio 3 : 5 and together they add up to 64. Find B.
steps: The real number is a sum, so match it to parts added: 3 + 5 = 8 parts.
One part = 64 / 8 = 8.
B has 5 parts, so B = 5 x 8 = 40.
Quick check: A = 3 x 8 = 24, and 24 + 40 = 64. It fits.

checks.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 2 : 7 and their sum is 45. What is one part?
checks.why: A sum matches parts added: 2 + 7 = 9 parts. One part = 45 / 9 = 5.

checks.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7 and the bigger one is 18 more than the smaller. What is the bigger number?
checks.why: A difference matches parts subtracted: 7 - 4 = 3 parts = 18, so one part = 6. The bigger number is 7 x 6 = 42.

lessons.title: Joining two ratios
lessons.plain: When one name appears in two ratios, make that name the same number in both.

teach.x: Sometimes you get two ratios that share a name: A : B = 4 : 5 and B : C = 3 : 4.
B is 5 parts in the first and 3 parts in the second. Those are different-sized parts, so the two ratios cannot be read together yet.
Fix it by making B the **same number** in both. A number that both 5 and 3 go into is 15.

items.x: Multiply the first ratio by 3: 4 : 5 becomes 12 : 15.
Multiply the second ratio by 5: 3 : 4 becomes 15 : 20.

teach.x: Now B is 15 in both, and you can write one line: A : B : C = 12 : 15 : 20.
Multiplying every number of a ratio by the same thing never changes the ratio. 4 : 5 and 12 : 15 are the same statement.

example.q: A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. Write A : B : C.
steps: B is 3 in one ratio and 4 in the other. Both go into 12.
Multiply the first by 4: 2 : 3 becomes 8 : 12.
Multiply the second by 3: 4 : 5 becomes 12 : 15.
B is now 12 in both, so join them.

checks.q: A : B = 1 : 2 and B : C = 3 : 4. What is A : B : C?
checks.why: B is 2 and 3, so use 6. First ratio x 3 gives 3 : 6. Second ratio x 2 gives 6 : 8. Together: 3 : 6 : 8.

checks.q: Is 6 : 10 the same ratio as 3 : 5?
checks.why: Divide both numbers of 6 : 10 by 2 and you get 3 : 5. Multiplying or dividing both sides by the same number keeps the ratio.

lessons.title: A number that several numbers go into
lessons.plain: Finding one convenient number that 10, 12 and 15 all divide exactly. Its formal name is the LCM.

teach.x: Many questions become easy if you can find **one number that several given numbers all go into exactly**. For 10 and 15, the number 30 works: 30 / 10 = 3 and 30 / 15 = 2, with nothing left over.
The smallest such number is called the **LCM** (lowest common multiple). You do not need a formal method for it. This simple routine is enough:

items.x: Take the **biggest** of the numbers.
Go through its multiples: once, twice, three times it.
Stop at the first one that all the other numbers go into.

teach.x: For 10, 12 and 15: the biggest is 15. Try 15 (10 does not go in), 30 (12 does not), 45 (no), 60. Yes: 60 / 10 = 6, 60 / 12 = 5, 60 / 15 = 4. So 60 is the number.
If you cannot spot the smallest one quickly, any common multiple will do the job. For 10 and 15, using 150 instead of 30 gives the same final answer; the numbers along the way are just bigger.

example.q: Find a number that 12 and 18 both go into exactly.
steps: Take the bigger number, 18, and go through its multiples.
18: does 12 go into it? No.
36: does 12 go into it? Yes, 3 times.

checks.q: What is the smallest number that 6 and 8 both go into exactly?
checks.why: Multiples of 8: 8 (6 does not go in), 16 (no), 24 (yes, 4 times). 48 also works but is not the smallest.

checks.q: What is the smallest number that 10, 15 and 20 all go into exactly?

lessons.title: Average means total
lessons.plain: The moment you see an average, turn it into a total. Totals are easy to work with.

teach.x: The average of a group is the total shared out equally: average = total / number of people.
Turn that around and you get the only form you will ever need:
**total = average x number of people**
Make this a habit. When a question says "the average age of A, B and C is 30", write "total = 90" straight away and forget the 30. Averages are awkward to move around; totals simply add and subtract.
One more rule about totals and time. Each person grows 1 year per year, so a group's total grows by **people x years**. Three people, 5 years later: the total is 15 more, not 5 more.

example.q: The average age of A, B and C is 30 years. A is 25 and B is 28. Find C.
steps: Average to total: 30 x 3 = 90.
A and B use up 25 + 28 = 53.
C is what is left: 90 - 53 = 37.

checks.q: The average age of 4 friends is 22. What is the total of their ages?
checks.why: Total = average x people = 22 x 4 = 88.

checks.q: Three sisters have a total age of 60 today. What will their total age be 4 years hence?
checks.why: Each of the three grows 4 years, so the total grows 3 x 4 = 12. 60 + 12 = 72.

lessons.title: A percent of a number
lessons.plain: Finding 24% of 5,000 without a calculator, by going through 1% and 10%.

teach.x: "Percent" means "out of a hundred". 24% of something is 24 of its hundredths.
The easiest way to find any percent is to find **1%** first. 1% of a number is the number divided by 100: move the decimal point two places left. 1% of 5,000 is 50.
Then multiply. 24% of 5,000 = 24 x 50 = 1,200.
For bigger percents, **10%** is a handy stepping stone (divide by 10). 30% of 1,600 is 3 lots of 160 = 480.
You will also use this backwards all the time: if you know that 36% of a sum is 1,440, then 1% is 1,440 / 36 = 40, and the whole sum, which is 100%, is 4,000.
That backwards step, "find 1%, then multiply by 100", is the most useful single move in arithmetic for this exam.

example.q: 15% of a number is 90. What is the number?
steps: The whole number is 100%: 100 x 6 = 600.
Check: 10% of 600 is 60 and 5% is 30. Together 90.

checks.q: What is 12% of 2,500?
20% of a sum is Rs 800. What is the sum?

lessons.title: Percents that are simple fractions
lessons.plain: 25% is a quarter, 20% is a fifth. Knowing a few of these makes awkward percents easy.

teach.x: Some percents are just familiar fractions wearing a different coat. 50% is a half. 25% is a quarter. When you recognise them, you can divide instead of multiplying, which is quicker and safer.
"25% of 480" is a quarter of 480: 120. No need to go through 1%.

This matters most for the percents that look ugly as decimals. Exam papers write 16.66% or 16 2/3% when they mean **one sixth**, and 33.33% or 33 1/3% when they mean **one third**. Treat them as the fraction and they become easy.
Here are the ones worth knowing. Read through them now; they will settle in as you meet them in questions.
A percent above 100 works the same way: 125% is 100% + 25%, which is one and a quarter, or 5/4.

example.q: What is 16 2/3% of 180?
steps: 16 2/3% is one sixth.
One sixth of 180 is 180 / 6 = 30.

checks.q: What is 12.5% of 640?
checks.why: 12.5% is one eighth, and 640 / 8 = 80.

checks.q: 66 2/3% of a number is 160. What is the number?
checks.why: 66 2/3% is two thirds. If two thirds is 160, one third is 80, and the whole is 240.

lessons.title: Percent and fraction words
lessons.plain: How to turn "25% more than" or "two-thirds of" into a simple ratio.

teach.x: Questions often compare two people with a percent instead of a ratio. You can always turn it into a ratio, and then it is an ordinary ratio question.
The method: call the person you are comparing **with** 100. Then write the other person next to it.

items.x: "A is 20% **less than** B": B is 100, A is 80. A : B = 80 : 100 = 4 : 5.

teach.x: The one trap worth learning now: **"more than" adds to the 100, "of" does not.** "200% more than B" is 300 against 100, which is 3 : 1. "200% of B" is 200 against 100, which is 2 : 1. Read that small word carefully.
Fractions work the same way. "A is 2/3 of B" means A : B = 2 : 3.
You do not need to memorise the table below. It is here so you can look things up until they stick.

rows: The words say A is ... B

example.q: A's age is 40% more than B's age. Write A : B.
steps: Call B 100.
40% more means add 40: A is 140.
A : B = 140 : 100. Divide both by 20.

checks.q: "P is 50% more than Q." What is P : Q?
"P is 200% more than Q." How many times Q is P?
checks.why: "More than" adds to the 100: Q is 100, P is 100 + 200 = 300. That is 3 times.

lessons.title: Let the options help you
lessons.plain: Every question comes with five answers. Use them to check your work, and sometimes to find it.

teach.x: In this exam you never have to produce an answer from nothing. One of the five options is right, and that is useful in two ways.
**1. Check before you move on.** Put your answer back into the question. If every sentence of the question is still true, you are done. This takes a few seconds and catches most slips.

**2. Test options when you are stuck.** Ages come out as whole numbers. If a person has 8 parts of a ratio, that person's age must be a multiple of 8. Options that are not can be crossed out without solving anything.

And always read the **last line** again before you mark. The question may ask for the age 5 years ago, or for the sum, when you have just found today's age of one person. The option for today's age is usually sitting there waiting.

example.q: The ages of M and T are in the ratio 5 : 8. T's age five years ago was one of: 30, 35, 40, 45. Which can it be?
steps: T has 8 parts today, so T's age today is a multiple of 8.
Add 5 to each option to get today's age: 35, 40, 45, 50.
Only 40 is a multiple of 8.

checks.q: You solved a question and found B = 42 today. The question asks for "B's age 4 years ago". What do you mark?
checks.why: The last line asks for 4 years ago: 42 - 4 = 38. Marking 42 is the most common slip in this topic.

checks.q: A's age is 7 parts of a ratio. Which of these can be A's age?
checks.why: A's age must be a multiple of 7. Only 42 = 7 x 6 is.
